News.title: Chelsea fined £150,000 by FA for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants as statement issued
News.content:
Chelsea fined £150,000 by FA for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants as statement issued

Chelsea have seen an appeal against a £150,000 fine rejected by an independent regulatory commission following offensive chanting by their fans at an FA Cup tie against Charlton

View 2 Images Chelsea have issued a statement after being punished (Image: Bryn Lennon/Getty Images)

Chelsea have been fined £150,000 by the FA over their supporters' anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting during an FA Cup tie against Charlton in January.

‌



‌



The Blues beat the Championship side 5-1 at the Valley in the third round on January 10. They have now been slapped with a punishment and a warning by the FA, who have also imposed an action plan on the club.

‌



Chants in the 56th minute of the match were found to be "improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief".

‌



Chelsea admitted the charge but appealed against the fine, only to see their appeal rejected by an independent regulatory commission. The FA's written reasons noted that although the chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

Chelsea said in a statement: "We unequivocally condemn this behaviour. Sectarian abuse – chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group – and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

‌



"Such behaviour only serves to cause hurt to others and does not represent the values we hold as a club. We want to create a safe and inclusive environment for all, and we have a shared responsibility in delivering this.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary.

‌



View 2 Images Chelsea beat Charlton 5-1 in the FA Cup back in January (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

"Discriminatory behaviour may constitute a criminal offence and supporters found to have breached the club’s regulations will face disciplinary action, including possible match bans or membership suspensions. We will also require all those who may be sanctioned to take part in the Kick it Out programme as we believe education is as important as sanctions in order to root out this behaviour for good.

‌



"We understand that further incidents risk additional sanctions against the club and are doing everything we can to inform and educate supporters, as well as develop our existing initiatives to prevent, detect and respond to discrimination in future.

"We know Chelsea fans do not want to see any form of discrimination in our game, and we ask for their support in fostering a welcoming environment at Chelsea matches going forward."

Article continues below

The fine comes a day after the FA itself was given a suspended away ticket ban by UEFA for the "racist and/or discriminatory behaviour of its supporters" during England's 3-2 win over Spain last weekend.

The FA have been given a one-match ban, which is suspended for two years, along with a £12,600 fine.

News.title: Andy Burnham gets a taste of things to come in Brussels as he sets sights on Brexit
News.content:
Andy Burnham was treated to Brussels waffle at lunch with European leaders on his first big EU summit.

But along with a tasty dessert - and a joke too good to pass up - the PM also got his first proper taste of how tricky doing business with the EU can be.

On the face of it, the summit was a success for the UK, with deals to ease the post-Brexit burden on business and drive down the cost of the weekly shop.

Negotiations had been underway for months, and Mr Burnham was supposed to turn up for a victory lap that would set the stage for a dramatic rethink of Britain's relationship with the bloc.

‌



But as British PMs before him have learned to their cost, any negotiations with Brussels can be fraught with risk.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Careful choreography and pitch-rolling by No10 was derailed when an EU official told reporters the deal would not be adopted until the UK agreed to cut tuition fees for European students.

No10 scrambled to clean up, with a flurry of frantic briefings and WhatsApps lighting up my phone over a confusing morning.

‌



The deal is done and a new bill will be brought to Parliament next week to implement the changes. But negotiations on tuition fees will continue into the next six months on a "different sheet of paper" as European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen described it.

To Brexit veterans, it's all very familiar. And it serves as a reminder to the Prime Minister of the challenges ahead if he wants radical change to the UK's relationship with the bloc.

Mr Burnham thinks Brexit has been a disaster for Britain - he's made that abundantly clear. And he thinks the public agrees with him.

But how far he is willing to go is unclear. He dramatically reopened the Brexit debate in September by suggesting he wanted to get closer to the EU - and all options are on the table.

‌



Keir Starmer's Brexit red lines - no customs union, single market or freedom of movement - look set to be consigned to the dustbin at the next election.

Significantly, Mr Burnham said today that he's gone as far as he can with "incremental" deals in this Parliament. His focus now is on the bigger picture.

Getting much closer to Brussels carries risks back home. The old Brexiteer flank is rearming, ready to do battle to keep Britain out of the EU.

While plenty in Labour welcome closer ties, some Labour MPs in Leave-voting constituencies are sceptical, including some members of the Cabinet.

‌



This summit serves up a reminder that dealing with the EU can also be fraught with risk. The bloc has changed since 2016, swinging to the right at a time when the UK has been shifting to the left. Brussels has its own aims, and it can play hardball when it wants to.

News.title: King Charles 'will willingly pay huge mansion tax bill' despite royal exemption
News.content:
King Charles 'will willingly pay huge mansion tax bill' despite royal exemption

King Charles will reportedly pay the new 'mansion tax' on qualifying royal residences from April 2028, despite the Crown being exempt from the annual property surcharge

View 3 Images Buckingham Palace revealed the King paid £12.9m in tax in 2024-2025 (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

King Charles is set to foot a ‘mansion tax’ bill, despite the Crown being exempt.

‌



‌



The King will reportedly cover the annual surcharge on all qualifying royal properties when it comes into force in April 2028. His decision follows the precedent set by his mother, Elizabeth II, who began voluntarily paying income tax and capital gains tax in the 1990s in which Charles later followed suit.

‌



Rachel Reeves announced the high-value council tax surcharge (HVCTS) in her final Budget as chancellor in 2025. Around 165,000 homes in England are expected to be affected, with owners facing annual charges of between £2,500 and £7,500.

‌



Royal residences have different ownership arrangements. Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle are held on behalf of the Crown, while Sandringham and Balmoral belong privately to Charles, who inherited them from his mother.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Sandringham House belongs privately to the King (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

‌



Residents evacuated as huge sinkhole swallows road and garden in Kent READ MORE :

In a bid to promote greater transparency following increased security of royal finances, Buckingham Palace chose to disclose the Kings’ personal tax bill in June. The disclosure, described as an “historic first” showed Charles paid £12.9m in tax in 2024-2025.

The Crown’s exemption is set to remain under the surcharge “consistent with the wider tax system”, according to a Treasury source. Government guidelines states: “The Crown is not within the scope of the taxing acts and can claim total relief unless an Act specifically makes it liable.”

‌



Discussions over which royal properties would qualify for the exemption is reportedly ongoing. This is to be made by Parliament rather than the royal.

Similar to the Crown, Ministers living in official residences such as No 10 will not have to pay the charge themselves. After the 2025 Budget, the Government confirmed the responsibility would sit with owners.

‌



Other members of the royal family could also face a mansion tax bill, depending on whether they own their homes or hold a long lease. For Prince William, that could mean picking up a bill for his father’s country home.

View 3 Images Other royals may face a charge on their properties (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Charles has used Highgrove in Gloucestershire since 1980, but the property belongs to the Duchy of Cornwall, which William now holds as Duke. The prince’s own tax payments were made public earlier this year, with Kensington Palace revealing he paid £7.76m in income tax in 2024-25.

Other royals could also face charges on their homes. Princess Anne owns Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire, given to her by the late Queen as a wedding present in 1976. Prince Edward leases his £30m Bagshot Park home from the Crown Estate. But because the agreement lasts 150 years, responsibility for the surcharge could fall to him.

Article continues below

William and Kate’s lease on Forest Lodge could put them in a different position. Their agreement for the eight-bedroom Windsor Great Park home lasts 20 years - just one year below the threshold for a long lease.

The couple paid £42,000 in stamp duty on the agreement, but any mansion tax liability would sit with the Crown Estate.

News.title: Andy Burnham Brexit reset live: Nigel Farage slams deal after EU and PM plan to 'disrupt illegal immigration gangs'
News.content:
Andy Burnham travelled to Brussels in the hopes of finalising a Brexit reset deal to push for closer ties with the EU - the deal is now done, with the PM describing it as a 'landmark' moment

Reform leader Nigel Farage has slammed Andy Burnham's Brexit reset deal with the European Union.

Earlier today, Mr Burnham said his "landmark" Brexit reset deal with the EU will benefit everyone in the UK, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen described it as a "turning point".

Farage claimed that the PM's reset "was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024". Mr Farage claimed the deals were an "overturn more than it was anything to do with a reset", adding: "The most significant thing that happened today is the European Community have accepted the United Kingdom back in a large chunk of the single market."

Mr Burnham has said the UK and EU are "stronger together" and finalised the agreement in Brussels this afternoon. There had been concerns that the EU wanting the UK to allow European students to study at British universities for the same price as domestic students would delay any deals today, but that was not the case.

The package includes agreements covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.

Announcing the deal earlier, Mr Burnham said there had also been "significant progress in the agreement on collaboration, on data sharing, so that we can disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

Mr Burnham has told business leaders he wants to put the UK "on a better path" and that his EU deal was "completely in step with where people are". Ahead of the talks, the PM said: "Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighbourhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."

News.title: UK lashes out at Putin for reckless attack on Poland - as the Mirror reports on military exercise just 30 miles away
News.content:
Britain lashed out at the Kremlin today after it fired three deadly weapons into Poland just over 30 miles from where hundreds of UK troops were performing exercises against Russia.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was furious with Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s latest act of mindless aggression as he attended Exercise Koalicja in Eastern Poland. The drama - witnessed on the ground by the Mirror - followed this week’s Shenzen summit, in which President Trump fawned over despots Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.

During the military display of coalition potency, the Mirror asked Mr Streeting if Putin’s attack on Poland just miles away had cast a shadow over the ‘Coalition of the Willing’ manoeuvres.

Mr Streeting said defiantly: “We have seen the words of Putin ring utterly hollow with his actions overnight. He claims to want peace with Europe, he says he doesn't see conflict with Europe, and yet, once again, we see another example of Russian provocation.

View 11 Images The NATO exercise was a major milestone in the UK's contribution to the Coalition of the Willing (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Trump gets warm welcome from Xi and Putin, but the US leader is being played READ MORE :

“And we also see the European response, which is one of Unity. It should be clear by now, like, every time they provoke Europe, every time they try and provoke NATO, it makes us stronger and more resilient.”

It had been a day of high-tension in Poland, witnessed first-hand by the Mirror who woke to air-raid warnings about Russian missiles heading into Poland. Shortly afterward, missiles and a high-powered drone slammed into Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem, in south-eastern Poland.

They were between 30 miles and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises were taking place. The second missile hit Rudnik nad Sanem, roughly 32 miles away from Nowa Deba.

View 11 Images The exercise took place in Nowa Dęba near Rzeszow, Poland (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

A Mirror team was on the ground to witness the 11-nation exercises, in which the Multi National Force-Ukraine - or the ‘Coalition of the Willing’ - have taken part. They came amid sky-high tension between the Kremlin and the West, in particular the UK, which has played the lead role in backing Ukraine with weapons and funding.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said foreign troops entering Ukraine in the event of a peace deal will be seen as a provocation. But a non-NATO force of more than 11 of the countries agreed to gather the Multi National Force-Ukraine in Poland to practise for bolstering Ukraine’s military and prevent post war Russian aggression.

View 11 Images CCTV caught the flash from an explosion in Bilgoraj County, eastern Poland (Image: AFP/UNKNOWN/AFP via Getty Images)

The MNF-U is in total a coalition of 35 countries and is being led by Britain and France, with the current HQ in Paris, shortly to move to Permanent Joint Force HQ in Northwood, outside London. These exercises were marred by the actions of the Kremlin’s troop opening fire, the impact zones so close to the military demonstration.

Last night Polish air defences were on high-alert after the Russian attack, which included a Kh-101 cruise missile and happened during a massive Russian aerial assault on Ukraine.

View 11 Images Wes Streeting with the Mirror's Defence Editor, Chris Hughes (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Mr Streeting told the Mirror: “What Putin did overnight once again reinforced European unity. Every time he tries to divide us he achieves the exact opposite.

“So, the response to the actions overnight in Poland is stronger European Unity with Poland. The reaction to the bombardment of Kyiv and the Ukrainian people this week, is for Ukraine's allies to step up and do even more to support Ukraine.

View 11 Images Streeting told the Mirror that Putin's latest actions just solidified Europe's unity (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

“Putin needs to understand that until he is prepared to negotiate a peace that is acceptable to Ukraine, we will continue to support Ukraine for as long as it takes.”

He said Putin’s actions were directed to try and ruin Exercise Koalicja, in which 300 UK troops are operating with a 2,800-strong force including 1,100 French soldiers. Troops from the UK, France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey are taking part in the exercise. The United States is not contributing troops to the mission.

Mr Streeting added: “Well, you heard very clearly what the Deputy Prime Minister of Poland said. Be very clear that they believe that this incursion into Polish airspace was not a coincidence with today's demonstration and the exercise that's taken place here.

View 11 Images Mr Streeting watched a stunning display of coalition air power during the exercise (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

“And the responses have been resolute from our European allies, and so it's really important for us to emphasise that the multinational force of Ukraine is a coalition of nations that are ready to step forward once hostilities cease, to help Ukraine with rebuilding. And so for Putin to seek to provoke Poland and to provoke European allies in this way is not only highly irresponsible for Putin. Is it also self-defeating.”

Earlier, Mr Streeting watched a stunning display of coalition air power including live fly-bys with French Rafale and UKGR4 Typhoon warplanes. The troops of British 7 Brigade - AKA the ‘Desert Rats’ of WWII fame and the French troops - whose unit is 7th Armoured Brigade - simulated going on patrol.

Casualty evacuations were displayed using large-sized drones to carry injured troops, as French soldiers scoured the skies for Russian drones, fingering Mistral ground to air missile systems.

View 11 Images The MNF-U is preparing for a time when Ukraine and Russia have agreed to stop the war (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

One told me: “The Mistral is to be used to shoot down airplanes, helicopters or enemy drones and with this system we are safe here. Working with the British troops and forces from the other nations has been a great experience as we are learning from each other all the time.”

The MNF-U is preparing for a time when Ukraine and Russia have agreed to stop the war and a non-NATO force enters the country at the request of President Volodymyr Zelensky or his government.

Air raid sirens sounded in Poland

Later Mr Streeting was asked by the Mirror if Trump’s tri-lateral meeting with China and Russia has hit how the west supports Ukraine.

He told us: “I think one of the consequences of Putin's war in Ukraine has been a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO.

View 11 Images A residential building on fire in Zhovti Vody, Ukraine, after Russian missile attacks (Image: AP via AP)

“We're now more united as a continent than ever. NATO is larger and stronger and is growing stronger month by month, year by year, as we're all investing heavily in our defensive capabilities.

“So Putin strategically has achieved the exact opposite of what he has aimed to do, which is a weaker and more divided Europe.” He even hinted that the military exercise and the MNF-U’s defiance of Putin shows European countries are showing they can go-it alone with the US.

View 11 Images Firefighters putting out a blaze in Kyiv after strikes (Image: UKRAINIAN EMERGENCY SERVICE/AFP via Getty Images)

He told The Mirror: “I think that, you know, when the history books about this period are written, the Ukrainian war will not only be seen as an illegal and unnecessary and unprovoked invasion of a sovereign European country, I think it will also be seen as a galvanising of European defence and security, and Europe taking greater responsibility for the defence of our own continent.”

During his time on the ground, Mr Streeting met young UK soldiers as well as senior officers - all of whom spoke about their pride in their equipment and training.

One young member of the Army told him: “It’s been great working with the other countries. We have been able to learn from one another and I am proud of what we’re achieving.”

View 11 Images Kyiv was pummelled by overnight Russian attacks (Image: UKRAINIAN EMERGENCY SERVICE/AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Streeting told the Mirror: “This exercise has been a really impressive display. It's been a really impressive show of European unity. It's been a very real demonstration that the multinational force for Ukraine is ready for when hostilities ceases to step forward and to assist Ukraine in rebuilding.

“But I've got to say, proud that I am of the whole team effort. Of course, I'm especially proud of the 300 British troops who've taken part in this exercise. And I hope that back home people see that, because not only do we have extremely capable warfighters in our armed forces, we've also got innovators, engineers, people with just the most extraordinary, ingenuity.

“And it makes me really proud of our country. And, you know, yes, of course, we've got challenges. And there's, of course, more than a decade of under- investment has consequences.

“But at the same time, you know, we mustn't let talking our country down become a national pastime when, despite those challenges in the armed forces, we've got some fantastic people, some extraordinary capability.”

News.title: Man murdered British woman Sonia Exelby after convincing her to travel to US for 'sadistic pleasure'
News.content:
Man murdered British woman Sonia Exelby after convincing her to travel to US for 'sadistic pleasure'

The twisted killer Dwain Hall posed as a mentor to gain Sonia Exelby's trust before murdering her in Florida - he's now been sentenced to life in prison for kidnap and first-degree murder

View 4 Images Ms Exelby met Hall through a fetish website, the court heard (Image: Facebook)

Dwain Hall, 54, has been found guilty of the kidnap and first-degree murder of 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, who he groomed on a fetish website before he convinced her to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

‌



‌



Sonia's body was discovered in a shallow grave in Marion County on October 17, 2025, just five days after she was reported missing from her home in the UK. She was found to have sustained four stab wounds to the left side, with injuries reaching up to seven inches dept.

‌



Hall was sentenced to life in prison, after the unanimous guilty verdict at a court in Ocala, Florida. Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt told the court that Sonia had flown to the US on October 10, 2025, and was "brutally murdered by a predator, a man who called himself Alpha Sadist, a man who was sexually aroused by the rape and torture of women".

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Dwain Hall has been sentenced to life in prison for kidnapping and murdering British Sonia Exelby (Image: Florida Department of Law Enforcement/Press Association)

UK lashes out at Putin for reckless attack on Poland - as the Mirror reports on military exercise just 30 miles away READ MORE :

Jurors heard Hall had spent two years manipulating Sonia online, posing as her mentor while he targeted her because of her mental illness. They described the murder as "for his own sadistic pleasure". Hall demanded Sonia pay $4,000 for him to kill her. The 54-year-old mechanic worships the Egyptian god of death.

‌



Sonia had struggled with her mental health throughout her life, had a history of self-harm and had previously attempted suicide, which led to her being manipulated by Hall. This was reflected in an email she sent to herself as she flew abroad last year.

She wrote: "As soon as the wheels leave the ground, I wish I was home, can't get off the plane…oh god, I feel so sick, why am I here, why?"

‌



Sonia’s last message to a friend, which was not shown to the jury, took place on her second night of suffering at Hall’s hands. She said: “I f***ed up really bad I think it’s too late, I’m so scared.”

View 4 Images Sonia's body was discovered in Marion County on October 17, 2025 (Image: Facebook)

‌



Hall was tracked down by police through the attempted use of Sonia's credit card by the roadside assistance company he owned. In a horrific deleted video, which was submitted as evidence, Hall can be heard instructing Sonia to explain why she was there and why she is "such an awful person".

In response, she says she has "crushed everyone who ever loves me".

‌



Hall says: "How did you want to die? What was your chosen way to die? Kind of describe that. What have you been consenting to here today?" She says: "You mean the way that you're talking about killing me? Yeah, is that what you mean?".

After a pause she says: "Be stabbed." Hall responds: "Yeah, that's what you want. But the last day or two, what has your treatment been? What did you ask for leading up to that?".

‌



She replied: "I can't remember. We talked about so many different ways."

Hall later said: "And this is how you wanted to die, right? You wanted to be beaten and made to suffer because you're such a piece of sh*t? Say it." Sonia replied: "I needed to be beaten and suffer because I'm such a piece of sh*t."

‌



During the investigations, police digital forensics experts discovered horrific images of rape, torture and murder on Hall's mobile phone. The jury also viewed extensive footage of Hall being interviewed by detectives, in which he initially denied any knowledge of Sonia, before ultimately making a complete retraction to "clear my conscience". He claimed he had been unwilling to reveal details about Sonia as he had made a promise not to.

View 4 Images The jury heard evidence over four days at the trial (Image: Fox 13)

‌



He told law enforcement officers that he had been "mentoring" the 32-year-old online, "wanted to make her life better", and did not want her to take her own life. His earlier statements, which he later withdrew, had been "Sonia's cover story", according to Hall.

Hall had groomed Sonia on a 'fetish website' which she also used to communicate "with many different men". The site has since been shut down.

‌



Addressing the jury on Friday, Ms Berndt for the prosecution said of Sonia: “She was beautiful. She was kind and she was deeply loved by everyone who knew her. And she also suffered from mental illness for most of her life. She should be alive today.”

Sonia had the support of her loving family and friends, Ms Berndt said. She added: “But no-one could save her from the defendant, the Alpha Sadist. Think about what he must have said to her over those two years, how did he manipulate her to get her to leave her home and travel thousands of miles to come here?”

‌



She told the court: “He took advantage of a severely depressed, mentally-ill woman who was incapable of making any rational decisions.”

The court heard that Sonia's consent was not a defence to the crime of first-degree murder.

‌



Ms Berndt added: “If you believe that she came here and she 100% wanted this man to kill her, he can’t do that. She cannot consent to that. He can’t do it. This man does not have the right to kill her, even if she wants to die.”

Her family previously shared a heartbreaking tribute to their "magic" sister who gave "so much of herself to other people". The tribute, penned by Sonia's eldest sister Gemma Isaj, said the hearts of her loved ones were broken following her death.

‌



"She had this incredibly calming, gentle and completely non-judgemental nature," the tribute said. "A magic healing hug that would wrap comfort around you. You could talk to Sonia about anything, and she would never make you feel judged. Sonia was a person who just wanted to help.

"She couldn't bear to see anything hurt. She was even vegan because she couldn't stand the thought of an animal suffering so that she could eat."

Article continues below

Sonia's siblings said they did not want Sonia's life to be remembered because of how it ended. "We want people to know how kind she was," the tribute added. "How compassionate she was."

When life is difficult, Samaritans are available day or night, 365 days a year. You can call them for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org

News.title: Chilling CCTV shows killers laughing as they buy knives before stabbing dad to death
News.content:
Chilling CCTV shows killers laughing as they buy knives before stabbing dad to death

Kieron Barnes, 20, and Tobias Agbaje, 21, were jailed for life at Canterbury Crown Court for murdering 19-year-old father Ashton Harrington in Whitstable, Kent.

Pair jailed for life after killing a Whitstable father

Chilling CCTV footage shows two killers laughing as they buy hunting knives just two days before stabbing a teenage dad to death.

‌



‌



Kieron Barnes, 20, and Tobias Agbaje, 21, were filmed inspecting knives in a shop before murdering 19-year-old Ashton Harrington in Whitstable, Kent, in the early hours of April 3.

‌



The pair have now been jailed for life after being found guilty of murder following a trial at Canterbury Crown Court.

‌



Barnes was sentenced to a minimum of 22 years behind bars on Friday, while Agbaje must serve at least 25 years. Both men also admitted possession of a bladed article.

Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

View 5 Images Ashton Harrington, 19, was stabbed to death in Whitstable, Kent. (Image: Kent Police / SWNS)

‌



Gran suffers horrific injuries trying to save screaming pet from vicious dog attack READ MORE :

Police were called shortly after 2am when a resident heard people screaming for help as they gathered around Ashton, who had suffered several stab wounds and stopped breathing.

The young father was pronounced dead at the scene. Barnes and Agbaje were arrested ten days later, on April 13.

‌



View 5 Images Kieron Barnes and Tobias Agbaje were caught on CCTV buying hunting knives two days before the murder. (Image: CPS / SWNS)

In their investigation, officers found that a friend had given Barnes and Agbaje a lift in their car on the day of the murder.

‌



During the journey, Barnes saw teen dad Ashton, who was sitting in another car with friends, and ordered the driver of the car he was in to stop the vehicle.

Barnes and Agbaje then brandished large hunting knives and ran towards Harrington, who tried to run away but was left fatally wounded. The murderers then fled the scene.

‌



The knives were recovered by police after members of the public found them discarded near the scene.

View 5 Images Tobias Agbaje and Kieron Barnes (Image: Kent Police / SWNS)

‌



A receipt found in Agbaje’s home in Herne Bay, Kent, showed he had bought the knife just two days before the murder – and CCTV confirmed he and Barnes had both bought the knives at the same time.

Footage shows the two men in tracksuits, along with another identified figure, looking at knives in a display case before selecting a large one from the shopkeeper.

‌



Agbaje and Barnes, of Sittingbourne, then smile and laugh as they hold one of the two knives in front of the counter.

They then hand over cash to pay for the knife, before Agbaje leaves the shop.

‌



View 5 Images Moment Tobias Agbaje was arrested (Image: Kent Police / SWNS)

A further review of CCTV showed that the pair had gone to Agbaje’s home after the killing, and were heard saying they hoped the victim was dead.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Emma Lawry, of Kent Police, said: “This was a tragic case in which a young man who should have had his whole life ahead of him was senselessly murdered.

“Kieron Barnes and Tobias Agbaje had no legitimate reason whatsoever to be in possession of the large hunting knives they bought, and they are solely responsible for the loss of a life.

‌



View 5 Images Moment Kieron Barnes wa sa (Image: Kent Police / SWNS)

“As demonstrated in this case, carrying a knife is not a game, it brings devastating results for all concerned.

‌



“My team and I are continuing to support Ashton Harrington’s family, who have suffered a terrible loss and have shown remarkable courage during this investigation.”

Following Ashton’s death, his mother, Camille Harrington, paid tribute to him.

‌



In a statement released through Kent Police, she said: “He was the most loyal, loving, funny boy with the biggest personality and he could light up a room with his smile and laugh.

“He was loved by all that knew him.

Article continues below

“He was most happy when he was with his friends and daughter, who he absolutely doted on.

“I'm so glad he spent his last day with his daughter and myself, and I will cherish this forever.”

News.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
News.content:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

News.title: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
News.content:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Daniel Thomas jailed for 15 months for slashing dinghy
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

News.title: Man guilty of murdering woman he groomed on fetish site
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.

Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.

Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.

The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (Â£3,000) for him to kill her.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

Hall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.

The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.

Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years".

"He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said.

"And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."

Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."

News.title: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
News.content:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

"This is simply unacceptable."

News.title: 'Dishonest' police officers sacked for lying over fatal crash searches
News.content:
Two officers who lied about carrying out missing person searches linked to a crash in which three people died have been sacked after being found guilty at a police misconduct hearing.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

Members of Smith's family described the verdict as "an important step towards accountability".

Following the proceedings, Smith's mother Emma Borg said the family had to repeatedly revisit the "most painful period" of their lives.

She said her family felt their honesty and credibility was being "questioned" at a time when they "trusted the police to do their jobs".

"Instead, the dishonesty established during these proceedings undermined the missing persons' investigation and the trust our families desperately needed to have in those responsible for helping us," she added.

Lauren Doyle, Smith's sister, said they "never wanted to spend years scrutinising police decisions" and called the outcome of the proceedings an "important step".

She added: "Our search for answers continues. We will never lose sight of why we started."

News.title: Secret UK cyber operation protected tens of thousands of fridges from hackers
News.content:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

News.title: UK braces for coldest night of autumn so far with temperature of -10C forecast
News.content:
The coldest night of the autumn so far was on Thursday night when the temperature got down to minus 8.4C (18F) at Tulloch Bridge, Highland.

Temperatures for many of us have been up and down recently due to cold Arctic air temporarily sweeping southward across the UK.

Southern areas of the UK have mostly held onto milder air from the Atlantic.

During Friday though a northerly wind will once again bring some of the colder air from the Arctic, and bring a colder day for most of the UK.

Any early cloud and rain in southern England will clear and for most of the UK it will be a bright day with some sunshine. A few wintry showers are possible across Scotland.

By night, temperatures will drop with frost expected widely, mostly across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Although it is likely to be the coldest night of the autumn so far, with minus 10C predicted in rural Scotland, we are a long way off the coldest November night on record, when a temperature of minus 16.1C was recorded in Cumbria in 1912.

We came closer to that record low temperature in 2025, when the UK experienced the coldest November night in 12 years with minus 12.6C in Moray.

News.title: Man jailed for murder of woman drowned in Thames
News.content:
A man has been jailed for life with a minimum of 22 years and six months after he murdered a woman, who was found drowned in the River Thames, while serving a suspended prison sentence.

The body of Jennifer Symonds, 44, was recovered from the river at Phyllis Court Club in Henley-on-Thames on the morning of 6 March 2026.

Last month, Nelio Gouveia, 45, of Phyllis Court Drive, Henley-on-Thames, pleaded guilty to her murder during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court.

During a hearing at the same court on Friday, Gouveia was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder and ordered to serve at least 22 years and six months behind bars.

It can now also be reported that Gouveia had been serving a two-year suspended prison sentence for a violent attack on a woman at the time of the murder.

Jailing him on Friday, Judge Jay said Gouveia's actions "stemmed from your propensity in certain circumstances to violence against women".

Reacting to the sentence, Gouveia, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey tracksuit and clutching white rosary beads, looked down at the floor.

His defence had earlier told the hearing that "he doesn't feel he is worthy of forgiveness and is deeply remorseful of what he has done".

News.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
News.content:
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTCâNCIâAACR Symposium 2026, external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year, external.

In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

News.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
News.content:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

News.title: Two men dead after glider crashes into Loch Leven
News.content:
Two men have died after a glider crashed into Loch Leven.

Police, ambulance, fire service and the coastguard were called to the scene near Kinross at about 11:00.

The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield near the loch, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight" but it was not clear what had caused the crash.

Police Scotland said the deaths were not being treated as suspicious and inquiries were ongoing to establish the full circumstances.

The Scottish Gliding Centre spokesperson added: "The incident is currently under investigation by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

"Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations."

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it had launched an investigation and sent a team of inspectors to the accident site.

Local airspace restrictions remain in place.

News.title: Sex abuse teacher arrested for missing sentencing
News.content:
But Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to Harrow Crown Court, and Judge Karim Ezzat issued an arrest warrant.

She could not be found at her home by Metropolitan Police officers on Friday morning, the court heard.

A Met spokesperson said: "On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow Crown Court for sentencing.

"A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.

"At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.

"She has been taken into police custody. A new sentencing date will be set by the court in due course."

Earlier, prosecutor Neelam Gomersall had said Bowen's partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers turned up, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall told the court that there was "no evidence" Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and information from her partner was "suggestive of refusal rather than inability" to attend.

Defence barrister Mark Kimsey said: "Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn't answer."

He said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been "concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages" from her.

News.title: Pontins fined £1m after grandmother's death
News.content:
Pontins holiday park resort has been fined Â£1m after a grandmother died in a "catastrophic incident" that was "an accident waiting to happen", a judge ruled.

Wendy Jones, 68, of Hereford, died six months after a 40m (131ft) section of air conditioning duct and ceiling collapsed onto guests at Pontins' Brean Sands resort, Somerset, in February 2019.

On Friday, Pontins' parent firm, Britannia Jinky Jersey, was sentenced at Bristol Crown Court to pay a Â£1m fine.

Jones' son James Havard-Jones said: "There is a temptation to describe what happened as an accident. I cannot do that. An accident is something unforeseeable. This was not unforeseeable. This was preventable."

Contractor Stephen Bennison also received a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months.

They both admitted failure to discharge a duty under health and safety laws.

News.title: No sign of missing men after fishing boat Kilda recovered near Orkney
News.content:
Police say there is no trace of two missing men after a fishing boat that went missing near the Isle of Lewis a month ago was recovered near Orkney.

Three men were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October.

The body of crew member Douglas Craigie was found by search teams the following day but two other men - Norman Murray and Murdo Morrison - are still missing.

Officers said the vessel had been fully examined after it was brought ashore to Kirkwall, but the pair remain unaccounted for.

The wreck was spotted semi-submerged in the North Sea east of Orkney on Wednesday morning, and a specialist vessel recovered it from about 40 miles (64km) out to sea on Thursday before bringing it to Kirkwall.

The Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) has started an investigation into the loss of the Kilda.

It is understood it will be kept in a secure yard while investigations are carried out.

News.title: House ramming charges in connection with A66 crash
News.content:
Police have charged a number of men with ramming houses and vehicles prior to a crash which killed two police officers and five young men.

Two men and a teenage boy appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court on Thursday over events before the fatal head-on crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough in August.

Cleveland Police said the charges related to two vehicles, a Volvo and Land Rover, suspected of being used to destroy or to cause damage to houses and vehicles in Middlesbrough on 22 August.

It included a property on Ruskin Avenue, which was the house of Gye Worthy, the father of Cole Worthy who was one of the young men killed.

Kai Inico, 21, from Shildon, was charged with conspiracy to cause criminal damage, conspiracy to steal, criminal damage with intent to endanger life and burglary with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was remanded in custody ahead of an appearance at Teesside Crown Court on 10 December.

A 16-year-old, who cannot be named because of his age, was charged with conspiracy to cause criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life and burglary with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

Jason Turnbull, 45, from Thornaby, was charged with burglary with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was released on conditional bail ahead of an appearance at Teesside Crown Court on 10 December.

Cleveland Police said another man had also been charged last week.

Mitchell Keenan, 19, was charged with conspiracy to destroy/damage property, conspiracy to steal a motor vehicle, damage to property with intent to endanger life, burglary with intent to inflict grievous bodily harm. He was remanded in custody ahead of an appearance at Teesside Crown Court on 10 December.

The fatal head-on crash happened in the early hours of 22 August.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Worthy, both 17.
