News.title: European leaders condemn Russia’s ‘intentional provocation’ as missile hits Poland
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Leaders across Europe have roundly condemned Russia after a cruise missile landed in Poland while Vladimir Putin’s forces carried out a major bombardment of neighbouring Ukraine, fuelling fears that the war in Ukraine is spilling further into Europe.

Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said the incursions appeared to be an “intentional provocation” from Russia, coming as Poland is set to host “Coalition of the Willing” military exercises with Ukraine’s allies.

Warsaw said it had scrambled jets and appealed to its Nato allies for help after detecting 11 foreign objects threatening its airspace, including three that it said had made it through.

Poland said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in the southeast of the country, about 30 miles from the Ukrainian border. The crash location is also about 47 miles from where thousands of European troops were taking part in the military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine.

Mr Tusk said there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian, adding: “It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation.”

“Today, it is clearer than ever before that Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe,” he said.

British prime minister Andy Burnham condemned the violation as “utterly unacceptable”, while his defence minister, Wes Streeting, said Europe would not be divided or deterred from its support for Ukraine.

open image in gallery A flash of an explosion is seen near Chmielek, in Bilgoraj County in eastern Poland, some 300km from Warsaw ( AFP/Getty )

Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said he had spoken to Mr Tusk about the “grave violations of Polish airspace overnight”. Mr Rutte said: “We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.

“This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.”

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also offered her “full solidarity” to Poland. “I also want to strongly condemn this violation of the Polish airspace. We stand in full solidarity with the Polish people,” Ms von der Leyen said during the press conference in Brussels.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on Nato’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance.

Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the attack early on Friday involved a Russian Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile, another missile he did not identify, and a drone.

He said that the incursions were unlikely to have been accidental, having occurred just ahead of Poland hosting defence ministers from Britain, France and the Baltic states.

Poland would ask the Nato military alliance for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank, he added.

open image in gallery Polish prime minister Donald Tusk and his British counterpart Andy Burnham pictured together in Berlin on Thursday ( Reuters )

Investigations were meanwhile opened into the incidents in Nowy Lipowiec, Molodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said.

Footage shared on social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the village of Chmielek, near Nowy Lipowiec, showed an explosion in the distance.

“I was making coffee, getting the kids ready for school, and then I heard a whistling sound. And then a thud – a dull, muffled kind of impact,” said resident Natalia Szponar. “I was a little panicked. I felt a bit scared.”

Andrzej Borowiec, mayor of neighbouring Aleksandrow county, said an object around seven metres long had fallen at 5.40am GMT (6.40am local time) on Friday.

“Smoke was rising – black smoke... something that looked like one large, distinct mushroom cloud,” he said.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin met with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China this week – an unprecedented summit compared to Yalta ( AFP/Getty )

European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilise the continent.

US President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Another envoy, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, in what could be a step towards compromise.

Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Russian president Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.

Overnight strikes killed at least eight Ukrainian civilians and wounded more than two dozen, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, calling it “one of the largest” attacks Russia has undertaken in recent months. Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, he said.

“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” Mr Zelensky said in a post on social media platform X.

open image in gallery Defence Secretary Wes Streeting meeting British solders while attending the Exercise KOALICJA demonstration in Poland ( PA )

Europe has long been vying for inclusion in the US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia, but is yet to find a seat at the table. Ukraine has been supportive of Europe’s inclusion.

Speaking an EU-UK summit press conference in Brussels, Britain’s Mr Burnham said: “The incursion into Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly.

“And from a British point of view, [we] send a strong message of solidarity to Prime Minister Tusk and the Polish people, who we will support always in any way that we that we can.”

The prime minister continued: “As I said at the [recent] Coalition of the Willing [meeting], everyone is losing in this war. Everybody, and Russia is losing the most – when you see the number of young people, Russian young people, their deaths at the front line.

“Nobody is winning; this is senseless. No ground is being taken, minimal gains.”

Mr Streeting, speaking at a joint press conference in Nowa Deba, Poland, said it was another example of a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.

“Europe will not be deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said.

“We will not allow Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the frontline in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere.”

News.title: Fiona the hippo fans left reeling over coincidental Macy’s Christmas display
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Macy’s has unveiled a hippo-themed holiday display hours after beloved hippo Fiona died, leaving fans reeling.

Fiona, the world-famous hippo who won hearts across the globe after surviving a premature birth, died Thursday at Cincinnati Zoo, 11 days after swallowing a young visitor’s knit hat.

On Thursday evening, department store Macy’s unveiled its hippo-themed holiday installation, in a nod to the retailer’s famous blue inflatable hippo balloon that vanished into the sky at the 1931 Thanksgiving Day Parade. It is also a reference to the hol track, “I Want a Hippopotamus for Christmas.”

As part of the festivities, a blue hippopotamus balloon was paraded down New York City’s West 34th Street ahead of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade next week. The display outside the flagship store includes a blue hippo next to Santa and a Christmas tree, perched on the main entrance by the main clock. A window display also shows a hippo’s head among a sea of blue balloons.

While the installation was praised as a festive spectacle, fans of Fiona couldn’t help but notice the sweet but unlikely coincidence.

open image in gallery Fans of the beloved hippo Fiona have been left reeling after Macy’s coincidentally unveiled a hippo-themed holiday display on the same day she died ( Getty Images for Macy's, Inc. )

open image in gallery Fiona, the beloved hippo who rose to fame in January 2017 when she was born six weeks premature, died after swallowing a knitted hat ( Reuters )

“It’s a sign from the universe that Fiona is smiling down on us,” said one Instagram comment.

“Consider this a tribute to our fair Fiona,” said another person, as one added: “What a weird coincidence.”

“Awwww it's to honor Fiona (and you can't convince me otherwise),” said another.

“I need to know what was happening in the Macy’s PR dept when Fiona died hours before they unveiled the hippo,” someone else chimed in as another wondered, “Are we living in a simulation because what are the odds.”

Fiona rose to fame in January 2017 when she was born six weeks premature. At birth, she weighed just 29 pounds, 25 pounds below the lowest birth weight ever recorded for her species. She became so famous that she inspired a beer line, an ice cream flavor and all kinds of clothing.

After her death Thursday, fans have been leaving cards and flowers at her statue at the Ohio zoo.

open image in gallery Macy’s unveiled its holiday display Thursday, themed around the 1931 balloon that went missing ( Getty Images for Macy's, Inc. )

In the days before Fiona’s death, keepers at Cincinnati Zoo had been caring for her around the clock, attempting to help her digest and pass the hat. Staff kept Fiona hydrated, offered her special treats, and closely monitored her movements.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote on Thursday afternoon.

“The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.

“The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover. We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are,” the zoo continued.

“Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.”

Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike added: “We are in shock at the moment. We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”

News.title: Lulu reveals she spent her birthday at ex-husband John Frieda’s bedside as he died
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Scottish singer Lulu has revealed she was present at the bedside of her ex-husband John Frieda when he died.

Earlier this month, the celebrity hairstylist and beauty entrepreneur died aged 75, with an official post on his hair salon’s account confirming he "passed away peacefully surrounded by his family".

Frieda was married to the artist between 1977 and 1991, and the couple had a son, Jordan.

While Lulu initially posted a brief homage to Frieda on Instagram after his passing, she has now provided further details.

Speaking on Kaye Adams’s How To Be 60 podcast, Lulu explained she was present when he died on November 3, which fell on her 78th birthday. She was among a group of relatives gathered at Frieda’s bedside.

She said: "I’ve never seen anyone die before. And this was such an incredible, uplifting experience because it was only the closest family, intimate family. I think there were 13 of us all together at his bedside. And it was wonderful."

open image in gallery Frieda passed away earlier this month at the age of 75 ( Getty )

The singer continued: "Both my parents died before I came in the room. My father actually died in the night. We were all in bed, and my mother died before I got there. I never watched anyone die and I’ve always been slightly wary of it, of course."

However, speaking after watching her ex die, she said: "It’s not secretive. It’s not dark. It’s not frightening. This was wonderful for me. So as sad as we were as a family, you know, John’s wife and his young kids, my son, our grandchildren… I mean, it was on some level sublime.

"I don’t think that everybody’s passing is as beautiful. Maybe, maybe, I don’t know. But this was an incredible experience. That’s what I got for my birthday. That was my birthday present."

Lulu also mentioned that Frieda had been suffering from pain prior to his death, adding that it brought her solace to know he was no longer in distress.

"I would be driven slightly crazy knowing he was in pain," she said.

She went on: "But ultimately, sad, sad, sad, sad to lose. The physical form, I think, is the thing that we as human beings find [losing] hard. Of course. But I believe the soul is with us always. I talk to my mother every day. I get answers, I get replies, I get signs. So that’s the kind of path that I follow and it’s very comforting."

Decades after their marriage ended, Lulu recalled a recent conversation in which Frieda remarked that they were "closer now than we’ve ever been".

"I think that was true. I think that’s a beautiful thing. And I adore his new family. You know, they’re not new, but it’s been a long time with Avery (Frieda’s wife). And we’re all just so connected in that sort of love around him," she added.

Following their divorce, Frieda went on to marry Frances Avery Agnelli in 2019.

On 9 November, Lulu shared what she described as their final photograph together, taken in September 2026.

She wrote on Instagram: "Our last photo together Sept 2026. A lifetime of memories. Rip Johnny."

In the picture, both are smiling while looking away from the camera as Frieda places his arm around the Scottish singer.

News of Frieda’s death was first shared via his hair salon’s official Instagram page on 4 November.

open image in gallery Lulu recalled how Frieda’s passing was ‘wonderful’ in some ways as his closest family were all by his bedside ( PA )

It said: "It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully… surrounded by his family.

"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.

"His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us. We will continue to do him proud."

The statement concluded: "Our thoughts are with John’s family and everyone who loved him. Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts."

Born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951, his father was a salon owner in Ealing, while his grandfather worked as a Fleet Street barber.

After working in his father’s business, Frieda joined the House of Leonard salon in London, working as assistant to Leonard Lewis – the stylist behind the haircut that launched Twiggy's career.

He opened his own salon in 1976 at the age of 25, going on to work for British Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar, as well as styling clients such as Twiggy, Jackie Onassis and Sir Mick Jagger.

In the 1980s, Frieda collaborated with American haircare executive Gail Federici on a product range, bringing Frizz-Ease to market in 1988.

In 2002, he sold his haircare company to the Japanese group Kao for 450 million dollars (£260 million).

He is survived by his wife, four children and two grandchildren.

News.title: Customer sues In-N-Out Burger and claims staff failed to stop racist attack on her family
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A California mother has filed a lawsuit against In-N-Out Burger, accusing employees at a Los Angeles restaurant of failing to intervene or contact police during a prolonged anti-Asian attack against her and her 17-year-old daughter.

Julie Choi filed the complaint Wednesday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, seeking unspecified damages for emotional distress as well as punitive damages for alleged misconduct by the fast-food chain, as reported by the Los Angeles Times.

The lawsuit stems from a May incident at a Sherman Oaks location, where Choi had taken her daughter to celebrate the end of a difficult school exam. According to the complaint, the altercation began when a female customer pushed Choi’s daughter into people standing in line ahead of her.

When Choi turned to the woman and asked, “Did you push my daughter?” the woman allegedly replied, “Yeah, b****,” used an anti-Asian slur and advanced toward them aggressively.

A security guard stepped between the woman and the pair, though the complaint states the assailant continued to “menacingly approach and taunt” them. Choi said she asked the guard to remove the woman from the building, but he told her he was not permitted to physically handle the customer.

open image in gallery In-N-Out Burger is facing a lawsuit from a California mother who claims staff at a Sherman Oaks location stood by as an aggressive customer shoved her 17-year-old daughter, shouted anti-Asian slurs and poured soda on them before being served food ( Getty/iStock )

For several minutes, the woman allegedly trailed the mother and daughter inside the restaurant, yelling racist remarks, mocking East Asian accents and languages, and calling them “entitled Asian b*****s,” according to the court filing.

Despite the ongoing harassment, employees allegedly allowed the angered woman to place a food order, pay in cash and take an empty fountain drink cup.

Bystander video reviewed by the Los Angeles Times captured an In-N-Out worker handing the woman her change while she continued to shout expletives and a racial slur. The woman then filled the cup at the soda machine and dumped the liquid over Choi and her daughter before walking out of the restaurant while still yelling slurs, the lawsuit states.

After the woman left, Choi spoke with the restaurant manager, who claimed he had already phoned the police but was told officers would not respond because neither Choi nor her daughter required paramedics. Addressing the guard's inaction, the manager told Choi that “security can’t touch anyone unless an aggressor touches someone first,” according to the complaint.

open image in gallery A complaint filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court claims a restaurant manager falsely told Julie Choi he had called the police, despite LAPD confirming no calls were logged from the business that night ( AFP via Getty Images )

Choi pointed out that the assailant had shoved her daughter twice and thrown soda on them in direct view of the guard. The manager said he would file an internal report, advised them to leave and walked them to their vehicle, later sending Choi a text message stating that officers never arrived.

However, when Choi contacted the Los Angeles Police Department the following day, she learned that no calls had been placed from the restaurant the previous evening, the complaint alleges. LAPD Lt. Alondra Garcia confirmed to the Los Angeles Times that no call was logged from the restaurant's address that night, though police did receive a 7:52 p.m. report regarding a battery investigation at the nearby intersection of Van Nuys Boulevard and Moorpark Street. Garcia noted there were no additional records detailing that call or whether officers were dispatched.

Police later took a statement at Choi’s home and informed her that the incident constituted a hate crime, according to the lawsuit, though the suspect remains unidentified.

open image in gallery According to the lawsuit, an on-duty security guard stood by as a woman followed the Korean American mother and her teen daughter around the Los Angeles restaurant, stating he was not permitted to physically remove the aggressor ( Getty Images )

Choi, a Korean immigrant who moved to the U.S. in the 1980s, said her daughter collapsed in tears after the confrontation and remains anxious in public spaces six months later.

“I felt just so sad for her that she had to see this ugly side of humanity,” Choi told the Los Angeles Times. “Whenever we go anywhere now, she looks around the room to see if there’s anything she should be concerned about. What happened to me and my daughter shouldn’t happen to anyone else because of the color of their skin or where they’re from.”

In-N-Out spokesperson Patty Peña declined to comment on the allegations, citing the pending litigation.

The lawsuit follows a separate high-profile incident of anti-Asian harassment at a Northern California In-N-Out in 2022, in which a man was arrested on two hate crime charges in Contra Costa County after directing racist and homophobic remarks at two Korean American college students filming a video.

News.title: V8 engines returning in 2030 in bid to ‘reconnect with DNA’ of Formula One
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Formula One will ditch its current controversial engines and return to V8s in a move the governing FIA has described as “an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA” of the sport.

The unanimous agreement means the more popular V8s will make a comeback in 2030, 17 years after the sport abandoned them in favour of “road relevant” engines.

It is hoped the 2.1-litre V8 turbo-hybrid power unit will not be as complex as the current engines – a 50-50 split between combustion and battery power – which were introduced only this season but have been heavily criticised by drivers and fans alike.

Four-time world champion Max Verstappen considered quitting F1, having compared the new rules to “Mario Kart”, while Fernando Alonso said the sport in its current guise should be known as the “battery world championship”.

The FIA also believe a V8 comeback will help rediscover the ear-piercing sound which became synonymous with F1. The new engines will be powered by sustainable fuels.

“This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula One,” said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem ahead of this weekend’s race in Las Vegas.

“From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide.

open image in gallery Max Verstappen considered quitting the sport (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

“Our vision is clear: lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.

“I want to thank all involved for their collaboration. This is an important step forward and demonstrates what we can achieve when we work together to deliver the best possible future for our sport.”

The call for simpler engines reignited after last month’s farcical race in Malaysia when multiple cars broke down following a software glitch.

The event had to be suspended for nearly an hour because new software had to be downloaded on to the cars.

News.title: Crunchy, chewy and charitable, the Girl Scout cookie is an emblem of empowerment
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ding dong — the Girl Scout cookies are here!

Whether delivered door to door, sold outside a grocery store or even dropped by drones, the arrival of Girl Scout cookie season is a time-honored tradition that people anticipate for months.

More than century ago, a simple idea of a bake sale run by a Muskogee, Oklahoma, troop of Girl Scouts spread in a grassroots way across the country. In a few years, troops were sharing homemade recipes for shortbread cookies that could be easily baked, wrapped in wax paper and sold for a quarter a dozen. Today hundreds of thousands of scouts sell cookies each year, giving them entrepreneurial experience and money to fund troop activities.

As a former scout and scout leader, the cookies were a staple in my house: stacked up by the hundreds in our hallway, hauled from one Kmart to another, peddled and pushed at every shopper or distant relative or random passerby.

Through sleet, snow, wind and rain, I would be out selling cookies multiple nights and weekends, often poorly calculating change by doing math on my mittened fingers. These days, scouts are more often swiping a credit card or holding up a QR code. No more counting out quarters from a cash box.

As a leader, I watched scouts learn to find their voice when approaching an adult with a box or an order sheet. Some kids just enjoyed counting sales and inventory or competing for who could sell the most. A portion of each sale helps fund camps, trips, community projects and other activities. I could rely on cookie sale proceeds to make sure everyone in our troop got an opportunity to go camping, even if their family couldn't afford it.

Wanna start a lively discussion? Ask a crowd which is the best Girl Scout cookie flavor. People hold steadfast to the cookies they grew up eating, whether it’s the hugely popular Thin Mints, the shortbreads perfect for a cup of tea, the chocolate-covered peanut butter cookies or the caramel and coconut circles. My favorite has always been the Tagalongs, so don't come at me.

Today there are more ways to enjoy Girl Scout cookies. They've had gluten-free, nut-free and vegan versions and even ones that dogs can enjoy. Plenty of other brands have tried to jump aboard the train with products like cookie-scented candles, Thin Mint-flavored coffee, Lemon-Up doughnuts and yes, even a line of shampoo, deodorant and body washes that smells remarkably like Do-si-dos.

The secret to the cookie success was only marginally about the crumbly, crunchy treat that keeps people buying them. The true pleasure was a little charitable giving, packaged in a reward for yourself.

___

News.title: Bowen Yang apologizes for using slur on podcast
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Former Saturday Night Live comedian Bowen Yang has apologized for using an antisemitic slur on his podcast.

The 36-year-old had been the subject of social media backlash after using the offensive term to refer to singer Regina Spektor during a recording of his podcast, Las Culturistas, which he co-hosts with Matt Rogers.

In a post on Instagram, Yang wrote: “I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history, especially since we’ve repudiated antisemitism on the show as recently as the last two weeks.”

He continued: “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.”

The origins of the term trace back to Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and the white supremacist movement.

open image in gallery Bowen Yang used a slur that was popularized by the KKK ( AFP/Getty )

Yang had been heavily criticized for his use of the slur by social media users including Meghan McCain, who wrote on X: “Bowen Yang using antisemitic slang that was popularized and mainstreamed by KKK leader David Duke is really just chefs kiss for the guy who got Shane Gillis fired from ‘SNL’ for racism. Well done buying this hate mongering podcast Disney.”

As of earlier this week, Las Culturistas is available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

Actor Michael Rapaport posted: “Bowen Yang, Matt Rogers & soooo many people LOVE preaching inclusion, compassion & protecting the dolls. UNTIL IT COMES TO JEWS. They dismiss the GREAT Regina Spektor for supporting Israel. Funny how it’s ALWAYS Jewish Zionists they single out. Never Black, Christian, Muslim or LGBTQ Zionists.

“The self-appointed COOL KIDS CLUB is judgmental, mean & needs fixing Girl…. Faye Dunaway would NEVER,” he concluded, referring to Yang’s Instagram handle @fayedunaway.

This is not the first time Spektor has been on the receiving end of antisemitic attacks. In July, her concert in Portland, Oregon, was interrupted by pro-Palestine protesters, prompting her to tell them they were “just yelling at a Jew.”

open image in gallery Regina Spektor has been on the receiving end of multiple antisemitic attacks this year ( Getty )

Spektor, who is Jewish and emigrated with her family to New York from the Soviet Union as a child, was filmed by a fan as she addressed an audience member who started shouting “free f***ing Palestine” during her performance at Revolution Hall.

After the first audience member interrupted the show, another fan apparently began repeating: “Free, free Palestine.”

Spektor told her audience at the time: “The only reason I even speak English is because I came here to escape this s***. I only speak English because I came from a country where people treated Jews as othered, and I’m being othered here and it sucks.

“It’d be nice if one of my family’s generation didn’t have to go to a new country and learn a new language and just stay put. Have nice lives, you guys.”

The Independent has reached out to Spektor for comment.

News.title: Macaulay Culkin returning for Home Alone sequel: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Macaulay Culkin has reportedly signed on for a Home Alone sequel.

The 46-year-old is best-known for playing Kevin McCallister in the first two films in the franchise, 1990’s original Home Alone and then the 1992 follow-up film Home Alone 2: Lost in New York. A third film was made in 1997 without him, and three more movies followed that.

Now, he will reportedly return for another sequel, according to Puck. The film is being produced by Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and their Point Grey Pictures.

Puck reported that Rogen and Goldberg will work with Culkin on a script.

The Independent has contacted Disney for comment.

open image in gallery Macaulay Culkin is reportedly returning to the ‘Home Alone’ franchise ( Getty )

Rumors of a new Home Alone film began circulating earlier this year when Culkin signed with influential Hollywood talent agency CAA on the heels of a People report that Disney was working on a new installment in the film series.

A source told the publication at the time that the reboot came from Culkin’s own idea, commenting: “It’s in the early stages, very early. It’s just an idea and an almost green light from Disney.”

The source added: “Disney loved Macaulay’s idea and everyone wants to see this happen.”

In November last year, Culkin openly spoke about a potential sequel idea during his “A Nostalgic Night with Macaulay Culkin” tour.

During an appearance in Long Beach, the actor said: “I kind of had this idea, I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard, and I’m not really paying enough attention, and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me, and then I get locked out.”

open image in gallery Culkin appears as Kevin McCallister in a new ad for McDonald's ( McDonald's )

Puck’s new report comes just days after Culkin revisited his Home Alone character in an ad for McDonald’s promoting a new meal named after the hit film franchise.

The Home Alone meal was announced Tuesday, just one day after the 36th anniversary of the film’s release in theaters.

The ad pokes fun at Culkin’s character Kevin McCallister, who was famously left behind when his family leaves for vacation.

In the fast food chain’s ad, he stands in the middle of a deserted McDonald’s location, shuttered due to a snowstorm, and laments: “Everyone disappeared, again.”

He then dons a name tag introducing himself as “Kevin” before stepping into the role of a McDonald’s employee, taking orders and preparing meals while simultaneously revealing the contents of the Home Alone meal.

News.title: Violence and mistrust hamper Ebola response
News.content:
Six months after the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola virus flared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the outbreak is far from under control.

Scores of new cases of the deadly haemorrhagic fever are being recorded every day and half of those diagnosed go on to die.

The official toll of 11,000 cases and more than 5,400 deaths is likely to be a vast underestimate and the outbreak is more than halfway to becoming the largest ever recorded.

Beyond the bare figures, aid agencies and emergency responders are also increasingly warning about the chaos, disorganisation and violence hampering the response.

Among the most worrying markers is that with 400 to 500 new cases reported every week, some two-thirds of deaths are occurring outside Ebola treatment centres.

Epidemiologists warn that figure is a sure sign cases are spreading undetected and that the tracking and quarantining of suspected patients is not working.

The outbreak has become like a deadly game of whack-a-mole, with new hotspots emerging just as responders manage to gain control over some of the early epicentres.

“Progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), warned this week.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Genocide verdict puts Netanyahu on notice
News.content:
The finding by the world’s top court that the military junta in Myanmar is guilty of genocide will send a shiver through Israel’s legal and military establishment.

No case is directly transferable from one country to another: each is judged on its own merits.

But the legal precedents set in the case against Myanmar are certain to shape the allegations of genocide against Israel over its actions in Gaza following the massacre by Hamas on Oct 7, 2023.

Perhaps it was the Court’s forensic and coldly logical presentation of the 191-page historic judgment, but as it was read out over the course of almost three hours in a hushed courtroom in The Hague, it was impossible not to see parallels.

Unlike other war crimes and crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide hinges on being able to establish “genocidal intent”.

Without it there can be crimes of mass killing, rape and even widespread ethnic cleansing. But there can be no finding of genocide unless those directing the violence “intentionally” planned to destroy a group “in whole or in part”.

Moreover, genocidal motivation must be found to be the “single” reasonable explanation for a defendant state’s actions.

Lawyers in Israel – like most international lawyers – have long stressed how high that bar is, with some believing it was insurmountable without a written document of the “final solution” type filed away by the Nazis.

But Thursday’s judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) blows that assumption out of the water.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino confirms Bruno Fernandes decision after private talks with Man Utd captain
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino confirms Bruno Fernandes decision after private talks with Man Utd captain

Mauricio Pochettino has spoken privately with Bruno Fernandes since touching down in Manchester and has revealed the outcome of their talks ahead of the Liverpool game

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino held his first Manchester United press conference on Friday (Image: Sky Sports News)

Mauricio Pochettino has confirmed that Bruno Fernandes will remain Manchester United captain, despite uncertainty continuing to surround his long-term future at the club.

‌



‌



Fernandes has recently rejected two offers of a new contract with United and the exit of Michael Carrick following a desperate start to the season has cast doubt on his plans. The 32-year-old was dropped after openly criticising the tactics in the thrashing by Como and has worn his frustration publicly for all to see this season.

‌



His contract is due to expire at the end of the season, although United do hold the option to extend it by 12 months. He rejected a big-money move to Al-Hilal in the summer of 2025 and has also been courted by Fenerbahce.

‌



Fernandes has been club captain since July 2023 and boasts an outstanding record of 113 goals and 111 assists in 341 appearances since his £47million transfer from Sporting Lisbon in January 2020. Pochettino has spoken to the Portugal international and is backing him.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



"Bruno is our captain and I think he's a very important player, but all the players need to feel that they are important, from the top to the bottom, or from the bottom to the top," he said in his first press conference on Friday ahead of a trip to Anfield.

"But Bruno is our captain, and he's a very important player. I think we will have time after to talk about the things that you are asking me."

‌



He added: "We spoke yesterday, I spent three hours chatting with all the players individually yesterday. I think I missed some injured players but in the next few days we will talk with everyone.

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes' future at Manchester United is uncertain (Image: Getty Images)

"It was very nice contact. It is important to listen to the players and what they need to say about areas on and off the field."

‌



United chiefs are understood to be relaxed about Fernandes' future, despite him snubbing two contract offers. He will wear the captain's armband when United bid for their second league win of the season against Liverpool on Sunday.

Pochettino has inherited a struggling team that sits 18th in the Premier League and has won just three times in all competitions this season. Like the vast majority of his team-mates, Fernandes has not been at his best this season, but still has six goals and three assists in 14 appearances.

Article continues below

United's new manager wants to create unity and build a new culture at the club, but has already said he wants more involvement in decisions in future. "I was in all my career a coach, head coach, manager. It does not change too much," he said.

"I know as head coach I am the guy who tomorrow will decide the squad for Sunday, pick the 11, make the changes. I know in the future I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that affect the squad. At the end of the day, Manchester United is a football club."

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino sends immediate January transfer plea to Man Utd chiefs
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino sends immediate January transfer plea to Man Utd chiefs

Mauricio Pochettino addressed the media for the first time since being appointed Manchester United's new manager, as he previewed Sunday's Premier League game away to Liverpool

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino wants assurances from Manchester United's owners (Image: MUTV)

Mauricio Pochettino has told the Manchester United hierarchy that he wants to be involved in any transfer decisions and reminded his bosses that they work for a 'football club'. Pochettino, 54, outlined his stance in an effort to avoid running into the same problems as his predecessors.

‌



‌



Former manager Erik ten Hag recently bemoaned how Scott McTominay was sold without his approval, while ex-boss Louis van Gaal once labelled United as a 'commercial club, not a football club'. In his first press conference ahead of Sunday's game against Liverpool, Pochettino was asked to define his role and how much of a say he'll have.

‌



"I was in all my career a coach, head coach, manager. It does not change too much," the Argentine replied. "I know as head coach I am the guy who tomorrow will decide the squad for Sunday, pick the 11, make the changes.

‌



"I know in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that affect the squad. At the end of the day, Manchester United is a football club."

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Pochettino's comments come little over a month before the January transfer window is due to open and after United CEO Omar Berrada told Sky Sports: "When we find the right opportunity, we will spend, but we won't spend for the sake of it."

Michael Carrick suffered the consequences of a lacklustre summer winner and was sacked earlier this month, having overseen just one win from the Red Devils' first 10 Premier League games this season. Pochettino, who's signed a two-and-a-half-year contract, is tasked with turning things around and restoring confidence in the squad that he's inheritated.

‌



"It is normal when you don't win games that the confidence starts to go down," the former USA manager acknowledged. "I think the players need to feel from us that you believe and trust in them, and show that you know what you are doing. That is important.

Will Manchester United beat Liverpool? Give us your prediction in the comments section.

‌



View 2 Images The Glazers have entrusted Sir Jim Ratcliffe with Manchester United's football operations (Image: Catherine Ivill - AMA/Getty Images)

"With the schedule we have ahead we have to settle on our principles. The players are intelligent, they have quality. Sometimes it is unlocking some things that didn't appear for different reasons."

‌



Pochettino flew into Manchester on a private jet from Cincinnati on Wednesday and has had a busy week, starting Friday's press conference only a few minutes after finishing training. "My first target is to sleep, but I cannot sleep," the ex-Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea boss admitted.

"The target is to know the people, the staff, all the people at the club, the players, and to try from the beginning to have an impact. We try to be positive.

Article continues below

"Our most important job is to get the best from the players. We have talented players in the squad. That is our main focus."
