Democratic strategist James Carville called out Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., during a podcast on Thursday over her remarks directed at House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., calling her the "ultimate urban progressive."

"But in terms of Hakeem being speaker, there was an incident that illustrates just how clueless and how the progressive urban left has no idea of what the Democratic Party is," Carville said during a "Politicon" podcast. "Let me refer you to Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, she's from Seattle, she is the ultimate urban progressive, and she said of Speaker-to-be Hakeem Jeffries, who is actually a Black person, that he needs to be on a short rope. This woman is so f---ing ignorant of Black history."

Jayapal said in an interview with Talking Points Memo last week that Jeffries would have "a relatively short rope to show that kind of urgency" as speaker. Jayapal said she wanted his help to secure votes for Medicare for All.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES WINS OVERWHELMING SPEAKER-DESIGNATE VOTE AS PROGRESSIVES' REVOLT FALLS FLAT

She later clarified on X that she meant "a short window to act" and condemned the use of lynching imagery to intimidate anyone.

Jeffries was elected to become the next House speaker on Wednesday. He brushed off the "no" votes from progressives after winning the votes.

JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES

Carville said that Jayapal was, "So f---ing ignorant of the history of the country that she comes from."

"It's a rather sensitive word to a lot of people, not just Black people, to be talking about that. There's a horrific history in this country, Ms. Jayapal, which you're not aware of, of what I guess you would call it, extrajudicial lynchings. Yeah, that's what we're talking about. And I think it's very important that these people submit themselves to self-education," Carville added.

DEMOCRATIC LAWMAKERS ERUPT AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL JOURNALIST CALLS HAKEEM JEFFRIES AN ‘AIPAC MONKEY’ IN VIRAL RANT

Jayapal told Talking Points Memo in the interview published on Nov. 10 that she wanted to see a new Senate leader, but pointed out there were no challenges to Jeffries. She said a challenger would have changed everyone's calculus.

"I think he will have a relatively short rope to show that kind of urgency and perhaps abandon some of the caution that everybody notes as one of his qualities," Jayapal said of Jeffries. "He is cautious and sometimes that can be good, but in a moment where you have this kind of anger and need, demand for bold reform, in order for him to be successful and to hold a speakership, he’s going to have to be able to respond very quickly to that."

CHARLAMAGNE BLASTS AOC FOR ‘BEATING AROUND THE BUSH,’ PRESSES PROGRESSIVES ON BACKING HAKEEM JEFFRIES

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital in a statement, "I don’t think Jayapal was making a lynching reference, and she clarified what she meant. But ‘short rope’ was an incredibly careless phrase to use about the man poised to become the first Black speaker. Carville overreaches if the argument is that criticizing Jeffries is somehow off-limits. The more interesting problem is that parts of the far left have a real blind spot when Black Democrats do not fit their preferred story about ‘the base.’"

Shroff added, "Black Democrats somehow disappear from the picture whenever the far left finds them inconvenient and when you call it out, you get accused of ‘identity politics.’ You can challenge Jeffries all you want. Just don’t pretend the loudest people online are the whole Democratic Party."

HAKEEM JEFFRIES CONFRONTED ON 'YOU'RE NEXT' CHANTS FOLLOWING NY DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST VICTORIES

Carville previously told Fox News Digital the progressive movement is insular, saying its acceptance of political allies depended on whether it considered them part of the group.

"I find that whole, you know, progressive whole thing very exclusionary in nature," Carville said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They only want you if they think you’re one of them, you know. I’m not a fan."

Jayapal and Jeffries' offices did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: Dozens of FBI and DOJ personnel are investigating Peltola's Alaska victory
World.content:

At least 50 FBI agents and more than a dozen lawyers from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) are working on an investigation into Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, and her alleged involvement in recruiting a candidate with the same name as her opponent, Fox News has learned.

The Associated Press projected Peltola's victory on Tuesday, forecasting that she'd defeat incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, with 50.1% of the electorate's votes.

However, senior DOJ officials have opened an investigation into Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives to determine if any laws were broken in an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, a third candidate with almost the exact same name as the incumbent senator, to run.

Attorney General Todd Blanche "sees the Peltola fraud as so egregious, he is putting a lot of resources into the criminal investigation," an ally close to Blanche told Fox News Digital.

ALASKA DEM PELTOLA DEFEATS SULLIVAN, FLIPPING 9TH GOP SENATE SEAT AFTER 'DECOY DAN' UPROAR

The DOJ has sent over 200 subpoenas as part of the probe, which sources told Fox News is focused on the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC).

At least five field offices are involved in the effort and nearly 100 letters have been sent out informing involved parties to preserve their records.

TIM SCOTT DECLARES ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT A 'CRIMINAL OFFENSE' AS DOJ INVESTIGATION ROCKS ALASKA

High-profile elections attorney Marc Elias, whose law firm represents the Peltola campaign, was one of the recipients of a preservation letter.

A federal grand jury is meeting in Alaska once a month to review evidence, Fox News has learned.

DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES

Sen. Sullivan has previously slammed Peltola for allegedly scheming to get the alternate Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

"This was a secret project that they had. And then they worked on it for over a year. And then she consistently lied about it," Sen. Sullivan said.

SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’

Peltola, for her part, denies ever knowing anything about recruiting efforts to get Daniel J. Sullivan, aka "Decoy Dan," on the ballot.

"I just want to clear the air," Peltola told supporters during an October speech in Juneau.

PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING'

"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan," she said.

A New York Times bombshell report released in October claimed that Peltola campaign staffers and senior aides at the DSCC jointly plotted to get the "Decoy Dan" on the ballot in an effort to confuse voters.

MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT

The DSCC has also denied involvement in the alleged scheme.

Peltola, according to the AP, garnered 144,486 votes to Sen. Sullivan's 131,965 votes. A third candidate, Republican Gerald Heikes, received 6,105 votes. All other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan, received 5,561 combined votes.

Alaskan officials have yet to certify the state's election totals, having previously targeted Nov. 25, as the date to certify.

"And what did the same Senate Democrats who just gave sanctimonious speeches do? They rammed through 22 federal judges in November and December before leaving," Cruz said of Democrats, referring to their actions following the 2024 elections.

Cruz pointed out that after President Joe Biden lost the White House and Democrats lost control of the Senate in the 2024 election, Senate Democrats "rammed through" 22 federal judges before Republicans took control in January 2025.

World.title: Marsupial Gear co-founder Hannah Graham reveals the pressure behind her dream Arizona elk hunt
World.content:
Hannah Graham has a pretty firm rule when it comes to hunting: One hunt a year.

The co-founder of Marsupial Gear, a hunting equipment company she started with her husband, Jim, in 2015, has three young kids and a busy schedule. So these days, one hunting trip is about all she can squeeze in.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

And she'd already checked that box with an oryx hunt earlier in the year.

But when Jim entered her name into Arizona's highly competitive elk tag lottery — figuring the odds of drawing were slim anyway — Hannah suddenly found herself with an opportunity many hunters spend decades chasing.

"I was shocked," Graham told OutKick OutDoors.

Her husband called with good news and bad news: She'd drawn an incredible elk tag. The catch? She was going hunting again.

Watch Hannah Graham's full interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

Arizona distributes a limited number of elk tags through a draw system, with applicants accumulating bonus points over time to improve their chances. Still, some people wait decades for the opportunity.

For Graham, who had very little elk-hunting experience, the significance of her good fortune didn't fully sink in until she was standing in the Arizona wilderness, surrounded by bugling bulls.

"It wasn't, I think, probably until the morning of day one of my hunt when the bugles were going off that I realized, 'Oh, this is what everyone was so excited for me for,'" she said. "I've never heard anything like it. It was spectacular."

But with that excitement came pressure.

Graham was accompanied by her husband, close friend Nash Clark and a group of experienced hunters who had volunteered their time to help her succeed. She also felt the weight of representing a well-known hunting brand.

"I put a lot of pressure on myself," she admitted. "It's not necessarily anyone putting pressure on me."

With everyone so excited about her opportunity, she recalled thinking, "Oh my gosh, I cannot fail at this."

The hunt itself was unlike anything Graham had experienced. Rather than spending hours glassing for deer, she found herself racing through difficult terrain, chasing the sounds of bugling elk.

"The first day we walked over 10 miles, literally. But we were, like, chasing bugles all day long. They were going off everywhere," she said. "It was like every hunter's dream I was experiencing."

And those elk weren't exactly waiting around for her.

"We were not walking 10 miles. We were jogging, quick running, just to keep up with the pace they were walking," she laughed.

When the dream hunt gets real

Eventually, the crew located an impressive bull and worked to get Graham into shooting position. But when the opportunity finally came, things didn't go exactly as planned.

Her first muzzleloader shot struck farther back than intended, leaving the bull wounded and forcing the group to continue the pursuit.

"It's not a good feeling," Graham said. "I want it to be, ideally, lights out."

RILEY GREEN FILLS THE FREEZER AFTER SCORING MASSIVE BUKL ELK WITH A BOW IN THE UTAH MOUNTAINS

She explained that, despite all her practice, shooting at a range and shooting in the field are two very different things.

"I'm shooting on the ground at the range practicing, and then here I'm standing up in a rush because I've only got 10 seconds to make it happen because they were just moving through the trees," she said. "Real life and range life are very different."

As the group worked to recover the bull, Graham's nerves began to take over. She missed two subsequent shots, and by the time she had another opportunity, she said she was struggling to maintain her composure.

"I was just shaking. I couldn't focus. I feel like people were talking to me, and I couldn't hear what they were saying," she recalled.

That's when her friend Nash stepped in.

"He literally was standing right next to me," Graham said, recalling how he helped calm her down and focus on the shot. "The last words I heard were, 'Hannah, just slowly pull the trigger.'"

With Nash coaching her through those final moments, Graham was able to steady herself and make the shot.

"I was able to hone in on what I was doing, and I just slowly pulled the trigger," she said.

HUNTING. FISHING. WILD STORIES. IT'S ALWAYS OPEN SEASON! WATCH AND SUBSCRIBE ON YOUTUBE!

Then came the words she'd been desperate to hear.

"He's dead," Jim told her.

"I just felt like the weight of the world lifted off my shoulders," Graham said. "It was very emotional. It was incredible."

Even recalling the experience during our interview brought those feelings rushing back.

"I cried," she said. "I could cry now thinking about it."

Despite the emotional roller coaster, Graham said she wouldn't trade the experience for anything.

More than just a trophy

And although she harvested a magnificent bull, the most meaningful part of the hunt wasn't necessarily the animal itself. It was the friends who devoted their time and energy to helping her succeed.

"There were so many guy friends that just wanted to see me succeed, and that was the most incredible part of it," she said, explaining that each member of the crew played an important role, including contributions that never made it into Marsupial Gear's documentary, "One Hunt a Year."

"I literally was brought to tears after the hunt multiple times because I was so moved by how nice every single guy was on there."

For Graham, that's what makes hunting so special.

"Everyone should try hunting once. Try one big game hunt once with friends," she said. "It's such a bonding experience when you really go after it and you're successful, and everyone's working as a team. It's such a cool thing to experience."

As for whether the experience convinced her to abandon her one-hunt-a-year rule?

Not quite.



She's looking forward to a javelina hunt with her oldest son this spring. And although Jim continues encouraging her to put in for more tags, Graham says she's taking things one year at a time.

World.title: Trump calling Putin ‘my friend’ at APEC summit sparks backlash
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, is wanted by the International Criminal Court on allegations of war crimes, and is accused of overseeing a yearslong campaign of election interference, sabotage and cyberattacks against the West.

So when President Donald Trump pointed to the Russian leader and declared, “He’s my friend,” at the historic Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China on Thursday, the reaction from some of America’s closest European allies was one of alarm and disbelief.

“God, protect us from such friends,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X shortly afterward.

“The optics of embracing Putin and calling him a friend cause us some concern,” Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, told a news conference Thursday. He added that it posed the question of whom Trump considered a closer friend, Putin or Poland, and “if push came to shove, which friend would he choose?”

Their comments came hours before Poland’s defense minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, accused Russia of violating the country’s airspace overnight with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone. Elsewhere, Estonia said it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months.

Much of the criticism of Trump’s remark has come from Poland, historically one of Washington’s closest allies in Europe but whose officials have grown increasingly wary of Trump’s dealings with Russia. The country, which borders Ukraine, Russia and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, has long been among the most outspoken European governments warning about the threat of Russian aggression. Its security strategy also relies heavily on the United States and NATO.

More broadly, the word “friend” also caused fresh alarm among other European governments, some of which are openly warning that Putin may expand his aggression beyond Ukraine and attack them, too.

Ultimately, there is widespread concern that elevating Putin alongside Trump and China’s Xi Jinping will legitimize and embolden a leader whom Western governments have sought to isolate over his record of grave human rights abuses and aggression against other countries, allegations he has routinely denied.

The joint declaration made by Trump, Putin and Xi after their meeting made no mention of Ukraine but condemned the International Criminal Court, which has issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was “very incomprehensible” that Trump would meet with Putin, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those who warned against the meeting becoming a rerun of the Yalta Conference of 1945. The summit toward the end of World War II saw President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively carve up occupied Germany and other parts of Europe.

Others, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, were more restrained. Asked whether Trump had “fallen for Putin’s charm offensive,” he replied that it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had “talked about the horrific loss of life, including the loss of young Russian lives, and he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also defended the principle of nuclear powers meeting to pursue diplomacy.

Burnham and Rutte were speaking at a meeting in Berlin of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of nearly 40 countries working to support Ukraine and provide security guarantees.

They were joined by Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, the U.S. envoys tasked with brokering peace between Moscow and Kyiv.

Trump called into a meeting of dozens of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, telling the group that Putin was ready to end the war, according to five European officials briefed on the discussions. He also encouraged the Europeans to make a deal so they can stop spending money on Ukraine and spend it on their own countries, the officials said.

Kushner also mentioned the call in a post on X but said it was up to the president to reveal what he said.

“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He’s not looking to impose anything unilaterally,” Kushner said. “Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. That’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard.”

The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on the criticisms about Trump’s comment about Putin. But Trump defended his description of the Russian president in an interview with Reuters, saying that “it’s nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy.”

This is far from the first time Trump has spoken warmly about Putin, joking in 2013 about becoming his “new best friend.” Once in office, Trump said in 2018 that the pair “got on very well,” and in 2022, he described Putin’s initial moves against Ukraine as “genius” and “savvy.” In 2023 and again in 2024, Trump recounted telling Putin, “We’re friends.”

However, this week was the first time Trump made the declaration to Putin’s face, in front of television cameras at one of the most hotly anticipated meetings of recent years.

“It’s one thing to say in an interview, ‘We get on,’ as Trump has in the past; it’s quite another to see him crossing a room in the hotel in China with an effusive smile on his face and gushing about ‘my friend,’” said Jonathan Eyal, international director of the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It all felt very natural and very real.”

The condemnation was not confined to one side of the Atlantic.

In the United States, Democrats were openly scathing. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called Trump’s words “embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” while Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described Trump’s “friend” as a “murderous war criminal.”

Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said: “Putin is not my friend. He’s not your friend. He’s not a friend of this country, and when the president of the United States refers to him in that way, it emboldens him.”

Republicans were more circumspect. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida called Putin a “thug” but acknowledged that Trump needed to work with him.

Bill Browder, a British American financier who spearheaded the international campaign for Russian sanctions and has become one of Putin’s most prominent critics, also described his “revulsion and disgust” at hearing Trump’s words.

“He’s a guy who’s a geopolitical menace, and he should not get any kind of respect, let alone from the American head of state,” Browder told NBC News in a telephone interview. “To be elevated to the top table with genuine superpowers is an unbelievable symbolic position to sit in.”

When asked about Trump’s comment at the end of the news conference following the “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in the German capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy only shrugged and walked offstage.

World.title: For the Washington Spirit, will the third time be the charm in the NWSL championship?
World.content:
The Washington Spirit hope the third time will be the charm as they face the Kansas City Current at home in the National Women’s Soccer League championship Saturday.

Although the club won the title in 2021 and is considered to be among the most consistent in the league, the Spirit have fallen short in two consecutive years. They lost in 2024 against the Orlando Pride, who won their first championship after repeatedly failing to qualify for the playoffs, before falling in the final yet again to the last-seeded Gotham FC in 2025.

This time, however, they’ll be able to claim home-field advantage.

Every year, the NWSL chooses a neutral site to host the championship game ahead of the regular season. This year’s host just happens to be Audi Field, home of the Spirit and its MLS counterpart, D.C. United.

The stadium is well known for the way the crowd’s roars reverberate, giving the field the nickname “Rowdy Audi.”

“What we feel at Audi, I think, is something unique,” Spirit head coach Adrián González told reporters this week. “It’s a huge push of energy, a huge motivation, and sometimes with the game you have some adversities ... and that extra energy is a blessing, because we need them.”

An inaugural NWSL team, the Spirit have made the league’s championship five times but have only reached the summit once, in 2021, star Trinity Rodman’s rookie season.

Rodman, who recorded an assist on the game-winning goal that year, has become the face of the franchise with the backing of owner Michele Kang.

Washington Spirit midfielder Andi Sullivan plays against the Portland Thorns at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 8. Jamie Sabau / Getty

But the team’s struggle to overcome late-season injuries has hampered the squad in the playoffs since. This year has been luckier, as they were able to activate veterans Ashley Hatch and Casey Krueger late in the season.

Another addition has been Tanzanian forward Clara Luvanga, a former Al-Nassr player whose speed and hunger for goals has made her difficult to defend against. Luvanga scored once and had two assists in the Spirit’s quarterfinal win against the Portland Thorns, showcasing her relentless energy in front of the net, which wears down the opposition.

This season has also been Rodman’s best to date.

The 24-year-old recorded 12 goals in the regular season before adding another two on the score sheet against the Thorns. It’s a comeback story for Rodman, who spent much of 2025 recovering from a recurring back injury.

But the Spirit aren’t the only team looking for redemption.

Izzy Rodriguez, a defender for the Current, called it “surreal” to know the team will be back in the final. She said she’s ready to take in the moment and bring the competitiveness to the pitch.

“Every playoff game has been a really tight game — that’s what you’re going to get in this league,” Rodriguez said Wednesday. “But I think we’re going to go out and be the best we can be.”

The Current, an expansion team founded in 2021, made the final for the second time in franchise history.

Kansas City had an incredible season last year, securing the postseason’s No. 1 spot at the fastest pace in NWSL history. But in a shocking upset, the Current were defeated by the last-seeded Gotham FC in the quarterfinals. It was a bitter end for the Current, who saw major roster turnover and injuries to key players early in the season.

Kansas City Current midfielder Croix Bethune plays in the semifinal match against Gotham FC in New York on Sunday. Ira L. Black / Getty

Expectation that the team would return to winning form at the start of the year, despite having forwards Temwa Chawinga and Michelle Cooper out with injuries, was unrealistic, according to head coach Chris Armas. This season came with a lot of change that led the team to discover a new version of itself, he added.

“It just seemed like every time we steadied this ship, there was something there,” Armas said. “And on the inside, we just kept talking about staying steady, consistent, sticking to the process. ... I give the players a lot of credit, honestly.”

In perhaps an ironic twist of fate, one of the saving graces for the Current this year has been the acquisition of former Spirit player Croix Bethune.

The 25-year-old was drafted by Washington in 2024, winning Rookie of the Year in her first season even after missing the final two months with a torn meniscus suffered by throwing the ceremonial first pitch at a Nationals game.

Her return the following year was lauded by both teammates and supporters as the young star seemed to rebound quickly early in the 2025 season.

But Bethune was traded in February in a million-dollar transfer, with the Current paying the Spirit $900,000 in transfer funds and an additional $100,000 in allocation money. The deal was a preseason stunner as Bethune was a beloved fixture on the Spirit roster.

To make matters worse for Spirit fans, this year has been Bethune’s best by far. The young midfielder had five goals and 11 assists and played nearly 2,200 minutes in the regular season. She was named the NWSL’s Midfielder of the Year on Wednesday night.

Bethune will return to Audi on Saturday night to face her former team and fight for the biggest title of her career. The young star said she’s confident it will be an “amazing game” as both teams are on a roll in the postseason.

“Going to Audi, it is tough for opponents to play against them because the stadium itself is great,” Bethune said Sunday after winning the semifinal game. “The fans show out for them. But K.C. does the same thing. ... I’m sure they’ll be there in D.C., too.”

World.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on companies that build AI data centers overseas
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he plans to restrict U.S. companies from building data centers overseas — the latest instance of the president embracing the construction of massive tech facilities that a majority of Americans oppose.

Back in Washington after a trip to Asia, Trump said the restrictions were necessary to prevent AI infrastructure from leaving U.S. shores.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump told reporters in the White House briefing room.

“We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country,” he said.

He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad.

“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” he said.

The comments signaled a potential new headache for the artificial intelligence industry, on a day when stock markets tumbled and not even the record-setting IPO this week of Anthropic could soothe investors’ fears about the sustainability of AI stocks.

They were also the latest example of Trump’s forceful advocacy for AI data centers, a position that puts him squarely at odds with the majority of Americans.

“You ought to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said Friday. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don’t shut them off.”

Trump has previously attacked state and local efforts to roll back data center construction, saying in August that they should only be stopped if communities “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” Trump wrote in a social media post.

During this year’s midterm elections, data centers proved a key sticking point for voters, who overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised to curb their proliferation.

On Wall Street, the massive wins by Democrats who pledged to rein in data centers put a fresh dent in an already-ailing AI stock trade, as investors digested the prospect that tech companies’ computing resources would be further crimped.

Since Nov. 4, the S&P 500 has declined approximately 9%, though a confluence of other factors has also contributed to the brutal sell-off.

President Donald Trump at a press briefing with AI executives at the White House on Sept. 29. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

It is not clear how Trump’s foreign data center ban would be implemented; a White House representative did not immediately reply to a request for comment Friday.

Trump admitted that he had not yet told his staff about the plan.

“I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump mused. “I’m telling them now — they’re here, many of them are here — and we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can’t. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it.”

World.title: Zohran Mamdani tears Achilles while playing soccer against NYC press corps

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will be hobbling in a walking boot for at least the next six weeks after forgetting that he’s on the doorstep of middle age — he tore his Achilles while playing soccer.

The first-term mayor of America’s biggest city paid a heavy price for scoring a goal in a friendly match between City Hall and the New York City press corps Thursday night.

Mamdani showed up on crutches to Friday’s news conference announcing the plan to close the Rikers Island jail. He admitted that he didn’t properly stretch.

“For those who don’t know, we played a friendly game against the press corps last night, soccer, which we won 10-5 and I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch,” the Big Apple’s chief executive and devoted Arsenal supporter told reporters.

Mamdani at City Hall on Friday. Michael Appleton / New York City Mayor's Office

“I forgot that I was 35, and soon after, I tore my Achilles,” Mamdani said. “I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks. I will play soccer in about nine months.”

The link between middle-aged weekend warriors and ruptured Achilles tendons is well known.

“Middle-aged adults doing sports activities are more likely to get this kind of injury,” according to the Columbia University Irving Medical Center. “Tears also happen in older adults.”

World.title: Anthropic shares tank after huge IPO as the Nasdaq erases 2026 gains
World.content:
A bruising stock market sell-off gathered steam Friday, despite high hopes that Anthropic’s record-setting IPO a day earlier would revive sentiment around the flagging AI trade.

Instead, Friday’s downturn was led by Anthropic itself, whose shares were down more than 11% after rising 17% on its first day on the Nasdaq Composite.

The S&P 500 was trading nearly 2% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, and is now 10% off from its most recent high, entering what’s known as “correction territory.”

Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also sold off.

The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index’s longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank.

For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn.

Samyukta Lakshmi / Bloomberg via Getty

Given the importance the AI trade has played this year in propelling markets and economic growth writ large, its derailment over concerns about costs, debt, profitability and political risk could have broader implications.

Deepening worries about AI revenues tied to exports of advanced technology to China compounded Friday’s sell-off.

The Jensen Huang scandal pulling down Nvidia appeared to broaden Thursday, when a short-selling firm issued a report raising questions about whether Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, may also have had shipments to Asia diverted to mainland China.

Alongside the stock sell-off, there has been an increase in purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeing signs of weakening growth amid higher interest rates from the Federal Reserve and a stalling economy in China.

“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.

Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.

“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”

Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Modera Wealth Management, called the recent sell-off “a garden-variety correction.”

But he noted that overall returns have still been respectable this year, “especially against a challenging backdrop of rising rates, persistent inflation and fears about an AI slowdown.”

But a prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth.

“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.

World.title: Deadly Russian strikes hit 3 Kyiv bridges after Putin vows revenge for Crimea attacks
World.content:
KYIV, Ukraine — Three bridges in Kyiv were hit Friday in a massive Russian ballistic missile attack, officials in the Ukrainian capital said, hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed “painful” revenge for strikes on his prized bridge linking Crimea to Russia.

The attacks, which started in the early hours of the morning and continued well into the day, damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges connecting the left and right banks of the Dnipro River, which flows through the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a post on Telegram.

The aftermath of an overnight Russian strike on an industrial area in central Kyiv on Friday. Ted Turner / NBC News

At least six people were killed and 15 injured in those strikes, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a separate post. Two others were killed in separate attacks across the country, which saw nine regions hit overnight, he said.

The strikes on Kyiv forced authorities to restrict traffic on the bridges, impacting the movement across the capital. Klitschko asked residents not to drive private cars into the city “unless absolutely necessary” and suggested employers let staff work remotely.

Russia has been hitting Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges since early October, causing multiple closures, disrupting metro services and causing traffic jams.

But it is the first time that Russia hit three different bridges in a single night, and it has left most of the main road crossings over the Dnipro simultaneously damaged or restricted.

An NBC News team in Kyiv heard air raid sirens going off every few minutes overnight, accompanied by loud explosions.

After dawn broke on the rainy and foggy Friday morning, firefighters were seen putting out the flames from a strike on an industrial area in the capital.

It’s part of the daily reality for Kyiv’s residents after Russia escalated both the number of ballistic missiles it was firing at the capital and the frequency of attacks.

The latest strikes came hours after Putin said that Moscow would retaliate after Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week.

World.title: Brazen train heist of Nikes and Crocs nets ring of bandits $22 million in cargo, officials say
World.content:
More than a dozen modern day rail bandits were arrested after allegedly stealing about $22 million of Nike sneakers and other products from Southern California cargo trains and selling them on the black market via social media, officials said Thursday.

The imported goods, which also included Crocs footwear and equipment made by Milwaukee Tools, were taken off Los Angeles and Long Beach freight trains connected to some of the nation’s busiest ports, according to federal authorities.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash.”

The defendants would disable air hoses that run “along the length of the trains” which then “would cause a sudden loss of air pressure, causing the brakes to unexpectedly engage” and force “an emergency stop of the entire train,” according to the indictment.

Once the trains were brought to a halt, defendants would raid cargo cars fulled with merchandise, load pilfered goods into their trucks and vans before transporting “the stolen cargo to stash houses” around Southern California, the indictment said.

From there, some stolen goods were then allegedly sold to retailers who didn’t have any agreement with brands such as Nike.

One buyer, identified only as “Company 1” was a “sneaker and streetwear resale brand with headquarters in Los Angeles, California” that “bought and resold desirable or ‘high heat’ sneakers,” according to the indictment.

“Company 1 was not an authorized Nike reseller, meaning that it was not a business contractually approved by Nike to buy and resell Nike sneakers,” the court document said.

Some other stolen cargo was just sold directly by the thieves, officials said.

One of the defendants, 36-year-old East L.A. resident Jose Angel Aguilar Espinosa “would advertise the stolen products to potential buyers, including through his social media accounts” before selling them “to buyers for a profit,” the indictment read.

A Union Pacific train passes shipping containers in Los Angeles on Sept. 2, 2025. Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty

The court document included numerous photos defendants allegedly took of themselves, proudly mugging for the camera with their loot.

The men were indicted on suspicion of conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. They could face between 5 and 20 years behind bards if convicted on all charges.

Nathan Daniel Angel, a 21-year-old East Los Angeles resident, was identified as “the crew’s leader,” according to a statement by the Department of Justice.

The defendants also included Angel’s father, 38-year-old Daniel “Rayo” Angel and the leader’s uncles, 23-year-old Rodolfo Angel, also known as “Rudy” and “Flaco,” and Jose “Joe” Luis Angel, also 23.

It wasn’t immediately clear if Espinosa, the three Angels, Donta “Dret” Hedgeman, 27, Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, Daniel Garcia, 36, Carlos Robert “JD” Estrada, 28, Angel “Fluffy” Sanchez, 24, Ruben Mario “Bubu” Banuelos, 26, Fredy Marquina, 25, Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, or Ricardo Mares, 32, had hired or been assigned criminal defense lawyers to speak on their behalf on Friday.

World.title: 4.2-magnitude earthquake rattles Los Angeles area
World.content:
An early-morning 4.2-magnitude earthquake rattled the Los Angeles area on Friday.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the earthquake struck about a half-mile north-northwest of Commerce, California, which is about 7 miles from downtown Los Angeles.

The map shows the location of a 4.4-magnitude earthquake near Commerce, California, on Nov. 20, 2026. USGS

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted about the quake on social media, saying it likely woke up many Angelenos.

"While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX," Bass wrote. "The LAFD and City teams will continue to monitor and update as needed."

People reported feeling the quake as far away as Lancaster, California, about 80 miles north of downtown L.A., and Poway, California, about 115 miles to the south, the USGS said.

Shortly after 5:30 a.m., the LA Fire Department provided an update that no significant infra/structure damage or injuries were noted. The spokesperson added that the LAFD Earthquake Mode is complete and normal operations will resume.

"Use this event as a reminder to prepare for inevitable earthquake activity in our region," the LAFD said.

World.content: Trump speaks to reporters after Putin-Xi summit President Trump spoke to reporters Friday following his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Matt Gutman anchored CBS News' special report. More

World.title: Russia missiles pummel Ukraine and hit NATO soil in Poland
World.content:
Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.

The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance.

"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."

NATO and Allied planes responded to the incident, including Polish F-16s, Swedish JAS 39 Gripens, a Dutch A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aerial refueling aircraft and others. NATO and Allied ground-based air defenses were also alerted.

Members of the Polish military gather near the site where an object fell near the border with Ukraine on Nov. 20, 2026. Kacper Pempel/REUTERS

"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure."

"Hard to regard it as a coincidence"

Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post. Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council.

"Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.

Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.

Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.

The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend."

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."

NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.

Members of the Polish Army take part in the Koalicja 26.2 military exercise at the Land Forces Training Range in Nowa Deba, Poland, Nov. 20, 2026. Patryk Ogorzalek/Agencja Wyborcza via REUTERS

Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine, about 60 miles west of where the Russian weapons landed Friday.

"It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post.

The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin — whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little.

The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv, citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

"We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."

At least 8 killed, dozens wounded in Ukraine

Ukrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.

Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

"Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."

A man stands amid the debris of an office building that caught fire after it was struck during Russian missile and drone attacks in Kyiv, Ukraine, Nov. 20, 2026. Thomas Peter/REUTERS

A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.

Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official.

"The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery."

"A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."

World.title: Maps and charts show record number of measles cases in U.S. this year
World.content:
So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. By November, the number of cases topped 5,000, more than double the previous year's total.

The ongoing outbreaks resulted in the U.S. losing its official measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

In August, health officials in Pennsylvania reported the state's first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years. Several more deaths associated with measles were later reported as the state's outbreak surged, and deaths were also reported in New York and Wisconsin.

Measles is one of the most contagious of all infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective.

The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC.

Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases in 2025, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children.

Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years, the total was much lower.

Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates.

CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. The figure has declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year — a critical threshold to keep people safe. Only 10 states hit the 95% threshold last year.

"When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity)," the CDC states.

"I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids," Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing.

World.title: 6 reasons stocks are falling, and what you should do about it
World.content:
The stock market is having its roughest patch since the early days of the pandemic.

Stocks renewed their slide on Friday after tumbling the previous day, with the S&P 500 on track to mark its seventh consecutive day of losses. That would mark its longest losing streak since February 2020, when investors fled the market amid the panicked early days of the pandemic.

The Nasdaq stock index fell sharply, sinking 865 points, or 3.5%, in early afternoon trading. The S&P 500 dropped 2.1%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.7%. Here are six factors souring investors' mood, and what experts say you should do about it.

Fears that AI investments might not pay off

Investors are increasingly concerned that the enormous spending on data centers and other infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence may not deliver the hoped-for returns. Anthropic, the first AI lab to go public, has shown rapid revenue growth, but its regulatory filings also point to massive losses — about $104 billion for the first nine months of 2026 alone.

"Those figures explain both the frenzy and the nerves," said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory group. "From here, the market will judge whether the software layer can turn breathtaking growth into lasting profit, and Friday's wobble shows the judging has already begun."

Anti-data center laws could take root

With Democrats set to gain the upper hand in Congress, investors are bracing for new laws that could restrict data center construction when newly elected officials take office in January. Although the shifting political winds aren't expected to halt that buildout, even a modest slowdown could impact the financial results for a range of big tech companies investing heavily in AI.

"The Blue Tidal Wave win and fears about an anti-AI/anti-data center DC" are contributing to the selloff, said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, in a report on Friday.

The Fed raising interest rates

The Federal Reserve is expected to hike interest rates at its December meeting, as inflation remains well above the central bank's 2% annual target. Raising rates tamps down inflation, but it also makes borrowing more costly, tempering consumer spending and business investment.

"The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%" without intervention from the central bank, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday.

A crackdown on chip exports

The revelation that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a spy for the People's Republic has sparked calls for stricter export rules to China. The ensuing turmoil at Nvidia, including Huang's resignation, has prompted the Commerce Department to move to restrict sales of advanced AI chips to China.

"The chip industry globally is witnessing a far larger impact from Washington's new export restrictions than initially expected," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a report.

Fears over Trump's saber-rattling

Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. That's raising fears that new hostilities could cause a renewed spike in oil prices, adding to inflationary pressures.

"The Iran war remains in a dangerous liminal stage," Crisafulli said.

Government shutdown risks

Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a U.S. government shutdown. But there's a risk that efforts in Washington, D.C., to broker a deal could break down, as some congressional Democrats are pushing to block any funding bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.

Shutdown risks could also intensify next year under a divided government, according to Oxford Economics. The Democratic-controlled Congress could "bring bruising fights over shutdowns and the debt limit, while doing little to curb tariff, immigration and geopolitical uncertainty," analysts with the investment adviser said in a report this week.

What experts advise

Investment pros say that while it's important to stay informed, it's best not to sell stocks in a panic, as that can lead to losses that are tough to recover from. For instance, investors who sold in February 2020 may have lost out on the sharp market gains that followed as the economy recovered from the pandemic.

"We have seen so many peaks and valleys over the decades, with many investors asking us over the last few weeks, is this a March 2000 moment (pre-dot.com bubble) or Fall 2007 vibe (financial crisis buildup)," Ives wrote. "This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting [that] this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years, and that is the wrong move in our view."

World.title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
World.content:
Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

The commemorative statue of 1st Sgt. Bradley Kasal being carried by Lance Cpl. Chris Marquez and Lance Cpl. Dan Shaffer, after taking heavy fire during the Second Battle of Fallujah in 2004. U.S. Marine Corps Cpl. Juan C. Bustos/DVIDS

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."

The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."

Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.

Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.

Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.

When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."

Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"

Daniel Gillan, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillan said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillan said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillan said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillan also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.

"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillan said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."

One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."

"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.

The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.

Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.

When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.

Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."

When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.

His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.

The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.

James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.

Editor's note: An earlier version of this article misspelled former JROTC cadet Daniel Gillan's name. The article has been updated.

World.title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
World.content:
A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

toggle caption i John McDonnell/AP

A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.

Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.

The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Sponsor Message

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."

The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.

"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.

Sponsor Message

NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.

On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.

That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.

Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.

And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.

She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.

"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.

Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.

The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

World.title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
World.content:
Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
