toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images

President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.

Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.

Loading...

In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.

While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.

"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."

Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.

But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.

"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."

Sponsor Message

The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.

On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.

Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.

"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"

But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.

"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.

The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."

"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."

Sponsor Message

To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.

"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.

But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.

The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

World.title: How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
World.content:
How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement

toggle caption i Andre Calder

Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.

The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.

Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.

Sponsor Message

YouTube

In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.

"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."

But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.

Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.

"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.

The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."

Sponsor Message

"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.

When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."

"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."

The journey to the stage

Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.

Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.

"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.

Sponsor Message

On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.

"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.

A night to remember

By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.

Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.

toggle caption i Andre Calder

They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.

When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.

Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.

As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.

"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."

Sponsor Message

"We're being seen. We have something to say," he added. "Younger folk, older folk — they can say, okay, we see Black people playing in orchestras. Which is a serious thing."

toggle caption i Andre Calder

For Wright, who grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, the ensemble has built a musical bridge she always wished existed.

"When I stepped outside, I was hearing Beyoncé or Brandy," she said. "But when I was practicing in the house, I was practicing Vivaldi." "We come to the edge of the stage, we can meet as many audience members as we can and we talk to them," Wright said. "Some of their children are playing the violin or the viola, and they'll ask us to take a picture or they'll ask us to make a video to inspire their daughter. Because sometimes when their daughter is practicing, they don't get to see the end result. Because practicing can take quite a bit of time. So they want us to show their daughters and send these videos to them to help inspire them."

"My goal is making sure [audience members] leave feeling something awesome or something great," Wright added. "And that's what we're doing. We treat every show as if it's our last."

World.title: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results
World.content:
Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during a White House press conference Friday, saying the U.S. took the stage from a position of strength.

"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," he said, though the historic summit between the three countries yielded few tangible results.

But Trump offered little in actual results of the meetings, beyond a joint statement on unity over some issues, such as continuing to discuss reducing nuclear risks.

Sponsor Message

Trump, flanked by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gave a wide-ranging opening statement that veered from recounting his trip and who he met with to asides about Iran, the U.S. Federal Reserve, his quest for a Nobel Peace Prize and domestic manufacturing.

Trump also said he and Chinese President Xi were agreeing to "joint guardrails" amid the race to develop artificial intelligence, a notable acknowledgement about the risks involved.

Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."

Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S.

"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off. And there's always somebody else in this country. But if it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.

Trump said he only wants "older chips" from the U.S. to be sold to China, in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. "We want only older chips, and we don't mind if none go, but only older. You have to understand, China makes chips too, and if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves," he said.

Vance and Rubio both spoke before the president took questions, with the vice president saying he missed the president and Rubio, who was on the trip with Trump, also recounting the highlights from overseas.

Sponsor Message

Historic meetings in Asia

Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.

Ahead of the press conference, Trump said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.

Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.

While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.

"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."

World.title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
World.content:
Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain

toggle caption i Texas Department of Criminal Justice/AP

HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.

And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.

The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.

Sponsor Message

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"

Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."

Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

Sponsor Message

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.

She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.

Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.

Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."

"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.

"David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."

Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."

Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

Sponsor Message

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

World.title: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
World.content:
Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.

toggle caption i Finn Gomez/Getty Images

🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.



Sponsor Message

🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.

The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.



🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Claire Harbage/NPR

Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Rockstar Games

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Being Heumann chronicles Judy Heumann, the "mother of the disability rights movement," and her coalition as they embark on a historic 1970s sit-in to advocate for disability rights legislation.

📺 TV: In the new British comedy-fantasy Small Prophets, a man summons magical spirits in an attempt to locate his long-missing girlfriend.

📚 Books: Longtime host of Reading Rainbow LeVar Burton shares his journey in his new memoir, Take My Word for It. He reflects on his life, both in and out of his iconic roles, and the unexpected twists he's encountered.

🎵 Music: On Graceland Way, singer-songwriter and harpist Mikaela Davis blends psychedelic and alternative country, showcasing her boundary-pushing harp play.

🎮 Gaming: After years of waiting, fans can now revel in the Bonnie-and-Clyde love story in Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is poised to steal the crown as the biggest entertainment launch ever with up to $5 billion in projected first-week sales, according to estimates.

❓ Quiz: What a week! A new James Bond was named, SpaceX made history and the Alaska Senate race was called. Think you were paying attention? Let's find out.

Sponsor Message

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i STR/AP

A new Pew Research Center report shows that by 2035, Muslims will become the largest religious group globally, surpassing Christians. The Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced that Fiona, the famous 9-year-old hippo, has died after failing to pass a hat she ingested more than a week ago. (via WVXU) Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a bill yesterday banning New York City's 160-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry. Animal rights activists have fought for decades to end the practice. (via Gothamist)



This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
World.content:
Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

There is a certain thrill in spotting a dollar bill on the ground. It's free money! Well one lucky person found a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her aunt's closet, under a pile of fur coats. The Smithsonian magazine reported the painting, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I," is part of a three-part series based on Keeffe's time in northern New Mexico. O'Keeffe has described her time there as particularly impactful.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i

The woman's aunt received the painting as a graduation gift from her parents way back when. They bought it for $3,800. That's the equivalent of $42,000 in today's dollars. This week, it sold at Christie's for $4,878,000 million. Double check your closet, people.

Coming up:



Why old software is so risky

Why Steam is pulling in less revenue from NEW games

What cohost Adrian Ma is reading this week

News We're Watching

This has been a long and strange week of outages from United Airlines to Apple Pay to the F.A.A. It's got many people thinking about this seemingly omnipresent threat of cyberattack. The agencies and companies experiencing the outages insist they're unrelated to cyberattacks. But there is a lot of concern right now about how vulnerable the U.S. is to these digital threats with the combination of fast-growing AI and decidedly fragile infrastructure.

Case in point, earlier this month, Europe faced ANOTHER hack on its supermarket refrigeration. Grocery stores and butcher shops across seven countries saw their fridges and freezers turned up to more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

It wasn't some complicated, sophisticated attack. It was hackers that found a vulnerability in old software. A vulnerability that had existed for a long time.

"That's where attackers see a big opportunity," said Aaron Mitchell, CEO of HeroDevs. "That's an easy way for me to get access and start to do some real damage."

After all, there is a lot of old software out there. Ones that touch utilities, hospitals, and critical infrastructure - or airlines. In some cases, companies didn't feel much urgency to address security gaps.

toggle caption i JOHAN NILSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

HeroDevs is a cybersecurity firm that does the addressing FOR companies. They help maintain support for a certain kind of software called open-source. When a software reaches end-of-life, and a company has moved on to new ideas, they might pay HeroDevs to maintain it and (importantly!!) patch vulnerabilities.

That could be more important than ever because AI is helping find a record number of these vulnerabilities. Last week, VulnCheck, a cybersecurity consulting firm, posted that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been found and disclosed so far this year, more than double than 2025. Hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities 33% faster compared to 2025.

Sponsor Message

In other words, vulnerabilities in outdated software are a prime target for hackers.

"About half of all exploits that happen, known exploits of a vulnerability, are happening on versions that are no longer supported by the maintainer," said Mitchell. "That number is rapidly growing."

This is a problem because countless websites, companies, and governments have outdated software somewhere.

Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that's built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.

"It was a huge deal, and for the whole week the whole internet was kind of on fire trying to get this thing patched," said Mitchell.

Still, in some cases, Mitchell said there were documented cases of websites that DID get exploited.

This is one example of how a small entrance for bad guys can be so dangerous. But these little doorways keep popping up. On Tuesday, an AI company revealed a critical vulnerability in Java known as Java4Shell prompting websites and companies to quickly take actions to patch against it.

As we can see and perhaps even feel, hackers are taking advantage. The most common cyberattack on utilities involves outdated software. Early this month, a cyberattack hit French blood banks, looking to increase temperatures using a similar tactic to the refrigeration hacks, although French authorities caught the attack in time and stopped it.

Richard Horne, the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said that "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long." In 2028, the UK predicts AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

For now, Aaron Mitchell says, exploitation of vulnerabilities isn't taking off as much as it could be, "but every day that goes by, we get that much closer to the edge."

Sponsor Message

Just yesterday, Axios reported President Trump's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his role. He did not want to serve an additional two-year term, leaving an important role to be filled.

Today's Indicator

We got this economics podcast before GTA VI

If you HAVEN'T listened: This is the week of Grand Theft Auto VI. The wildly hyped game has already collected more than $1.5 billion in pre-sales. But the game itself is almost like a cover charge for an entire digital world, and, importantly, economy.

"Take-Two Interactive learned from GTA V that selling a product at retail is great, but better yet, what if you could continue to sell expansions and in-game events and items over a longer term?" said Joost van Dreunen, a professor at the NYU Stern School of Business.

toggle caption i RALF HIRSCHBERGER/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

GTA VI isn't launching its story mode with micro-transactions. That will likely come with the online mode of the game, expected to be released next year. The story mode can hook players into the world, and the online mode can keep them there. THEN you might start wanting to buy a few things. In the current GTA Online, based in the previous game's world, you can buy a digital yacht for $100 real US dollars.

LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE

If you HAVE listened: Overall, Steam is doing just fine, but in 2024, new releases accounted for just 29% of Steam revenue. In 2025, 27%. This year, it's down to 21%, according to the Alinea Insight substack.

To reporter Ricky Mulvey, this means people might not want new games and GTA VI is an exception to the rule.

"What is the purpose of playing a game? Not just the coolest, most advanced graphics," Ricky said. "I want to talk to my friends"

Other reasons back catalogue items are doing well: they're a fraction of the price. Plus, who can keep up with the latest and greatest console?

Sponsor Message

Rest of the Week



Listener Mailbag

Listener Chris Browett sent in a question from Virginia Beach, VA

Question: Longtime fan, and I really enjoyed the episode on the death of the sitcoms. I've been rewatching old shows lately and just finished White Collar. It made me realize how much I miss full length seasons. They give you something to look forward to week after week. Eight episode seasons are over before they even start. The new economics make sense for most shows, but what about the big franchises like Star Wars, where Disney earns money from licensing and merchandise anyway? More episodes would mean more material to sell around, so why not lean into longer seasons? As streaming bills creep toward a regular cable bill, do you think that math changes?

Reporter Ricky Mulvey's Response

Hi Chris! Glad you enjoyed the episode and thanks for writing in. You're kind of describing an economic concept called "marginal utility". Or how much enjoyment do you get from your tenth episode of a binge watch versus the eighth? I imagine that this is the concept that the streaming execs are looking at too.

How much more likely are you to buy a Star Wars shirt after five episodes or ten? Does it matter?

Add into this the incredible cost of some streaming shows. Disney's Andor cost more than $20 million per episode. I think these higher production costs are a key reason why you see shorter seasons too.

And I think that as streaming bills creep toward cable bills the move is to live events. Streamers are looking to give you a reason to watch live and not cancel. You've seen this with Netflix adding the WWE and the Women's World Cup in 2027, Apple adding Formula 1, and Amazon with Thursday Night Football.

Sponsor Message

Cheers,

Ricky

In Our Spare Time

Co-host Adrian Ma read The Hot Young Widows Club

Recently, I read a book that deeply resonated with me called The Hot Young Widows Club.(Okay, actually, I listened to the audiobook. But I've been assured by various totally unbiased friends that listening to audiobooks counts as reading.) This memoir by Nora McInerny, written after she lost, in quick succession, a pregnancy, her husband, and her father, is one of the sharpest articulations of grief that I've ever read (or listened to).

And somehow, amazingly, it is also funny. This book made me cry. And laugh. And very often, cry and laugh at the same time. She manages to vividly capture the soul-wrenching pain and messiness of grief, while telling it to you in a comforting, conversational style, like you're commiserating with a best-friend over bottomless cups of diner coffee. If you've lost a partner, or are wondering how to support someone who has, I think you'll find this book helpful.

World.title: GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war
World.content:
GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war

toggle caption i Finn Gomez/Getty Images

Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who has defended President Trump's war with Iran, said Friday that he opposes tying government funding to an end to the conflict as Congress struggles to avert a shutdown before Christmas.

"We're not going to shut down the war. That is President Trump's power. He's exercising his constitutional authority," Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, told Morning Edition.

Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to keep federal agencies operating, giving Democrats leverage in the Republican-controlled Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to advance. But both parties face divisions. Democrats disagree over whether to use the funding deadline to force an end to the war, while Republicans are weighing bipartisan negotiations against a party-line approach to securing additional military spending.

Sponsor Message

Johnson said Republicans would prefer to negotiate a spending agreement with Democrats rather than use budget reconciliation, a procedure that could allow them to approve defense funding without Democratic support.

"I think we'll give them one more chance," he said, referring to negotiations before the Thanksgiving recess.

Johnson, who previously supported military aid to Ukraine but later opposed additional funding, warned that temporary spending measures would hinder military modernization and weapons procurement. He pointed to the changing nature of warfare in Ukraine as an example.

A shutdown could furlough hundreds of thousands of federal workers or delay their pay just weeks before Christmas. Johnson said he hoped to avoid one but warned that Republicans would need Democratic support.

The war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran has killed thousands of people, threatened U.S. military bases across the region and become a point of contention in the American midterm elections. Asked what he wanted to see happen in Iran, Johnson said he hoped Iranians would rise up against their government and that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.

"I want to see the Ayatollahs on the dustbin of history," he said.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

World.title: Trump says he's working on 'a deal that's fair' with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump floated the prospect of reaching a trade deal with Canada soon but said more work needs to be done to get there.

In a news conference at the White House on Friday after returning from his trip to Asia that included a brief meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Trump said he's working on a trade deal with Canada.

"While more work remains to be done with Canada, Prime Minister Carney was very nice," Trump told reporters. "One of the things he wants to do is build a Keystone pipeline for us — and we like that. But, you know, got to do a lot more than that."

Trump repeated several of his most frequently stated grievances, claiming Canada has been ripping off the U.S. for years and insisting his country doesn't need energy, vehicles or lumber from its northern neighbour.

"That being said, we're working on making a deal that's fair," Trump continued.

The U.S. president complained about the trade deficit with Canada, and put the figure at " about $80 billion." That's closer to the actual goods trade deficit (in 2025) of $48 billion US than the $200-billion figure he has often used.

"I said, when it's down to zero, come over and let's start talking," Trump said.

WATCH | Canada seeking interim trade deal with U.S. aimed at reducing key tariffs: Canada pursues tariff relief through interim U.S. trade deal | Duration closed caption 2:45 Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke briefly with U.S. President Donald Trump at the APEC summit in China as Canadian negotiators pursue an interim deal to secure relief from U.S. tariffs by the end of the year.

Trump's comments come as the Carney government seeks an interim agreement with the U.S. aimed at bringing down some of the most onerous tariffs on Canadian exports.

Trump held his news conference with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice-President JD Vance at his side.

In his own remarks, Rubio spoke of "unfairness and imbalance" in commercial relations with Canada.

"The president had an opportunity to visit with the prime minister and move the ball forward on getting to a final agreement that is good for American workers and fair to the United States of America," Rubio said.

World.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.

A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.

But for her family, that doesn't add up.

A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.

The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.

"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."

The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)

With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

Watch the full documentary, "The Invisble Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.

The next morning, they woke violently ill.

Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.

She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.

"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."

They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.

‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

'Things aren't going well'

That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"

Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.

"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"

Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)

The Böcek family

The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.

As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?

Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.

"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."

The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.

The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.

But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.

WATCH | An exterminator explains treatments to kill bedbugs: Safe extermination of bedbugs | Duration 1:26 Istanbul exterminator Birkan Cihan explains the difference between legal and lethal treatments to kill bedbugs.

Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.

"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said

The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.

In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.

Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.

In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)

'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."

We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."

Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)

Women and children

In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.

Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.

'This is not food poisoning'

Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.

She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.

Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)

She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.

"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.

"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."

She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.

"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.

"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."

She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.

"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)

150 bites

We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.

One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.

We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.

The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.

That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?

We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.

We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.

"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.

Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)

He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.

The extermination company is called Wolves.

A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.

Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.

The employee was cautious on the phone.

He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.

"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.

Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.

The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.

We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.

"Of course," she said.

WATCH | Honouring her sister's memory: A life without her | Duration 0:52 Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants her sister, Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, to be remembered.

'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.

While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.

"Those who are gone never come back."

Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.

"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.

"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."

After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

World.title: Despite early start, Canada's flu season may be 'far from peak' as holidays approach
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An early start to Canada's flu season has medical experts bracing for a range of possibilities, from influenza-free holiday gatherings to the risk of a second wave later this winter.

The latest national data shows nearly 15 per cent of flu tests came back positive in the week ending Nov. 14, up from close to 14 per cent of tests the week before. Outbreaks and hospitalizations are also up, Public Health Agency of Canada figures show, with influenza A detected in almost all test samples.

Roughly four in 10 positive tests were among older adults aged 65 and up — one of the groups at the highest risk of serious illness — though the H1N1 strain circulating this year can actually be worse for younger adults and children.

"We're really on a concerning trajectory in terms of both the volume and the speed of [the] rise of the cases right now," said Dr. Lynora Saxinger, an infectious diseases specialist and professor at the University of Alberta.

"And by the numbers, I'm very concerned about how difficult it might get."

WATCH | Why this flu season could be worse for young people: This flu season might be worse for young people | Duration 0:55 This flu season might be hitting younger people harder, and experts are saying everyone should take precautions against it.

Rise in infections putting pressure on hospitals

Influenza appeared relatively early this fall — weeks before the country's past two seasons — with the west coast bearing the brunt of those initial infections. Flu cases began appearing in B.C. by early October, and in Alberta, roughly a quarter of all flu tests were coming back positive in early November.

The ongoing rise in cases is already putting pressure on at-capacity hospitals, said Saxinger, who is based in Edmonton.

"[This week] I was seeing people in an ambulance bay. Many have basically been there for days," she told CBC News.

It's a mixed bag elsewhere in the country, said Dr. Allison McGeer, a Toronto-based infectious diseases specialist with Sinai Health System.

"B.C. is probably close to the peak of the wave by now. The peak in Ontario and Quebec is probably going to be early to mid-December," she said.

"And then, hopefully, that's it."

But she acknowledged that an early end to flu season — before the holidays are fully underway — may be wishful thinking, given the unpredictability of influenza in any given year.

H1N1 strain can impact kids, young adults

Canada-wide, Saxinger said the season is likely "far from peak," with the potential for another surge of flu in the months ahead.

In some years, the virus rises and falls twice in the same season. Though H1N1 is dominant this fall, it's possible another strain could spike later in the winter, leading to a distinct second wave of infections.

"We have had recent years where things have been very strange and we've actually switched strains partway through," said Saxinger. "And it's also very common to have influenza B come up at the end."

WATCH | What to know about Ontario's flu season this year: What you need to know about this year's flu season in Ontario | Duration closed caption 2:51 Want to avoid the flu this season? CBC's Talia Ricci has you covered with what you need to know.

Still time to get flu shot, experts say

The takeaway for Canadians? It's still worth getting a flu shot, even for young and healthy individuals.

Multiple experts agreed the early dominance of H1N1 this year could hit both kids and younger adults harder than usual, as many lack prior exposure to the similar virus strains that circulated decades ago among older generations.

"[B.C. has] seen a lot of emergency room visits, doctor's office visits; it's really gone up for young children, particularly zero to five, and then the young elementary age children," said Dr. Bonnie Henry, B.C.'s provincial health officer. "But we're not seeing it so much in adults yet."

Young adults who skipped the flu shot may have a higher risk of infection this year, Saxinger warned, though overall numbers still show more older adults testing positive.

"We will probably see a higher number of otherwise healthy people getting more severely ill this season," she said.

WATCH | Flu season strikes Quebec early as most people now have to pay for flu shot: Flu season strikes Quebec early — and most people now have to pay for the shot | Duration closed caption 1:50 Health officials are urging Quebecers to book their vaccinations early as influenza activity picks up, but universal coverage has officially come to an end. Here’s who qualifies for free doses and why provincial recommendations changed.

COVID, RSV seasons underway as well

COVID and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are also circulating at varying levels this fall, with the latest federal numbers showing more than six per cent of tests were recently coming back positive for COVID while less than one per cent of tests showed RSV.

After multiple severe RSV seasons in the wake of the COVID pandemic, McGeer said this "quieter than usual" year is giving the country a reprieve from a lesser-known infection that typically sends both the youngest and oldest into hospital.

With B.C.'s respiratory virus season the furthest along, Henry remains hopeful it won't be nearly as severe as other recent years given the relative lack of RSV cases. "We're happy that we're not having influenza and RSV at the same time," she added, "because that's where you really see the impact on … children's hospitals."

McGeer also stressed that highly effective vaccines and monoclonal antibody shots are available to protect against RSV — for infants, children, pregnant individuals and older adults — on top of the shots meant to ward off COVID and flu.

"This is going to be an 'everybody should take precautions' flu season," Saxinger said.

World.title: Supreme Court ruling for Quebec's secularism law coming on Nov. 27
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Supreme Court of Canada will issue its long-awaited ruling on Quebec's secularism law, known as Bill 21, on Nov. 27.

In a statement issued on Friday, Canada's top court said the decision will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET.

The law, which prohibits civil servants such as teachers and police officers from wearing religious symbols while on the job, was adopted in 2019 by the Coalition Avenir Québec government (CAQ).

The law quickly faced a constitutional challenge, with civil liberties groups arguing that the legislation discriminates against Muslim women who wear head coverings.

In April 2021, a Quebec Superior Court judge rendered a decision that described Bill 21 as a law that violates the basic rights of religious minorities in Quebec — but that those violations are permissible because of the Constitution's notwithstanding clause.

The notwithstanding clause allows governments, including provincial governments like Quebec, to temporarily shield laws from court challenges over fundamental rights violations.

The ruling by Justice Marc-André Blanchard also declared that the most contentious parts of the law — the religious symbols ban for many government employees — could not be applied to English schools.

The CAQ government at the time appealed that decision, stating that such an exemption would divide the province along linguistic lines and create two categories of Quebecers.

More to come.

World.title: Nasdaq wipes out 2026 gains, S&P 500 falls into correction territory
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The technology stock-heavy Nasdaq composite index has erased its gains for 2026, as artificial intelligence shares led a decline on Friday. The S&P 500, the benchmark U.S. stock index, also slipped into correction territory.

The Nasdaq fell below 23,241.99 points, eliminating a blistering run-up this year fuelled by investor enthusiasm for AI, and the companies seen to propel the technology's growth.

The Nasdaq is down 3.34 per cent, as of 1:19 p.m. ET.

Stocks also slipped lower on the larger U.S. indices. The S&P 500 index shed 2.07 per cent, entering correction territory, defined as a fall of 10 per cent or more from its most recent peak.

The Dow Jones industrial average, composed of 30 large blue-chip stocks, fell about 0.71 per cent on Friday. Nvidia, Goldman Sachs and heavy equipment-maker Caterpillar led the declines, while United Health, Walmart and IBM booked the biggest gains.

In Toronto, the S&P/TSX composite index is down 2.07 per cent. Canada's benchmark index has slipped about nine per cent since hitting an all-time high in August.

On Friday, information technology and materials stocks led the TSX lower. BCE, Telus and Quebecor were among the most influential stocks making gains, as investors digest news about proposed consolidation deals in Canada's telecom sector.

On the Nasdaq, Anthropic slipped over 14 per cent in a reversal from its big market debut on Thursday. The company behind the popular Claude chatbot was pitched to investors as a pure play on the AI boom.

Unlike the other AI "hyperscalers" on the market — such as Google and Meta — Anthropic's business is solely focused on building and selling AI models.

The company's Nasdaq-listed stock ended its first trading day on Thursday with a 17 per cent gain.

AI stocks have been losing ground recently, due in part to worries among investors that their market values and massive spending are unjustified.

Nvidia is among the heaviest weights on the market on Friday, falling about six per cent. Shares of Intel and SpaceX are also among the most influential decliners.

WATCH | Second day drop for Anthropic: Anthropic stock tumbles after first day on market | Duration closed caption 4:01 Anthropic made its public debut on Thursday, with a record-breaking IPO. While stock prices climbed as high as $111 US, the stock price fell to between $87 US to $89 US on Friday morning.

Tech stock analyst Dan Ives says the fear and anxiety behind today's tech stock sell-off is akin to levels seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and U.S. President Donald Trump's so-called "Liberation Day" tariff announcement last year.

Ives points to a "perfect storm" of factors roiling the tech trade. These include the leadership crisis at Nvidia , U.S. regulators putting tighter controls on China's access to AI chips and fears of a data centre slowdown in the U.S. driven by the "blue wave" of Democrat victories in the recent midterm elections.

"This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting this fourth Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years … and that is the wrong move in our view," he wrote in a note to clients on Friday.

World.title: Alberta separatist leaders pursue different paths back into UCP fold
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Moving on is hard to do.

A month after Albertans voted decisively to reject the prospect of a future vote on independence, many in the governing United Conservative Party are struggling with how to heal the breach blazed by the separatist sentiment that, polling says, was particularly entrenched in their ranks.

The party line is now one of unity. And the party has moved to enforce that, requiring both aspiring board members and leaders of local riding associations to sign a pledge to abide by the results of the referendum, prompting further questions about how unity is actually achieved, and how much disagreement must be embraced, tolerated or stamped out in pursuit of it.

The challenge is personified by the former separatist leaders themselves, several of whom spent months spreading the gospel of an independent Alberta before those dreams were crushed — who now must grapple with their own futures within Alberta’s governing party.

It’s a dilemma that has left Danielle Smith wobbling on a highwire as she tries to keep her party together while the independence movement, never that cohesive to begin with, has begun to turn on itself.

“As a sovereignty-minded individual, I have choices to make,” Chris Scott, founder of a group called Let’s Talk Alberta, told CBC News. He spent months crisscrossing the province in a branded motorhome but, after not getting the result he wanted in October, is now running for a seat on the party’s provincial board.

“Am I going to flog the dead horse for the rest of my life, or am I going to find alignments with those that have disagreed with me?” said Scott.

Chris Scott of the pro-independence group Let's Talk Alberta is seeking a spot on the UCP's provincial board. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Speaking on stage as part of a board candidate forum in Calgary Wednesday night, Scott told the audience that despite his disappointment, he didn’t see a future in trying to rip the party apart or take down the premier. There are plenty of people on both sides who want to strengthen Alberta sovereignty, he added.

“If we can set our emotions aside and start treating each other as what we’re supposed to be, which is one group instead of enemies, we really only can go up from here,” he said.

Two days after the referendum, Smith released a video in which she drew a line in the sand. Hers was not an independence party, and those few who “remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement” were invited to go elsewhere, she said.

The first time he watched the video, he was angry, Scott says. He saw it as the party leader telling those who believed in independence to find a different party. But once he set emotion aside, he watched it again and changed his mind. He concluded that Smith only meant that all members were welcome — but shouldn’t try to seek leadership positions and turn the UCP into a separatist party.

His bid for a board seat is a continuation of what he’s been doing all along, he says, in that he will continue to push for a strong and sovereign Alberta. But he plans to do it in a way that puts independence on ice, at least for now.

In his view, that puts him in compliance with Smith’s directive.

When he received the form sent to board candidates, asking them to respect the referendum, he signed it. He suggests that his fellow travellers in the independence movement who can’t move on aren’t able to see past their own anger.

“Any reasonable person would accept and abide by the outcome of the referendum,” he said. “That’s how democracy works.”

But not all of the separatist figureheads share Scott’s convictions.

Mitch Sylvestre maintains that in his neck of the woods, meaning the farmland and oil country around northeastern Alberta, separatism remains a going concern.

The sporting goods store owner, who helped craft the first petition calling for a separatism referendum, argues that the independence-leaning part of the party helped bring Smith to power, and she won’t stay there without them.

Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, spoke to reporters after the remain side was projected to win in the Alberta referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Unlike Scott, Sylvestre already has a firm perch in the United Conservative Party, as president of the Bonnyville-Cold Lake riding association. He’s one of the presidents who have refused to sign a pledge to respect the results of the referendum and signed his name to public letters calling on the requirement to be dropped.

He intends to stay with the party and continue what he sees as his ongoing educational campaign, but said he couldn’t answer a question about whether that meant pushing for independence.

But he took a less positive view about the calls for unity expressed at the recent meeting of UCP members.

“We’re not the problem,” he told the CBC News, speaking the morning after the Calgary event.

“I’ve been saying forever that we’re going to work within the UCP, but they’re trying to kick us out,” he added. “The unity has to come from their side.”

It would be impossible for Smith to remove all the separatists from the party, given how many there are, says Duane Bratt, a political scientist at Mount Royal University. In the weeks before the vote, polling suggested that slightly more than half of party voters favoured separation.

Instead Smith has appeared to implement a “don’t ask, don’t tell,” policy, Bratt said, citing a phrase first applied to Smith by political blogger David Climenhaga . There are longstanding rumblings about the convictions of some of her MLAs, but she has turned a blind eye to those who haven’t spoken publicly, he said.

But if the challenge for the party is unity, Bratt said, the general public — who showed up to the polls to firmly reject the idea of independence — is going to want to know that their governing party is not a separatist one.

To do that, Smith will likely have to remove a few high profile separatists, Bratt argues. The party has already kicked out Jeff Rath , another high profile separatist whose membership was recently revoked after publicly clashing with Smith over her leadership.

Jeff Rath, the lawyer for the Stay Free Alberta petitioners, says the premier can't ignore Alberta separation anymore. (Emily Fitzpatrick/CBC)

In an email, the party’s executive director told Rath his “words and actions” made clear that he did not support Smith or the party. Rath told CBC News that the party declined to tell him which of his social media posts triggered the move and that leaving the party hadn’t hampered his efforts to remove Smith from leadership.

He also attended the recent UCP meeting and said the unity talk had fallen on deaf ears.

“The people that she wants to unify with, she’s basically told it’s her way or the highway,” he said.

The question now, Bratt said, is whether Rath’s ouster will be enough to convince Albertans that the separatists are no longer in control over the party.

“The question, ultimately, is how many bodies have to be tossed,” he said.

Removing Rath may not be sufficient, he said, and it would be far harder for Smith to remove someone like Sylvestre, who already has standing with the party.

“That’s a challenge for her,” he said.

But as far as Sylvestre is concerned, the demands by, and on, the premier aren’t his concern.

“We’ve had three different premiers in the last 12 years,” he says, alluding to the political turmoil that saw Jim Prentice, Jason Kenney and Smith all take turns as head of an Alberta conservative party.

“Leaders can come and go.”

World.title: Nikhil Gupta sentenced to over 19 years in prison for plot to kill U.S.-Canadian activist
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in prison in a federal court in New York on Friday after admitting guilt in a plot to kill dual U.S.-Canadian citizen Gurpatwant Pannun.

U.S. District Judge Victor ​Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence for Nikhil Gupta, 55, at a hearing in Manhattan federal ⁠court.

Gupta earlier this year pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering in the case. He has been jailed in Brooklyn, N.Y., since his June 2024 extradition to the U.S. from the Czech Republic, where he had been arrested a year earlier.

The plea and sentence on Friday come amid a wave of threats and violence in North America targeting Sikh separatists, headlined by the fatal shooting of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., in June 2023. Then-prime minister Justin Trudeau accused agents of the Indian government of involvement in the killing, which the government in New Delhi denied.

Supporters of an indendent Khalistan are shown outside the federal courthouse building in New York City on Friday, ahead of the sentencing of Gupta. (Kris Reyes/CBC)

Nijjar was a prominent official in Sikhs for Justice, an organization that advocates for a sovereign state in India called Khalistan. Pannun has served as counsel for the group.

"This is the accountability for India's authoritarian [Narendra] Modi regime and this is the first step," said Pannun outside the court before proceedings began. "But we're looking for accountability that all those who directed and financed this assassination plot and my friend's murder in Canada, they should be held responsible."

Prosecutors said an Indian foreign intelligence service ​official, Vikash Yadav, recruited Gupta in May 2023 to orchestrate Pannun's assassination. According to court ⁠papers, Yadav arranged through dealings that Gupta brokered to pay $100,000 US to a purported hitman, who was actually an undercover officer ⁠for the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, to assassinate Pannun.

Gupta and Yadav arranged to have $15,000 US in cash delivered to the undercover ⁠officer ⁠as an advance payment for the murder, court ​papers show.

"This case cuts to the very core of American ⁠values," prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court, according to Reuters. "We don't condone the use of violence to silence ⁠voices ⁠in this country, ever."

Addressing the ​court, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by Indian independence leader ​Mahatma Gandhi.

"I'm sorry to ⁠Mr. Pannun. I'm sorry to the communities I hurt. I'm sorry to my own family," Gupta said.

Yadav faces an indictment but is not in U.S. custody.

Even with Gupta convicted, Pannun said this summer he had received warnings from the RCMP and FBI about threats to his life under their "duty to warn" protocols.

Pannun sends message to PM Carney

Pannun, who obtained Canadian citizenship in the early 2000s and has maintained a residence in Ontario, told the Associated Press at the time that he was "unfazed and undaunted" by the attempts to silence him.

India's government has denied being involved in the violent incidents.

India Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to visit Canada on Dec. 11 and 12 and expected to meet with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"Accountability before trade; do not sell the sovereignty of Canada," Pannun said when asked what message he had for Carney.

WATCH | Charges announced in 2023 homicide in Winnipeg suburb: Suspected Bishnoi gangster wanted in 2023 Winnipeg murder | Duration closed caption 2:00 Winnipeg police say Satinderjeet Singh, a suspected Bishnoi gang lieutenant also known as Goldy Brar, is wanted in the 2023 killing of Sukhdool Singh Gill — an alleged member of a rival gang.

Four Indian nationals await trial in B.C. in connection with the Nijjar killing after being arrested in Edmonton and Ontario in the spring of 2024. Federal officials in California charged two men earlier this summer with ordering the killing — Lawrence Bishnoi and Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar.

Neither Bihnoi nor Singh are in U.S. custody.

Singh, who is now on FBI's Ten Most Wanted fugitive list, has also just been linked to a 2023 homicide in Winnipeg, which occurred just three months after Nijjar's slaying.

B.C. Lt.-Gov. Wendy Cocchia is seen at the legislature on Feb. 12, 2026. She will lead a swearing-in ceremony for the province's next premier, Lorne Doerkson, on Friday. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
