World.title: Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension
World.content:
Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension

20th Friday, November 2026 - 14:21 UTC Full article

Guests and the Northlands school pupils' choir at the British ambassador's residence in Buenos Aires, during the reception marking King Charles's birthday.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

“In international relations, as in personal relationships, there can be good days and not-so-good days,” Cairns told some 800 guests from politics, the judiciary, business, diplomacy and culture gathered at the ambassador's residence. “I am the 56th British ambassador to Argentina, and as such I will continue working to strengthen the ties between our two countries. I am convinced we will enjoy more good days than not-so-good days.”

As an example of that strength, the ambassador recalled last year's celebrations of the bicentenary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and announced that next year the 45th anniversary of the “South Atlantic conflict” will be marked “with respect and sensitivity, working together with veterans and the families of the fallen in both countries to promote reconciliation and friendship”. Cairns also highlighted values associated with the monarch, such as diversity, inclusion and care for nature: “Countries are stronger when their societies are diverse and open.”

The celebration, held as a garden party, included the British and Argentine national anthems performed by the pupils' choir of Northlands school, performances by the Orquesta de los Barrios, a programme for young musicians from disadvantaged backgrounds, and a mural by artist Costhanzo featuring British and Argentine icons. The event was sponsored by British and Argentine companies, including Pan American Energy, BP and Standard Chartered.

The reception took place two days after Javier Milei's government rejected Princess Anne's visit to the islands as a “provocation”, and nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rules on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project.

World.title: Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise
World.content:
Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise

20th Friday, November 2026 - 04:27 UTC Full article

A person walks past the Central Bank of Brazil headquarters in Brasília.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

The intervention follows several days of falls on the São Paulo stock exchange and a sharp depreciation of the real, which makes imports more expensive, especially fuel, and puts pressure on inflation. Investors doubt the government's ability to control spending and stabilise public debt, which exceeds 92% of gross domestic product.

The spending containment plan, already approved by the Senate, will be voted on next week in the Chamber of Deputies. The government estimated savings of between 50 billion and 60 billion reais in 2027, between US$8.4 billion and US$10.1 billion, although the figure may change due to amendments made in Congress. One of its pillars caps growth in public spending above inflation at 2% a year, down from the current 2.5%. Part of the market considers the plan insufficient.

The adjustment has drawn criticism from the Brazilian left, particularly from sectors to the left of the Workers' Party, who fear cuts to health and education. Lula said on Thursday that “some comrades” had not understood the proposal and pledged that, as long as he is president, “there will be no reduction in the rights the Brazilian people have won”. He told the market that he too wants fiscal control, but criticised the moves of recent days: “What is really happening is that there are people trying to make money from speculation, from rumours.”

Lula, re-elected on October 25, has not announced who will be his economy minister for the term that begins on January 5, another source of uncertainty. The current minister, Dario Durigan, expressed concern about the pace of the economy in 2027, although he ruled out a recession. According to the Central Bank's latest survey of analysts, published on November 16, growth will slow from 2.3% in 2025 to 1.7% this year and 1% in 2027. The benchmark Selic interest rate stands at 13.75% a year, after the Central Bank halted a cycle of five consecutive cuts in November.

World.title: Colombia to euthanise hippos for the first time: ten animals in four months
World.content:
Colombia to euthanise hippos for the first time: ten animals in four months

20th Friday, November 2026 - 04:24 UTC Full article

A female hippo with her calf in the Magdalena River basin, Colombia.

Colombia's government will for the first time carry out chemical euthanasia on hippopotamuses, an invasive species in the country since drug lord Pablo Escobar brought the first animals to his estate in the 1980s. The Environment Ministry announced on Wednesday that ten animals in Antioquia department, located near populated areas, will be put down over the next four months.

Colombia's government will for the first time carry out chemical euthanasia on hippopotamuses, an invasive species in the country since drug lord Pablo Escobar brought the first animals to his estate in the 1980s. The Environment Ministry announced on Wednesday that ten animals in Antioquia department, located near populated areas, will be put down over the next four months.

The measure is part of the first phase of the national plan for the prevention, control and management of the hippopotamus, which also includes sterilisation, relocation and confinement, along with population monitoring, work with communities and environmental education. The pilot phase has a budget of about 500 million Colombian pesos, and the next would require more than 8 billion, funding that has yet to be confirmed. The ministry is working with experts from South Africa on techniques for capturing hippos in water, and has not ruled out moving animals to a wildlife rescue centre in India.

Among the animals selected is one that appeared in late July in the river used daily by 23 schoolchildren in Puerto Nare, and those seen a week ago in a video crossing a road at night in Puerto Triunfo. At least three people have been injured in attacks in the Magdalena Medio region, one of whom is now in a wheelchair.

“Ethically and environmentally it is the best measure. And it had to be taken sooner or later,” said David Echeverri of Cornare, the regional environmental agency that has managed the species for 15 years and has castrated 58 animals. “What we want is for it to be as soon as possible and painless,” he said. Echeverri stressed that it is a long-term plan: “We will be able to say the problem is over when the sterilised hippos die of old age and the problematic ones are gone. That is years away.”

The decision marks a turnaround for Environment Minister Fabio Arjona, who on taking office had proposed a sanctuary for the species and said that “it is cheaper to keep them than to kill them”.

Some 250 hippos live in Colombia, spread over about 2,000 square kilometres of the basin of the Magdalena River, the country's main waterway. The Humboldt Institute warns that, without control, they could reach 1,000 by 2035. Scientists warn of their impact on native species and water quality. The only previous lethal intervention was in 2009, when an animal known as Pepe was shot.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi hold their first three-way summit, rich in symbolism but short on announcements
World.content:
Trump, Putin and Xi hold their first three-way summit, rich in symbolism but short on announcements

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:38 UTC Full article

Putin, Xi and Trump arrive together for their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen.

US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three powers in Shenzhen on Thursday, an encounter rich in symbolism that ended with a commitment to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks but no concrete measures.

US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three powers in Shenzhen on Thursday, an encounter rich in symbolism that ended with a commitment to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks but no concrete measures.

“We are truly making history,” Trump said during the nearly hour-and-a-half meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lower the risk of those weapons being used,” he added. “Everything possible must be done to prevent a nuclear war,” Xi said, adding that “the seeds sown at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root”. Putin recalled that the three countries were “the victors of World War II” and share “responsibility for maintaining international peace and security”.

According to the declaration issued after the meeting, the three leaders committed to “engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation”, and agreed to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. The text also states that “the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”, upholds respect for the immunity of state officials and calls for reform of the United Nations. The International Criminal Court has an outstanding arrest warrant for Putin.

The New START treaty, which limited the US and Russian nuclear arsenals, expired in February 2026. Trump has proposed replacing it with an agreement that includes China, which in turn demands that Washington and Moscow first reduce their arsenals. “We need more than diplomatic theatre and photo opportunities,” Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, told AP.

The summit marked a new step in Putin's return to the international stage. Trump, who had not met him since their Alaska summit in August 2025, called him a “friend”. “God protect us from friends like that,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk responded on X. European governments and Ukraine had feared the three leaders would discuss the country's future without Kyiv at the table.

Trump and Xi will meet again at the G20 summit on December 14 and 15 at the Trump National Doral resort in Florida. Putin has not decided whether he will attend. “I will think about it. We will see,” he said.

World.title: UK Parliament briefing details London's response to Argentina's offensive against Sea Lion
World.content:
UK Parliament briefing details London's response to Argentina's offensive against Sea Lion

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:35 UTC Full article

Flags of Britain's Overseas Territories fly near the Houses of Parliament in Westminster, London.

The House of Commons Library has published a research briefing setting out the response of Andy Burnham's government to Argentina's legal, economic and diplomatic offensive against the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides whether to order a halt.

The House of Commons Library has published a research briefing setting out the response of Andy Burnham's government to Argentina's legal, economic and diplomatic offensive against the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides whether to order a halt.

The document, prepared by researchers Patrick Butchard, John Curtis and Philip Loft, is not a government statement but an analysis intended to inform lawmakers, Infobae reported. It reviews four fronts of Argentina's offensive this year: the reaffirmation of sovereignty at the UN General Assembly, sanctions against some 60 individuals and companies linked to exploration, the revival of construction at the Ushuaia naval base, and the case before the Hamburg tribunal. “The UK government has said it will contest the legal case and introduce protections for businesses operating” in the islands, it summarises.

Those responses include the business guidance published in September by Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran, which states that the islanders “have the right to develop their natural resources as they see fit”, with the government's “full support” for companies. In October, London announced measures under its Protection of Trading Interests legislation so that British companies “can continue to make commercial decisions in accordance with UK law” despite Argentine sanctions.

The briefing devotes a section to the United States. It recalls that Donald Trump said in August his administration was reviewing its traditional neutrality on sovereignty over the islands, and that Burnham subsequently raised with him “the economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and the US”. Citing Argentine media, it says Washington's concern over possible sanctions on US companies may have led Buenos Aires to slow down its sovereignty defence bill.

That bill suffered a fresh setback on Wednesday: the Chamber of Deputies session called to debate it collapsed for lack of quorum, with 126 deputies present, three short of the 129 needed, after the Provincias Unidas and MID blocs refused to take their seats over objections to the articles on foreign interference and freedom of expression.

Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno defended the legal route the same day. “This arbitration focuses on the exploitation of natural resources while the underlying issue has not been decided,” he told a legal forum in Buenos Aires. “Once a drop of oil is extracted, that drop cannot be recovered.” Quirno said that, whatever the decision on November 28, “the arbitration continues”.

Sea Lion, operated by Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum about 220 kilometres north of the islands, has estimated reserves of 1.7 billion barrels and is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

World.title: Ueno Bank collapse claims Paraguay’s attorney general and the head of Itaipú
World.content:
Ueno Bank collapse claims Paraguay’s attorney general and the head of Itaipú

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:27 UTC Full article

In the case against the businessmen, ten executives of the Vázquez Group, which owned Ueno, are in custody

Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolón resigned on Tuesday in the face of imminent impeachment, and the Paraguayan director of the binational Itaipú dam, Justo Zacarías Irún, was dismissed on Wednesday, in the latest wave of departures triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank. At least a dozen senior officials have left their posts since the bank was taken over on November 3, among them President Santiago Peña, who was removed from office and is in prison.

Rolón submitted his resignation to President Pedro Alliana after the Chamber of Deputies opened impeachment proceedings against him for alleged misconduct in office. He had been criticised for delaying raids and stalling investigations linked to the bank and to Peña. Deputy prosecutor Alba Rocío Cantero has taken over on an interim basis.

Zacarías Irún, dismissed by Alliana along with the Paraguayan members of Itaipú’s board, is accused of depositing US$163.8 million of the entity’s funds in Ueno Bank in breach of internal rules. The dam, shared with Brazil, is one of the Paraguayan state’s largest sources of revenue.

Peña, charged with breach of trust, self-serving administration and now also criminal association, was moved to a barracks on the outskirts of Asunción, to an ordinary room, after it emerged that at the Presidential Escort Regiment he had occupied a luxury room with a gym. Alliana dismissed the unit’s commander, José David Daiub Fatecha. Prosecutors also raided the homes of the former president’s brothers and seized documents on a company set up in Luxembourg in 2024.

The list of departures includes former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, in pre-trial detention; his interim successor, Liana Caballero Krause, who lasted a week in the post and is in custody; the Superintendent of Banks, Holger Insfrán, charged with breach of trust; and Interior Minister Enrique Riera. Opposition lawmakers are also demanding the departure of Comptroller General Camilo Benítez for failing to flag the irregularities.

The string of removals is unsettling the ruling Colorado Party. “Where does this end? And where do we begin a process of institutional reconstruction?” asked the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Raúl Latorre, who called for dialogue with the opposition ahead of the 2028 general election.

In the case against the businessmen, ten executives of the Vázquez Group, which owned Ueno, are in custody, among them chief executive Federico Miguel Vázquez and the bank’s president, Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors have seized 27 vehicles, including several Rolls-Royces and a Lamborghini, three aircraft and a yacht.

World.title: IMF warns global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II
World.content:
IMF warns global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:51 UTC Full article

“The level of global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II. This requires urgent attention,” Georgieva said

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Thursday that global public debt will soon reach 100% of world gross domestic product, the highest level since World War II, and called for “urgent attention” to government finances.

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Thursday that global public debt will soon reach 100% of world gross domestic product, the highest level since World War II, and called for “urgent attention” to government finances.

“The level of global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II. This requires urgent attention,” Georgieva said at the plenary session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The warning comes amid a rebound in global inflation, which the IMF chief attributed both to the energy crisis caused by the war in the Middle East and to rising technology demand linked to the construction of artificial intelligence infrastructure. That rebound, she said, has led to tighter monetary policy through interest rate rises in many countries, making debt more expensive to service.

In the same speech, Georgieva highlighted that 2026 has been the first year in which artificial intelligence has had a tangible impact on global growth, and called on countries to prepare quickly for the changes it will bring.

World.title: IMF’s Georgieva at APEC: countries must “quickly prepare” for artificial intelligence
World.content:
IMF’s Georgieva at APEC: countries must “quickly prepare” for artificial intelligence

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:36 UTC Full article

“We are facing the fastest transformation in the history of humanity,” the Bulgarian economist said

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Thursday urged countries to “quickly prepare” their digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers for the rise of artificial intelligence, speaking at the plenary session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

“We are facing the fastest transformation in the history of humanity,” the Bulgarian economist said. “Countries must quickly prepare their digital infrastructure, their labour markets and their workers for AI, and prevent risks, especially in ensuring financial stability and cybersecurity,” she added.

According to Georgieva, 2026 has been “the first year in which AI has had a tangible impact on global growth”, acting as a counterweight to the effect of the war in the Middle East on energy supplies. “While the energy crisis will eventually dissipate, AI is here to stay. It will be the most significant factor for competitiveness, productivity and growth in the medium term,” she said.

Artificial intelligence is among the priorities of the agenda promoted by China at the summit, alongside the defence of free trade and regional connectivity. The Shenzhen meeting culminates on Thursday with the first three-way encounter between the presidents of China, the United States and Russia.

World.title: Organilleros: Is Mexico City’s centennial profession at risk of disappearing?
World.content:
Unlike his fellow street organ players, Don Miguel Santiago García has not been in this line of work his entire life.

“I’ve been playing the organillo for eight years,” the musician tells me, “and I do it with great pride.”

The organillo, or street organ, arrived in Mexico during the Porfiriato, at the dawn of the 20th century, and was originally designed to play German and Swiss polkas.

Organ owners rented their instruments to musicians, who used them on the streets to earn a few coins — a trade that has remained virtually unchanged for over a century.

Beyond being an integral part of the capital’s sonic and cultural landscape, this craft supports hundreds of families, like Don Miguel’s.

At 65 years old, Don Miguel leaves his home in the Gustavo A. Madero borough, north of Mexico City, at 6:00 a.m., Monday through Friday, arriving in the Historic Center around 7:30 a.m.

He takes public transportation, and after a commute of more than an hour through the capital’s traffic, he emerges from the Pino Suárez Metro station to retrieve his organillo from a local warehouse.

By 9:00 a.m., he’s standing on Isabel La Católica Street, near the Museo del Estanquillo, turning the crank that makes the instrument sing — just as he and his colleagues have done for more than a century.

Despite the long tradition of street organ players in Mexico City, Don Miguel could well be one of the last of his kind in the city.

An inherited musical craft

Don Miguel started playing the organillo to support his daughters’ families.

“They brought me into the business,” he says with a toothless grin, “because they had children of their own, and they simply didn’t have the time anymore.”

Unlike Don Miguel, who inherited the work from his daughters, other organ grinders come from a lineage dedicated exclusively to the trade, which is unique to Mexico City.

Along Isabel La Católica Street, several of his colleagues take turns playing the instrument. “It’s easy money,” he explains.

Organilleros can be identified by their traditional beige uniforms and police-style caps, as well as the 20-kilogram (44-pound) instrument they rest against their bodies.

“The instrument isn’t ours,” Don Miguel says. “The woman who rents it to me charges 100 pesos a day.”

Typically, Mexico City’s street organ players spread out across the surrounding area — most notably along Madero Street, where they have long been a part of the Historic Center’s soundscape.

Today, roughly 700 street organ players work in Mexico City, 337 of whom are affiliated with the Unión de Organilleros del Distrito Federal y de la República Mexicana A.C. The others operate independently.

All of them, however, are subject to a poorly regulated working arrangement that offers few labor protections.

A centennial profession without a fixed salary

Traditionally, Don Miguel says, organilleros do not earn a fixed wage, instead living off what passersby give them throughout the day.

“Some days go well, and some days go poorly.” On a good day, he can bring in as much as 300 or 400 pesos (US $16 to $21) — “especially in December, when there are so many people here in the Historic Center.”

On a bad day, however, Don Miguel says he barely earns “enough to cover the rental cost of the instrument.”

In contrast, pet sitters in the Roma and Condesa neighborhoods can make in a single house visit what an organillero might make in an entire day.

What’s more, if an organillero fails to make enough money, they can’t simply work extra hours, hoping to close to the gap.

“By 5:00 p.m.,” Don Miguel says, “I no longer have permission to continue, because other colleagues are coming in who will be there until 10 p.m.”

Today, street organ players in Mexico City cannot operate without a state permit. To bring some semblance of formality to the industry, the Mexico City government issues a “Non-Salaried Worker Credential” through the Labor and Employment Promotion Ministry (STYFE). This license is granted to artists and individuals who work independently in public spaces, providing a degree of regulation for how they earn their living.

Despite the precarious labor conditions facing the country, these long-standing, traditional professions remain active — and organilleros are resisting disappearance by submitting formal petitions to the Mexico City government.

A new breath of life

Street organ grinders like Don Miguel rarely have contact with the authorities.

They do so through a leader “who handles those administrative matters and organizes us by street,” he says. Generally, these leaders belong to the Union, which works to protect the craft.

For instance, Excélsior notes that through the union, the workers sought greater protection for fine-tuning their instruments, as well as suitable spaces for training and properly maintaining the barrel organs.

It was a necessary battle. Back in 2000, organ grinders were nearly brought to the brink of extinction, largely due to a lack of knowledge and spare parts needed to maintain their instruments.

All of their hard work and advocacy paid off in May, when the city government published a decree recognizing organilleros and their music as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Mexico City.

“The presence of organ grinders in public spaces […] fosters a sense of community and social interaction,” the decree states.

Essentially, this recognition provides the organilleros with greater protection from the state, enabling them to practice their profession safely.

The Mexico City government also organizes an annual Organillero Festival, featuring musicians from Mexico and Chile who perform and compete throughout the Alameda Central.

“Every year, we compete against the Chileans in the Alameda,” Don Miguel says. “Sometimes they beat us, because they bring along people who dance while others play, but generally, we Mexicans are better.”

These government actions aim to secure a place for organ grinders in public life, so that this living tradition may be preserved with dignity.

“Before television or radio existed, this instrument already brought joy to people,” Don Miguel says. “We have to protect it.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Singer Gabito Ballesteros detained after his Querétaro show was halted over banned narco-ballads
World.content:
Mexican singer Gabito Ballesteros was arrested on suspicion of a firearms offense and later released after authorities shut down his concert in Querétaro over lyrics they said glorified crime. Now, the show’s promoter faces a fine of 117,310 pesos (about US $6,150).

The situation at the Querétaro International Livestock Fair involved two separate issues: restrictions on lyrics performed at public events, and a federal firearms investigation after police found a pistol in a vehicle carrying Ballesteros and four companions.

Querétaro state police arrested Ballesteros, 27, at about 4 a.m. Saturday at the fairgrounds after his concert was halted. As the police confronted him, he livestreamed from inside his SUV and sang part of another restricted song, “Cuerno Azulado.”

After he refused to get out of his SUV, police had it towed away with him inside and turned him over to federal prosecutors. He was released later Saturday following some 17 hours in custody, after his defense presented valid weapons permits, the news source Infobae reported.

The Sonora native is a leading performer of corridos tumbados, which blend traditional Mexican storytelling ballads with hip-hop and other urban influences. Some songs celebrate wealth and criminal power; narcocorridos specifically tell stories about drug trafficking and cartel leaders.

Authorities in Querétaro, one of several states that have moved to ban narcocorridos, say lyrics glorifying organized crime normalize violence. El Marqués, the municipality hosting the fair, prohibits permits for concerts featuring songs that promote criminal behavior or glorify organized crime.

The restrictions concern lyrical content, rather than a blanket prohibition on corridos.

Organizers said Ballesteros twice departed from a setlist reviewed and approved by authorities. Municipal officials issued a warning after the first violation, then cut the sound when he performed “AMG” — the hit version of which features Ballesteros, Peso Pluma and Natanael Cano.

Ballesteros said he had not been told that song was prohibited, the newspaper El País reported.

Its lyrics pair luxury-car imagery with threats. A passage quoted by El País translates to: “With Nike sneakers on, I’m a crook, and that’s just how it is. I’m good with numbers; I write everything down in my notebook. I’ve got a blacklist for anyone who fucks with me.”

The newspaper Milenio ran the full lyrics.

Federal prosecutors said officers saw a firearm inside the vehicle and seized a pistol, two magazines and 34 rounds of ammunition.

The concert fine is separate from the firearms investigation and falls on the promoter, not Ballesteros. El Marqués imposed the maximum fine under the municipal provision cited in its ruling, Infobae reported.

Romualdo Moreno, president of the Regional Livestock Union of Querétaro, identified Fernando Hernández as the promoter responsible for artist bookings and logistics. Moreno said the union owns the fairgrounds but handles livestock matters, not artist bookings.

State officials say Ballesteros is not banned from returning, but future performances must comply with local regulations, including approved setlists.

With reports from Milenio, Infobae, El País and Diario de Querétaro

World.title: Sheinbaum leaves Shenzhen after a blitz of bilateral meetings at APEC
World.content:
After what she described as a “very productive and successful” four-day visit to Shenzhen, President Claudia Sheinbaum left China on Thursday evening local time to return to Mexico.

While at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting, she addressed business and political leaders on Thursday, and held bilateral talks with several of her counterparts, including Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump.

She also addressed the APEC CEO Summit, visited a “smart hospital” and met with members of the Mexican community in China at a Mexican restaurant in Shenzhen, the East Asian nation’s tech capital.

Here is an overview of Sheinbaum’s visit to China, her first trip to Asia since becoming president in October 2024.

Sheinbaum’s economy-class flight goes viral in China

To get to Shenzhen, a city in southern China near Hong Kong, Sheinbaum spent more than 20 hours in economy class on a China Southern Airlines flight that stopped off in Tijuana after departing Mexico City early Sunday morning. She has previously traveled on commercial flights to events in Brazil and Canada.

Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that Sheinbaum’s “move to join the masses in economy class on a flight to the APEC summit in Shenzhen has struck a chord with the Chinese internet.”

“A hashtag about her arrival has been seen 10 million times on the Chinese social media platform Weibo,” the news agency wrote.

After arriving in Shenzhen on Monday morning, Sheinbaum hustled to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet with Mexican citizens residing in China.

Afterward, she praised “the extraordinary Mexicans who have decided to live their lives [in China],” adding that “we should find ways for them to stay connected with Mexico.”

Mexico ‘guarantees’ conditions for investment, Sheinbaum tells CEOs

In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum promoted Mexico as an investment destination.

“We have a privileged geographic location, an extensive network of trade agreements, an economy integrated into the world’s major markets, natural resources, expanding infrastructure and, above all, the human talent of a hardworking people,” she told the event.

“Mexico guarantees conditions for investment, certainty and a long-term vision for development,” Sheinbaum said.

Discurso de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum en APEC CEO Summit 2026. Shenzhen, China

Watch this video on YouTube

She also touted Plan México — the federal government’s overarching economic and industrial policy — saying that it has a “humanist vision” in which “the economy is at the service of the people” rather than the other way around.

By speaking at the APEC CEO Summit, Sheinbaum had the opportunity to court investment from major companies in APEC economies and beyond.

The event attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland, according to the Xinhua news agency.

Sheinbaum talks with Xi, Trump, Carney and other leaders in a 3-day blitz of bilateral meetings

Between Tuesday and Thursday, Sheinbaum held bilateral talks with leaders of several APEC countries, including China, Canada, Vietnam and the United States.

In her meeting with President Xi on Tuesday, Sheinbaum declared that her visit to China marked the beginning of “a new era” in Mexico’s relationship with the East Asian country.

She told the Chinese president that her government was “interested in strengthening cooperation in areas related to science and technology, agriculture, clean energy, water resources, health and, of course, culture and tourism.”

For his part, Xi said that China and Mexico “should first continue to treat each other with sincerity, deepen political mutual trust” and “keep growing bilateral relations in the right direction,” according to a statement issued by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

There was no indication that trade tensions related to Mexico’s imposition of new and higher tariffs on imports from China were discussed in the meeting between the Mexican and Chinese leaders.

Sheinbaum also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday, with both leaders expressing support for the renewal of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). The Trump administration announced in July that it had decided not to renew the USMCA “in its current form” through 2042, creating uncertainty over North American trade even though the three-way free trade pact remains in effect.

Sheinbaum has stressed that the agreement can be renewed through 2042 “at any time,” and trade negotiations between both Mexico and the United States and the U.S. and Canada appear to be making progress.

After her meeting with Trump on Wednesday, Sheinbaum said that Mexico-U.S. trade negotiations are “very far along,” but didn’t say when a bilateral deal might be reached.

According to a statement from Carney’s office, the Canadian prime minister and Trump, in their meeting in Shenzhen, “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.”

Bilateral trade deals between Mexico and the U.S. and the U.S. and Canada would likely make the U.S. government more willing to back an extension of the USMCA to 2042.

Regarding the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship, Trump is particularly concerned about the United States’ large trade deficit with its southern neighbor, while the Mexican government is pushing for a reduction of U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum also held a bilateral meeting with Vietnamese President Tô Lâm, during which she expressed Mexico’s interest in “deepening ties between both nations.”

On Thursday, she met with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. In addition, she held talks with Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, and reportedly had a brief exchange with Chilean President José Antonio Kast.

‘We are living at a decisive moment for humanity,’ Sheinbaum tells APEC Leaders’ Meeting

During a four-minute address at the APEC Leaders’ Meeting on Thursday, Sheinbaum declared that “we are living at a decisive moment for humanity.”

“Scientific and technological advances, [including] artificial intelligence, are opening up enormous possibilities, yet we continue to face profound inequalities,” she said.

Les comparto mi discurso en la Reunión de Líderes Económicos APEC China 2026. https://t.co/oLbaJv9qDT — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) November 19, 2026

“Faced with this reality, it is worth asking ourselves: What kind of world do we want to build, and what kind of relationships do we want to establish between our economies? In Mexico, we believe that development should not be measured solely by economic growth, market size or technological leadership,” Sheinbaum said.

“Even in the age of artificial intelligence, it must be measured above all by people’s lives: by whether every woman and every man can live with dignity, and whether families have housing, food, employment and education. This is the vision that has guided us in Mexico in recent years,” she said before highlighting that over 17 million people in Mexico have been lifted out of poverty between 2018 and 2026, according to World Bank data.

“That should be the purpose of our economies,” Sheinbaum said.

‘A very productive and very successful tour for Mexico’

At a press conference on Thursday before embarking on the long return journey to Mexico, Sheinbaum said that her “tour” of Shenzhen was “very productive and very successful for Mexico.”

She highlighted that Mexico signed memorandums of understanding with China in areas including the environment, science and renewable energy and reiterated that her meeting with Trump was “very good.”

“We have made significant progress on several issues we have been working on regarding what … [U.S. authorities] call ‘non-tariff barriers’ — virtually all of which have been addressed — as well as on our interest in reducing [U.S.] tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminum, and their derivatives,” Sheinbaum said.

She reaffirmed her belief that the commencement of a “new era” in the Mexico-China relationship will not affect ties between Mexico City and Washington.

“As you know, we have a trade agreement with the United States [and Canada]. The economies of Mexico and the United States are highly integrated,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that Mexico wants “greater cooperation” with China, but stressed that a free trade agreement with the East Asian export powerhouse is not on the horizon.

“At the moment, we have no plans for a free trade agreement with China,” Sheinbaum said before emphasizing the importance of trade between Mexico and the United States, which are each other’s largest trade partners.

The president said that she and the officials who accompanied her to Shenzhen, including her economy, foreign affairs, environment, energy and tourism ministers, are leaving China “very happy” and “very satisfied.”

“It has been a great experience,” Sheinbaum said.

“Representing the people of Mexico is a privilege. And I believe everyone recognizes the moment Mexico is going through right now. It has been an extremely successful tour, both in terms of our relationship with China and with all the other countries,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she didn’t yet know whether she would attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in Vietnam in 2027. Mexico will host the annual event in 2028 at a location yet to be announced.

Sheinbaum is scheduled to arrive in Mexico City on China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 late Thursday night Mexican Central Time, before leading an event in the capital on Friday to mark the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution.

World.title: Congress approves Animal Welfare Law, spelling out pet owners’ legal responsibilities
World.content:
Congress has approved a new General Law on Animal Welfare, Care and Protection, establishing new obligations to ensure the care and protection of pets in Mexico.

The new law recognizes animals as sentient beings and subjects of care, and establishes that abandonment, mistreatment and cruelty may lead to penalties and the requirement to make amends for the harm caused.

The legislation also includes amendments to five other laws related to animal health, environmental protection, wildlife, civil protection and film production.

What are the new obligations and sanctions?

According to the bill, pet owners must provide their animals with suitable food and constant access to drinking water. Owners must also keep their pets in a clean and safe environment, protected from harsh weather.

The bill also regulates the sale of animals, which can only take place in authorized shops — not public markets or online platforms like Facebook. Sales must meet the criteria for traceability and include a mandatory veterinary inspection.

Failure to meet the new legal obligations may result in fines, administrative detention of up to 36 hours, business closures and revocation of permits, among other penalties.

What is considered animal abuse under the new law?

The law defines acts of mistreatment or cruelty as behaviors that may lead to death with prolonged suffering; killing healthy animals without a legal justification; administering harmful substances such as alcohol or drugs and performing mutilations for aesthetic purposes, such as ear and tail docking.

Other prohibited acts include tethering animals in a way that could cause them injury or strangulation; denying them access to food, water or rest; and using them as targets for attacks during the training of other animals for shows, sporting activities or security work.

Expanding on last year’s dolphin show ban, the bill also prohibits the use of wild animals in circuses, dog fighting, and the use of animals in demonstrations or television contests. It also prohibits using animals for political or commercial advertising, school festivities, or as contest prizes.

Finally, the law says that euthanasia may only be justified in cases of injury, serious or incurable illness, suffering, or other conditions that compromise the animal’s well-being.

The bill has been forwarded to the presidential office (Presidencia) for publication in Mexico’s Official Gazette (DOF) and immediate entry into force.

With reports from Grupo Animal and El Financiero

World.title: Mexican security forces dismantle 3 drug labs in Sinaloa and Michoacán
World.content:
Federal authorities dismantled three narco labs, seizing drugs and chemicals worth an estimated US $74.6 million in two separate joint operations carried out earlier this month.

In a Nov. 17 press release, the Security Cabinet said that intelligence work allowed Navy personnel — in coordination with the Security Ministry, the Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and state police officials — to identify and locate clandestine laboratories in the states of Sinaloa and Michoacán.

En #Sinaloa y #Michoacán, autoridades federales localizan e inhabilitan tres laboratorios para la elaboración de metanfetamina. https://t.co/HYVXaSot2u https://t.co/WYilOHxC0y — Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana (@SSPCMexico) November 17, 2026

In total, authorities seized 2.4 metric tonnes and 1,000 liters of methamphetamine, 11,630 liters of chemical precursors and 2,210 kilos of dual-use substances. No arrests were reported.

“With these actions, the institutions of the Security Cabinet weaken the capacity of criminal organizations to produce synthetic drugs by disabling facilities, chemical precursors and equipment used for their production,” the press release said.

The first operation took place in Sinaloa near the town of Tanques, in the coastal municipality of Elota, halfway between Culiacán and Mazatlán.

There, authorities found a clandestine laboratory with approximately 1,000 liters and 800 kilos of methamphetamine, 800 liters of chemical precursors, 210 kilos of dual-use substances, as well as various materials used for the production of synthetic drugs.

In a second operation in the remote village of Zirúcuaro, Michoacán, about 145 kilometers south of the state capital Morelia, two clandestine laboratories were located.

Marines seized approximately 1,600 kilos of methamphetamine, 10,830 liters of chemical precursors and nearly 2,000 kilos of dual-use substances. They also seized tanks, makeshift reactors, improvised equipment and material used for the production of synthetic drugs, as well as two vehicles.

All materials from the three laboratories were seized and turned over to the appropriate authorities, while the hardware and machinery used to manufacture synthetic drugs found at the three locations were destroyed.

These operations followed an action carried out on Nov. 6 in the municipality of Atempan, Puebla, where Navy personnel, in coordination with federal, state, and municipal authorities, dismantled another clandestine laboratory and arrested two men.

The Security Cabinet said that federal authorities have dismantled more than 2,800 clandestine labs and methamphetamine production and storage sites since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office on Oct. 1, 2024.

With reports from Milenio, El Financiero and Zeta

World.title: Misifú, the crime-fighting cat, thwarts a would-be robber in Puebla
World.content:
Streaky the Supercat now has a crime-fighting colleague in Puebla after a night-time hold-up was foiled by a heroic kitty earlier this month.

The feisty feline protected his home turf valiantly, forcing the aspiring attacker to retreat from the premises, in a manner that would have made Captain Americat proud.

The attempted robbery took place on the evening of Saturday, Nov. 7, at a family grocery store in the San Ramón neighborhood in the southern outskirts of Puebla city.

🐱🐾 ¡El michi se puso la capa de héroe! Un gatito fue parte de la defensa de una tienda durante un intento de asalto en una tienda en la primera sección de San Ramón, ubicada en la calle Bugambilias, #Puebla. Las dueñas se enfrentaron al ladrón el pasado 7 de noviembre y ahora el sujeto es buscado por las autoridades. 🚨 #Noticias #Entérate #Viral #TráficoPuebla — TraficoPuebla (@Trafico_Puebla) November 18, 2026

A man wearing a black hoodie sweatshirt and a baseball cap entered the establishment and asked the shop assistant, Lidia, for some information about an over-the-counter medication.

Shortly thereafter, he returned wearing a mask, the hood pulled up over his head, and, while menacing the attendant, threatened to use a weapon he claimed to have concealed in a backpack unless they opened the cash register.

As he approached Lidia, her daughter came rushing out from behind the counter with a weapon of her own — her kitten Misifú.

The young woman held the cat by the back of its neck and thrust it toward the thief’s face while he had yet to brandish the unidentified weapon. Misifú lashed out, its claws extended and began hissing and scratching the would-be thief on his raised hands, causing him to back away and eventually retreat from the store.

The owner of the store then emerged from behind the counter and followed the suspect out the door, after which the wannabe crook can be seen walking down the sidewalk in the video from the security cameras that captured the entire cat-astrophic incident.

Thus far, there has been no official report on the identity of the alleged purr-petrator and police are still searching for the suspect. However, since the video has been circulated widely on social media his cronies are no doubt mocking him mercilessly for being hiss-terically thwarted by a 10-pound ball of fur.

Following the incident, the victims requested increased police presence in the area to prevent further crimes that could endanger business owners and residents.

With reports from TV Azteca, Milenio and MegaNoticia

World.title: MND Local CDMX: From folklórico and Santa runs to little devils, Christmas is here
World.content:
From Christmas pageantry at Chapultepec Castle to mischievous devils in Coyoacán and hundreds of Santas racing through Santa Fe, Mexico City has plenty of festive ways to celebrate the holiday season. Whether you’re looking for traditional Mexican posadas, folkloric performances, family-friendly theater or a chance to don a Santa suit and hit the pavement, here are some seasonal events worth adding to your December calendar.

Oh, and don’t forget about the medieval Christmas fair we shared a couple of weeks ago.

Okay … Let’s get into it.

Ballet Folklórico brings Mexican Christmas traditions to Chapultepec Castle

Mexico City’s historic Chapultepec Castle will once again provide the backdrop for “Navidades en México,” a unique Christmas-themed performance by the Ballet Folklórico de México de Amalia Hernández, with seven shows scheduled in December.

The production celebrates Mexico’s Christmas traditions through folkloric dance, music and theatrical performances, exploring the blend of Indigenous and Spanish influences that shaped the country’s holiday celebrations.

According to the organizers, the show is divided into three acts. The first recreates the Annunciation and a live Nativity scene, complete with farm animals brought in especially for the performance. The second celebrates the gifts brought by the Three Wise Men through regional dances inspired by traditions from Oaxaca, Yucatán, Chihuahua and Tamaulipas, as well as Tlaxcala, Michoacán and Veracruz. The final act recreates a traditional Mexican posada, featuring folkloric dances and Christmas carols performed by a choir of more than 50 people.

The event takes place outdoors, so organizers recommend dressing warmly and arriving at least 45 minutes before the show. General admission seating is available, and late arrivals will not be permitted once the performance begins.

The production is recommended for children aged 6 and older. Chapultepec Castle, for those who don’t know, sits on top of a hill. As such, free transportation vans will be available for visitors with disabilities and older adults, while other attendees can use a paid shuttle service to reach the castle.

Dates : Dec. 17, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27 and 30. Every show begins at 7 p.m.

Location: Av. Heroico Colegio Militar 172, Bosque de Chapultepec I Secc, Miguel Hidalgo, 11580 Ciudad de México

Cost: 1,180-1,708 pesos

Tickets and additional information are available through Ticketmaster Mexico. Meanwhile, if you can’t make the show but want to see a folkloric ballet performance, check out Ballet Folklórico de México de Amalia Hernández on Instagram.

Mischievous devils and posada traditions take over Coyoacán

A traditional Mexican Christmas pastorela returns to Coyoacán for its 37th year, combining live theater, music, fireworks and an interactive celebration of the country’s holiday traditions.

“Diablos Revolucionarios: Pastorela Tradicional de Coyoacán” will run from Dec. 18–27 at the Casa de Cultura Jesús Reyes Heroles in the southern Mexico City borough. Written by Luz María Meza and directed by Jorge Sandoval, the production features a cast of more than 20 performers.

For nearly four decades, the family-friendly performance has chronicled the journey of several shepherds as they make their way to witness the birth of Jesus. There’s just one problem: A group of mischievous devils continuously try to derail their plans.

The production combines Mexican humor with live music and fireworks, culminating in a Nativity scene accompanied by performances from folkloric group D’Santos.

But the experience extends beyond the stage. Following the performance, visitors can walk through the cultural center’s gardens alongside a procession of pilgrims, singing traditional posada songs and taking part in a recreation of the customary request for lodging. The evening also includes piñata raffles and a snack of tamales and atole.

Admission includes a candle, a welcome serving of ponche and post-performance refreshments.

Unfortunately, we can’t tell you how much tickets cost, as they don’t go on sale until Nov. 20, at which point they can be purchased via Boletia or the venue’s box office.

Dates: Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays from Dec. 18-27, with two performances beginning at 6 p.m. and 8 p.m.

Location: Av. Francisco Sosa 202, Santa Catarina, Coyoacán, 04010 Ciudad de México

Tickets go on sale Nov. 20. In the meantime, though, you can learn more about the event at Cartelera de Teatro.

The Santa Run brings a sea of Santas to Mexico City’s Parque La Mexicana

Hundreds of Santa Clauses are expected to take over Mexico City’s Parque La Mexicana on Dec. 13 for The Santa Run, an annual Christmas-themed sporting event that combines running, family activities and holiday festivities.

The 2026 edition will offer three distances: a 10-kilometer race, a 5-kilometer race and a 1-kilometer walk. The event is open to participants of all ages, with children, people using wheelchairs and even furry four-legged companions welcome to join the shorter route.

There is one important requirement: participants must wear the event’s official Santa Claus costume throughout the race. The outfit, which comes with registration, includes a jacket, trousers, belt and hat. Special costumes are also available for dogs.

The 5K and 10K races will begin at 7 a.m., while the 1K walk is scheduled to start at 7:15 a.m.

In addition to the outfit, registration includes a commemorative medal, a race number, hydration along the route and access to a post-race Christmas celebration featuring a concert and prize raffle. Participants will also receive breakfast provided by Fisher’s restaurant, while part of the registration proceeds will go toward purchasing gifts for children with cancer.

Date: Sunday, Dec. 13 at 7 a.m.

Location: Av. Luis Barragán 505, Santa Fe, Contadero, Cuajimalpa de Morelos, 05348 Ciudad de México

Cost: 690-950 pesos

Registration is available through the event’s official website, The Santa Run México, or check them out on Instagram for more information.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Just how big is Mexico’s tourism economy?
World.content:
Incredible food. Beautiful beaches. Friendly people. Archeological wonders. Cool cities. Pueblos mágicos. And much, much more.

It’s no wonder that Mexico is one of the world’s most popular tourism destinations.

Mexico welcomed a record-high 47.8 million international tourists in 2025, making it the world’s sixth most-visited country.

With such a high number of international tourists, it’s no surprise that tourism is a major contributor to the Mexican economy. Holidaying Mexicans also inject large amounts of money into the economy.

So, exactly how big is Mexico’s tourism GDP? What contribution does it make to Mexico’s overall GDP? Which states are most and least dependent on tourism?

Find the answers in this “Mexico in Numbers” article!

Mexico’s tourism GDP exceeded 2.7 trillion pesos in 2024

Federal Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez Zamora reported last December that Mexico’s tourism GDP in 2024 was 2.71 trillion pesos, representing a year-over-year increase of 2.5% in real terms.

Based on the Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate on Monday (18.53), that amount is equivalent to US $146.25 billion.

Rodríguez also reported that tourism’s share of Mexico’s overall GDP in 2024 was 8.7%.

Mexico leads OECD in tourism’s share of GDP

Among countries that belong to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Mexico ranks equal first with Iceland for tourism’s share of GDP, according to data published in the report “OECD Tourism Trends and Policies 2026.”

Published in August, the report includes data from either 2023 or 2024 for 33 OECD countries.

In Mexico and Iceland, tourism contributed to 8.7% of GDP.

The only other OECD country where tourism contributed more than 8% of GDP was Portugal.

What are Mexico’s most and least tourism-dependent states?

According to federal Tourism Ministry (Sectur) data, the Caribbean coast state of Quintana Roo — home to tourism destinations such as Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Cozumel — is easily Mexico’s most tourism-dependent state.

Data published by Sectur in a 2024 report shows that tourism-related activities generated 49.2% of Quintana Roo’s GDP in 2022.

Baja California Sur and Yucatán had the next-highest shares, with tourism accounting for 17.3% and 16.1% of their GDP, respectively. The former state’s tourism destinations include Los Cabos and La Paz, while among the latter’s are Mérida and the ancient Maya city of Chichén Itzá.

Campeche had the smallest tourism share of any state economy in 2022, with tourism accounting for just 2.8% of its GDP. The Gulf coast state’s economy is heavily dependent on offshore oil production, although it does have two UNESCO World Heritage sites: the “Historic Fortified Town of Campeche” and the “Ancient Maya City and Protected Tropical Forests of Calakmul.”

After Campeche, Coahuila and Durango had the smallest tourism shares of state GDP in 2022, at 3% and 3.2%, respectively. The graph below shows data for all of Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Nelson Mandela Bay Coalition Deal Nears
World.content:
The DA holds the most seats in Nelson Mandela Bay but not enough to govern alone, and its provincial leader is aiming for a signed deal by Tuesday.

Andrew Whitfield, the Eastern Cape leader of the Democratic Alliance (DA), said on Friday 20 November 2026 that coalition talks in Nelson Mandela Bay are making “good progress behind closed doors”. The metro surrounds the port city of Gqeberha, formerly Port Elizabeth, and still has no governing majority after the local elections.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), which runs the country’s elections, declared the final results of the November 2026 local elections. The DA won 53 of the 120 council seats in the metro with 44.17% of the vote.

A majority needs 61 seats, so the DA is 8 short and cannot elect a mayor on its own. Published tables give the African National Congress (ANC, which has led South Africa’s national government since 1994) 32 seats, the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF, a left-wing party) 7 and the Patriotic Alliance, a smaller party, 4.

“We have identified parties we’d prefer to work with and we are all finding consensus in our discussions,” Whitfield said on Friday. “With coalition partners we have chosen, we will have a stable partnership for the next five years.”

After the election the DA was reported to be in talks with the Freedom Front Plus (FF Plus, a conservative minority-rights party, 3 seats), ActionSA (a party led by Herman Mashaba, 2 seats) and the United Democratic Movement (UDM, an Eastern Cape party, 3 seats). Whitfield has not confirmed which parties are in a deal, and he said so plainly: “Unfortunately, I cannot tell you which parties we are working with until an agreement has been signed.”

Retief Odendaal is the DA’s mayoral candidate and a former mayor of the metro. It is not clear whether Whitfield or Odendaal would become mayor if the DA bloc takes control.

The ANC won 32 of the 120 seats, the second-largest bloc on the council. Whitfield says the DA’s own talks are already at an advanced stage.

The metro’s first council sitting, planned for this week, was postponed to allow talks to conclude. The date now in view is Tuesday 24 November 2026, the day Whitfield names.

Coalitions here have been fragile before. In November 2021 the ANC’s Eugene Johnson beat the DA’s Nqaba Bhanga by 60 votes to 59 with the help of smaller parties, and Odendaal became DA mayor in a council vote in September 2022.

Nelson Mandela Bay is not alone in this. Cape Town was the only metro where one party won an outright majority, and Johannesburg and Tshwane have no governing majority either.

Whitfield’s target is Tuesday 24 November 2026, the day he hopes for “a great birthday”. Readers can follow the other metros in our South Africa coverage.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a platform where people trade real money on outcomes, the market “Next Mayor of Nelson Mandela Bay (Port Elizabeth)?” had US$45,302 traded in total at 2:01 p.m. ET on Friday 20 November 2026. Traders priced Retief Odendaal at 89%, another candidate, Andile Lungisa at about 6%, and every other name below 4%.

These prices are bets, not polls. The market cannot say whether any coalition has the 61 seats needed to elect a mayor.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the DA need coalition partners?

It won the most seats but not a majority of the council. Partners would close that gap and let it govern with a stable majority.

Who could run the metro if the DA talks fail?

The ANC has 32 seats and would need several smaller parties to reach 61. No party has published a signed agreement.

When will the new council meet?

The first sitting was postponed from this week, and the date now in view is Tuesday 24 November 2026. The delay gives the parties time to finish their talks.

World.title: Senegal Presidency Spokesman on Article 52
World.content:
Senegal's Constitution lets the president dissolve the National Assembly, but bars it early in a legislature and while emergency powers are in use.

Photo: Iolanda Pensa / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Politics: Senegal

Me Abdoulaye Tine (“Me” is short for maître, the title of a Senegalese lawyer), the Presidency’s spokesman, said on Friday 20 November 2026 that President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has “other possibilities… notably Article 52”. He spoke on a Dakar radio morning show, the day after Faye put the revised budget into force by decree.

A report of the interview says Tine raised dissolving the National Assembly as an option, but his quoted sentence does not use the word. On our reading of the Constitution, Article 52 is an emergency clause that bars dissolution while it is in use, and the dissolution clause is Article 87.

When. Dissolution is barred until around 2 December 2026; we found no announcement of one.

The dispute began on Friday 22 May 2026, when Faye ended Ousmane Sonko’s term as prime minister. Sonko, who leads Pastef (African Patriots of Senegal for Work, Ethics and Fraternity), the party with the Assembly majority, then became president of the Assembly.

The Assembly rejected the revised 2026 budget, a mid-year correction known as the “loi de finances rectificative”, on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Faye answered on Thursday 19 November 2026 with a decree forcing the budget into force.

The National Assembly building in Dakar (Photo: Photowalk, Lamine Niang, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

Article 68 of the Constitution gives the Assembly “soixante jours au plus”, sixty days at most, to vote finance bills. If a bill is not definitively voted in that time, it “est mis en vigueur par décret”, meaning it is put into force by decree.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Kabila's armed group seizes three South Kivu towns” Get the brief

Tine said on 20 November that Faye has more options than the decree route. His sentence did not say which of them he would choose.

Article 52 covers a “grave and immediate” threat to the state that interrupts the regular working of public powers. The president may then take any measure to restore it after addressing the Nation, but cannot revise the Constitution, and the Assembly “se réunit de plein droit”, meaning it meets by right.

Legislative measures taken under Article 52 must go to the Assembly for ratification or they lapse. The article also says the Assembly “ne peut être dissoute pendant l’exercice des pouvoirs exceptionnels”, meaning it cannot be dissolved while those powers are in use.

Article 87 is the dissolution clause: the president may dissolve the Assembly by decree after hearing the prime minister and the Assembly’s president. It adds that dissolution cannot happen during the first two years of a legislature.

The current legislature opened on Monday 2 December 2024, so that bar ends around 2 December 2026. A dissolution decree would then have to set the election between 60 and 90 days after its publication, and deputies keep their mandates until the new Assembly’s election is proclaimed.

The split with Faye’s former party is open: on Tuesday 17 November 2026 Pastef’s national council announced that Faye and 31 others had automatically lost party membership. Pastef won 130 of the 165 Assembly seats in the November 2024 election, and the Assembly refused the first part of the 2027 budget on 18 November.

The fight matters abroad because the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reached a staff-level agreement on 1 September 2026, a preliminary deal for a US$2.2 billion, 36-month programme that still needs approval from its Executive Board. IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said on 12 November 2026 that a completed budget framework is one of three conditions, alongside corrective steps on misreported debt and financing assurances.

We found no announcement of a dissolution as of Friday 20 November 2026, and the Presidency has not announced one. The next dated marker is around 2 December 2026, when the two-year bar in Article 87 falls away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can President Faye dissolve the National Assembly now?

Not on the text of Article 87, which bars dissolution during the first two years of a legislature. We found no announcement of one.

Does Article 52 allow dissolution?

No, its own text says the Assembly cannot be dissolved while exceptional powers are in use. On our reading it is a clause for grave threats to the state, not a route to early elections.

Why does the budget fight matter outside Senegal?

A completed budget framework is one of three conditions for the IMF board to approve the loan programme. The IMF has named no deadline.

Sources Sources: Constitution of Senegal (2001, as amended), Articles 52, 68 and 87; Me Abdoulaye Tine, Presidency spokesman, radio interview of 20 November 2026; presidential decree of 19 November 2026; Pastef national council, announcement of 17 November 2026; International Monetary Fund, staff-level agreement of 1 September 2026 and spokesperson briefing of 12 November 2026.

World.title: Senegal Spent US$7.3 Billion in Nine Months
World.content:
For investors in Senegalese debt, the nine-month figures show revenue at 63.8% of its yearly target. Spending has used 60.8% of credits.

File photo. The Dakar coastline seen from the air, Senegal, December 2010. Photo: Jeff Attaway, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Economy: Senegal

Senegal’s state spent FCFA (CFA franc) 4,370.7 billion (US$7.3 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, according to the Quarterly Budget Execution Report published on Friday 13 November 2026 by the Ministry of Economy, Finance and Planning. That is 60.8% of the spending credits, the limits opened for the year, so 39.2% was still unspent on 30 September.

The numbers arrive while the budget itself is in dispute. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye put a revised 2026 budget into force by decree on Thursday 19 November 2026, 16 days after the National Assembly, Senegal’s parliament, voted it down.

Key Facts Who. Senegal’s Finance Ministry under minister Cheikh Diba, which runs the state budget.

What. FCFA 4,370.7 billion spent, US$7.3 billion, or 60.8% of yearly credits.

Where. Senegal’s general budget, with a deficit of 2.5% of GDP (economic output) so far.

The state took in FCFA 3,785.2 billion (US$6.3 billion) over the nine months, or 63.8% of its annual target of FCFA 5,932.2 billion (US$9.9 billion). Domestic revenue rose 16.8% against the end of September 2025, the ministry’s report says.

The gap between FCFA 3,785.2 billion (US$6.3 billion) of revenue and FCFA 4,370.7 billion (US$7.3 billion) of spending is the deficit. It stands at FCFA 585.5 billion (US$980 million), or 2.5% of GDP, which is 47% of the annual target.

That nine-month deficit compares with a full-year deficit of 7.6% of GDP in the revised bill, against 5.4% first planned. The National Assembly, where the ruling Pastef party (African Patriots of Senegal for Work, Ethics and Fraternity) won 130 of 165 seats in November 2024, rejected that bill on Tuesday 3 November 2026.

Stalls around Sandaga market in central Dakar in January 2019 (Photo: Balou46, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons).

The rejected bill put the full-year deficit at FCFA 1,735.2 billion (US$2.9 billion) and energy subsidies at FCFA 790.3 billion (US$1.3 billion), against FCFA 250 billion (US$418 million) in the original plan. President Faye then enforced it through a budget decree, number 2026-2416, on Thursday 19 November 2026.

Amadou Ba, a Pastef lawmaker, tabled the rejection motion in the Assembly. The 2027 budget has met resistance too.

On Wednesday 18 November 2026 the Assembly refused to adopt the first part of the bill. Finance Minister Cheikh Diba’s bill sets a 2027 deficit target of 4.7% of GDP.

On Tuesday 17 November 2026 Pastef’s national council recorded that President Faye had lost his party membership under its statutes. The president and the party that holds the Assembly majority now disagree openly over the budget.

Most of the nine-month money went on running costs. Ordinary spending reached FCFA 3,302.7 billion (US$5.5 billion), or 75.4% of its credits, including wages of FCFA 1,142.5 billion (US$1.9 billion) and current transfers of FCFA 1,049.9 billion (US$1.8 billion).

Interest and debt-service charges took FCFA 874 billion (US$1.5 billion). That is a large fixed cost that the state must pay before any new project.

Capital spending, meaning investment in projects, was far slower at FCFA 1,068 billion (US$1.8 billion), or 38.1% of credits. Of that, FCFA 641.3 billion (US$1.1 billion) came from domestic resources and FCFA 426.7 billion (US$714 million) from external financing.

Tax revenue came to FCFA 3,484.3 billion (US$5.8 billion), short of target by FCFA 127.1 billion (US$213 million). The report attributes the shortfall to the Economic and Social Recovery Plan, known as PRES, the government’s programme for the economy.

The same report puts real economic growth at 6.1% in the second quarter of 2026 and inflation at 1.0% in September. Dakar hosted the Youth Olympic Games, which ended on 13 November 2026.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global lender, agreed with Senegal’s staff on Tuesday 1 September 2026 on a 36-month Extended Credit Facility, a type of IMF loan, worth about US$2.2 billion. Its board has yet to approve it.

IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack said on Thursday 12 November 2026 that the board must see a completed budget framework, corrective measures on misreported debt and financing assurances. The loan therefore waits on the same budget that the president and the Assembly are contesting, and no board date has been set.

No vote date for the 2027 budget bill is confirmed either. Until the Assembly and the president settle the legal status of the 2026 budget, the ministry’s nine-month report is the latest official account of how the state has spent its money.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the nine-month figures tell investors?

They show revenue at 63.8% of its yearly target and spending at 60.8% of its credits. They do not settle whether the full-year deficit lands near the plan or the revised bill.

Why does the budget decree matter for the IMF loan?

The fund wants a completed budget framework before its board votes. A challenge to the decree’s legal footing makes that framework harder to call settled.

What happens next?

The Assembly must keep working on the 2027 budget, and the IMF board must schedule its review. Neither date has been confirmed.

Sources Sources: Quarterly Budget Execution Report to 30 September 2026, Ministry of Economy, Finance and Planning (13 November 2026); IMF press release PR26282 (1 September 2026); IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack (12 November 2026); National Assembly vote on bill no. 40/2026 (3 November 2026); presidential decree no. 2026-2416 (19 November 2026). US$ conversions at US$1 = FCFA 597.7 (RT market rate, 20 November 2026).

World.title: Nigeria Opposition Presses Tinubu on Subsidy
World.content:
A policy announced in 2023 is back in the campaign. The opposition says the president must explain it; a former minister points to the law and the finances.

Another view of the NNPC headquarters towers in Abuja, in an undated photo. The photo does not show the monthly report. Photo: Naziftm / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

POLITICS · NIGERIA

Nigeria’s opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) has accused President Bola Tinubu of putting the World Bank’s advice ahead of Nigerians’ welfare when he ended the petrol subsidy. Bolaji Abdullahi, the party’s national publicity secretary, made the charge in an opinion article published this week.

It tests how voters will judge a reform announced on 29 May 2023, because Nigeria votes for president on 16 January 2027. Nigeria is a major oil producer and a member of OPEC, the oil producers’ group, so what its drivers pay at the pump is watched far beyond its borders.

A policy announced in 2023 is back in the campaign. The opposition says the president must explain it; a former minister points to the law and the finances.

Tinubu announced the end of the petrol subsidy in his inaugural address at Eagle Square, a parade ground in Abuja, on 29 May 2023, saying “The fuel subsidy is gone”. He said the 2023 budget made no provision for subsidy payments, and that the money would be redirected to public spending.

Pump prices rose sharply afterwards. In its June 2022 Nigeria Development Update report, the World Bank had estimated that gasoline subsidies would cost the government about 5 trillion naira (about US$12 billion at the 415 naira to the dollar of 14 June 2022) in forgone revenue that year.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Kabila's armed group seizes three South Kivu towns” Get the brief

On Tuesday 17 November, Babatunde Fashola, a former Lagos governor and former federal minister, defended the removal in a television interview. He said the lender’s position indicated Nigeria would no longer be financed if it kept paying for petrol, and that the Petroleum Industry Act, the 2021 law that overhauled the oil sector, calls for market-based pricing.

Fashola added that Nigeria would struggle to find the crude and the financing to pay for a subsidy. He also said Atiku’s plan would be hard to finance.

Abdullahi answered in an article titled “Who Governs Nigeria, Tinubu or the World Bank?”. “International institutions are entitled to offer recommendations.

They are not elected to govern Nigeria. The President is,” he wrote.

Eagle Square in Abuja, the Nigerian capital, where Tinubu gave his inaugural address in 2023. File photo. Photo: Tofibobo2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
