World.title: The Costa Rica I Remember and the Changes I Have Seen
World.content:
I like going to the weekly feria in Perez Zeledon. Unlike much of the Costa Rica I know, it is largely unchanged over the past thirty years. Same location, same set up, same rows and rows of vendors selling fresh fruits, veggies, and assorted other agriculture and artisanal products. I once had a booth there, selling my homemade breads and cookies. I can stand at the spot where I had a booth and look out and see the same scenes I saw thirty years ago. There is a comfort in that kind of familiarity.

As time passes, not everything stays the same. Change is inevitable. Things that once were fade into distant memory. While I can stand in that spot at the feria and remember being there thirty years prior, once I step outside, I am in a Costa Rica where much has changed. There have been major changes– in infrastructure, with new highways and bypasses, and in construction, with thousands of new houses, and a San Jose skyline that features dozens of high rises that have sprung up in that time span. But there are also smaller changes, more subtle, less noticeable at first, that have occurred. Here is my own list of 20 random changes I have seen in Costa Rica:

The disappearance of the Lada Niva. The Russian made 4×4, cheapest on the market, could be classified as a vanishing species. I personally can’t remember the last time I saw one on the road. The machete wielding landscapers have been replaced by gas powered weedwhackers. We traded the rhythmic whinging of the machete for the incessant drone of the machine. Whatever happened to the amateur blood pressure takers? They once roamed the cantinas and public areas, dressed in medical garb, blood pressure measurement devices in hand. For a small fee they would let you know how serious your hypertension, though the accuracy of their units was always in doubt. Informal, front of the house bars were once fairly common. Up front, a small bar with uncomfortable wood block chairs, with a door that separated the bar from the living area. It was always a bit odd when the door opened and you would see a family sitting around in their living room while at the bar, borrachos sang along with a ranchero tune. While on the topic of bars, many will remember the days of a free boca with every drink order. You could get a full meal with 3 or 4 beers. Some bars kept it basic with only ‘sustancia’, others offered small portions of meat, chicken or fish. Now virtually extinct. In a good change for taller people like myself, the 6-foot high doorways have been universally adjusted. I banged the top of my head more than once in older Tico houses and cantinas. Likewise, most buses have more legroom than previous, thanks to a new generation of larger Ticos. Speaking of which, large doesn’t always mean tall. My first years in Costa Rica, I marveled at the overall fitness of the country. Everybody looked like a soccer player or a cowboy. Today the country deals with the health issues brought on by poor diets and lack of exercise. Obesity rates are up everywhere in the world, so Costa Rica is hardly alone. I remember a time when people looked ahead as they walked down the street. They are still around but the number of distracted walkers is astronomical compared to the pre-cell phone epoch. For every person you saw back then who was reading a book or newspaper as they walked down the street, today there are ten staring into their phones. At least. Cooking con leña – The wood fired cooking of meat, The Cocina con Leña, was once as common as fried chicken, but is now more artisanal, offered up in higher-end restaurants. The masses eat it fried, skin and all. My barrio in San Isidro de el General has paved streets, I remember when it didn’t. But I’m not complaining. We still have one-lane bridges. Relics of simpler days. Medical care was once incredibly cheap. People come here because it still is a good deal. How’s this for a good deal?: In 1991 my son was born in a private clinic in San Jose, the doctor an accomplished Costa Rican who had worked in well known US hospitals. An anesthesiologist was called in as my son was delivered by caesarian. His mother spent four nights, and a 24-hour nurse on call. The total bill was $1,100. Here’s another: In 1992, I had emergency surgery to remove an ulcerating parasite from my intestines. I spent 10 nights in the hospital after surgery. Had daily doctor visits and nurses always around. The cost was $800. Adjusted for inflation, $2,700 and $2,000. Still astounding.

The rest of the list is what I call the Virtually Extinct list:

World.title: Dollar Hits Its Third Record Low in a Week in Costa Rica
World.content:
The U.S. dollar fell to a new all-time low against the Costa Rican colón yesterday, its third record in a week. The weighted average on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR), closed at 444.45 colones. That was 0.40 below Wednesday’s record of 444.85, which in turn broke the previous low of 446.10 set on Nov. 13.

The dollar began 2026 at 497.07 colones and has since lost 52.62 colones, or 10.6% of its value. It now sits 36% below its all-time high of 696.76 colones, reached on June 21, 2022. For anyone paid in dollars and spending in colones, the decline is direct. At Thursday’s average, $2,000 converts to about 888,900 colones, compared with roughly 994,100 colones at the start of the year, a difference of about 105,000 colones.

The BCCR’s reference rates for today were 442.31 colones to buy and 446.48 to sell. Prices at bank windows vary by institution. The new low coincided with the release of the 2026 State of the Nation report, which divides the past decade of exchange-rate movement into four stages.

From 2016 to 2020, the rate was relatively stable with a slight tendency to depreciate, ranging between 535.47 and 628.85 colones. It stayed below 600 on 1,068 of 1,251 trading days. In 2021 and 2022, the pandemic and global shocks, including the shipping container crisis, drove a sharp depreciation of the colón. The dollar peaked at its record 696.76 in June 2022 before falling back below 600 by the end of that year.

Between 2023 and 2025, the colón appreciated and returned to pre-pandemic levels, with the rate ranging from 488.06 to 596.73. It dipped below 500 in only 33 of 751 sessions. In 2026, that appreciation accelerated. The rate has moved between 444.45 and 499.39 colones this year, setting several new lows in a data series that began on Dec. 6, 2007.

According to the report, an oversupply of dollars has been the main driver since 2023, and that pattern persisted into 2026. BCCR president Róger Madrigal has maintained that market forces determine the exchange rate. The Central Bank has shifted from supplying dollars to absorbing part of the surplus. It has said it will buy dollars when necessary to prevent abrupt movements that do not reflect economic fundamentals.

Seasonal factors are adding pressure. The high tourism season, along with companies converting dollars to pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes, typically increases the supply of dollars in November and December.The State of the Nation report notes that a low exchange rate creates clear winners and losers. Households and businesses that earn colones but carry dollar debts or costs need fewer colones to meet those obligations.

Those who earn in dollars but spend in colones must convert more dollars to cover the same expenses. Domestic producers face tougher competition from cheaper imports, which can squeeze margins and limit investment and hiring, and exporters have asked the BCCR for additional measures to counter the appreciation, mainly during 2026.

Projections from several institutions compiled in September placed the year-end rate between 440 and 465 colones. Analysts have said the dollar could keep falling through the end of the year, and the drop has already raised the cost of retiring in Costa Rica.

Today’s Monex session will show whether the dollar sets yet another record before the weekend.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Vice President Takes Over Trade With a 12.5% US Tariff Still in Place
World.content:
Costa Rica’s first vice president, Francisco Gamboa Soto, takes charge of the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex) today, while keeping his post as vice president. The ministry has been without a permanent head for more than three weeks, since President Laura Fernández dismissed Indiana Trejos on Oct. 28 and ended Costa Rica’s bid to join a major Pacific trade pact.

Casa Presidencial announced the appointment on Thursday evening, Nov. 19. According to the presidency, Gamboa will run the ministry as an additional charge on top of the vice presidency, and the choice reflects his experience in public management and economic policy. The government did not announce any change in trade policy alongside the appointment.

The move puts a senior member of the government in charge of the ministry responsible for trade agreements and foreign investment at a delicate moment. Costa Rican exporters still face a 12.5% duty on most goods sold to the United States, and growth in the free zones that host most multinational employers has nearly stalled.

Gamboa, an economist, has spent most of his career in trade and industry. He directed business intelligence at the export promotion agency PROCOMER from 2006 to 2014, served as executive director of the Chamber of Industries from 2015 to 2019 and later headed institutional relations at Banco Nacional. He was minister of Economy, Industry and Commerce under former president Rodrigo Chaves before becoming first vice president in May 2026.

He was also the official who signed Trejos’ removal. With Fernández traveling in Europe, Gamboa signed Agreement No. 110-P dismissing Trejos effective at noon on Oct. 28, and Agreement No. 111-P naming Arianna Arce Camacho as interim minister, according to decrees published Nov. 3 in the official gazette La Gaceta.

Fernández announced the dismissal in a video released Oct. 28, in which she also said Costa Rica would not sign its accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). The bloc’s 12 members include Japan, Canada, Mexico, Chile, Peru, Australia and the United Kingdom. The president questioned the transparency of the negotiations and said productive sectors had not received the full text of the treaty despite her instructions.

Trejos had defended the process before lawmakers, arguing that the terms concluded in May could not be renegotiated. Chaves had announced the close of substantive negotiations on May 6, 2026, two days before leaving office, and the signing had been scheduled for Nov. 23.

Instead, Fernández confirmed on Nov. 11 that the government would not resume the accession process, and Arce sent a letter on Nov. 13 informing member countries that Costa Rica would not sign. Agricultural groups had raised concerns about foreign competition and the effects on domestic production, though people linked to the process have also pointed to political calculations ahead of the 2028 municipal elections.

Former foreign trade minister Manuel Tovar has described the CPTPP as the most important of all international trade agreements, while the government has not said who is accountable for the public money spent on the talks.

Gamboa now inherits a ministry whose direction remains unclear. How he handles the fallout with the CPTPP members and the trade relationship with the United States, Costa Rica’s largest export market, will shape conditions for the companies, farmers and workers who depend on the country’s exports.

World.title: How Costa Rica’s San Jose Airport Manages Thousands of Wildlife Encounters
World.content:
Costa Rica is famous for its biodiversity, but at the main international airport in San Jose, sharing space with wildlife creates an unusual challenge: keeping aircraft safe while protecting the animals that wander onto airport grounds. Between January and October 2026, Juan Santamaría International Airport monitored 22,014 animals on its grounds, according to airport operator Aeris. Of those, 19,001 were driven off through preventive wildlife management measures, about 86% of all animals recorded.

The most frequent visitors by far were great-tailed grackles, known locally here as zanates, with 14,568 birds chased off during the ten-month period. These familiar black birds, common across Costa Rica’s towns and cities, made up more than three-quarters of all the animals driven away from the airport.

Other species frequently moved along included swallows, with 2,234 dispersals, followed by vultures with 988, crested caracaras with 287, and parakeets with 252. While birds are an everyday sight across Costa Rica, their presence near runways and aircraft movement areas creates real safety concerns. Bird strikes, which occur when birds collide with aircraft, are a recognized aviation hazard, so airports run wildlife management programs to reduce the chance of encounters during takeoff, landing, and other operations.

At Juan Santamaría, the approach involves more than simply chasing birds away. Aeris runs a continuous wildlife monitoring program to identify which species frequent the airport, where they gather, and what conditions may be drawing them in. Arturo Zamora, Aeris’ operations and safety manager, said understanding wildlife behavior is essential for pinpointing higher-risk areas and putting preventive measures in place.

To keep animals away from sensitive areas, the airport uses controlled pyrotechnics, laser lights, sound-producing equipment, and camera traps. According to Aeris, the program follows standards set by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and Costa Rica’s RAC 139 aviation regulations.

Teams also carry out regular inspections to find and remove anything that might attract wildlife, such as standing water, nesting spots, shelters, and perches. When scaring animals away doesn’t work, they may need to be captured. Between January and October, Aeris carried out 107 captures, 89 using cage traps and 18 by hand. Depending on the case, the airport coordinates with wildlife rescue centers and specialized organizations.

The program’s work also reaches beyond animals that could interfere with flights. As part of its Friends of the Bees certification, Aeris has responded to 14 bee swarms so far this year, working with Costa Rica’s Fire Department to rescue and relocate the insects and protect these important pollinators.

Outside the airport perimeter, the operator has also backed community animal welfare efforts, including a sterilization campaign for 24 dogs and cats, and organized lessons on responsible pet ownership with students from León Cortés School in the nearby community of El Coco.

World.title: Costa Rica Ranks Among the 10 Safest Countries to Visit in 2027
World.content:
Costa Rica is the only Central American country named among the 10 safest destinations for travelers in 2027, according to the Risk Map 2027 released by Swedish risk-management firm Safeture and travel intelligence company Riskline. The annual map rates every country on Riskline’s five-level scale of Low, Moderate, Medium, High and Extreme. It weighs security, crime, health and environmental risks, and access to medical care.

Costa Rica appears on the list of standout safe countries alongside Bhutan, Canada, Chile, Denmark, Iceland, New Zealand, Singapore, Slovenia and Switzerland. Riskline’s analysts chose those countries from every region of the world. The list is not ranked. Within Central America, Costa Rica, Belize and El Salvador share the region’s lowest risk rating. Panama and Nicaragua are rated Medium. Guatemala and Honduras are in the High category.

El Salvador’s rating is one of the biggest changes on the 2027 map. The country moved from Medium to Moderate, making it one of only six countries worldwide whose risk level improved over the past 12 months. The others were the Maldives, Bangladesh, Cameroon, Mozambique and Nepal.

That puts El Salvador in the same tier as Germany, Finland and Cyprus, which all slipped from Low to Moderate this year. Honduras is the region’s most prominent concern on the map. San Pedro Sula, its second-largest city, is one of the 10 least safe cities in the world, alongside Kabul, Port-au-Prince, Bamako, Goma, Guayaquil, Port Moresby, Quetta, Sana’a and Tehran.

Fifteen countries moved to a higher risk level this year. Most of them are in the Middle East, where Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates jumped from Moderate to High. Saudi Arabia and Jordan rose from Medium to High, and Iran moved up to Extreme. Closer to home, Cuba rose from Moderate to Medium.

The 10 least safe countries on the 2027 map are Colombia, Haiti, Iran, Myanmar, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Yemen, and the West Bank and Gaza. “This year’s map shows how quickly the risk picture can change,” said Jonas Brorson, chief marketing officer at Safeture.

The two companies say the map gives a broad picture and does not replace a full risk assessment. Ratings can also vary a lot within a single country. A separate 2027 assessment by security firm Global Guardian also placed Costa Rica and Panama among Central America’s most stable destinations. That report identified Guatemala and Nicaragua as the region’s most serious concerns.

Costa Rica’s place on the safest list comes as the country continues to deal with drug-related violence, which has kept homicides near record levels in recent years. Most of that violence is concentrated in specific urban and coastal areas and involves criminal groups, not visitors.

The full Risk Map 2027 can be downloaded free at safeture.com/riskmaps.

World.title: Costa Rica Hit by 3.6 Million Malware Attempts as Hackers Shift to Targeted Attacks
World.content:
Costa Rica had about 3.6 million attempted malware infections between September 2025 and September 2026, according to the latest Latin America threat landscape report from cybersecurity company Kaspersky. That is the second-highest figure among the five Central American and Caribbean countries in the report. The Dominican Republic led with 4.2 million, followed by Costa Rica, Guatemala with 3.4 million, Panama with 3.3 million and El Salvador with 1.2 million.

Kaspersky’s previous annual report, which covered a slightly different period, put Costa Rica at 3.9 million attempts. Across Latin America, Kaspersky said it blocked 592 million malware infection attempts over the 12 months, an 18% drop from the year before. Brazil and Mexico accounted for the largest totals, with 330 million and 102 million respectively.

The company cautioned that the decline does not mean the region is safer. Rather than relying mainly on mass campaigns built to infect as many devices as possible, attackers are increasingly concentrating on specific targets, particularly government agencies and large industries.

Government institutions accounted for 27.3% of blocked malware attempts across Latin America, followed by process manufacturing at 12.5%, retail and wholesale trade at 11.5% and healthcare at 8.3%. The report does not break those shares down by country. Costa Rica knows what a targeted attack on the state can cost. In 2022, the Conti ransomware group crippled Finance Ministry systems and other public institutions, prompting the government to declare a national emergency.

The figures reflect detections among users of Kaspersky’s own products, so they point to trends rather than the total number of attacks in each country. Among the most common threats the report identified are pirated programs and unauthorized license activation tools. These downloads often ask users to switch off their antivirus first, which gives malicious software an easy way in.

Once installed, spyware bundled with pirated software can harvest passwords and other confidential data, exposing individuals and organizations to fraud or extortion. Adware is another frequent problem. Although it is mostly associated with unwanted ads and browser redirects, some programs can also steer users toward fraudulent websites and more serious threats.

Fabio Assolini, Kaspersky’s lead security researcher, said many people in the region still put their digital security at risk to get paid software for free, and that criminals exploit that demand by hiding highly malicious files inside copies of expensive programs. Assolini said the overall drop in detections reflects a change in strategy, as attackers move away from simple mass-distributed malware toward professional operations capable of causing greater financial and operational damage to governments and major industries.

Kaspersky recommends a zero-tolerance approach to pirated software, downloading programs only from developers’ websites or official app stores, installing security updates promptly, and using reliable security software at home and at work. The regional decline may look encouraging, but the report suggests the more important question is no longer how many attacks are occurring, but how much damage a single successful one can cause.

World.title: Costa Rica Is Latin America’s Priciest Place to Retire as the Dollar Hits a Record Low
World.content:
Costa Rica is regularly ranked among the best places in the world to retire, but one analysis of cost-of-living data found it is also the most expensive country in Latin America in which to retire comfortably. A record-low dollar is widening that gap for retirees whose income arrives in U.S. currency.

The analysis, published in September by Bloomberg Línea using NetCredit and Numbeo data compiled by Visual Capitalist, estimated that $556,000 in savings is needed to retire comfortably in Costa Rica. That placed the country 16th worldwide and first in Latin America, ahead of Uruguay at $451,000 and Mexico at $356,000.

The same analysis put the U.S. figure at about $738,000, meaning Costa Rica still costs roughly a quarter less than retiring at home. Its estimates assume nearly 15 years of retirement and exclude taxes and health care costs, and the authors noted that results can vary significantly by city, housing and lifestyle.

Costa Rica’s standing in lifestyle rankings remains high. International Living’s 2026 Global Retirement Index placed it third with a score of 87.6, behind Greece and Panama, and ranked it first in the index’s climate category. A separate index by Global Citizen Solutions ranked Costa Rica’s Pensionado visa fourth in the world.

The exchange rate is now eroding the cost advantage those rankings rely on. The dollar closed at 444.85 colones on Nov. 18 in the central bank’s Monex market, the lowest level since the platform began operating in November 2006. It started 2026 at 497.07 colones, a decline of 10.5%, and analysts expect further declines before year-end.

For a retiree living on a $1,000 monthly pension, the minimum income required for Pensionado residency, the difference shows up every month. At January’s rate, $1,000 converted to about 497,000 colones; at Wednesday’s rate, it brings about 445,000, roughly 52,000 colones less each month, or about $117 at current rates. Banks also pay less than the Monex average when they buy dollars from customers.

International Living’s index estimated monthly living expenses in Costa Rica at about $1,500 for a single person to roughly $4,000 for a couple seeking a comfortable lifestyle. The Bloomberg Línea analysis cited high housing costs, prices for some foods, transport, electricity, imported goods and exchange-rate risk as factors behind Costa Rica’s higher requirement.

The pressure on the dollar is seasonal and expected to continue, as the high tourist season, year-end aguinaldo bonuses and tax payments increase the supply of dollars in the country. International Living’s next index is expected in the coming weeks; the 2026 edition was released in December 2025.

World.title: Court File Alleges Diablo-Linked Group Tortured US Surfer Kurt Van Dyke for His PINs
World.content:
The men who killed American surfer Kurt Van Dyke in February allegedly belonged to a group linked to Alejandro Arias Monge, the alleged drug trafficker known as “Diablo,” according to the court file in the case. The file also alleges that Van Dyke was bound and tortured to force him to reveal the PINs for his bank cards.

Van Dyke, 66, was found dead on Feb. 14 in Hone Creek, near Cahuita on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. A Santa Cruz, California, native known in surfing circles as “King,” he had run Hotel Puerto Viejo for decades. His killing was first reported as a robbery.

Two suspects are in custody. A 31-year-old woman surnamed Arroyo Ramírez, who had a long relationship with Van Dyke, and a man surnamed Gutiérrez Víctor were detained on Nov. 12. On Nov. 15, the Talamanca Criminal Court ordered both held for six months of pretrial detention while prosecutors investigate them for aggravated homicide.

Neither has been charged or convicted, and both are presumed innocent. The allegations described below come from the prosecution’s case file and have not been tested in court.

According to the file, the plan took shape on the morning of Feb. 14. Arroyo Ramírez allegedly persuaded Van Dyke to come to her home in Hone Creek under false pretenses. Prosecutors allege that once he was there, she sent WhatsApp messages telling the others he was unprotected and how to get in.

The file states that the attackers entered, immobilized Van Dyke and tied his hands and feet. They then allegedly tortured him and inflicted stab wounds as they tried to obtain his bank PINs. Prosecutors attribute the killing to a structured group acting together to seize his assets and take his life.

A neighbor called 911 at 10:35 a.m. to report that armed men had broken in, restrained both people inside and stolen the woman’s car and phone, according to the file. Security cameras recorded Van Dyke calling for help at about 10 a.m. Investigators found no sign of forced entry.

The medical-legal report concluded that Van Dyke died of asphyxia caused by compression of the neck, with a fractured hyoid bone, and that he had been tortured. He was found under a bed with his hands and feet bound, a sheet around his head and multiple stab wounds. Investigators allege that the woman staged the robbery and reported her own vehicle stolen to conceal her role.

The car was later recovered in good condition, and investigators determined that her account did not match the evidence. The file also describes alleged threats in the months before the killing. On Jan. 4, Arroyo Ramírez allegedly demanded $1,500 from Van Dyke and threatened to send people from Diablo’s group to harm another former partner of his and their son.

Arias Monge was captured on July 24 in San Bernardino de Sarapiquí at the end of an operation authorities named Némesis, and he is being held at La Reforma prison. Reports on the file have not said whether he is a suspect in the Van Dyke case. Investigations into his network have already reached a police officer and two Pococí judges.

The case is being handled under file 26-000171-0829-PE by the organized crime unit of the Limón Prosecutor’s Office, under the supervision of the deputy prosecutor’s office for money laundering. The OIJ is still looking for two more men believed to have taken part in the attack.

Anyone with information can contact the OIJ’s confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: Audit fallout
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness delivers the keynote address during the official opening of the Trelawny Adult Care Residential Facility in Falmouth on Thursday. (Photo: JIS)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has charged that some of the findings in the latest auditor general (AuG) report on the management of Hurricane Melissa donations by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) should not have been included, as they raised concerns that could have been cleared up with readily available information.

At the same time he reiterated plans for a revamp of ODPEM, transitioning it into a national resilience organisation.

Speaking at the official opening of Trelawny Adult Care Residential Facility (formely infirmary) on Thursday, Holness said the Government had already started addressing structural and operational gaps within the agency, with the findings contained in the auditor general report further underscoring areas in need of continued strengthening.

He pointed out that the Government had commissioned an independent review of ODPEM in 2024, with the findings received in 2025.

Holness noted that the review highlighted several challenges, with recommendations for changes to the agency’s leadership, staff upgrades, system improvements, and a clearer mandate.

“We will move swiftly to address the issues at ODPEM, including the staffing issues, and appoint permanent leadership, and restructure it. So, we are well advanced in what we need to do to restructure ODPEM, and those things will probably move with a little bit more speed now,” declared Holness as he argued that some of the matters raised in the October report were of serious concern, but that others could have been clarified before being presented as findings.

“The report, in some instances — some of the points that have been itemised — are of great concern, as I have said, but some of them are easily explained, and probably should not have been a part of the report. For example, the report of 200 houses donated by the Government of China, only 30-plus can be accounted for.

“That is absolutely something that should never have been in a report, because you can easily see where they are. There are reports even before, where Minister [Robert] Montague and [a] Member of Parliament [in] Westmoreland toured facilities where some of the houses were stored, and so it is there. The ODPEM has come out and they have clarified that they have [been] handed over to the Ministry of Economic Growth and [Infrastructure Development], that has the duty to build the platforms,” said Holness.

The Auditor General’s Hurricane Melissa Relief Initiative Audit: Compliance Audit Report on Management and Distribution of In-Kind Donations, which was tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, listed 200 prefabricated houses, valued at approximately $139.1 million, among 1,332 fixed assets donated to the Government for response to the October 2025 Category 5 storm which devastated sections of the island.

The audit found that ODPEM had not provided receipt forms for the houses and had not entered the internationally donated assets in its inventory records or fixed asset register.

The auditors also reported that they had verified the existence of 31 prefabricated houses. The report did not conclude that the remaining houses had been stolen or were missing; rather, it identified gaps in the documentation and records needed to account for the donated assets.

Despite his belief that some things should not have been in the report, Holness also defended the role of the auditor general.

“The auditor general is an important part of our democracy that it is able to do this. There are other countries that don’t have this, but this is an important part. The society, however, has to develop the understanding of what the reports mean before drawing conclusions,” said Holness.

The prime minister also addressed concerns about relief supplies that had spoilt, describing the matter as one of inventory management and agreed with the auditor general that there is a need to ensure that older goods are distributed before newer supplies.

During a physical inspection of Warehouse 3 on June 18, the auditor general’s team found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, as well as insects on the packaging of some consumable items. The report noted that the other items inspected were within their usable dates.

The audit further found that ODPEM had not maintained adequate store records to allow auditors to compare the physical stock with the quantities received and distributed. It also noted that rice remained in storage about three months after an infestation of weevils had been reported.

Holness said the circumstances surrounding donated goods, including their expiry dates, should be considered before conclusions are drawn.

“Normally your first in is your first out, and you have to have a process to look at the date of expiration that comes in on some of the items that you have, so you try to either dispose of them, or send them out. It is a complicated issue… I won’t go any further than to say that when you are dealing with donated items, the expiration dates are sometimes close to the use date. So you have to bear that in mind when you make your conclusions on that finding,” he argued.

Holness also addressed ODPEM’s use of donated funds to pay Customs clearance fees for relief goods, acknowledging that the spending did not follow the instructions given for how the money should be used.

The auditor general found that ODPEM spent approximately $45.1 million from its Donation Account on brokerage and related clearance fees, as well as warehouse rental and utility expenses. Of that amount, $32.97 million was used to clear goods intended for private organisations.

The donated funds had been approved to support the Government-Directed Roof Repair and Semi-permanent Housing Solution Programme under the broader Shelter Recovery Programme.

ODPEM acknowledged in its response to the audit that the brokerage fees fell outside the approved expenditure, but said the payments were considered necessary to prevent delays in releasing relief consignments.

Holness said the decision was made at the executive level of ODPEM and was not a decision made by the Government’s executive leadership.

“But I suspect they may be thinking that, if they didn’t pay, they wouldn’t get the goods, or if they didn’t pay, the goods would stay on the wharf, generating more fees that the Government would have to pay,” added Holness.

World.title: Sandals South Coast reopens under US$250-million ‘Sandals 2.0’ upgrade
World.content:
The entrance to be revamped Sandals South Coast showing the heart-shaped porte-cochère lobby. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Just over a year after taking a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, the reimagined Sandals South Coast officially reopened its doors on Thursday with Executive Chairman Adam Stewart declaring the property’s rapid transformation a triumph of Jamaican resilience and teamwork.

According to Stewart, Sandals Resorts International (SRI) has invested no less than US$250 million across three of its hurricane-damaged Jamaican properties — Sandals South Coast, Sandals Montego Bay, and the rebranded Sandals Caribbean Cay (formerly Sandals Royal Caribbean) — to usher in a new era for the brand.

“My dad taught us, never waste a good crisis,” declared Stewart, referring to the philosophy of his late father and Sandals founder, Gordon “Butch” Stewart.

“We have spent no less than a quarter-billion US dollars taking Sandals from what it was to what we now call Sandals 2.0: New restaurants, new pools, new architecture, new designs, new features, new amenities. So, you know, we have a message to our competition: While you are trying to get back to baseline, catch us if you can,” added Stewart.

Stewart was addressing the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated resort in Westmoreland. The hotel, which sustained severe damage during the Category 5 storm, was rehabilitated by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects, engineers, and hospitality workers over a compressed 10-month period and welcomed its first guests of 448 on Wednesday,

The remaining two badly damaged properties are slated to reopen on December 18, 2026.

Stewart praised the scale and speed of the rehabilitation effort at the 380-room property located in Whitehouse.

“What the team of Sandals demonstrated here was nothing short of a miracle. Two-plus years of work compressed into 10 months. We worked with American and Jamaican architects until the coffee couldn’t help them any more,” Stewart told the gathering.

The ceremony drew bipartisan representation from political leadership, tourism officials and stakeholders and Stewart commended the country’s political maturity in the aftermath of Melissa.

“Jamaica as a country, even on both sides of the political divide, it is amazing the maturity, it is amazing the advancement that we have made as a country, how we can talk about complex things and how we can find solutions to make sure that love for country is never far away from our performance and what it is that we’re doing,” Stewart stated.

He revealed that during the recovery period, Sandals kept its team members on payroll with full benefits and 50 per cent of their gratuities. The hotel also hosted and housed team members who were stranded in their communities.

Stewart pointed out that during the COVID-19 pandemic in Jamaica (2020-2021) and in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, the hotel housed and fed essential personnel — including members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF), Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), air traffic controllers, embassies, non-governmental organisations, and the staff and contractors of Jamaica Public Service (JPS), which occupied a third of the resort — free of cost.

He also recounted the harrowing hours during and after Melissa when for hours Sandals executives lost contact with the property until former General Manager O’Brian Heron — now president of the Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) and SRI’s newly promoted head of operations — managed to send a WhatsApp message.

Stewart highlighted Heron’s heroism during the height of the storm where he risked his life to ensure the security of his team members.

Meanwhile state minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright lauded SRI for its 45-year contribution to Jamaica’s economy, workforce, and global brand.

Seiveright described the home-grown hospitality giant as an “economic powerhouse” and “one of the greatest entrepreneurial success stories this region has ever, ever produced.”

Highlighting the resort chain’s vast footprint, Seiveright noted that Sandals employs approximately 20,000 people across the Caribbean, including more than 7,000 in Jamaica.

Sandals South Coast employs between 900 and 1,000 workers — primarily from surrounding communities — making it one of Westmoreland and western Jamaica’s largest private-sector employers.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang hailed the reopening of Sandals South Coast as a defining symbol of national resilience.

According to Chang, Jamaica’s tourism sector and its security apparatus are emerging stronger a year after the historic storm made landfall in Westmoreland.

“Melissa wrote a chapter about what we lost, today, Sandals South Coast writes the next chapter about what we rebuilt,” declared Chang.

“Let’s say Jamaica is open. Jamaica is safe. Jamaica is back. Sandals are back, leading the way,” added Chang.

World.title: Ras-I comes into his own with Kingman Live
World.content:
Ras-I to host Kingman Live on December

For years Ras-I has been steadily building his place in reggae music, carving out an identity through introspective songwriting, conscious lyrics, and a willingness to draw from his own lived experiences. The artiste is now preparing to embrace a new chapter in his journey, one that will see him step into the spotlight as the headliner of his own live production.

Dubbed Kingman Live, the event represents more than another performance opportunity for the rising reggae sensation. It is the culmination of years of artistic development, a growing connection with audiences, and the determination of a team that has been working to bring the vision to life.

Originally conceptualised for 2023, Kingman Live had to be put on hold when the pieces failed to fall into place. Rather than force the production, the artiste and his team opted to reassess their plans and wait for a more opportune moment.

In the intervening years, the artiste has continued to build momentum, with the release of his album and a succession of singles helping to expand his reach.

“The album, the momentum from singles release and everything, we started to gain a lot more traction and then corporate came on board, and that was very instrumental because we know how challenging it is to produce live events. It nuh cheap at all. So my team and I — Apryl included — decided that now was the right time. Di people dem ready for Kingman Live and we ago give it to dem,” he said.

That reference to Apryl McIntosh carries particular weight. McIntosh, Ras-I’s manager, passed away recently. Her death left a significant void in both his professional and personal life. Her contribution to the development of Kingman Live makes her absence especially poignant.

“Kingman Live wouldn’t be happening at all without Apryl, and so, of course, we have to honour her memory in a special way. We will definitely want to have a tribute section to her,” he shared.

The loss has also forced Ras-I to confront grief while navigating the demands of an industry that rarely pauses. He admits that he is still processing McIntosh’s passing, taking each day as it comes and accepting that healing does not follow a predictable pattern.

“Everybody have dem own way of grieving, mine is day by day. Every day is different; some days you’re up, other days you’re not. Some days the emotions high,” he said.

Music has naturally become one of his anchors during this period. Whether listening to other artistes, revisiting his own catalogue, or simply allowing himself to be immersed in sound, he finds comfort in music. His faith also provides reassurance, while activities such as playing football offer an opportunity to disrupt negative thought patterns.

“Through the Almighty, I just gwaan hold it and know say this too shall pass. I just always try to break the cycle, do something that mash up the negative momentum… play ball,” he explained.

That ability to draw from life’s difficult moments is also reflected in his approach to songwriting. Rather than relying solely on imagined scenarios, Ras-I uses his experiences as the foundation for his music, allowing his artistic expression to evolve alongside his personal growth.

He views each new experience as an opportunity to create, particularly as he continues to navigate the demands and rewards of a developing career.

“I just write about my experiences daily. As you grow in the industry, there are fresh experiences, so every time I break a new barrier, there’s new material,” he said.

It is an approach that has informed both his album and the collaborations featured on the project, with the artiste explaining that many of the songs were born out of similar moments of personal and professional progression.

And while the emotional demands of the past months have presented their own challenges, his attention remains firmly fixed on delivering a memorable experience when Kingman Live takes place.

He said preparations are progressing well, despite the need to bring additional personnel on board following McIntosh’s passing. He is confident in the new additions to the team and says the musicians and artistes involved are equally prepared to deliver.

“The band is ready, I am ready, and all the artistes on board are ready — the ones announced and the ones not on the flyers, because we have a whole heap of special guests passing through,” he revealed.

For audiences, he promises an evening centred on the kind of live musical connection that has become increasingly important to him.

Rather than an elaborate spectacle designed around social media moments, Ras-I wants to recapture the uncomplicated enjoyment of attending a show, discovering music, and connecting with artistes in real time.

“People should just expect good vibes. Remember when we used to go show and just ‘fuljoy’ the music, the live entertainment, that’s what it will be like,” he said.

He sees the production as an opportunity to introduce audiences to artistes they may not necessarily know beyond a handful of songs, giving them the chance to experience their music in a more intimate and meaningful setting.

For him, that is part of a wider conversation about the importance of live entertainment in Jamaica’s musical landscape.

“Kingman Live is my way of saying we need more live events, because we have a lot of music and you can only experience it the right way through in-person vibes — not through a phone screen from a 30-second video, but the real feeling, drum and bass with conscious lyrics,” he said.

It is perhaps an appropriate reflection of where Ras-I finds himself at this stage of his career. Having spent years developing his craft and gradually building an audience, he is now taking greater ownership of the spaces in which his music can be experienced.

There is still much to navigate, both personally and professionally, but Kingman Live offers a tangible reminder of how far he has come.

And, as he prepares to take centre stage, the moment is as much about celebrating that growth as it is about acknowledging the people and experiences that helped bring him there.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: BARITA SEEKS $9.3B IN FRESH FUNDING
World.content:
BARITA Investments Limited is returning to the public bond market with plans to raise up to $9.3 billion through a combination of Jamaican- and US-dollar-denominated securities, as the investment company seeks to strengthen its balance sheet and secure funding for new investment products.

In a prospectus published on Tuesday, Barita outlined a three-tranche bond offer comprising two US-dollar instruments and one Jamaican-dollar instrument, with interest rates ranging from 7.25 per cent to 10.50 per cent and repayment periods of two to five years.

The company is seeking to raise US$10 million in each of the two US-dollar tranches, with the option to increase each to US$15 million if demand permits. The Jamaican-dollar tranche targets $3 billion, with provision to increase the amount to $4.5 billion.

Investors in the first tranche will earn annual interest of 7.25 per cent over two years, while the second tranche offers 10.50 per cent over three years. The third tranche carries an interest rate of 8.25 per cent over five years.

Barita intends to use the proceeds to strengthen its capital base, improve liquidity and support the development and introduction of new investment products as it works to diversify its earnings.

“Continued emphasis on disciplined risk management, recurring income generation and balance sheet resilience, alongside selective participation in emerging investment and capital market opportunities, should support Barita’s competitiveness and long-term earnings growth,” the company stated in its prospectus.

Although Barita outlined the broad purposes of the fundraising, it did not specify how much would be allocated to each activity. Transaction costs associated with the offer are expected to remain below $200 million.

“We will strengthen liquidity and diversify our funding sources. With policy rates higher in Jamaica and the United States, we will manage the maturity and repricing of assets and liabilities and adjust funding terms where appropriate to protect net interest margins,” said Barita chairman Mark Myers in the company’s fourth quarter report ending September 30.

The bond offer also enters a market recently buoyed by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited’s $63.50-billion acquisition of the remaining minority shares in Scotia Group Jamaica Limited (SGJ), a transaction that has returned a substantial amount of capital to investors and potentially created fresh demand for investment securities.

Barita has been actively deploying capital into different opportunities over the last year. This included the acquisition of Barita Fund Managers Limited (formerly JN Fund Managers Limited) in January for $3.81 billion. The acquisition expanded Barita’s assets under management by at least $52 billion and contributed $789.5 million to Barita’s net operating income (NOI) and $60.2 million to net profit.

Barita also acquired Key Homes Limited from MJR Real Estate Holdings Limited in December 2025 as it brings some of its real estate plans to its balance sheet. The consideration for this deal was a series of debentures over five years valued at US$111.53 million ($17.63 billion). Key Homes owns a 101 acre property known as Windsor Estates in St Ann. This acquisition contributed $897 million in fair value gains to Barita’s NOI and increased its investment property balance to $20.23 billion.

The investment firm reported a 136 per cent increase in its net operating income from $8.70 billion to $20.47 billion for its financial year ending September 30. The bulk of this improved earning capacity was attributed to $13.27 billion in gains on its investment activities. Accordingly, Barita raked in $4.68 billion in realised gains and $8.59 billion in unrealised gains, with $7.09 billion arising in the fourth quarter.

Although revenue generation improved during the year, operating expenses doubled from $4.64 billion to $10.78 billion, which included $2.38 billion in credit loss provisions for amounts in doubt. There was also a sevenfold increase in the loss from its associate during the year.

Despite the higher costs, Barita’s profit before tax grew 126 per cent to $8.85 billion while net profit doubled from $3.01 billion to $6.03 billion. These figures are unaudited and subject to final review in the upcoming audited financial statements by newly appointed auditor PwC.

“We are tightening control of technology, administrative and transformation spending, simplifying processes and using targeted automation to lower the cost of serving clients. This work goes hand in hand with modernising our systems and improving digital service. Our aim is to improve operating leverage so that more of our revenue growth translates into earnings,” Myers explained on the 2027 objectives.

Barita’s balance sheet moved by 32 per cent to $196.17 billion, reflecting the benefits of its Barita Fund Managers and Key Homes acquisitions. The investment firm’s pledged assets reached $116.28 billion as it continued to grow its repurchase agreement (repo) book with its clients.

Equity increased by four per cent to $36.59 billion as Barita recorded unrealised losses on some investments and proposed a $3.25 billion dividend to be paid on November 30.

The investment firm is working to develop some of the real estate properties under its alternative investment portfolio. Three of the sites held by MJR Real Estate are in active pre-development, with demolition work completed former Ice Factory on Harbour Street and former Eden Gardens property on Lady Musgrave Road. MJR Real Estate is owned by the Barita Real Estate Unit Trust.

“Over time, we expect completed developments to broaden the portfolio’s sources of return through proceeds from sales and recurring income from leasing and operations, complementing the Group’s securities and asset management businesses,” Myers noted.

This is the company’s second public bond offer following its June 2025 bond listing where it raised $4.74 billion and US$20 million from investors. Tranche I and tranche III from that listing are scheduled to mature in June 2027, with US$10.22 million and $1.37 billion payable to investors, respectively.

Barita intends to apply to list the different tranches on the JSE’s Bond Markets. Barita currently has five securities listed on the JSE Bond Market and two securities on the JSE USD Bond Market.

Investors seeking to purchase tranches I or III must subscribe to a minimum of US$1,500 and apply in multiples of US$100 for higher amounts. The tranche II offer requires a minimum of $50,000 and increments in multiples of $1,000 for higher amounts. Applications can be made on Barita’s Boss website or through selling agents such as Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB), Barita Fund Managers, Proven Wealth Limited or VM Wealth Management Limited. The offer opens on November 25 and is scheduled to close by December 29.

World.title: ITALIAN JOB
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) dribbles away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. Lyle is one of Jamaica’s top players at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup, where they will play Italy today at 10:00 am in their opening match. (Photo: JFF Media)

Jamaica’s Under-17 Reggae Boyz will begin their FIFA Under-17 World Cup campaign against European champions Italy on Friday at 10 am, and Jamaica Football Federation President Michael Ricketts is confident that the team is adequately prepared and has urged Jamaicans to rally behind the youngsters.

Jamaica, appearing in its third Under-17 FIFA World Cup and first in 15 years since they last competed in 2011 in Mexico, are paired in Group E with Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The Jamaicans will be hoping to make a positive start against the Italians before facing Uzbekistan on November 23 and Ivory Coast on November 26.

Despite acknowledging the difficulty of the assignment, Ricketts is confident that the team is adequately prepared and has urged Jamaicans to rally behind the youngsters.

“We will open our World Cup campaign against Italy and obviously, this is going to be a tough encounter. In fact, I think we are in a very tough group. But the important thing is that we are here and we are going to represent ourselves and our country well,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer.

“I think they are mentally and physically well prepared. We’re just hoping that they will execute on the field tomorrow and we’ll get a good result,” he added.

Jamaica qualified for the tournament after winning all three of their Concacaf group matches, with forward Jahmarie Nolan playing a significant role, scoring four goals and providing two assists.

The likes of Jamone Lyle, who like Nolan recently made his senior debut, as well as Tyrique Robinson, Dwayne Burger, Justin Hayles, Nathaniel McCarthy, Jaeshawn Edwards, Kelvin D Brown, and Kelvin O Brown, should carry the fight for Jamaica.

The team’s qualification represents another milestone for Jamaica’s youth football programme, particularly following the Under-15 team’s appearance at the World Cup just a month ago, as the federation tries to qualify all its teams.

“Being to a World Cup is no ordinary achievement and we must express our gratitude to all the key stakeholders, who would have contributed to the success of our youth programmes. Just a month ago, our Under-15s were at the World Cup and they also did so very well,” Ricketts said.

The Under-15 World Cup and Festival was open to all 211 FIFA member associations and did not require qualification.

Meanwhile, the JFF president also credited the federation’s technical staff, which is supported by FIFA, for contributing to the development of the country’s youth programmes.

“I must express my gratitude to the coaches, the technical staff, administrative staff and all those who have contributed to the growth and development of our youth programmes. Our TDS programme, which of course is supported by FIFA, has done so very well and that probably would have been the framework that would have contributed so significantly to our youth programmes,” he added.

Jamaica’s history at the Under-17 World Cup has been mixed.

Their first appearance came in 1999 in New Zealand, where they lost all three group matches without scoring a goal.

They returned to the competition in 2011 in Mexico, where they recorded their first point with a 1-1 draw against France. Zhelano Barnes scored Jamaica’s first goal at the tournament.

Now, 15 years later, the Young Reggae Boyz have another opportunity to improve on that record and make a lasting impression on the global stage.

Ricketts is calling on Jamaicans at home and abroad to give the team their full support as they embark on the latest chapter in the country’s football history.

“I want all of Jamaica to rally around our youngsters and, of course, give them as much support as you can as we embark on another historic exercise,” he said.

World.title: Business set to ‘pickup’ for CAR Jamaica
World.content:
Carwyn Brown, sales executive, CAR Jamaica, with the all-new Musso Grand pickup. (Photo: Rory Daley)

CAR Jamaica launched its newest model, the all-new KGM Musso Grand, on Friday, November 13, at their Lady Musgrave Road showroom.

“The Musso is one of the best-selling pickups on its side of the world, and we know for sure it will do well here in Jamaica because we have a great extensive pickup culture here in Jamaica,” Mellisa Bailey, general manager, CAR Jamaica, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

The Musso is a long-time name for fans of the Ssangyong brand, now KG Mobility. Originally an SUV, the Musso had a dual cab pickup version called the Musso Sport Utility Truck, or Musso Sports. For 2027, it’s a traditional body-on-frame four-door pickup only.

Powered by a 2.2-litre four-cylinder turbo diesel, it drives a six-speed automatic transmission with part-time four-wheel drive, and has all the technology, safety, and convenience features expected in a modern pickup.

Making the Musso unique is its two trim levels. The standard Musso is a small, shorter vehicle, with a 122-inch wheelbase and a full body length of 203-inches.

In Musso Grand trim, the vehicle gains 4.4-inches of wheelbase and 12 inches in body length, the large majority of which is in the rear tray for more cargo space. The Musso can handle a payload up to approximately 2,400lb and tow up to approximately 7,700lb.

“The Musso is perfect for a work-life balance,” explained Carwyn Brown, sales executive, CAR Jamaica.

Brown expects the Musso to appeal to lifestyle pickup buyers and expand the company’s reach into the commercial vehicle segment.

Both the Musso and Musso Grand are available with a six-year warranty and several service packages.

The third brand CAR Jamaica is set to represent was finally revealed by Bailey at the Musso launch.

“Car Jamaica is definitely expanding. We are excited to bring a full electric option, Xpeng, out of China. The launch for that is coming soon,” she said.

World.title: BOJ rate hikes raise mortgage payment fears
World.content:
At a time when Jamaicans are already struggling with punishing cost of living, homeowners carrying hefty mortgages are expressing fresh concerns following two consecutive policy interest rate hikes by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ).

It has raised fears among them that monthly mortgage payments could climb further and place additional financial pressure on their already stretched pockets.

The BOJ raised its benchmark policy rate on September 29 by 50 basis points from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent – the bank’s first rate increase since November 2022 – and again on Thursday to 6.5 per cent, a decision the central bank said was taken in the context of “an upside risk that inflation could remain above the target range until late 2027”.

READ: BOJ increases policy rate to 6.5% as inflation pressures persist

Jamaica’s annual inflation rate eased to 8.2 per cent in October from 8.6 per cent in September, but remained above the Bank of Jamaica’s target.

The policy rate is what the BOJ pays deposit-taking institutions on balances held at the central bank, and serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs.

One woman, who is in her eighth year of mortgage payments, said she is apprehensive, maintaining that her budget cannot handle any more pressure.

“You budget for a certain amount that your mortgage rate will be, and you don’t know what percentage it’s going to be increased by and when they do it, they’re not going to give you a grace period or anything,” she said.

The mortgager reflected on the 2022 rate hike, and the subsequent cycle of five cuts that brought it down from seven per cent.

“A [few] years ago, when the interest rate went up, our mortgage went up and so did the home insurance, and then when the BOJ reduced the rates, the mortgage went down,” she explained.

With the interest rates up again, she said she is “of course” worried.

“Because right now, I am maxed out; I don’t have any extras. Nothing working with…I’m maxed out. If it increases, I don’t know what I would do. I [would] just hope that eventually it’s going to decrease again.”

There are some Jamaicans, however, who say their mortgages have not decreased since that 2022 spike, as some commercial banks were slow to reduce their lending rates, prompting calls for a reduction from lobby groups including the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica (PSOJ), Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association (JMEA) and Jamaica Chamber of Commerce.

One male mortgager said the 2022 increase added a huge chunk to his payment that he is still grappling with.

“By itself, it added $28,000 to my monthly payments. What’s worse is that mere days after being informed about the interest rate increase, I was informed that the peril insurance rate has been increased as well, resulting in another increase in my monthly payment,” he explained.

That was four years ago, and unlike some, he says, he has not gotten any relief. Now with the BOJ increasing rates again, the possibility of additional hikes is distressing.

“I am very apprehensive about the possibility of another increase, because I simply cannot afford it. I am paying approximately $40,000 more in monthly mortgage payments in just four years, when my salary hasn’t budged. Considering all the other increases in cost of living, the struggle is real,” he lamented.

One female mortgager who borrowed directly from the National Housing Trust and is about halfway through paying off a 25-year mortgage said her relief at not necessarily being subject to an increase because of the interest rate hike is immense.

“I am terribly relieved because since that time there have been adjustments based on policy changes so the mortgage I started out with is not the mortgage I now pay,” she explained, adding, “I am very relieved, and I am still thinking and trying to find a way to exit the agreement before the 25 years because…I really look at it now, and I don’t want to be trapped that long.”

Another male mortgager, who is nearing retirement age and has around $8 million left to pay on his own mortgage, was less concerned about any potential increases.

“I think, yeah, there are people who legitimately would want to worry about these things. I really don’t. I have the mortgage already, I have to pay it. The only thing I could maybe try to do is shop around for another entity, financial company that might offer me a better rate. But that’s a lot of hassle,” he said.

Realtor and CEO & Qualifying Director for Easton Douglas Consultants Ltd, Kari Douglas explained that it was unlikely that the increase would drastically affect the housing market locally, maintaining that there are factors in purchasing a home that carry more weight than the current interest rate.

However, she did have advice for potential homeowners.

“A rate increase raises the cost of borrowing, so buyers should test their budget, confirm whether their rate is fixed or variable, and buy only what they can comfortably carry if rates move again. Take the time to get a proper valuation so you’re paying a price that the market supports and borrowing against real value,” she urged.

Douglas said prospective purchasers should also shop around and compare the rates, fees and terms of different banks, building societies, and credit unions to ensure the lowest possible rates.

World.title: ‘I will not be baited into a one-sided apology’, says Burchell
World.content:
Nekeisha Burchell

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Member of Parliament (MP) for St James Southern, Nekeisha Burchell, has stated that she will not be baited into a one-sided apology over statements she directed at the MP for St Andrew West Rural, Juliet Cuthbert-Flynn, during a tense sitting of the House of Representatives on November 17.

Burchell, while responding to an off-mic quip from Cuthbert-Flynn about her ability to adequately prepare for parliamentary debates, said “mi go a gud, gud school enuh. Mi neva run fi a living”.

Cuthbert-Flynn, a four-time Olympian and minister of state in the ministry of national security and peace, and other Government MPs were incensed by the remark. The member for St Catherine East Central, Alando Terrelonge, rose on a point of order to demand that Burchell withdraw the statement. He accused Burchell of disrespecting athletes. She eventually withdrew the remark after she was ordered to do so by deputy speaker of the House, Heroy Clarke.

The next morning, the dispute erupted into a below-the-belt war of words when Cuthbert-Flynn posted on social media that she was “proud to have earned my living on my feet”.

Burchell has come under pressure to apologise to both Cuthbert-Flynn and Jamaican athletes in general.

But, in a video posted to social media on Thursday, she indicated that there will be no such apology even while stating that, “I have tremendous respect for Jamaica’s athletes, and the discipline and sacrifice behind their achievements”.

Burchell said she has since spoken with athletes, adding that, “I’ve taken the time to speak with managers and leaders in the sporting fraternity and generally they understood this was a personal retort directed at Juliet, not an attack on athletes as a group”. She said if there’s any athlete who took offence, “no disrespect was intended”.

Describing Cuthbert-Flynn as chief heckler, Burchell said she has observed since entering the Parliament, that Government members “throw stones and hide their hands. When somebody responds, they present themselves as the victims and demand one-sided apologies”.

She accused the Government of using its parliamentary majority to condemn the response “while ignoring the attacks that provoked it – kind of how they deal with Beenie Man”, she said. “I was baited into a retort, but I will not be baited into a one-sided apology that pretends the provocation never happened”.

Burchell insisted that there cannot be one standard of respect for the majority and another for the minority. She has declared that she will not be bullied into silence.

The first-term MP who represents the opposition People’s National Party has often locked horns with Government members. She began her video by expressing regret for “allowing myself to be drawn out in Parliament this week, and I shouldn’t have”. She outlined her educational and professional achievements before entering representational politics, moving from Mt Alvernia High School to the University of the West Indies, to the London School of Economics.

“I built a career running campaigns across the Caribbean and working in different countries, just making a name for myself.

“So imagine standing in Parliament trying to make a contribution, and somebody across the floor is repeatedly questioning your education, your ability, and tell you that you didn’t even write your own speech? Me, who has been writing speeches for presidents, prime ministers and business leaders for nearly two decades,” Burchell said.

“And she just wouldn’t stop, the remarks kept coming, getting more personal and insulting, while I’m on my feet trying to concentrate,” she added.

Responding to Cuthbert-Flynn’s comment that she made her accomplishments on her feet, Burchell said, “I understood exactly what she’s saying; she was suggesting that while she worked for her achievements, I somehow slept my way to mine. Burchell said it’s the same sexual insinuations she has had to endure since entering representational politics, from both males and females.

World.title: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
World.content:
British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers.

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry



The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.



The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.



The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.



Of the more political parts of the agreement, the Youth Experience Scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

World.title: Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy
World.content:
A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling.

Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa.

They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what.

Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.”

World.title: France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership
World.content:
The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7.

The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said.

If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year.

In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets.

“I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.”

Fewer politicians

A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency.

World.title: Latvian leader calls for closure of EU borders to all Russians
World.content:
Latvia was among the 11 countries that signed a Swedish-led letter in June urging Brussels to restrict visas for Russians. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner suggested to POLITICO in October that the European Commission could present a proposal next year.

Kulbergs warned that Russia’s hybrid attacks on NATO’s eastern flank were intensifying. “The situation is escalating,” he said, adding that Latvian and Estonian special forces had arrested eight people on Estonian soil last weekend who had “concrete instructions to attack a production facility in Estonia that supports Ukraine.” Russia, he said, “is behind this.”

He called the coming months “a winter of truth,” arguing that Russia was striking Ukraine’s water, heating and power supplies because it was making little progress at the front, while also trying to sway public opinion in Germany and elsewhere. “Putin wants the Germans to be frightened and to demand that their government stop supporting Ukraine,” he said.

Kulbergs dismissed fears that Thursday’s summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen amounted to a new Yalta as “an exaggeration,” arguing that the Russian leader had been humiliated. The Yalta summit in February 1945, where U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin shaped Europe’s postwar order, is widely seen as having left much of Central and Eastern Europe under Soviet domination.

Kulbergs urged larger countries, especially Germany, not to give in to war fatigue. “It is entirely possible to be pro-European, to support Ukraine vigorously, to stand up to the aggressor — and still win an election by a large margin,” he said.
