It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: EU warns against COP31 becoming a ‘fossil fuel summit’
World.content:
The draft document calls on countries to scale up carbon storage and capture technologies (CCUS) to meet a specific target, and includes a pledge to raise the share of electricity in global energy use to 35% by 2035 — including power generated using fossil fuels.

France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has heavily criticized the inclusion of CCUS targets.

“When it comes to carbon capture, we’re completely opposed — and this is a real red line — to any figures, any targets, or any quantified objectives,” French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters on Friday.

Dated Nov. 19, the letter asks Australia and Turkey, who are jointly presiding over this year’s global climate talks, to address these demands.

“The EU always prefers an ambitious negotiated outcome but cannot accept agreement at any cost,” the letter warned.

World.title: Tusk: Russian cruise missile incursion into Poland seems ‘intentional’
World.content:
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Trump said that “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” referring to previous incidents.

“To put it mildly, I don’t always agree with the American side’s assessment and interpretation of these incidents,” Tusk said in the press conference.

He added that U.S. officials have access to the wreckage from Friday’s incursion. “I think that in this particular case, no one will try to pretend anymore that this was just an innocent accident,” Tusk said.

Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the objects fell at three locations in southeastern Poland: Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz. The object found at Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Ch-101 cruise missile, he said. A second object was also believed to be a missile, Kosiniak-Kamysz added, while the third was probably a jet-powered drone.

Tusk pointed to a possible connection to military exercises by the “coalition of the willing” in nearby Nowa Dęba. Led by France and Britain, the drills involve 11 countries preparing to deploy a multinational force to support Ukraine after a ceasefire.

“We can’t rule out the possibility — and this is a hypothesis — that the provocation was also connected to the exercises taking place in Poland,” he said.

World.title: German defense minister apologizes for calling US criticism of Ukraine strikes ‘stupid’
World.content:
“But I also made clear — and he sees it the same way — that we simply have different views on this.” The two sides “agree to disagree,” Pistorius said.

The apology follows a public clash at Tuesday’s meeting of Ukraine’s military backers in Brussels. Colby questioned the effectiveness of Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and other targets, arguing they had done little to end the war or halt Russian advances.

In a joint news conference following the meeting, Pistorius said: “Criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military … targets is quite a stupid thing.”

The minister on Friday acknowledged that his language had been inappropriate, explaining that he had reached for the wrong expression while responding to a question in English. “I shouldn’t have done that,” he said.

During Tuesday's conference, U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting also backed Ukraine, but used less colorful language to show his disagreement with Colby, saying: “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war.”

The exchange highlighted differences between Washington and Berlin over Ukraine’s military strategy at a time when Germany is helping finance the development and production of Ukrainian long-range weapons and is Kyiv's largest financial backer.

World.title: Marine Le Pen’s party faces scrutiny over alleged leaks from interior ministry
World.content:
A senior civil servant is under investigation for reportedly passing on confidential judicial information to the National Rally.

PARIS — French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Friday summoned a senior civil servant who is under judicial investigation for allegedly leaking confidential information to the far-right National Rally.

Hugues Moutouh, the senior state representative in the Centre-Val de Loire region, is under investigation by prosecutors in Paris for reportedly passing on information about judicial investigations into Marine Le Pen’s party, according to multiple French outlets including Le Monde, which first reported on the allegations.

The investigation was opened in July and Moutouh has not been formally charged, Le Monde reported. Civil servants are bound by professional confidentiality, and sharing information on a judicial investigation is also an offense under French law.

World.title: Thousands protest across Europe demanding better wages and services
World.content:
Workers and students took to the streets across Europe on Friday, demanding higher wages, better living conditions and greater investment in public services.

 

The demonstrations follow weeks of protests over rising housing costs, worsening education conditions and increased military spending, with many calling for peace and more funding for healthcare and welfare.

Italy: Protesters demand higher wages and better public services

In Italy, a 24-hour strike called by the Italian General Confederation of Labour (CGIL) trade union sparked demonstrations in more than 100 locations.

Protesters criticised stagnant wages, rising living costs and what organisers described as the government's failure to improve public services and protect workers' rights.

The protests also drew opposition leaders, who joined demonstrations and criticised Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government over wages and social spending.

The strike, which coincided with the International Day of Student Mobilisation, affected both public and private sectors, disrupting public transport in several cities, as well as schools and some health facilities.

Planned strikes by air transport workers were cancelled for Friday, although separate walkouts involving airport staff remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice airports.

Authorities deployed additional police in several Italian cities where multiple demonstrations took place.

Croatia, Austria and Germany: Students call for education over military spending

In Croatia, students boycotted classes and protested in around a dozen cities, demanding more investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.

In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more education funding and less spending on weapons. Police dispersed the demonstration following reported disturbances, using pepper spray and making several arrests.

In Germany, demonstrators called for greater investment in education and opposed a possible return to compulsory military service. The rallies followed protests on 31 October that drew thousands of people into the streets, with violence reported in some cities.

World.title: Europe Tonight: EU and UK strike post-Brexit reset deal as Russian missiles hit Poland
World.content:
EU and UK sign Brussels summit deal

At today’s summit in Brussels, EU and UK leaders agreed to ease barriers on food exports, link carbon emissions systems, and launch a youth mobility scheme. Both sides also pledged to debate their future relationship, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalling a potentially closer arrangement after the next election.

 

Russian missiles hit Poland amid reports of US peace trade-off

Two Russian missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during deadly strikes on Ukraine overnight an incident Warsaw condemned as an intentional provocation. The attacks came hours after Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin jointly vowed to pursue global peace, and amid reports that Washington is considering NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv ceding the Donbas region. We bring you full analysis on what this means for European security.

COP31 runs into weekend overtime over four sticking points

Finally, negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya are pushing talks into the weekend after failing to reach a deal on its final scheduled day. Talks remain deadlocked over four key issues: a concrete roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, ensuring the 35% by 2035 electrification goal relies on clean energy, delivering climate finance, and guaranteeing a just transition that leaves no one behind.

When and where to watch Europe Tonight?

You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.

In just 28 minutes, our new format brings the day's top stories through a European lens, with live analysis and debate with MEPs and leaders.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 20th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Researchers find that cats tailor their communication to get human attention
World.content:
Researchers have found that cats are remarkably good at getting our attention and adapting the way they communicate with us. They use a combination of vocalisations, eye contact and body language. And we humans seem more than happy to play along.

 

A purr with a hidden message

One particularly interesting study, published in 2009 by researchers at the University of Sussex, examined how cats use purring when they want food.

Led by researcher Karen McComb, the team identified a distinctive type of purring known as "solicitation purring". This special purr contains a high-pitched sound that resembles a human baby's cry, making it particularly difficult for people to ignore.

It is a clever acoustic trick that seems to work remarkably well on their human housemates.

This insistent purr combines the familiar deep rumble with a high-pitched sound resembling a baby's cry. People who listened to recordings of this type of purring rated it as more urgent and less pleasant than ordinary purring. It seems we are particularly sensitive to sounds that remind us of a baby crying for attention.

A friendly blink: body language is part of the repertoire, too

Cats don't just use their voices to get their way. Their eyes also play an important role in how they communicate.

A 2020 study published in the journal Scientific Reports explored what is known as slow blinking. This is when cats gently narrow their eyes before closing them briefly.

The researchers found that cats responded to slow blinking from their owners, often blinking back. They were also more likely to approach people who had given them this friendly signal.

Slow blinking is therefore considered a form of positive communication between cats and humans. Anyone wanting to tell their feline companion "I like you" can try a gentle, slow blink. Who knows – you might even get one in return.

Cats don't just miaow at random – they deliberately communicate with their humans

Just how skilfully cats use their voices is illustrated by a new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil. For the experiment, researchers observed 38 pet cats sitting in front of a closed plastic box containing their favourite food. The cats could smell the food but were unable to open the box themselves. Each cat was observed for one minute, first with an attentive person present and then alone.

The results were striking: when a person was in the room, the researchers recorded a total of 86 miaows. When the cats were alone, that number dropped to just 20. While miaowing, the animals also frequently sought eye contact, alternating their gaze between their human companion and the food box.

The researchers suggest that cats direct their vocalisations specifically at people they hope will help them. However, whether the animals consciously follow a particular strategy remains an open question.

Archive. The governor of New Hampshire, Chris Sununu, is greeted by a kitten on 28 July 2021 at the Salem Animal Rescue League animal shelter in Salem, New Hampshire. AP Photo

A cat may therefore know exactly when it is worth appealing to a human – and when it is better not to bother.

They even know their own names

Anyone who thinks their cat only responds when food is involved may be underestimating these little furry companions.

A study published in 2019 in the journal Scientific Reports found that domestic cats can recognise their own names, distinguishing them from other words and even from the names of other cats.

The cats responded differently to hearing their own names than to hearing similar words. That does not mean, however, that every cat comes running when called. Unlike dogs, which often trot over eagerly at the sound of their name, cats seem to prefer to acknowledge the information first and then decide, entirely on their own terms, whether responding is worth the effort.

Humans don't always understand cats

As skilfully as cats communicate, understanding one another is not always straightforward.

A study published in 2024 in Applied Animal Behaviour Science examined how well people can interpret cats' signals.

For the study, 630 people were shown videos of cats in different situations. The researchers assessed how accurately participants could identify the animals' emotional states based on their vocalisations, body language or a combination of the two.

The results were striking: when people could both see a cat's body language and hear its vocalisations, they correctly identified its emotional state in 91.8 per cent of cases. When relying on sounds alone, the figure dropped to 72.2 per cent.

Participants found it particularly difficult to recognise when cats were feeling uncomfortable or unhappy.

A miaow alone does not necessarily reveal what is going on inside a cat's head. Anyone hoping to understand their feline companion should also pay attention to its ears, tail, eyes and overall posture.

Manipulation or simply very good communication?

Over generations of living alongside humans, cats seem to have developed ways of communicating that are particularly effective with us. Whether they consciously manipulate their owners is difficult to establish scientifically. What the studies do show, however, is that cats are remarkably good at picking up on human attention and adapting their signals accordingly.

An insistent purr, a gentle blink or a well-timed miaow can sometimes achieve more than even the most convincing argument.

Perhaps cats have simply figured out how humans work.

World.title: Morocco commits €366 million to build a national defence industry by 2035
World.content:
King Mohammed VI has allocated 4 billion dirhams (€366 million) from the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development to launch a national defence industry roadmap, the Moroccan Royal Cabinet announced on Wednesday.

 

The plan sets 2035 as its target date, with three main goals: creating around 50,000 direct and indirect jobs, meeting 40% of the Royal Armed Forces' and security services' equipment needs through domestic production, and generating more than 65% of defence industry revenues from exports.

The roadmap will be backed by a new strategic agency responsible for implementing national defence industry policy and supporting investors, alongside an industrial holding company to organise the production ecosystem and mobilise public and private capital.

Two new industrial zones dedicated to defence manufacturing will be created in Ben Guerir and Benslimane, adding to existing defence zones in Nouaceur and Sidi Yahya.

Morocco is seeking to leverage its existing expertise in automotive, aviation and electronics manufacturing to develop a domestic defence sector.

Priority areas include drones and autonomous systems, land and naval systems, defence electronics, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. The strategy also covers dual-use technologies with both civilian and military applications.

According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Morocco ranks among Africa's leading importers of major weapon systems.

International partnerships

Morocco has begun forming partnerships with foreign defence companies. The Indian group Tata Advanced Systems is cooperating with Morocco to manufacture WhAP 8×8 armoured vehicles in Berrechid, aiming to progressively increase the share of locally produced components.

Moroccan company MMI manufactures military turrets and remotely controlled weapon systems, forming an initial base for broader domestic production.

The Emirati defence group EDGE signed two agreements with Morocco's National Defence Administration at the Marrakech Air Show in October.

The first is a memorandum of understanding to explore manufacturing small arms and aircraft engines in Morocco through local partnerships.

The second covers supplying Desert Sting 16 and Thunder P-31 guided munitions to the Royal Moroccan Air Force for integration into its fleet of unmanned combat aircraft.

The king also instructed authorities to establish a specialised academy offering advanced training programmes in partnership with industrial companies, drawing on Moroccan civilian and military expertise, including professionals based abroad.

A programme to channel young talent into the sector and adapt vocational training to defence industry needs — particularly in engineering, electronics and digital fields — was also ordered.

World.title: Spain requires data centres to draw 80% of their electricity from renewables
World.content:
The Spanish government has approved new rules for data centres that set renewable energy consumption requirements, water and energy efficiency standards and digital sovereignty obligations, with the aim of aligning the growth of these infrastructures with the capacity of the electricity system and the country’s environmental commitments.

 

The Royal Decree, approved on Friday by the Council of Ministers, requires data centres to prove that 80% of their electricity consumption comes from renewable sources, with hourly matching between generation and consumption and additionality criteria to drive new clean production capacity.

The regulation provides for long-term power supply contracts, self-consumption and energy storage. It also establishes a voluntary transitional regime for operators that agree to the possibility of being disconnected with priority when this is necessary to safeguard the stability of the electricity grid.

Stricter energy and environmental requirements

The rules introduce provisional limits on water and electricity use in data centres: they will have to use water more efficiently and cut the energy needed for their operation, while European criteria are finalised. The text also incorporates into national law other transparency and water and energy efficiency requirements laid down by European regulation, adapting them to Spain’s specific circumstances.

The regulation introduces sustainability reporting obligations for the largest facilities and sets specific data protection and digital sovereignty requirements for high-category information systems under the National Security Framework.

In these cases, the most sensitive data must remain within the European Economic Area and controls will be tightened on access from third countries to administration, maintenance and support tasks.

Failure to comply with certain obligations may lead to financial compensation and sanctions, including suspension of grid access and connection rights for up to three years. Projects that are already being processed will generally have six months to adapt to the new conditions.

35 GW between permitted capacity and projects in the queue

The decision comes at a time of strong growth in demand for digital infrastructure in Spain. Third Vice-President and Minister for Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, said that data centres currently have 15 gigawatts (GW) of granted access capacity to the electricity grid, while a further 20 GW remain on the waiting list.

The minister warned that, without control measures, the expansion of these facilities could generate an additional cost of up to 5,000 million euros per year in the electricity system, according to government estimates: 4,000 million from the impact on wholesale prices and another 1,000 million from capacity mechanisms.

"In the absence of this Royal Decree, we would see an impact of 5,000 million euros on our bills," said Energy Transition Minister Sara Aagesen. "We have different scenarios, but it would lead, for example, to industrial consumers having to pay 25% more for the electricity they use," she added. These figures are government forecasts for a hypothetical scenario, not costs already incurred or savings guaranteed by the new rules.

17,142 million euros of investment in the electricity grid

At the same time, the government has approved new electricity grid planning up to 2030, providing for investments of 17.142 million euros to expand and reinforce infrastructure and meet rising demand. The plan includes capacity for new forms of consumption, including data centres, although it is not specifically dedicated to these facilities.

Spain is seeking to consolidate its position as a destination for international investment in data centres, drawing on its renewable resources, connectivity and strategic location in Europe.

The new regulation is designed to tie that growth to greater energy and environmental efficiency, in a context where the availability of electricity, water and connection capacity has become one of the key factors in the development of these projects. The impact on ongoing projects and future investment will depend on how the new obligations are applied and on the deadlines set out in the final text.

World.title: France investigates suspected confidential leaks to Le Pen's far-right party
World.content:
French authorities are investigating whether a former senior Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information about judicial investigations to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party, months before the presidential election.

 

According to Le Monde newspaper, Hugues Moutouh, now prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region, is suspected of sharing information about investigations into the financing of the party's 2022 and 2024 election campaigns.

Judicial investigation

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed on Friday that an investigation had been opened and that he had summoned Moutouh for a meeting.

The Paris prosecutor's office told The Associated Press news agency it was investigating possible breaches of professional confidentiality and investigative secrecy, as well as the handling of information obtained through these offences.

No one has been formally charged, prosecutors said, adding that investigators searched the National Rally's headquarters on 9 November.

Le Pen has not commented on the case.

"If the facts are confirmed, they are obviously very serious," Nuñez told BFM TV.

Further controversies ahead of the election

The investigation adds to a series of controversies involving Le Pen's party less than six months before France's presidential election.

In September, Jordan Bardella, Le Pen's choice for prime minister if elected, was accused of making antisemitic remarks as a young party member. Bardella, 31, strongly denied writing the comments reported by investigative website Mediapart.

Le Pen, 58 is also facing legal challenges after being sentenced in July to a year of home detention with electronic monitoring following an embezzlement conviction. She has appealed to France's highest court and believes she will not have to wear the device.

Despite her legal troubles, Le Pen leads opinion polls ahead of next year's presidential election to succeed Emmanuel Macron.

World.title: Deepening EU–Canada ties: From critical minerals and defence to erasmus+
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Europe and Canada have always been natural allies, through both good times and bad, and are growing even closer. It´s not only politics, trade and security, but culture, sports and way of life that joins us. Next year will mark a historic milestone when Canada will compete at the Eurovision Song Contest for the first time. May the best song win!

 

Canada is a trusted democratic partner

For Europe, Canada is a trusted democratic partner. As Canada´s Prime Minister Mark Carney said when addressing the European Parliament: “Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication”. And those shared values are translating into concrete cooperation.

Trade is obvious area where the partnership has delivered tangible results.

Trade is obvious area where the partnership has delivered tangible results. Since the provisional application of Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), bilateral trade in goods and services has grown by around 80%, rising from €72.1 billion in 2016 to €130 billion in 2025.

More opportunities lie ahead: critical raw materials and defence

And more opportunities lie ahead. For example, Europe is seeking to reduce its dependence on China, particularly in the supply of critical raw materials. Fortunately, Canada is one of the few democratic partners with the resources and capacity to supply the EU with minerals essential to batteries, semiconductors, defence, aerospace, renewable energy and telecommunications.

Canada is also a major producer of uranium, cobalt, nickel and zinc, as well as the world's leading producer of potash.

Europe must build a circle of trusted friends around our continent and, here, Canada plays a vital role.

During this time of Russian aggression, defence and security are of the utmost importance. Europe must build a circle of trusted friends around our continent and, here, Canada plays a vital role. Canada has stood firmly with Ukraine and contributes directly to European security through its leadership of NATO operations in Latvia.

Canada’s defence spending reached 2.0% of GDP this year, and its new federal budget sets out a path towards more than 4% by the end of the decade. This is an ambitious commitment, bringing Canada closer to the level of investment pursued by frontline allies like Poland.

Earlier this year, Canada also became the first non-European country to join the €150 billion defence procurement instrument, SAFE, though more remains to be done to better integrate Canada into European defence markets and defence industry development.

Education and research offer other chances for mutual benefits

Education offers another chance for mutual benefits. Canada consistently performs well in international education, remaining among the strongest OECD countries. According to PISA 2025, it outperforms most EU Member States in science and reading.

We can deepen this relationship by welcoming Canada into the Erasmus+ exchange scheme

We can deepen this relationship by welcoming Canada into the Erasmus+ exchange scheme, one of the most tangible benefits of European integration for young people. Following the launch of formal negotiations at the recent Canada-EU Summit in Montréal, Canada is poised to become the first non-European country associated with the programme, which funds people and organisations to study and train abroad.

Research cooperation is also moving forward. In 2024, Canada became associated with Pillar II of Horizon Europe, which supports collaborative research across a wide scientific and technological fields. Although this is an important milestone, there is still room to strengthen Canada’s participation. Negotiations on deeper participation have now begun and we fully support Canada’s closer integration into Horizon Europe.

Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together

Generations of Europeans have made Canada their home, contributing to Canadian society while maintaining ties with their countries of origin. These communities help sustain cultural links, connect businesses and create opportunities for younger generations to study and work on both sides of the Atlantic.

From critical minerals and trade to defence, education and research, there is considerable scope to work closer together.

The case for a stronger EU–Canada partnership is clear. From critical minerals and trade to defence, education and research, there is considerable scope to work closer together. Great partnerships, like great oaks, do not grow overnight. But with the right foundations, they can weather even the roughest political storms. We must make full use of the opportunities available under our existing treaties and agreements. Whether we describe this relationship as an alliance or an association matters less than what we achieve together.

In an increasingly uncertain world, Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together, whatever the political weather.

As the strongest political force in the EU political system with majorities in the main institutions, the Commission, the Council and the Parliament, the EPP is an effective broker. We are determined to drive the renewed political momentum between the EU and Canada forward. In an increasingly uncertain world, Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together, whatever the political weather. The timing of our visit couldn’t be better.

Andrzej Halicki, MEP, Vice-president, EPP Group

Zeljana Zovko, Vice-president, EPP Group

Łukasz Kohut, Vice-President, Subcommittee of the Human Rights

Loucas Fourlas, Chair, Delegation to the EU-Serbia Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
World.content:
Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023 .

Oil interests and climate promises collide at the COP31 summit To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

2028 climate report card risks delay

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Poorer countries are calling on the nations responsible for the largest share of greenhouse gas emissions to assume financial responsibility for adaptation efforts Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking off the record.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable. "We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

EU stresses need to 'protect the integrity of climate science'

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: at past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

Disinformation hindering climate action

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

DW was able to obtain a copy of a presentation which included misleading statements on the COP's electrification targets, one of the key goals at this year's talks. Turkey has proposed boosting global electrification to 35% by 2035, to reduce the world's reliance on planet-warming fossil fuels.

The contents of the presentation, said to have been leaked to some states in advance, was confirmed to DW by two countries. Its origin, however, could not be verified.

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs
World.content:
Skip next section Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in new German defense and technology investments.

During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz said, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation."

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry."

That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.

The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace."

Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations."

Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.

He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

World.content:
11/20/2026 November 20, 2026 German defense minister open to talks with Russia

Pistorius' comments on talks with Russia came while he was visiting Poland Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius "welcomed in every respect" a move by Russian President Vladimir Putin to consult Europeans on the future of Ukraine (see entries below for more details).

During a trip to the Polish capital Warsaw, Pistorius added that declining such an invitation to Moscow would send the "completely wrong signal."

"We need to talk. Only by talking can we ultimately achieve results," he said.

Pistorius said reaching an agreement was the goal — not simply sitting down in a room together.

"He [Putin] must now show that he truly means what he says and that he will then take the necessary steps to ensure that, at the very least, a ceasefire is established and that peace-sustaining stability can once again take hold in Europe," the German minister said.

The comments came the same day a pair of Russian missiles and a drone were reported to have violated Polish airspace (see entries below).

While Russian officials said Germany, France and the UK had been invited to send representatives to talks on Ukraine, no details about a time or place for such talks have been announced.

World.title: Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future
World.content:
Never before have young people faced so many challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents later in life?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

Erik Sczygiol was deputy secretary-general of the German Conference of Student Representatives until recently Image: Oliver Pieper/DW

Gen Z is better educated but faces a bleaker future

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Young people are underrepresented in the German parliament

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Florian Brod has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years Image: Oliver Pieper/DW

Political participation often remains purely symbolic

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

'Small extremist minority' turn Germany's youth protests violent To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
World.content:
German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

Can crisis reinvent the car again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Berger agreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and components Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside Germany Image: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."

PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Production remains resilient despite decline

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

Analysts call for faster reform

For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

World.title: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience
World.content:
The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

But it doesn't have to stay this way.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

What Brazil does differently from the US

Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:

Report cases within 24 hours

Investigate within 48 hours

Vaccinate people close to the case within 72 hours

It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why the US lost its measle-free status

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

In August 2026, when US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children, it came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. As PAHO's Jarbas Barbosa says above, avoiding vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear; Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners unprotected.

In the Texas counties, where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved. In 24 states, so many children were exempt that those states couldn't reach the 95% threshold even if every other child got vaccinated.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The 95% measles vaccination rule explained

It all comes down to math.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak start is likely to start.

In the US, where vaccination rates at kindergartens have dropped to 92%, that small difference is big enough to cause a measles outbreak.

The picture is mixed worldwide

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as this time (November) in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

What you need to know about measles

Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

World.title: Is Pakistan backing anti-Taliban groups in Afghanistan?
World.content:
The Taliban rulers in Afghanistan have accused Pakistan of aiding and sheltering armed resistance groups. The allegations come amid heightened tensions and are likely to deepen the rift between the two neighbors.

The Taliban authorities in Afghanistan claim that the Pakistani government is supporting armed Afghan groups that are opposed to their rule, an accusation Islamabaddenies.

Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi recently alleged that Pakistan had launched a "project to destabilize Afghanistan."

He claimed that "thousands of armed individuals have gathered along the Durand Line [Afghanistan-Pakistan border] to undermine the stability achieved in Afghanistan."

The accusations come after months of border clashes between Afghan Taliban and Pakistani forces.

In July, the Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF), an anti-Taliban group, reportedly clashed with Taliban forces in the Zebak district of Badakhshan, a northeastern Afghan province. The group said it also carried out attacks in Nooristan and Kunar provinces in October.

Another "resistance group," the United Front of Afghanistan, claimed it attacked Taliban forces in Kandahar province along the border with Pakistan.

"The people who created insecurity in Badakhshan crossed from Chitral [in Pakistan] and later fled back to Chitral. They had been brought in. Even Pakistani military personnel were with them," alleged Zabihullah Mujahid, the Taliban's main spokesperson, in an interview with DW's Pashto-Dari service in September.

Pakistan's Ministry of Information swiftly dismissed the allegations as propaganda.

Groups that oppose Taliban rule in Afghanistan say they are not supported by any external force, and their resistance is purely indigenous.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pakistan's 'leverage' amid tense ties

More than five years since returning to power in Kabul, the Taliban have consolidated their control over Afghanistan and largely suppressed both armed resistance groups and political dissidents.

Shinkai Karokhail, a former Afghan lawmaker, told DW it would be logistically difficult for anti-Taliban Afghan groups to cross the Pakistani border and enter Afghanistan without Islamabad's support, referring to clashes in Badakhshan and Nooristan provinces. "It is simply impossible," she said.

The Taliban themselves maintained close ties with Pakistan in the 1990s during their first stint in power. Some US officials have even claimed that Islamabad didn't relinquish its support to the Islamist group even after the 2001 September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States. Islamabad has always refuted these allegations.

Afrasiab Khattak, a Pakistani political analyst and former senator, believes that Pakistani support for anti-Taliban groups is "real."

"Taliban opponents come to Islamabad, hold meetings, and it is a part of Pakistan's policy toward Afghanistan," he told DW.

Qandil Abbas, an associate professor of politics and international relations at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, disagrees.

"Pakistan may provide political support [to Taliban opponents], but not military support," she told DW.

Ali Ahmad Jalali, a professor at the Near East South Asia Center for Strategic Studies at the National Defense University in Washington DC, said it is possible that Islamabad is backing opponents of the Taliban as "leverage."

"When such incidents take place along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, and given Pakistan's history of support for Afghan groups, it would not be surprising if Pakistan is supporting these groups," Jalali said.

Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Islamabad accuses Taliban of similar tactics

Pakistani officials have repeatedly demanded that the Taliban take action against anti-Pakistan militant groups, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group responsible for attacking Pakistani civilians and soldiers, and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), an outlawed armed separatist group active in its western Balochistan province.

Islamabad alleges that these groups organize and launch attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory with Taliban support.

"Meaningful progress requires Afghan authorities to address legitimate security concerns of neighboring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism," Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said this week at the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) summit in Islamabad.

The Pakistani government said on Friday that Afghanistan was not invited to participate in the ECO gathering as Pakistan does not recognize the Taliban regime in Kabul.

Jalali, who served as Afghanistan's interior minister from 2003 to 2005, argued that Islamabad is demanding something the Taliban may neither be willing nor able to provide.

"Pakistan wants the Taliban to cooperate in fighting against groups such as the TTP. But the TTP has long fought alongside the Afghan Taliban. There are ideological as well as friendly ties between the two. They seek a similar political system, and some Afghan Taliban members may even be among TTP fighters," the analyst added.

Experts also point to the Taliban's efforts to strengthen relations with India, Pakistan's long-standing regional rival, as a cause of concern for Islamabad.

Malek Sitez, an Afghan international relations researcher, argued that Pakistan was not keen on Kabul getting closer to New Delhi but added that Pakistan no longer had the kind of influence over Afghanistan that it had in the past.

Under Taliban shadow, Afghans in Pakistan look to Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is Pakistan seeking to remove the Taliban from power?

Despite accusations and counteraccusations from both sides, Jalali did not believe that Pakistan was seeking regime change in Afghanistan.

"I do not think Pakistan can or wants to overthrow the Taliban and replace them with another group," he underlined. Instead, he stressed, Islamabad's objective is to pressure the Taliban into cooperating against the TTP.

Aziz Barez, a political analyst, was of the view that Afghan groups opposed to the Taliban could not fully trust Islamabad, adding that they may welcome alleged Pakistani support but are also aware that such backing could be temporary.

"It is possible that Pakistan and the Taliban will resolve their differences tomorrow and become close allies again," he told DW.

Ahmad Waheed Ahmady and Helay Asad contributed to this report.

World.title: Germany face belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag
World.content:
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.

Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals—after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."

Historical success for Germany against Belgium

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway – a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

World.title: La distancia entre el PP y el PSOE se estrecha al mínimo pese a la victoria de Feijóo en el debate
World.content:
Alberto Núñez Feijóo ganó con claridad, en opinión de los ciudadanos, su cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez. La encuesta de urgencia realizada por 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la SER no deja lugar a dudas: el 43% de los entrevistados señala como triunfador al líder del PP, diez puntos más de los que apuntan al socialista. Pero no todo son malas noticias para el PSOE, porque el acumulado del tracking diario de los últimos cuatro días estrecha al máximo la diferencia entre los dos grandes partidos, apenas siete décimas, equivalente a un empate técnico.

El aparente contrasentido se explica por las diferencias entre las muestras. Y por un detalle relevante: el debate, con una media de 10 millones de espectadores de audiencia, fue mucho más seguido por los votantes del PP. Un 61,5% del total de simpatizantes del primer partido de la oposición asegura que siguió el cara a cara hasta el final, mientras que entre los del PSOE baja hasta el 49%. La encuesta de urgencia fue elaborada con una muestra de 500 entrevistas en línea, recogidas entre las 23.43 horas del jueves, recién concluido el programa, hasta las 8.27 de este viernes 20. Esos datos se han incorporado hasta engrosar otro contigente mayor de 2.000 entrevistas que reflejan las intenciones de voto manifestadas en los últimos cuatro días.

En el debate, Feijóo se mostró mucho más convincente que Sánchez (47,9% frente a 38,8%) y algo más competente (43,5% frente a 40,9%). Pese a aparecer como derrotado, el actual presidente aún fue visto como más carismático que su contrincante: 46,8% frente a 39%. El duelo dialéctico fue seguido por casi tres de cada cuatro de los entrevistados, aunque no llegan a la mitad los que afirman haber asistido íntegramente

En las opiniones sobre el cara a cara pesa de modo determinante la simpatía política de los entrevistados. Entre los votantes del PP y Vox, Feijóo es visto abrumadoramente como triunfador. Sin embargo, tres de cada cuatro simpatizantes socialistas eligen a Sánchez, así como uno de cada tres del Frente Amplio (FA), la misma porción de los que manifiestan que no ganó ninguno de los dos.

Los 500 entrevistados por 40dB. tras el debate también manifestaron su intención de voto y esos resultados se incorporaron a los recogidos en los tres días anteriores hasta conformar una muestra de 2.000. Con esa perspectiva más amplia, y a pesar del revés del cara a cara, el PSOE consigue su mejor resultado no solo desde el comienzo de la campaña, sino también de toda la legislatura, en la que el instituto demoscópico ha realizado barómetros mensuales para EL PAÍS y la SER. De ese modo la diferencia entre los dos grandes partidos se reduce a siete décimas, la mitad de la ventaja que el PP logró sobre el PSOE en las anteriores elecciones de 2023. Lo que no impide que el conjunto del bloque de la derecha conserve su amplia distancia, con 189 escaños, 13 más que la mayoría absoluta.

Los socialistas ganan un punto en esta última entrega del tracking, sumarían un 31,2% y, aun con cinco décimas menos que en 2023, obtendrían tres escaños más que entonces, hasta 124. El PP, con el 31,9%, quedaría un poco por debajo de su cosecha en las anteriores elecciones y se anotaría 131 diputados, seis menos que en el Congreso saliente. Pero la tendencia general de los populares desde el inicio de la campaña apunta a una recuperación, cimentada sobre todo en el freno a las fugas hacia Vox. La encuesta incluso advierte un pequeño flujo en sentido contrario, de antiguos votantes de la extrema derecha que ahora se decantan por Feijóo.

Aun así, Vox sería la formación que más crece comparado con los anteriores comicios, casi cinco puntos, hasta situarse en el 17,1%. El Frente Amplio y las confluencias territoriales en las que participa siguen sin sumar mucho más allá del 5%, mientras que Podemos quedaría fuera del Congreso.
