World.title: La contención de Sánchez en el cara a cara divide al PSOE por su “pasividad” ante Feijóo
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez recuperará esta tarde en Santiago de Compostela el espíritu combativo que se ha convertido en la marca de la casa de la campaña del PSOE después de concederle toda la iniciativa a Alberto Núñez Feijóo en el cara a cara. Un giro de 180º grados que resaltará todavía más la sorpresiva estrategia adoptada en el debate electoral: el perfil presidencialista y extremadamente contenido de Sánchez para evitar el cuerpo a cuerpo con el líder del PP no cumplió con las expectativas de líderes territoriales e incluso de miembros de la dirección federal del PSOE. Cargos que siguieron el debate en el cuartel general de los socialistas se quedaron “con ganas” de que Sánchez “hubiera dado más caña”.

“Los nuestros ya están convencidos y se ha dirigido a los indecisos. Nadie va a dejar de votar a Pedro por el debate. Es evidente que estaba calculado a diferencia de 2023, cuando Feijóo le desconcertó. Ahí sí que no hubo ninguna estrategia con la que escudarnos. ¿Qué vaya a surtir efecto? Ya veremos, es una campaña en la que se está innovando mucho, y esta es la última prueba. Lo que está claro es que el presidente nunca deja de sorprendernos", relativiza un responsable de la cúpula del PSOE. “Ah, que el debate no era para los nuestros”, ironiza otro integrante de la ejecutiva federal; “eso es una cosa y otra que Pedro me pareció alguien desconocido, porque puedes ser educado y no entrar al barro, pero ser contundente con la catarata de bulos de Feijóo”. “Feijóo colocó una piara y o eres cerdo o no sabes jugar. ¿Su primera intervención es admisible? ¿A partir de aquí a qué juego jugamos? Colocó de primeras el barro… ¿Y entonces qué haces?“, observa una ministra; explica que Sánchez ha sido recibido con aplausos en el Consejo de Ministros extraordinario.

La justificación oficial de La Moncloa y Ferraz es que esa apuesta por el centro, en una legislatura caracterizada por la política de bloques y una fortísima polarización, puede decantar el 29-N, el último escaño en juego, en algunos casos por unos cientos de votos, en las 18 provincias que el partido tiene señaladas como prioritarias. Pero a nadie se le escapa el contraste con el desempeño y energía de Sánchez en los mítines y entrevistas desde la precampaña. “Para nuestras bases fue un bajonazo, como si les hubiera caído encima una bomba nuclear”, resume un alcalde de una gran ciudad.

Montero: “¡Más debates y nos faltan escaños para rellenarlos!”

La perspectiva oficial no puede ser más diferente. “¡Más debates y nos faltan escaños en el Congreso para rellenarlos!”, irradió optimismo María Jesús Montero en el chat de la ejecutiva del PSOE, según fuentes conocedoras del mensaje. “Uno educado y propositivo. El otro mentiroso y marrullero. Cada uno definiéndose a la perfección”, escribió el exministro Óscar Puente, que forma parte de la dirección socialista, en redes sociales. “Vimos a un presidente sereno y constructivo frente al candidato de la crispación y la mentira”, ha apostillado hoy Pilar Alegría, secretaria general del PSOE de Aragón, en Tarazona (Zaragoza). Su homólogo extremeño, Álvaro Sánchez Cotrina, vio a “un Pedro Sánchez preparado para seguir siendo presidente y a un Feijóo preparado para seguir siendo el líder de la oposición”. “Cuando se tiene el privilegio de gobernar este país, no se puede estar entrando todo el día en el barro, en el insulto, en la descalificación y en la polarización”, ha sentenciado en Navalmoral de la Mata (Cáceres).

Pero incluso los defensores del plan reconocen en privado que se trató de una maniobra “arriesgada”. “Yo no entendí la estrategia, por muy enfocada que estuviera a la moderación, captar voto de centro, no ser faltón, no entrar al trapo de los bulos, ser educado... No sé si funcionó. Cuando me toca ir a debates, voy mentalizado de no calentarme, pero eso es una cosa y otra dar la sensación de pasividad, aunque fuera buscada”, comparte un secretario general autonómico.

“Hay muchas estrategias dentro de una campaña, y esta es la que se ha querido hacer en este momento”, defendió Rebeca Torró a su llegada del debate en Ferraz. La secretaria de Organización subrayó que el objetivo era “ganar en un determinado grupo de electores” que, según los trackings internos del PSOE, pueden suponer la victoria en las elecciones y revalidar La Moncloa, un escenario que no detecta ninguna casa de encuestas salvo el CIS. La fórmula para conseguirlo, incidió la número tres de los socialistas, era “retratar” a Feijóo dejándole hablar: “Podía haber aportado algo, no hizo nada salvo insultar, mentir y lanzar preguntas como una metralleta a lo Trump”. El ministro de Presidencia, Félix Bolaños, ha ahondado este viernes en esa línea en un acto en Cuenca: “Me da la sensación de que ayer nos estábamos dirigiendo a públicos diferentes, Feijóo lo hizo a ese electorado fronterizo del PP y Vox, y Pedro Sánchez a esos ciudadanos que son mayoría, que son sensatos, educados, que no insultan, no odian, no faltan al respeto, no interrumpen y que quieren escuchar propuestas”.

“La militancia no lo entenderá, pero había que dirigirse a un público no convencido para que nos vote”, concede un alto mando del PSOE que, como todos los cuadros consultados, está convencido de que el tono de Sánchez en el debate a cuatro de la próxima semana, con Santiago Abascal en el plató como potencial vicepresidente del Gobierno, será muy diferente. “Aceptemos que el cara a cara no era un debate para convencer a los convencidos. Puedo comprender la estrategia, pero he echado en falta su ironía —de Sánchez— para dejar a Feijóo en evidencia y rebatir su sarta de mentiras. Aunque igual eso podía espantar a esos votantes no ideologizados a por los que íbamos”, añade otro miembro de la cúpula del PSOE.

“En 2023 caímos en la trampa del PP de explicar que todo lo que decía Feijóo era mentira y eso es lo que esperaba el PP que hiciéramos. Feijóo mintió en el cara a cara más de 20 veces, por eso no entramos”, alegan en La Moncloa. Esa lógica no es compartida por quienes echaron en falta que Sánchez defendiera que la financiación de sus primarias en 2017 fue limpia. El presidente guardó silencio y el PP lo explotó a los pocos minutos, moviéndolo por las redes sociales. “Feijóo ya era así, otra cosa es que solo lo supiéramos en Galicia pero ya lo saben en el resto de España. Su único recurso es el barro, el insulto, la difamación y la mentira, más del 60% de los datos que dio eran falsos”, ha resaltado la alcaldesa de A Coruña, Inés Rey. “Cuando alguien interrumpe constantemente y no deja hablar al adversario, o no tiene nada que aportar o quiere ocultar su proyecto. A Feijóo nadie le compraría un coche de segunda mano”, ha abundado el ministro de Hacienda, Arcadi España.

Aun así, las llamadas a reivindicar a Sánchez no despejan el desconcierto en el PSOE. “Hemos perdido una gran oportunidad, entiendo que hay claves que desconozco y el consuelo es que responde a una estrategia. La cuestión es si la estrategia era la correcta”, discrepa un senador que, aparte, cree que Sánchez debería haber empleado “un lenguaje cercano para dirigirse al ciudadano normal”. “Hay que hablar para la gente, ¿qué son los consejos de transparencia, los mapas de riesgos o los grupos de interés? Habla a la calle", coincide un presidente de Diputación.

“Una cosa es parecer educado, limpio y aseado y otra es ser un saco de boxeo”, también se desmarca del discurso de Ferraz un dirigente andaluz. “La contención sacó de quicio a Feijóo. Si en el bloque de la corrupción se terminó hablando de aborto, es que Pedro le comió la tostada”, disiente otro mando de la misma comunidad. “Feijóo se equivocó con avalancha de datos que nadie sigue ni entiende. Sánchez le metió siempre encadenado a Vox y nunca respondió; también hay que destacar eso”, concluye un secretario provincial.

En lo que todo el PSOE coincide es en que el minuto de oro fue el mejor momento de Sánchez. El candidato socialista parafraseó la máxima del “Quien pueda hacer que haga” de José María Aznar, pero adaptándola al electorado progresista. “Quien pueda votar, que vote. Vota con toda tu alma. Vota con toda tu fuerza al PSOE”, animó a la participación. El primer mensaje de este viernes, a las 7.39, en el canal La fuerza de la gente a sus 88.000 seguidores decía lo siguiente: “¡Buenos días, gente! Primera misión del día: ¡Vamos a hacer que el minuto de oro del debate de ayer llegue a todos los rincones! Guarda, dale like y comparte, porque en democracia el poder lo tienes TÚ“.

World.title: Perro de marrón, poco mordedor y la inesperada web sorpresa del PP: el debate en las redes
World.content:
Texto en el que el autor aboga por ideas y saca conclusiones basadas en su interpretación de hechos y datos

—Cuidado con el perro.

44 minutos antes del inicio del debate, el PSOE lanzó este mensaje al grupo de WhatsApp de sus simpatizantes, La Fuerza de la Gente, donde albergan a 87.000 personas (poca broma). El perro apareció después en traje marrón. Y un perro de marrón… poco mordedor. Y llegaron las primeras críticas a X, antes Twitter, y antes nada porque no existía: “Qué color es ese por el amor de Dios”, escribió un usuario. “Es un color comunista”, dijo otro. “Que la de la lotería le deje la chaqueta”. La corbata era roja, eso sí.

Los populares, mientras tanto, fueron más rápidos, mucho más raudos que los socialistas en el debate de la pantalla de las redes sociales. Y dos minutos antes (¡dos minutos antes!) de que empezara el rifirrafe, el equipo de Alberto Núñez Feijóo lanzó por sorpresa una campaña digital con una etiqueta: #sanchezmiente. Y empezó a viralizarse, claro. “#Sanchezmiente. #Sanchezmiente. #Sanchezmiente”.

Sánchez ya había perdido. Y no lo sabía.

Por si fuera poco, también soltaron una bomba inesperada. Una web —sanchezmiente.com—, ya que igual no había quedado claro que, incluso sin comenzar a hablar, también se puede engañar a la gente. El PP (por si había dudas) fue con todo al cara a cara. Activó a todos los suyos para la guerrilla tuitera. Alcaldes, concejales, consejeros, incluso presidentes autonómicos. Todos tenían una orden: ¡tuitead!

El primero en decir que Sánchez había mentido sin decir ni mu fue el presidente aragonés Jorge Azcón, que escribió: “#Sanchezmiente”. Eran las 21.59. Horas antes, Isabel Díaz Ayuso tecleó: “Esta noche, un chupito todos cada vez que Sánchez diga ‘Ayuso’ o ‘Comunidad de Madrid’”. Si las cuentas no fallan, bebió solo un par de tragos. O dicho de otra manera: Sánchez ha estado de Ayuso intermitente.

La web sorpresa del PP, por cierto, se define así: “Verificación del discurso en directo. Datos, contexto y fuentes”. A la hora ya iban 20 supuestas falsedades de Sánchez que, sin saber esto, dijo durante el debate: “Va a dar usted mucho trabajo a los verificadores”. Y Feijóo respondió: “A usted se lo van a decir los verificadores”. La verificación en España está en un plan que ya lo adelantó El Mundo Today hace unos días: “Las cenas de Nochebuena tendrán que contar con un mínimo de dos verificadores”.

Muy comentado también fue el saludo entre ambos (616 días después —se dice pronto, se produce lejos—). Mientras tanto, la guerra digital iba en aumento, con críticas a la actitud tranquila de Sánchez ante la agresividad de Feijóo, que soltaba datos, ataques, frases contundentes. Quizá por eso comenzó a ser tendencia en España “Pedrito”. Otros pedían ya la entrada al plató de Candela Peña, que estaría en su casa, y quién sabe si hablándole así a la tele: “¡Ay, mi Peter!”. En X, incluso, se viralizó un vídeo de Alba Carrillo apuntando con el dedo a la cámara:

—¡Pedro Sánchez, haz algo ya, coño!

Pero nada. Ni rastro: perro de marrón, poco mordedor. Pepe Colubi estuvo más ávido: “Feijóo está interrumpiendo mejor que Sánchez”.

Llegó un punto en que hasta Gabriel Rufián estaba ya harto de Sánchez. Él mismo cogió su móvil y escribió: “Si Feijóo te come así en un debate, es que o no te lo has preparado o es que estás mal asesorado. O las dos”. Cómo sería la cosa que en el grupo de WhatsApp del PSOE comenzaron a hacer lo que no hacía su candidato: avivar a la parroquia con mensajes contundentes.

Primero, en minúsculas: “Feijóo ya recortó en Galicia”. Y luego, quizá al ver que aquello no tiraba, lanzaron las mayúsculas: “NO QUEREMOS RECORTES”; “CERO LECCIONES DEL PARTIDO MÁS CORRUPTO DEL SISTEMA ESPAÑOL”. Y así.

Al terminar —total, qué necesidad— ni pidieron votar a Sánchez como ganador. Se hizo el silencio en el grupo. El PP, por cierto, y quizá para entender cómo iban de sobrados, solo envió un par de mensajes a su parroquía guasapera en todo el día. El último fue a las seis de la tarde. “Nos vemos esta noche”. Y tanto.

World.title: El Supremo mantiene suspendido el voto a 163.000 nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’ aunque ahora vivan en España
World.content:
El Tribunal Supremo ha dado este viernes un paso más en la prohibición a que los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos voten el 29-N. A nueve días de las elecciones, la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo ha instado a la Junta Electoral a impedir que voten 163.355 nuevos españoles que han obtenido la nacionalidad por la Ley de Memoria Democrática, tanto si están inscritos en el Censo Electoral de Residentes Ausentes (CERA) como en el Censo de Residentes en España, a los que, hasta ahora, había dejado fuera de la suspensión. Los magistrados solo permiten que voten los 901 nacionalizados que han acreditado que son descendientes de exiliados por motivos políticos y quienes consigan certificarlo por vía consular antes del 29-N.

La decisión del Supremo llega después de que la Abogacía del Estado cifrara hace unos días en 113.326 los españoles nacionalizados por la llamada ley de nietos que viven en el extranjero y que, por tanto, no podrían participar en las elecciones del 29 de noviembre como consecuencia de la suspensión del derecho al voto decretada por el alto tribunal. Los servicios jurídicos del Gobierno habrían cifrado anteriormente los afectados por esa suspensión en 163.355 personas, pero el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE) redujo el número tras eliminar a los menores de edad, registros duplicados o a personas que no estaban actualmente inscritas en el CERA, que es el único censo que hasta ahora había ordenado modificar.

Tras ese baile de cifras, que el tribunal califica como “de difícil comprensión”, Vox y el partido Iustitia Europa reclamaron al Supremo que ordenara a la Oficina del Censo Electoral que adoptara, respecto de las personas inscritas en el censo de España, la misma medida de suspensión del voto que se había impuesto sobre el censo de extranjeros, ante la sospecha de que alguno de los electores que, según el Gobierno, no figuran ahora en el CERA estén en el CER. Y esto es lo que ha acordado este viernes el Supremo.

En su resolución, la sala insta a la Junta Electoral a garantizar que “ninguna de las 163.355 personas incluidas en el Anexo I de la Orden de 25 de octubre de 2022, de la Directora General de Seguridad Jurídica y Fe Pública [los nacionalizados como hijos y nietos del exilio], pueda figurar como elector en el Censo Electoral, sea en el de electores residentes ausentes que viven en el extranjero, sea en el de electores residentes en España, con excepción de las 901 personas que presentaron certificación consular, o cualesquiera otras que, con anterioridad al día de la votación, aporten dicha certificación consular”.

La medida del Supremo no implica extender la suspensión a más personas de las que ya lo tenían suspendido, pero sí que esas personas no podrán votar aunque se hayan trasladado a vivir a España y ya no estén inscritas en el censo del exterior. Las 163.355 personas que no podrán votar son aquellas cuyas identidades entregó el Gobierno al alto tribunal después de que la Sala de lo Contencioso diera el pasado 23 de octubre cinco días a los ministros Félix Bolaños y José Manuel Albares para que remitieran esa lista al alto tribunal, a la Junta Electoral Central y a la Oficina del Censo Electoral y les amenazara con una multa y posibles responsabilidades penales si no cumplían en el plazo fijado.

Estas personas se nacionalizaron al amparo de la ley de nietos en los consulados de España y, posteriormente, se tramitó su inscripción en el censo del extranjero. El Gobierno ha ido reduciendo esa cifra en sucesivos escritos presentados en el Supremo tras constatar que el listado incluía a personas que, aunque habían adquirido la condición de españoles por la Ley de Memoria, no estaban inscritas en el CERA de las próximas elecciones generales, por lo que no se les consideraba afectados por la suspensión. En este grupo se encuentran 9.707 registros correspondientes a menores de edad o a españoles cuya adquisición de la nacionalidad es posterior a la fecha de cierre del censo electoral del 1 de agosto, el vigente para el 29-N; y casi 3.000 nombres que estaban duplicados en el listado que envió el Gobierno al tribunal, lo que dejó la relación de nacionalizados afectados por la suspensión en 153.355 personas.

Pero, en una revisión posterior, la Oficina del Censo comprobó que solo 117.723 de estos nacionalizados estaban registrados en el CERA, una cifra que luego redujo a 113.326 tras otra comprobación. Los datos aportados por el Gobierno no aclaran dónde están registrados los otros más de 35.000 nacionalizados que Exteriores incluyó en el listado que envió al Supremo y que no están en el CERA. Este desajuste es el que ha llevado a Iustitia Europa y Vox a reclamar al tribunal que garantice que esas personas no puedan votar en el caso de que hayan pasado del censo extranjero al nacional.

“¿Dónde están los 35.925 registros que no aparecen en el CERA y por qué no se aclara su situación censal? ¿Figuran en el censo electoral de residentes en España (CER)? ¿Han sido trasladados desde el CERA? ¿No llegaron a inscribirse? El Gobierno no lo aclara en el informe remitido al Tribunal Supremo", advirtió Iustitia cuando reclamó a los jueces que exigieran garantías de que la suspensión del voto va a regir para todos los nacionalizados a los que identificó Exteriores, tanto si figuran en el CERA como en el CER.

La medida del Supremo no afecta a quienes hayan obtenido la nacionalidad por la ley de nietos, pero la hayan tramitado desde España, a través del Registro Civil. Iustitia Europa y Vox pidieron al tribunal que extendiera la suspensión del voto a este grupo, que nunca figuró inscrito en el CERA, pero la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo lo descartó.

World.title: Amenazas de muerte, insultos y humillaciones: el lado oscuro del liderazgo de Jensen Huang en Nvidia
World.content:
En una ocasión, el ex consejero delegado de la gigante tecnológica amenazó con arrancarle los brazos a un empleado, según una investigación de ‘The New York Times’

Las amenazas de violencia y los insultos personales formaban parte del estilo de dirección de Jensen Huang mucho antes de que Nvidia se convirtiera en una de las empresas más valiosas del mundo. El cofundador de la compañía, reconocida por sus chips para inteligencia artificial, utilizó durante décadas la humillación pública como una herramienta para presionar a sus empleados y exigirles resultados, de acuerdo con una investigación de The New York Times.

En uno de los episodios documentados por el diario, Huang amenazó a un subordinado con arrancarle ambos brazos y utilizar esos mismos miembros para golpearlo hasta matarlo. A otro empleado le dijo que le arrancaría la parte superior de la cabeza y que después se orinaría en su cerebro.

Las amenazas no se limitaban a intercambios privados. Una persona con conocimiento de otro incidente relató al periódico que Huang recorrió una sala en la que se encontraban varios gerentes mientras les decía que los mataría. Cuando llegó ante un empleado de unos setenta años, comentó que era alguien muy viejo y que todos esperaban que muriera.

Estos episodios forman parte de un patrón de comportamiento que, según más de una docena de empleados actuales y antiguos entrevistados por The New York Times, marcó la cultura laboral de Nvidia durante buena parte de su crecimiento. Los periodistas Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac y Tripp Mickle también revisaron cientos de páginas de documentos judiciales y otros registros que abarcan más de dos décadas.

La investigación describe una cultura en la que Huang recurría a ataques personales, comentarios violentos y reprimendas frente a otros trabajadores. En ocasiones, justificaba ese trato como una manera de impulsar el desempeño de sus subordinados. “Preferiría torturarte hasta convertirte en alguien extraordinario, porque creo en ti”, llegó a decir, según el reporte.

El comportamiento también provocó inconformidad entre algunos directivos. Uno de los casos más relevantes fue el de Michael Winston, quien se incorporó a Nvidia en septiembre de 2004 como vicepresidente sénior de Recursos Humanos.

Durante sus primeros meses, Winston quedó sorprendido por el ambiente del departamento y las prácticas de la compañía. En octubre de ese año, durante una reunión de dos días a la que asistieron alrededor de 50 empleados, presenció lo que describió como amenazas violentas y episodios de humillación pública por parte de Huang.

Winston aseguró que varios empleados se sentían aterrorizados y le pidieron intervenir. Posteriormente, confrontó al empresario y le advirtió que su comportamiento podía exponer a Nvidia a demandas judiciales. Sin embargo, Huang habría defendido esas prácticas como una especie de rito de iniciación.

En noviembre de 2004, Winston fue despedido. De acuerdo con sus notas y documentos revisados por el periódico, Huang le dijo que no encajaba en la empresa y amenazó con asegurarse de que nunca volviera a trabajar en Silicon Valley si presentaba una demanda.

Acuerdos extrajudiciales

El antiguo directivo presentó una queja ante el Departamento de Empleo y Vivienda Justos de California y preparó una demanda contra Nvidia y Huang. Antes de que el litigio llegara a los tribunales, ambas partes alcanzaron un acuerdo confidencial por más de un millón de dólares, una cifra que no se había divulgado anteriormente. Ninguna de las partes admitió responsabilidad ni conducta indebida.

La investigación también recuperó el caso de Stephen Pettigrew, antiguo abogado de Nvidia, quien demandó a la compañía en 2007 por presunta discriminación por edad y represalias. Su proceso terminó en un acuerdo extrajudicial en 2009.

El reporte señala que las prácticas de Huang persistieron incluso cuando Nvidia alcanzó una posición central en la industria de la inteligencia artificial. Algunos empleados describieron una relación de admiración y temor hacia el empresario: mientras unos reconocían su capacidad para anticipar el futuro tecnológico y llevar a la compañía a la cima, otros consideraban que su trato era extremo incluso para los estándares de Silicon Valley.

La investigación también apunta que algunos directivos reprodujeron ese comportamiento, incluida su hija Madison Huang, quien trabaja en la empresa y fue señalada por reprender a otros empleados.

Jensen Huang salió de la jefatura de Nvidia hace una semana, en medio de un escándalo que involucró varias relaciones extramatrimoniales, dos con empleadas de la compañía y una con una ejecutiva de la empresa Megaspeed de Singapur que funcionarios de inteligencia de Estados Unidos determinaron era una espía china. Pekín lo ha negado, mientras que el presidente Donald Trump ha afirmado que no estuvo en riesgo la seguridad nacional.

World.title: IDFA 2026 winners: Chinese family portrait takes top prize
World.content:
The Year of the Ghost, a Dutch-Chinese documentary about a filmmaker’s mother and sister after his father’s death, has won the top prize at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA).

Louis Hothothot’s film won three awards at Thursday’s ceremony at the Eye Filmmuseum. It took best film in the International Competition, which carries a €15,000 prize, as well as best editing and the €5,000 award for best Dutch film.

The festival’s 39th edition runs until Sunday, with 253 films from 80 countries. One of the five documentaries in our preview, You Can See Everything, came second in the audience vote.

These are the films that took the main prizes:



The Year of the Ghost

Hothothot was born in China in 1986 as a second child under the one-child policy and moved to Amsterdam in his twenties. His first film, Four Journeys, opened at IDFA in 2021. In this second film, Covid restrictions stop him from getting back to China in time to say goodbye to his father. He then follows his mother, who wants to stay in her husband’s home town to care for his spirit, and his sister, who is trying to get by as a single woman in a big city. The jury praised the film’s “bold honesty, a rare attention to detail, cinematic curiosity and love”.

Memories of Lightning

Riccardo Giacconi’s French-Italian film won best film in the Envision Competition for experimental work, also worth €15,000. Radio journalist Sibilla Scinti Roger (30) travels to an almost deserted village in Le Marche, central Italy, to make an audio documentary about a murder there in 1982 – and finds out the 14-year-old victim was her aunt. Scinti Roger also won the award for outstanding artistic contribution.

Hazara Town

Afghan-born director Khadim Dai won the award for best first feature and the international critics’ prize (Fipresci), as well as a special mention in the International Competition. The film follows his Hazara family, who fled Afghanistan 20 years ago and now face growing persecution in Pakistan. They have to decide whether to stay together or leave one by one, knowing they may never see each other again.

The Clearing

Dutch director Sabine Groenewegen won the award for best use of archive footage, sponsored by the media archive Beeld & Geluid. Her film is a feminist history of Dutch colonial rubber plantations in the Dutch East Indies, where local women were subjected to violence and sexual enslavement. On the festival’s opening night, Groenewegen also received the €50,000 Cultuurfonds documentary grant, which an anonymous donor gives every year to a Dutch documentary maker.

Women and War

The €5,000 audience award, announced on Friday, went to Elwira Niewiera’s German-Polish-Ukrainian documentary. Four women attend therapy sessions in a chalet in the Ukrainian mountains, each trying to recover from very different traumatic experiences of the war. Festivalgoers gave it an average score of 4.856 out of 5, just ahead of You Can See Everything on 4.842.

Other winners included Joël Akafou’s Lonan Tché for best directing and Tala Hadid’s Bardi, set among horse riders in central Morocco, for best cinematography. Raluca Lupaşcu’s A Modern Roma Fairytale got a special mention for best Dutch film, and Ant Hampton’s Dutch-Belgian All the Downtime won the DocLab award for digital storytelling.

The full list of winners is on the IDFA website.

World.title: Inburgering with DN: understanding education system acronyms
World.content:
International parents in the Netherlands often find the Dutch school system baffling: HBO, SBO, DUO, WO… the jargon is endless. So to help you pass this particular parenting test, our Inburgering course this month looks at educational acronyms and the like.

Lesson 65: educational jargon

Primary school in the Netherlands is relatively straightforward – although parents often face a bewildering number of school philosophies when deciding which school to entrust their offspring to. It is in groep 8, the final year of primary school, that the trouble really starts.

Doorstroomtoets

Previously known as the Citotoets and the Eindtoets Basisonderwijs, the doorstroomtoets is taken by children in their final year at primary school. The tests focus on language and arithmetic, and the results are used to help determine which type of secondary education children should go on to. In principle, the teacher’s recommendation takes precedence.

The Dutch love of tests and early streaming has been widely criticised, and more secondary schools now offer mixed-ability classes in the first and second years.

Secondary education itself is divided into three main streams. Schools may offer just one – typically in cities – or a combination.

VWO

VWO (voorbereidend wetenschappelijk onderwijs, or preparatory academic education) is the highest level of Dutch secondary education and is followed by some 20% of pupils. A VWO education takes six years, with pupils choosing a specialism (profiel) in the sciences or humanities after three. There are two variants: atheneum and gymnasium. Gymnasium pupils take Latin and Greek in addition to the dozen or so other VWO subjects.

HAVO

HAVO (hoger algemeen voortgezet onderwijs) literally means ‘higher general continued education’. It takes five years to get a HAVO diploma, which prepares school leavers for a hogeschool (see HBO below) rather than a university. Around 30% of pupils are in a HAVO stream. After three years, HAVO pupils also choose a specialism in the sciences or humanities.

VMBO

VMBO stands for voorbereidend middelbaar beroepsonderwijs (preparatory intermediate vocational education). Some 50% of pupils attend this type of secondary education, which is subdivided into four streams. It takes four years to complete a VMBO course.

The most academic VMBO stream is still widely known as MAVO (middelbaar algemeen voortgezet onderwijs, or intermediate general continued education), after the type of school it replaced in 1999.

Middle-class parents push hard to avoid a VMBO recommendation, hence the popularity of tutors and crammers – and exam stress – for 12-year-olds.

SBO, SO and VSO

Special needs pupils have their own category of jargon, depending on their age, the nature of their disability and how much care they need. The main types are speciaal basisonderwijs (SBO, special primary education), speciaal onderwijs (SO, special education) and voortgezet speciaal onderwijs (VSO, special secondary education).

Lighthouse Special Education in The Hague is the only international school for special needs pupils.

After secondary school, most young people move on to further education. Education is compulsory until 16, and until 18 for anyone who does not yet have at least a HAVO, VWO or MBO level 2 diploma.

MBO

MBO, or middelbaar beroepsonderwijs (vocational education and training), is the highest level of education reached by around 40% of the working population. There are four levels of MBO diploma, and students can either attend college full time or combine work and study.

HBO

There are two types of degree course in the Netherlands: the academic courses offered by universities and the more vocational courses (HBO, or hoger beroepsonderwijs) offered by hogescholen. Their umbrella body, the Vereniging Hogescholen, calls them ‘universities of applied sciences’ in English. The Netherlands has 36 hogescholen ranging from art academies to hotel schools and technical colleges.

WO

The Netherlands has 14 official universities offering wetenschappelijk onderwijs (research-oriented education), including the Open University. Delft, Eindhoven and Twente are universities of technology, while Wageningen focuses on agriculture and food. A bachelor’s degree takes three years, a master’s one or two.

DUO

If you have any connection to post-school education, you cannot avoid dealing with the education ministry’s Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs (DUO), which runs student finance and related services. DUO holds the diploma records that colleges and universities use to check whether you can enrol, organises the lotteries for popular courses and works out how much student finance you are entitled to.

After you graduate, DUO will follow you for years to make sure you pay back your student loan. DUO should not be confused with DUWO, which specialises in student housing.

World.title: Prosecutors hacked and wiretapped Tata Steel, court hears
World.content:
The public prosecution service (OM) hacked into Tata Steel’s internal communication network, wiretapped phones, and made video recordings as part of its investigation into alleged criminal pollution, it was revealed on Friday in Amsterdam’s district court.

During the first hearing of the case, the OM revealed it had conducted a “covert intrusion into Tata Steel’s corporate network”, broadcaster NOS reported. Documents were also taken, witnesses questioned and deposition measurements examined.

The case, which has been years in the making, accuses the steelmaker of intentionally ignoring harmful pollution stemming from its coke and gas plants in IJmuiden.

Police and prosecutors are allowed to use hacking techniques in criminal cases under highly specific circumstances. This has been allowed since 2019, NOS reported, and only in a handful of cases, including child pornography and criminal communication investigations.

A defence lawyer for Tata Steel said that there was “unfounded distrust” against the company, that its employees go to work to do the right thing, and that “wire tapping and hacking” had been used as part of an “unbalanced” criminal file.

The investigation is ongoing and could lead to the prosecution of individual executives of the company. The process is not expected to be completed until the first quarter of next year, the OM said, at which point it will also become clear if the current CEO Hans van den Berg could be charged.

The public health institute RIVM records an above-average rate of lung cancer for residents living around the plant, and soot regularly collects in the surrounding neighbourhoods, including school playgrounds.

Many people have suffered serious health problems, which they attribute to the plant.

In 2021, lawyer Bénédicte Ficq filed a complaint on behalf of 1,200 residents and the following year prosecutors began investigating. In July, the OM summoned Tata Steel to court on criminal charges.

Shortly thereafter, the government said it could pull out of a planned €2 billion subsidy package for the company if the criminal case raises “serious concerns” for the Dutch state.

World.title: Bruna and Readshop avoid bankruptcy, for now
World.content:
Audax, the parent company of the popular Bruna and Readshop shops, was granted two months of protection against creditors by a Breda court Thursday.

The move follows a provisional cooling-off period granted to the company earlier this month and a hearing earlier this week attended by more than 10 creditors and auditors, many of whom signaled they were willing to grant Audax more time to get its financial affairs in order.

Audax, which was acquired by Lector Capital in January 2026, has been experiencing financial difficulties for years. It says at the time of the acquisition, Lector agreed to invest €8.6 million in Audax, money they say never came through.

Audax is said to owe its suppliers more than €9 million. Some have demanded payment before delivering new products, which could impact the upcoming Christmas shopping season.

World.title: Exiled Colombian climate activist wins children’s peace prize
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A 17-year-old Colombian climate activist, Francisco Javier Vera Manzanares, has won the 2026 International Children’s Peace Prize given out by the Amsterdam-based KidsRights Foundation for “putting children’s rights at the heart of climate justice”.

The young activist is currently living in exile in Spain after receiving death threats over his activism in Colombia.

“Although our 17-year-old winner Francisco is an example of peaceful activism for climate rights defenders around the world, he has been forced to flee due to violent death threats against him,” KidsRights chairman Marc Dullaert told broadcaster NOS.

“It is shocking that peaceful child activists are threatened and that governments are unable to protect these children and their right to be heard.”

But in the imposing Peace Palace in The Hague Thursday afternoon, it was all celebration as Francisco received the prize from 72-year-old Kailash Satyarthi, an Indian child rights activist and 2014 Nobel Peace Prize winner.

“All children around the world have the right to live on a healthy, clean, dignified, and peaceful planet,” Francisco said.

Child activist

Francisco got involved in climate action in 2019 after seeing devastating wildfires engulf the Amazon rainforest. At just nine-years-old, he and six friends founded Guardians for Life, which today has more than 1,400 young members from across Colombia and Latin America.

He became the first child ever in Colombia to speak before Congress that same year.

According to KidsRights, Francisco “believes children are citizens of today, not just tomorrow, and should have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape their lives and futures.”

He’s served as a Child Advisor to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, helping to craft implementation guidelines on children’s rights and climate change.

Francisco’s work has led to the planting of more than 5,000 trees across Latin America and Europe and the training of some 10,000 young people in climate leadership, human rights and citizen participation.

More young winners

Francisco was chosen from 280 nominations across 57 countries. Former winners include Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who won the prestigious award in 2019.

Two finalists were also recognised at Thursday’s ceremony, Chilean justice activist Issaiah Guzman Arancibia (15) and 17-year-old Sufaira, a Rohingya refugee from Myanmar currently living in Bangladesh who works to prevent child marriages.

Some 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh refugee camps after a 2017 government crackdown that judges in the same Peace Palace ruled hours before the award ceremony was a genocide committed by Myanmar against its Rohingya population – the first time a country has been held responsible for committing genocide.

World.title: Students walk out against conscription and defence spending
World.content:
High school and university students nationwide will walk out of their classrooms at 1pm on Friday in a National Peace Protest against conscription and increasing defence spending, part of an international action day also taking place in 24 other countries including Germany, England and France.

“In our opinion, money is being taken away from care, education and housing to go to defence,” National Student Union (LSVb) chairwoman Evy Kras told RTL news. “At the same time, they want us to enlist. Young people feel betrayed and say: so far and no further. We want to be invested in us.”

She says these political spending choices are at the expense of young people, and that campaigns by the defence ministry paint an unrealistic picture of war. “They pretend it’s all very adventurous and flashy, but fighting in a war is not flashy.”

The LSVb, together with research and activist group Stop Wapenhandel, published a report earlier this week saying that defence spends €260 million annually on recruitment campaigns at schools and online. Meanwhile, they say, students have trouble making ends meet.

In at least 16 Dutch cities and dozens of schools, students will leave their classrooms at 1pm, fighting for an “affordable future”. In Amsterdam, students will gather at the Stopera, while in Utrecht, they’ll head to the Domplein and in Groningen to the Broerplein.

The Dutch group Stop the War Fever, which is organising the walkout, says on its website that the government refuses to work towards peace yet “pumps billions into weapons and war.”

Conscription

The group is asking to do away with conscription, move defence out of education and invest in the future of young people instead of weapons of war.

Currently, both men and women in the Netherlands aged between 17 and 45 must register for conscription, but since 1997, there has been no obligation to serve.

But the government is preparing legislation for a selective military conscription system that could be employed if it’s deemed necessary for security reasons.

Junior minister Derk Boswijk said in March that he couldn’t rule out the deployment of young people in the coming years.

“Many young people see it coming, now that the war is near at hand on the European continent,” student Camiel Breet told RTL News. “We want to fight against the cabinet’s plans.”

“This is the first post-Cold War generation that is both the generation of misfortune and grows up with the threat of war,” Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam professor of social change and conflict Jacquelien van Stekelenburg told RTL News. “A basic sense of peace is no longer self-evident for them.”

World.title: Tata Steel goes on trial accused of deliberate air pollution
World.content:
The criminal case against Tata Steel over alleged deliberate air pollution around its IJmuiden plant began at Amsterdam district court on Friday.

The public prosecution service (OM) accuses Tata Steel IJmuiden of intentionally and unlawfully releasing harmful substances into the air. The complainants say they suffer serious health problems and worry about local children, with soot accumulating in local playgrounds, broadcaster NOS reported. The public health institute RIVM has recorded above-average lung cancer rates in the area.

The case began in 2021, when lawyer Bénédicte Ficq filed a complaint on behalf of people living near the plant. Prosecutors opened an investigation the following year and announced in July that they would take the company to court. They are still considering whether individual managers can be held personally liable.

The case focuses on the plant’s coke-making ovens, where coal is heated at very high temperatures without oxygen to produce coke, a material used to make steel. If the coal is not heated for long enough, it remains partly unfinished (called raw coke) and can release harmful gases into the air and spread soot into the environment.

Tata says it is technically unavoidable that a batch is sometimes not heated for long enough. Prosecutors suspect the company accepts these incidents and deliberately does not report them. In July, Tata called the allegations “essentially unjust”.

Ficq told NOS it was “a tremendously important day” and said the emissions incidents were “foreseeable and avoidable”. She wants executives, including chairman Hans van den Berg, to be prosecuted as well.

€2bn subsidy at steak

The criminal case also affects a €2 billion state support package for Tata’s switch to greener steel. The cabinet said in July that it could pull out of the deal if the investigation raised “serious concerns”. According to NOS, talks have now been extended to March, and the trial is unlikely to be over by then.

Poland recently managed to prevent a planned Russian “false-flag operation” at the border that, if it had not been stopped, could have “ended tragically”, says a retired general who acts as an advisor to the defence minister. His statement follows a report earlier this week by a leading newspaper, based on statements by unnamed senior officials, that Poland had foiled an attempt by Russia to carry out a major “provocation” on the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Polish government figures, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, have confirmed that a Russian operation at the border was prevented, though they have not provided further details. Bieniek then revealed that, “based on information we received from both our allies and our own intelligence services, we managed to thwart an incident with potentially tragic consequences, because the planned false-flag operation could have ended tragically”. “For example, if a group of people crossed the border and later dressed in uniforms, whether Ukrainian or Polish, but were Russian citizens disguised as others, and carried out an attack on their target, the side whose uniforms were worn would naturally be blamed,” continued the general. “Fortunately, nothing of the sort happened,” he added. “Certainly this preventative action [by Poland] forced the other side to desist from these acts.” Bieniek’s comments followed a report published on Wednesday by the Rzeczpospolita daily, which said it had learned of a planned Russian sabotage operation on the border between Poland and the Kaliningrad exclave. The newspaper, citing unnamed high-ranking figures from the uniformed services, said that the planned incident could have involved Russia mounting an attack on one of its own facilities but blaming it on Ukraine. Such actions are known as false-flag operations. “It was supposed to be reminiscent of the Gleiwitz incident,” said one unnamed source, referring to a false-flag attack in 1939 staged by Nazi Germany, in which German operatives dressed in Polish uniforms. Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań. Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities. Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026 In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers. While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies. On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism. According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”. The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP. In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram. When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities. Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026 Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”. Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. World.title: Two Russian missiles and a drone hit Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This is a breaking news story and will be updated as more information becomes available. Two Russian missiles and what is likely to have been a jet-powered drone struck Poland today amid large-scale attacks on Ukraine, the defence minister has confirmed. On Friday morning, an image published by Polish media outlet Wirtualna Polska showed a crater in the ground with a fire burning in the middle of it. The website reported that it had been caused by an object landing in a field in the village of Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland, around 60 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. 🔴Tu spadł niezidentyfikowany obiekt. Mamy zdjęcie Niezidentyfikowany obiekt spadł w piątek rano na pole w miejscowości Nowy Lipowiec w powiecie biłgorajskim. Stało się to kilkaset metrów od zabudowań. Nikomu nic się nie stało. Mamy zdjęcie z tego miejsca… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 20, 2026 At a press conference later on Friday morning, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the object in Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile (the same type as one that entered Polish airspace and exploded in eastern Poland in July this year). The defence minister also revealed that another missile had fallen in the town of Rudnik nad Sanem and what is likely to be a jet-powered drone had struck in the village of Mołodycz. Both of those locations are also in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. He added that there were no reports of injuries or any damage to critical infrastructure as a result of the incidents in Poland, which he noted had taken place during “one of the largest Russian attacks on Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale war”. Kosiniak-Kamysz also suggested that the fact that these incidents had taken place now was “no coincidence”, given that military exercises of the Coalition of the Willing – a group of countries supporting Ukraine – are taking place in Poland not far from where the missiles and drone struck. Addressing the media on Friday afternoon, Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that Friday represented “another instalment in the Russian escalation”. He said that there was no doubt that the objects which had hit Poland were Russian. “I’m cautious in my wording, but it does seem that we’re dealing with an intentional provocation,” added the prime minister. NATO’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, announced that he had spoken with Tusk about “the grave violations of Polish airspace” and declared that the alliance “stands in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend”. Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend. This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of… — Mark Rutte (@SecGenNATO) November 20, 2026 During the early hours of Friday, operational command of Poland’s armed forces reported that they had “activated the necessary forces in response to Russia’s strikes on targets in Ukraine”. Such communiques have become common in recent months, as Poland has had to scramble its forces in response to Russia’s increasing strikes on targets in western Ukraine, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw that was hit by a jet-powered drone in September this year. In recent months, the Polish government has warned of intelligence suggesting the likelihood of “provocations” by Russia, including airspace and border violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Earlier this month, Poland claimed to have foiled a ground operation around the border with Kaliningrad. Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk claims that "individuals with flashlights" were observed at the Russian border last night. "We very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and resources there, and managed to prevent a provocation," he added https://t.co/kD5OmpNagf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. Back in November 2022, during the early stages of Russia’s war in Ukraine, two people died in Poland after a missile crossed the Ukrainian border and struck the ground. It later transpired to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile fired in response to Russian attacks. World.title: Poland hands e-commerce giant Allegro “greenwashing” fine for misleading tree-planting campaign
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service. The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland. UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests. The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted. In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels. 🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę! Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono. ❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać 🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI — UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026 The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers. According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period. Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer. UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said. The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree. UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision. “Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny. “If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”. When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices. The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska. World.title: Poland deepens regional gas cooperation with Hungary, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed memorandums with four of its neighbouring countries – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania – pledging to strengthen regional cooperation on natural gas supplies and the security of infrastructure. The initiative comes amid Poland’s efforts to use its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity and transmission links to establish itself as a regional energy hub, helping its neighbours, especially landlocked countries to the south, diversify supplies and reduce their reliance on Russia. The two memorandums of understanding were signed in Warsaw during a ministerial meeting at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC), co-organised by the US Department of Energy, Poland’s energy ministry and the Global Energy Centre run by the Atlantic Council. Rozpoczęliśmy 7. edycję Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC) – jednego z kluczowych forów współpracy energetycznej Stanów Zjednoczonych oraz krajów Europy Środkowo-Wschodniej. ⚡️ W Warszawie spotkali się przedstawiciele rządu Stanów Zjednoczonych, państw… pic.twitter.com/7t8kLluubF — GAZ-SYSTEM (@GAZ_SYSTEM) November 18, 2026 One of them, signed by Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – who collectively form the Visegrad Group – establishes a framework for closer collaboration between their gas transmission system operators and more effective use of existing infrastructure. In late 2022, for example, a new gas interconnector opened between Poland and Slovakia. However, since then, the pipeline has seen very little use, as Bratislava has continued to rely on Russian gas supplies. Hungary has also remained reliant on Russian gas. By contrast, Poland quickly phased out its imports of Russian energy after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It now receives most of its gas via a pipeline that runs from Norway through Denmark and through LNG that arrives by sea, sourced mainly from the US and Qatar. From autumn 2027, the EU will ban its member states from importing Russian gas. In September, Hungary’s energy minister said that his country will be ready to meet that deadline. Slovakia, however, is challenging the import ban at the European Court of Justice. As part of the new memorandum signed this week, the four Visegrad countries will assess the impact of phasing out Russian supplies on regional energy security. The second memorandum, signed between Poland’s Gaz-System and Lithuania’s Amber Grid and KN Energies – which operate gas and LNG infrastructure in the two countries – focuses on strengthening the resilience and security of energy infrastructure around the Baltic Sea. It provides for closer coordination between the companies, including information-sharing on threats and incidents, joint risk assessments, exchanges of expertise on infrastructure protection and crisis response, and joint training sessions and exercises. “The LNG terminals in Poland and Lithuania serve as critical supply hubs for…Central and Eastern Europe, significantly enhancing energy security and bolstering regional resilience,” said Sławomir Hinc, CEO of Gaz-System. But that “security depends on the resilience of every link in the chain”, added his counterpart at Amber Grid, Nemunas Biknius. “This regional agreement will enable us to strengthen that chain in a structured and coordinated way.” Poland has declared its ambition to become a hub for supplying gas to the CEE region, including Ukraine, in particular by expanding imports of LNG from the United States. In addition to its existing LNG terminal in Świnoujście, which opened a decade ago, it is planning to build two further floating storage and regasification units that will be located in the Bay of Gdańsk. The first of those, under construction in South Korea, is due to open in 2028. Last year, a record amount of natural gas was traded in Poland, surpassing the levels seen before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis that followed. World.title: Poland detains 123 men in operation against online child sexual abuse material
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Police and prosecutors have detained 123 people across Poland as part of a major operation targeting online child pornography. Among those arrested were some who had used AI to produce content depicting the abuse of minors. Around 170 searches took place, with prosecutors seizing a total of 1,096 electronic devices. Initial analysis indicates that almost 2.8 million files containing child sex abuse material were contained on them, said the National Prosecutor’s Office, which oversaw the operation. Those detained are all men, ranging in age from 18 to 73, and include a teacher and a doctor. All were Polish citizens apart from one Ukrainian and one Belarusian. Policjanci Centralnego Biura Zwalczania Cyberprzestępczości zatrzymali 123 osoby i zabezpieczyli ponad 2,8 mln plików z materiałami przedstawiającymi seksualne wykorzystanie małoletnich ‼️ Działania pod krypt. „INFERNO”, to już kolejna – 9 operacja CBZC przeciwko przestępczości o… pic.twitter.com/XBdNAmLjKz — Centralne Biuro Zwalczania Cyberprzestępczości (@PolicjaCBZC) November 19, 2026 The police’s Central Cybercrime Bureau (CBZC) reports that the detained teacher claimed “he was studying to obtain expert qualifications and was collecting and analysing the [abuse] material to check whether his psyche could withstand the associated strain”. The doctor, an anaesthesiologist, was found to be in possession of around 75,000 files containing child sexual abuse material. Prosecutors have already charged 94 of the suspects with producing, possessing and/or disseminating materials related to the sexual exploitation of minors. Those crimes carry a jail term of up to 15 years. Thirty-one of the suspects have been placed in pretrial detention. “Among those detained were people who used AI technology to produce materials depicting the sexual abuse of minors,” wrote the National Prosecutor’s Office. One suspect is also accused of taking photographs and videos of himself and children naked at a public swimming pool. In May this year, prosecutors announced the results of a similar operation against child pornography, which, by coincidence, also resulted in 123 people being detained. Among those detained at that time was a teacher accused of recording and photographing children, as well as another suspect accusing of grooming minors through a messaging app before encouraging them to perform sexual acts. World.title: Polish Supreme Court rejects government’s position on Constitutional Tribunal
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s rule-of-law crisis has taken another twist, after the Supreme Court (SN) issued a resolution effectively opposing the government’s position towards another top court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), and endorsing that of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. The SN found that TK rulings are only valid if issued by judges the president has sworn in and that they take effect even if the government refuses to publish them. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five TK judges, while the government has refused to publish 85 previous TK rulings. However, the government’s justice minister argues that the new SN resolution is itself invalid because it was issued by judges who were appointed unlawfully. Połączone izby Sądu Najwyższego o wyrokach Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jako podstawie wznowienia postępowaniahttps://t.co/DzgL6aDTGK pic.twitter.com/GpiGbWMvNn — Sąd Najwyższy (@SN_RP_) November 18, 2026 On Wednesday, the SN issued a resolution in response to questions over the validity of rulings issued by the TK. It found, among other things, that a valid TK ruling can only be issued by a panel of judges who, after being elected to the tribunal by parliament, have “taken an oath before the president, that is, in his presence”. Those latter words relate to a key dispute that has arisen around the TK. The government’s majority in parliament has this year chosen eight new TK judges, who would now form the majority on the 15-seat tribunal. However, Nawrocki has refused to receive the oath of five of those judges, citing concerns over the method of their appointment or their qualifications. Those five judges have instead arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies before a notary and then forwarded their oaths to the presidential chancellery. They and the government argue that this meets the requirement for them to take up their seats. However, Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former government, reject that position and say that the judges cannot take up their seats on the court until the president receives their oath in person. The Supreme Court has now effectively endorsed their stance. Meanwhile, the SN also addressed another contentious issue. Since March 2024, the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – has refused to publish any of the 85 TK rulings issued in that time. That is because, under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, three judges were unlawfully appointed to the TK. The current government argues that TK rulings only take force when published in the official Journal of Laws. Indeed, so did the former PiS government when, in 2016, it refused to publish TK rulings that contradicted its judicial policies. However, the SN has now deemed that valid TK rulings enter force even if not published. “In a situation where the body responsible for publishing TK rulings fails to fulfil this obligation…these abuses by the executive power cannot affect the universally binding force of TK rulings,” said SN judge Aleksander Stępkowski, quoted by the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily. However, the validity of the SN’s resolution is itself contested as it was issued by judges whose own status is questioned. That is because they were appointed to the court through the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS) after it was overhauled by PiS in a manner that brought it under political control and rendered it invalid, according to Polish and European court rulings. The current government has generally rejected decisions issued by such “neo-judges”, as it calls them. And that position was reiterated on Thursday by justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who wrote that “the neo-judges in the Supreme Court have adopted a so-called resolution”. “Any decision issued with the participation of even one person appointed through the politicised National Council of the Judiciary after 2017 is a non-existent judgement,” he added. Neosędziowie w Sądzie Najwyższym podjęli nibyuchwałę połączonych trzech izb (III CZP 41/26), uznając, że nieopublikowane rozstrzygnięcia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego mają moc powszechnie obowiązującą, a za wyrok TK można uznać tylko taki wydany przez osoby, które złożyły ślubowanie… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 The SN’s resolution comes as the TK itself is embroiled in a crisis. At the end of October, the eight new TK judges chosen by parliament this year took control of the tribunal and announced that its chief justice, Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, supported by Nawrocki and the SN’s chief justice, Zbigniew Kapiński (also a “neo-judge”), has rejected that move as an illegal “coup d’état” and claims he is still in charge of the tribunal. However, police have prevented him from entering the building. On Wednesday, just as the SN was issuing its resolution, the eight government-backed TK judges announced that they had lifted Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution at the request of Żurek. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court announces chief justice stripped of immunity to face charges
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government-backed judges who recently took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have announced that the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has been stripped of legal immunity in order to face criminal charges. Święczkowski, who was appointed to the TK under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, has condemned their takeover as an illegal “coup d’état” and says that any decisions issued by them have no validity. In a further development, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) announced yesterday that it has rejected a request by Święczkowski for an emergency order to suspend all proceedings against him at the TK. Trybunał Konstytucyjny zdecydował. Prokuratura może teraz stawiać zarzuty. Nikt nie stoi ponad prawem.https://t.co/trIEqa8Mh1 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 A statement published on Wednesday evening on the tribunal’s website announced that motions from the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, to strip Swięczkowski and the deputy head of the court, Bartłomiej Sochański, of immunity had been approved. The decision was made by the group of eight judges who dramatically took control of the TK on 30 October as riot police held back protesters outside. All of them were chosen by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, but opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them. After taking over the tribunal, they declared that Święczkowski and Sochański had been suspended for their failure to properly fulfil their duties. They also launched internal disciplinary proceedings against the pair, with hearings in those cases due to take place later this week. Separately, Żurek, who serves as justice minister in addition to being prosecutor general, filed multiple requests to the TK for Święczkowski and Sochański to be stripped of their immunity in order to face criminal charges. Most of those were approved today. Among the alleged crimes prosecutors wish to charge Święczkowski with are abuse of power and failure to fulfil duties for his refusal to allow five judges chosen by parliament this year to take up their seats on the court. Sochański is accused of the same offences. Święczkowski has argued that he cannot admit those judges because, under Polish law, they are obliged to first swear an “oath before the president” and have not done so. Prosecutors also allege that Święczkowski used violence against those five judges to physically prevent them from entering the judges’ chambers at the TK. The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 Further allegations against Święczkowski relate to his time serving as national prosecutor under the former PiS government. Prosecutors say that he abused his powers by making unauthorised use of material gathered from surveillance. They also accuse him of abusing his power by “maliciously” reassigning prosecutors to different locations as a form of punishment, despite there being no legal basis for doing so. However, although the TK today approved the lifting of Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunities, it did not consent to them being arrested and held in pretrial detention. It also rejected two additional requests from Żurek to lift Święczkowski’s immunity for other alleged crimes. The TK found the motions contained “formal deficiencies”. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski immediately rejected today’s decisions, saying that they had no legal validity. He describes the eight judges who have taken control as “usurpers”. However, on Tuesday, Święczkowski suffered another setback in his struggle to retain control over the TK after the European Court of Human Rights announced that it had rejected a request from him and Sochański for an interim measure ordering that all proceedings against them be suspended. The ECHR found that “the applicants had failed to demonstrate an imminent risk of irreparable harm to the core of their rights”. The decision stands in contrast to one made in May this year by the ECHR, when it ordered that the five judges Nawrocki has refused to swear in be admitted to the TK. Święczkowski ignored that order, arguing that the ECHR did not have the authority to issue it. European Court rejects request for interim measure in case concerning Constitutional Court of Poland. 🔗 https://t.co/I15bGXeeKF — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 17, 2026 Święczkowski has received backing from some other Polish institutions. President Nawrocki continues to recognise Święczkowski as the chief justice of the TK and has condemned the government-backed judges’ takeover of the court. The chief justice of the Supreme Court (a separate body from the TK), Zbigniew Kapiński, has also sided with Święczkowski and Nawrocki. Speaking to broadcaster RMF on Wednesday morning, Kapiński said that any decisions made by the eight judges who have taken over the TK “have no legal force”. Kapiński’s own status has also been subject to dispute. He was appointed to the Supreme Court under the PiS government through a judicial body overhauled in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to various European and Polish court rulings. On Monday, the central bank, whose governor is a longstanding associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, announced that it was suspending all outgoing payments from the TK’s bank accounts due to uncertainty over who holds legitimate control over the court. Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026 The recent dramatic events at the TK follow a decade-long crisis around the Polish judiciary, triggered by the contested judicial reforms and appointments made by the former PiS government and PiS-aligned former President Andrzej Duda. The current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that came to power in 2023 – has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK due to the presence of unlawfully appointed judges. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. The eight judges it has appointed now have a majority on the 15-person court, although five of them have not been sworn in by Nawrocki. The remaining seven judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were appointed when PiS was in power.
