World.title: EU, UK in ‘landmark deal’ on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions
World.content:
The European Union – United Kingdom summit on November 20 produced a “landmark deal” on food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions, but negotiations on university student fees – with the EU wanting its students to pay the same as British students in the UK – are to continue.

The joint statement, announced at a joint news conference by European Commission President António Costa, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, is part of efforts to “reset” the relationship between the bloc and Britain, 10 years after Brexit.

Costa said: “A strong partnership between the European Union and the United Kingdom is a strategic investment in Europe’s security. But it is also an investment in our shared prosperity, in innovation, competitiveness and resilience. Because there can be no strong defence without a stronger economy”.

“There is much more we can achieve together. We are not competing against each other, we are building win-win solutions together,” Costa said.

The European Union is a union of sovereign nations which respects sovereign natures, he said: “We respected the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016”.

“And I recall the words of the European Council after the referendum. We regret but we respect. And we will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long-term relationship with the European Union,” he said.

“Of course, we follow with great interest the debate you have relaunched about our common future. And as you know, we remain open to have the closest possible relationship between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”

Von der Leyen said: “We know the world around us is changing fast, making a closer and stronger partnership between the European Union and the UK the more important. And indeed, the spirit of our cooperation is win-win. Our economies are deeply connected.”

“Last year, we agreed on an ambitious agenda, and today we are delivering. First, we are bringing our people closer together. From next year on, the United Kingdom will once again take part in Erasmus+,” Von der Leyen said.

She said that negotiations had been concluded on a youth experience scheme. “It will allow 100 000 young people from each side to spend up to three years in each other’s countries. To work, to study, to volunteer, to simply travel.”

Von der Leyen said that negotiations had been concluded on an agreement on food and other agricultural products: “This is a big success. It is a two-way street”.

“For our businesses on both sides of the channel, it means easier trade and lower costs. And for our consumers, it means more choice and more affordable food, so lowering the living costs. We have also concluded negotiations to link our carbon markets.”

“The agreement will cut emissions, and it will generate investments in cleaner industries. It will help us advance our shared climate goals. Work also continues towards the United Kingdom’s participation in our electricity market,” Von der Leyen said.

Burnham said: “We’re 10 years on from Brexit, but I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe”.

“The agreement that we’ve reached together is a win-win. And it is in tune with public opinion in the UK. People can see the status quo isn’t working,” Burnham said.

“It’s not good enough for Britain. Three quarters of people say that they favour closer ties with Europe, according to the most recent polls. And that is because we’ve had a decade of drift, too much division, low growth in the economy, and higher prices in the shops,” he said.

“They want a better deal than the hard Brexit we ended up with. And today, together, we have delivered that better deal. As I say, it will be good for people in Britain, and good for people in Europe,” Burnham said.

“It directly addresses the biggest challenges of our times, and the biggest worries that people have. The cost of food. The cost of energy. The lack of growth in the economy, and the cost of doing business. The levels of illegal immigration. And the challenges facing our young people.”

Ffor people who are worried about the cost of the weekly shop, this deal will help, he said.

“By cutting the costs of exporting, it will help relieve pressure. At the moment, it can cost up to £1400 to export a single shipment of salmon. And obviously, that’s too high, and it will bring costs for business down.”

The deal would bring the cost of food down “and nd it opens up the possibility of lower electricity costs”.

There are so many businesses out there who are worried about the cost of doing business, Burnham said.

Burnham said that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey had “confirmed today that the UK Treasury has said that the deal struck here will add up to 0.5 per cent to UK GDP”.

“That is a £17 billion boost to the British economy. It is the single biggest growth measure that we could take in this Parliament,” Burnham said.

Brexit did take away opportunity from our young people, he said.

“And I can say to the young people of Britain, you will have, as a result of this deal, a new freedom. For anyone under 31, you will have much greater ease and ability to travel to any of the wonderful 27 member states of the European Union to live, to work, to study,” Burnham said.

“And that is such a positive note that we’ve been able to strike between ourselves so that the next generation can feel finally that people in our positions are directly doing something to recognise that they need more help and that they need more opportunity in their lives.”

Burnham said that a bill would be introduced in the British Parliament next week to implement this aspect of the deal.

(Photo: Council of the EU)

World.title: Two Russian missiles, Russian drone crash in Poland
World.content:
Two Russian missiles and a Russian drone have fallen in Poland, Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on November 20, as quoted by his ministry.

One missile exploded in Nowy Lipowiec, the other in Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone in Mołodycz.

“This attack by the Russian Federation on Ukrainian territory, with its impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

He said that the missile that fell in Nowy Lipowiec, Biłgoraj County, was a Kh-101 missile.

“Throughout the night, our and allied pairs of on-duty jets operated – Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripens. Our pilots had a Dutch Air Force refueling aircraft at their disposal in the air. Our reconnaissance system, a Saab early reconnaissance aircraft, was also activated and operating in the Podkarpackie and Lublin Voivodeship,” he said.

Patriot systems located around Jasionka Airport in Rzeszów and near Świdnik in the Lublin region have been activated, as had the Poprad and Pilica+ ground systems.

Helicopters are also participating in the operation, as they continue to operate in the air, as are three brigades of the Territorial Defence Forces.

“We are dealing with another provocation by the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“In my opinion, the date is not accidental. Today, the Coalition of the Willing exercises are taking place, involving several countries on Nowa Dęba near these locations,” he said.

“The Coalition of the Willing exercises, the presence of the Defence Ministers of France, Great Britain, and the Baltic states, eight chiefs of staff led by our most important allies. It seems the coincidence of these events is no coincidence,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“I will go to our allies, also with a request that they see what we have been facing here every day, every week, every month for four years. The threat to Nato and provocations from Russia are very serious. I will also request that the Alliance, the Secretary General, allocate additional forces and resources to support Operation Eastern Sentry. There are soldiers here from allied countries, for example, the Czech Republic, but more support is needed.”

We will not be intimidated, he said: “We will continue our actions, protecting above all our citizens, the Republic of Poland, and the strength of our Alliance”.

World.title: European prosecutors charge individual in 213.7M euro fraud probe into rail modernisation in Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Bulgaria has filed an indictment in the Sofia City Court against one suspect, following an investigation into a project for the modernisation of the Bulgarian railway infrastructure, EPPO said on November 19.

The project, which concerns parts of the railway section between Sofia and Plovdiv, is worth more than 213.7 million euro in EU financing.

The contract for the execution of the project was awarded to a consortium formed by three companies.

The accused is the legal representative of a company participating in the consortium.

According to the investigation, through the manager of the consortium, he submitted false information to the National Company Railway Infrastructure (NRIC) regarding the company he represented to illegally obtain EU funds.

His conduct enabled the consortium to be eligible to and to be awarded in 2019 the EU-funded grant agreement amounting to 213 714 235.14 euro.

Between 2019 and 2024, a total of 68 213 186.03 euro was paid out by the NRIC to the consortium, co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and the national budget.

In particular, the accused used the manager of the consortium, who had no knowledge of the relevant criminal circumstances, to declare that the company was not subject to insolvency proceedings. In reality, based on the evidence, it was declared insolvent already in 2012.

The investigation was supported by Bulgaria’s Interior Ministry National Police General Directorate and the State Agency for National Security.

Numerous searches and seizures were carried out throughout the investigation across various locations in Bulgaria, including company headquarters and private residences. Documents concerning the tender procedure and its implementation were also seized.

The initial crime report was submitted by OLAF, which also conducted a complementary investigation, EPPO said.

(Archive photo: NRIC)

World.title: Arrests in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Poland in probe into multimillion euro VAT fraud
World.content:
At the request of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Munich, three suspects were arrested this week in an investigation into a multimillion VAT fraud, EPPO said on November 19.

The arrests took place in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Poland. Searches and seizures were also carried out in those countries.

The criminal organisation under investigation is suspected of operating a cross-border VAT carousel fraud – a complex criminal scheme that takes advantage of EU rules on cross-border transactions between its member states, as these are exempt from value-added tax.

It is understood that they sold AirPods via companies and missing traders based in Germany and Bulgaria.

The activities of these suspects alone may have caused an estimated tax loss of 23 million euro in Germany.

With the support of national authorities from Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, searches were carried out at the premises of the suspects and companies under investigation.

These investigative measures are part of investigation Midas , targeting a transnational criminal organisation behind a 195 million euro VAT fraud scheme involving the sale of smartphones, small electronic devices and protective face masks.

(Archive photo: Interior Ministry)

World.title: EC opens two new infringement cases against Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Commission said on July 8 that it opened two new infringement cases against Bulgaria for failing to correctly transpose EU rules on deforestation and non-cash payments fraud.

In its latest infringements package, the EC said that it sent a letter of formal notice, the first stage in the infringement process, after Bulgaria failed to correctly implement the directive on non-cash payments fraud, which defines criminal offences and sanctions regarding fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment.

The Commission also found Bulgaria in breach of the EU Deforestation Regulation, which aims to ensure that key goods placed on the EU market do not contribute to deforestation and forest degradation, requiring member states to designate competent authorities responsible for implementing and enforcing the rules. Bulgaria did so for all commodities covered by the regulation, except rubber, the EC said.

Separately, the Commission also said that it was advancing an existing case by issuing a reasoned opinion, the second stage in the infringement process.

In that case, Bulgaria is accused of failing to correctly transpose the rules of the Seasonal Workers Directive, which outlines rules for the admission of third-country seasonal workers to the EU to meet seasonal labour demand.

(Entrance to the Berlaymont building, headquarters of the European Commission. Photo: EU Audiovisual Service)

World.title: FDI in Bulgaria in January-September 2026 was 3.96B euro
World.content:
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria in the first nine months of the year stood at 3.96 billion euro, the equivalent of 3.1 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), statistics from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) showed on November 19.

In January-September 2025, FDI was 2.38 billion euro, but the BNB originally reported 1.91 billion euro, which was revised upward later.

Investment in equity, including in the real estate sector, was 96.5 million euro (compared to an outflow of 10.5 million euro in January-September 2025) and the BNB figures showed 3.73 billion euro in re-invested earnings (compared to 3.33 billion euro for the first nine months of last year.)

Net receipts from real estate investments by foreign companies recorded an outflow of 11.1 million euro, compared to an outflow of 21.2 million euro in January-September 2025.

The central bank data showed 130.9 million euro in investment inflows as debt instruments, recorded as the change in the net liabilities of Bulgarian companies towards their foreign investor owners, compared to outflows of 935.3 million euro in the first nine months of 2025. Such financial flows include financial loans, suppliers’ credits and debt securities, BNB said.

By country, the largest direct investment in Bulgaria in the first three quarters of 2026 came from Greece (515.3 million euro), Luxembourg (487.1 million euro) and Switzerland (464.9 million euro). Notable net outflows were recorded towards the United States (-104.1 million euro) and Kazakhstan (-12.3 million euro).

According to preliminary figures, Bulgarian investment abroad increased by 406.8 million euro in January-September, compared to 379.2 million euro in the same period of last year, BNB said.

World.title: Defining Luxury: RSVP Symposium Comes to Hvar
World.content:
November 6, 2026 – More international attention on Croatia’s premier island, as the prestigious RSVP Symposium comes to Hvar Town, hosted by Suncani Hvar Hotels.

Long known as Croatia’s premier island, the island of Hvar has been taking significant steps in recent years to cement and develop that image, as its tourism offer diversifies and targets the more elite market. Significant investment in the Suncani Hvar Hotels portfolio, including the first five-star hotel on a Dalmatian island (Palace Elisabeth, opened in 2019) has seen a surge in arrivals from the sought-after American market, which is now firmly number one in terms of both tourist arrivals and overnight stays.

All photos by Mihoci Studio

Success breeds success, and Hvar Town was the venue last month for the latest gathering of the influential RSVP Symposium, a global membership community for luxury event planners, wedding designers, creatives, and industry producers. The three-day event took place from October 5-8.

More than 150 professionals from over 30 countries came to Hvar to exchange knowledge and industry insights, build meaningful international partnerships, discover emerging luxury destinations, and to connect buyers with destinations, venues and suppliers.

After successful editions around the world, Croatia – and specifically Hvar – was chosen as the next destination to showcase its luxury hospitality, culture, gastronomy and event capabilities to an international audience. Full credit for this goes to Suncani Hvar Hotels, who not only hosted the three-day event, but were also instrumental who brought the event to Hvar.

The RSVP Croatia Experience was built around the concept of The Power of K(no)w, Shaped by Place, Informed by Heritage, Powered by Modernity. As such, Hvar was an incredible choice. The home of the gala dinner, 5-star Palace Elisabeth, lies on the spot where organised tourism in Europe began in 1868; across the main square lies the oldest public theatre in Europe, also an RSVP event venue, and no other island in the world in Europe has more UNESCO heritage, some of which was reflected in the UNESCO agave lace adorning the gala dinner tables. Experience inspired by authenticity.

The event was not just a celebration of the island of Hvar, but Croatia in general, and it was an opportunity also to celebrate one of the great symbols of innovation and modernity from years gone by – the genius of Nikola Tesla, who was born in what is now modern-day Croatia. Beach Celebration – Electric Enlightenment – Inspired by Nikola Tesla and invisible energy was a spectacular addition.

RSVP Symposium held several key events over the three days, hosted at the various Suncani Hvar hotels, each with its own theme and showcasing of the island’s diversity:

Knowledge of Place

After arrival in Hvar, there was an immersive destination welcome, followed by an Evening Cocktail Experience – 1001 Dalmatia, which was hosted by Hotel Adriana. Highlighted was a contemporary interpretation of the Dalmatian lifestyle, inspired by the contrast of white limestone and the Adriatic Sea.

Knowledge of Heritage

After a full educational programme and networking opportunity, the Signature Gala Dinner – Veiled Intentions – Inspired by UNESCO-protected Hvar agave lace, was held at Palace Elisabeth, a chance to see Hvar’s rich heritage presented through a contemporary luxury lens.

Knowledge of Modernity

After the final conference sessions and future-focused discussions, there was a beach celebration – Electric Enlightenment – Inspired by Nikola Tesla and invisible energy, hosted at Beach Club Hvar. The evening included dynamic lighting, music and immersive entertainment. A wonderful celebration of Croatia as an innovative and creative destination.

Three days of showcasing history, heritage, tradition and the Mediterranean lifestyle while networking, socialising and exchanging views, and delegates headed back to their corner of the world more informed, energised and impressed by Croatia and its luxury opportunities. The possibilities to expand and develop Croatia’s luxury tourism market, using its key ingredients of nature, gastronomy, heritage and tradition have always been plain to see, but hosting events such as the RSVP Symposium enable those possibilities to reach the right and influential audiences.

World.title: Croatia Draws Republic of Ireland in Nations League Play-Offs
World.content:
Croatia will face the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League play-offs, with their place in League A on the line. The draw was made on Friday at UEFA headquarters in Nyon.

Slaven Bilić’s side will play the first leg away and the return leg at home, both in March 2027. The winner stays in League A for the next edition of the competition, while the loser drops into League B.

The first legs can be played on March 25 or 27, and the return legs on March 28 or 30. UEFA will confirm the exact schedule after the draw. The Croatian Football Federation has not yet chosen a venue for the home leg, with Osijek’s Opus Arena, Zagreb’s Maksimir and Split’s Poljud all under consideration.

The tie is decided on aggregate over two legs. If the scores are level, two 15-minute periods of extra time follow, then penalties if needed. There is no away goals rule.

Croatia finished third in Group A3 behind England and Spain, and ahead of Czechia, collecting six points from six matches, with both wins coming against the Czechs. Only the two best third-placed sides, Greece and Italy, stayed in League A automatically, leaving Croatia and Denmark among the teams heading into the play-offs.

The other play-off ties

League A/B: Bosnia and Herzegovina v Denmark, Hungary v Serbia, Slovenia v Wales

League B/C: Cyprus v North Macedonia, Estonia v Romania, Faroe Islands v Georgia, Belarus v Israel

World.title: Foreign Workers Must Learn Croatian in 2027, But is That Really Integration?
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Foreign workers must learn Croatian and be able to prove at least a basic level of it in 2027, but is that really integration into society? According to the law, it is, but according to experts, it’s far from enough.

You move from India, Bangladesh or Nepal to Croatia, an agency gets you a job, you learn about thirty basic phrases of its language, and according to the law, that’s enough to be considered “integrated.” Davor Kovacevic reports for Glas Slavonije that this is precisely what will be required of foreign workers in Croatia starting in 2027, as they will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at the A1.1 level in order to extend their residence and work permits.

However, is a basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, a senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is a clear “no,” and the data his institute collects shows that Croatia has only scratched the surface of a problem that will become increasingly complex.

there are more barriers than language

When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the daily lives of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out just one. Language barriers, inadequate housing, violations of labor rights, difficult access to healthcare, and social isolation, he says, are all intertwined, yet the common denominator of most of these problems is a lack of information. Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding to the new situation through regulations, though it remains an open question how much of it the administration manages to implement in practice. Stricter criteria for employers, for example, were meant to regulate the market, but they simultaneously increased the administrative burden, causing some workers to wait months for permit extensions.

The healthcare system is a particular problem, according to a November 2025 Institute survey conducted among 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously hampers regular healthcare. Language remains an obstacle even when workers try to find information on their own, as official institutional websites are often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of this, many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, and sometimes only, source of information becomes their employer or employment agency. “A series of very practical questions, from whether an employer can hold onto their passport, to whether they are entitled to unemployment benefits, to whom to contact if their rights are violated—remain without a reliable answer for a large number of workers. What Croatia lacks today is not primarily regulations. It lacks a system that will enable a foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” he pointed out.

acceptance from a society that was, until very recently, extremely homogenous

Balabanić views the obligation to pass the A1.1 exam simultaneously as an integration measure and an administrative condition, though he emphasised that its purpose should primarily be integration.

“Knowing the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first prerequisites for starting to feel like part of society. Still, such a low level of language proficiency does not in itself solve the issues of foreign workers’ legal security or their ability to navigate Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can genuinely exercise them,” Balabanić stated. Precisely for this reason, until a worker masters Croatian, information regarding residence, work, the healthcare system, and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and, Balabanić stresses, in one central place rather than scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mostly boils down to the relationship between worker and employer, the social dimension is equally important. Foreign workers need to become familiar with the norms and values of the society they are entering, while the local population must also accept that Croatia is becoming more culturally diverse.

Just how weak that readiness currently is was shown by a November 2025 survey by the Institute for Migration Research conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and only a negligible number of respondents as a family member.

“That is why I would say Croatia is still in the very early stages of integrating foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, accessible information, social contacts, and the readiness of the local population to accept new fellow citizens, we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić stated. When it comes to financing integration, Balabanić clearly points out that the state should bear the largest share of the costs.

a(nother) financial burden for employers

The Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK) pointed out that integrating a foreign worker places a serious financial burden on the employer. Through its own program “Welcome to Croatia,” HGK has so far included more than 400 foreign workers from 15 Croatian companies, while users of Croatian Employment Service (HZZ) vouchers for language learning are employed by 1,602 employers. According to HGK estimates, accommodation provided by the employer alone costs between 3,000 and 3,600 euros annually per worker, a language course costs between 300 and 500 euros, and administrative costs, such as residence and work permits, medical exams, and plane tickets, climb into the hundreds of euros. The new legal obligation will further increase costs, as the law stipulates that the cost of the standardised A1.1 exam is borne specifically by the employer.

taking responsibility

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily due to the needs of the domestic labour market and labour shortages in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest share of responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

This, he emphasised, doesn’t mean the responsibility must rest exclusively with the state. Local self-government plays an important role because integration happens within specific communities—the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, though Balabanić warns it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, as they already bear significant hiring costs. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have an obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the laws. It is precisely here that Balabanić sees a real danger of integration becoming something the state formally demands from a foreign worker without providing them the tools to actually fulfill that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration to be exclusively their personal problem,” he said. Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers facing overlapping adverse circumstances, those who went into debt just to reach Croatia through long chains of intermediaries, making it harder for them to refuse poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer upon whom they depend for their salary, accommodation, and information about their own rights.

the issue of language

Interestingly, employers themselves, according to an HGK survey on a sample of 572 companies, recognise the importance of language, with as many as 80 percent of respondents believing that learning Croatian would contribute most to easier integration of local and foreign workers in a shared work environment. However, HGK states that employers’ responsibility in practice already goes beyond merely paying for an exam. “It includes quality onboarding, mentorship support, and, where applicable, ensuring the adequacy of accommodation,” HGK stated. The Chamber believes that integration must remain a shared responsibility among institutions, employers, and workers.

World.title: Bjelovar Plans Extension of Brezovac Airport Following Wellovar Complex Completion
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Bjelovar is planning the extension of the Brezovac Airport following the completion of the Wellovar complex. The desire is to attract more visitors to the newly opened facility.

The airport in the Bjelovar settlement of Brezovac could accommodate smaller passenger aircraft in the future, and its development opens up interesting opportunities for Bjelovar’s tourism. Ivan Karacony reports for Bjelovar Live that this is particularly relevant now given that the Wellovar geothermal complex in Veliko Korenovo is now completed and is just a few kilometres from the existing runway.

In its draft budget for 2027, the City of Bjelovar foresees the continued preparation of the airport expansion project, including a new runway and additional facilities. If realised, this project would expand the airport’s current sports purpose and enable the reception of smaller aircraft with a capacity of three to 10 passengers.

With the opening of Wellovar, a large geothermal sports and recreation complex featuring 10 indoor and outdoor pools, Bjelovar gained an attraction that, alongside the logical idea we might call “Operation Airport”—could draw additional visitors from Croatia and abroad. At least those who wish to reach their tourist destinations by plane and shorten their travel time. Of course, this does not involve large passenger airliners and regular commercial routes, but rather smaller private and business aircraft that could use the expanded airport in the future. In this context, the proximity of the Brezovac airport, located approximately 1.9 kilometres as the crow flies from Wellovar, and between 3.5 and four kilometres from the heart of Bjelovar, is particularly intriguing.

This opens up the possibility for the future airport to take on a specific tourism role alongside its sports function. The option of arriving via smaller private and business planes could be an added advantage for Wellovar visitors, as well as for business guests and other tourists coming to Bjelovar.

bjelovar’s more tourism-oriented future

This conclusion is backed by the official explanation of the city budget. The City of Bjelovar lists proximity to the city center, the planned Zagreb–Virovitica expressway, and Terme Bjelovar, Wellovar, as key advantages of the future airport expansion. The explanation highlights the potential for connecting air and road transport with tourist facilities, as well as introducing a passenger program for smaller aircraft. In other words, linking the airport and Wellovar stands out as one of the most interesting possibilities for Bjelovar’s future tourism development, although a concrete program for such a connection has not yet been presented. Thus, everything is still at the idea stage, albeit a good idea.

a newer runway for smaller passenger aircraft

The existing airport in Brezovac is currently used for sport aviation, and its infrastructure consists of a runway as well as business and auxiliary facilities used by the Bjelovar Aeroclub (Zrakoplovni klub Bjelovar). The planned expansion includes building a new runway and additional facilities to broaden airport activities. Clearly, this is a plan, or rather, an idea, to create conditions for accommodating smaller passenger planes, giving the airport new value and a new purpose.

For the Brezovac Airport expansion project, 33,000 euros were planned in the 2026 city budget for preparing project documentation, including the conceptual design, preliminary project, and environmental protection and parceling studies. Furthermore, according to the City of Bjelovar’s draft budget, another 33,000 euros are planned for the “Brezovac Airport” project in 2027. The projection for 2028 is 50,000 euros, while a significantly higher amount, 200,000 euros, is foreseen for 2029. When all is said and done, the sum of planned and projected amounts from 2026 to 2029 reaches 316,000 euros. It should be emphasised that this figure does not represent the total estimated cost of expanding the airport, but rather the funds listed in the budget documentation for that period. Additionally, this does not mean that all the stated money has already been spent or that all projected amounts will ultimately be realised.

Whether Brezovac will become an airport for smaller passenger planes in the future remains to be seen. However, given the proximity of Wellovar and the growth of the tourist offer, such infrastructure could gain new value far beyond its previous role in sport aviation. If Bjelovar already has a tourist attraction that might make someone want to arrive by plane, it is only logical to consider where that plane could actually land.

World.title: Dubrovnik Wins Global Model of Sustainable Tourism Award
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – After many years being the unfortunate poster child of mass tourism and “overtourism”, Dubrovnik has managed to turn things around so successfully that it has won the Global Model of Sustainable Tourism award.

The City of Dubrovnik is the recipient of the international “Global Model of Sustainable Tourism Award,” which was presented to it during the 21st annual session of the Global Forum on Human Settlements. Dubrovniknet reports that the ceremony was held on November the 13th in Antalya, Turkey, at the time of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31).

This is an international recognition that acknowledges cities and initiatives whose approach contributes to sustainable development, responsible tourism management, and the preservation of natural and cultural heritage. This year’s Forum gathered more than 300 representatives from over 50 countries worldwide, and among the award winners were cities and projects from China, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, Colombia, Croatia, and other countries.

The Mayor of the City of Dubrovnik, Mato Franković, addressed the ceremony participants via video message, thanking the Global Forum for this valuable international recognition, which confirmed Dubrovnik’s long-standing commitment to developing a more sustainable and responsible tourism model.

Mayor Franković emphasised that since 2017, through the “Respect the City” initiative, the City of Dubrovnik has been systematically working to establish a balance between tourism development, the protection of the UNESCO World Heritage area, the preservation of natural and cultural heritage, and the quality of life of its residents. Through responsible destination management, data-driven decision-making, the application of innovations, and investments in sustainable mobility and green infrastructure, Dubrovnik demonstrates how tourism can be a driver of positive change for the benefit of the local community and the environment.

“We believe that the future of tourism is not in attracting an ever-increasing number of visitors at any cost, but in creating a sustainable balance that brings benefits to everyone. This award is a great honor for us, as well as additional motivation to continue being an example and sharing our experiences with cities around the world,” the mayor stated.

This year’s Global Forum on Human Settlements was held under the theme “Resilient Cities, Just Transition: Empowering Climate Action Implementation,” with a special emphasis on the role of cities in confronting climate change, strengthening the resilience of urban environments, and implementing concrete sustainable development measures.

As a reminder, last year at the 20th Global Forum on Human Settlements, held in Geneva, the “Global Model of Sustainable Tourism” award was also won by the Lokrum Reserve Public Institution, for a management model that successfully harmonises tourism activities with the protection of natural and cultural heritage and the preservation of biodiversity.

World.title: Iberia to Reduce Flights from Zagreb Airport in 2027
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – The Spanish airline Iberia is set to reduce the number of flights it operates from Zagreb Airport in 2027.

The Spanish airline Iberia will significantly reduce the number of flights between Zagreb and Madrid during the summer season of 2027. As Index reports, according to the current schedule, the company will operate for a shorter period than this year, with fewer weekly departures, and Zagreb Airport could lose almost 38,000 available seats. As originally reported by the portal Croatian Aviation, Iberia has withdrawn from sale all flights planned from the end of March to the beginning of June 2027. Instead of starting in March, the first flight to Zagreb is now scheduled only for the 3rd of June.

a significant reduction in august 2027

At the beginning of June, Iberia will have only two return flights per week, and three in the middle of the month. In June this year the company operated five return flights per week on the same route. The reduction will continue in July, when four to five return flights per week are planned, instead of this year’s eight. The biggest difference will be in August. While this year Iberia operated nine return flights per week between Zagreb and Madrid, next year it plans only five. That is a reduction of approximately 44 percent.

flights will stop operating almost one month earlier

According to the current schedule, Iberia will operate its last flight of the season on 12 September 2027. This year, the company flew the route until 11 October, which means that next year the season will end almost a month earlier. Croatian Aviation estimates that due to the reduced number of flights and the shorter season, Zagreb will lose more than 100 Iberia return flights and almost 38,000 available seats in both directions. This is a comparison of offered capacity, not the number of already sold tickets or passengers left without transport.

The reduction in Iberia’s flights comes after Austrian Airlines decided to cancel the Vienna–Zagreb route, and British Airways withdrew from sale its flights between Zagreb and London Heathrow for summer 2027. Qatar Airways has also reduced the planned number of flights between Zagreb and Doha.

zagreb airport still has a huge amount of international connections

Nevertheless, Zagreb will not be left without a direct connection to Madrid, as Croatia Airlines also operates on that route and this year introduced flights to the Spanish capital for the first time during part of the winter schedule as well. As for London, Ryanair has actually increased its flights from Zagreb to London Stansted, and Croatia Airlines will also continue operating their own flights connecting the cities.

Croatian Aviation recalls that Zagreb Airport increased fees for airlines this spring, at a time when airlines are facing rising fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East. However, it must be said that there is currently no confirmation that Iberia reduced the number of flights precisely because of the increase in airport fees.

The announced schedule for summer 2027 can still change, and at the moment Iberia still plans to operate between Zagreb and Madrid from the 3rd of June to the 12th of September.

World.title: New Routes and More Flights to Croatia in Winter Schedule
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – New routes and more flights are on the cards for Croatia as part of the winter flight schedule.

Croatian airports are going to be connected by regular routes to 26 markets during the winter flight schedule, which is one more than last winter. Poslovni reports that there will be 35 airlines operating in total, or three more than before. 77 percent of operations are directed abroad with 110 unique routes, representing an increase of three routes, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) has revealed.

HTZ collected the flight data for the winter schedule from Croatia’s airports in October. They add that the data shows positive trends continuing in the development of Croatia’s air connectivity with international markets.

“Continuous improvement of air connectivity is one of the important prerequisites for developing year-round tourism and strengthening Croatia’s international competitiveness. It is encouraging that even during the winter we see the arrival of new airlines, the introduction of new international routes, and an increase in the number of flights on a series of existing connections,” commented HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić, emphasizing the importance of connecting Croatia with new markets.

The HTZ highlights international routes such as Air China’s Zagreb – Bucharest – Beijing service, which continues to operate during the winter following its launch in September, as well as Ryanair’s Zagreb – Warsaw (Modlin) route, which will operate twice a week throughout the entire winter. British Airways will launch its Dubrovnik – London flights at the beginning of March 2027.

World.title: Vukovar: After 35 Years, a Mother Finds Her Son’s Remains
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – The siege of Vukovar and the subsequent massacre took place over three decades ago now, but after 35 long years, a mother has finally found her son’s remains.

For 35 long and painful years, the Bataković family didn’t know where Zlatko was. Index reports that they waited for an answer about his fate without a grave on which to place flowers and without the chance to properly say goodbye. After three and a half decades of uncertainty, his remains have finally been found, reports HRT. “When they told me, I felt such relief. Mum will finally get to light a candle at her son’s grave instead of in front of Our Lady,” said his brother Branko.

a quiet young man who grew up on the banks of the danube

Zlatko Bataković was 26 years old when he disappeared in wartime Vukovar. His older brother Branko remembers him as Džala, a quiet and peaceful young man who loved the Danube more than anything. “He would often come back from fishing without any fish. I would ask him: ‘So Zlatko, what do you even do there for 20 hours?’ He would reply: ‘Nothing, I just look at the water, it relaxes me.’ He would go to the Danube like that, sit and it would calm him. I couldn’t understand how someone could lose a whole day just looking at the water,” Branko recalls.

joining the national guard

Soon the time came when he could no longer sit peacefully by the river. In June 1991 Zlatko, together with three other young men from Mikluševci, enlisted in the Croatian National Guard. He had already made the decision and only came to tell his brother he was leaving. “It was the 10th of June 1991 when he told me: ‘Bajo, I’m joining the Guard.’ I asked him why, and he answered: ‘Bajo, better me than you, you’ve got two children, I have to go.’ Even then I didn’t understand it, but he left,” Branko revealed.

their final meeting

His brother last saw him in August, when he came to congratulate them on their wedding anniversary and birthday. That day Vukovar was being bombed and they came to pick Zlatko up. He started towards the vehicle but returned once more to his mother. “He came out. He was wearing a chain with a pendant that said Zlatko – we had bought it for him for his eighteenth birthday. He said to me: ‘I’m going now, I’ll give you all the money. Put it in the passport.’ I told him: ‘I won’t.’ And he answered: ‘You have to, you have to take it.’ He hugged me and kissed me,” his mother Veruška Bataković remembers.

She couldn’t know that she was seeing him for the last time ever. The war was becoming ever more brutal. Croatian defenders on positions around Vukovar were trying to stop the enemy forces. “I remember him telling me: ‘Nothing will come of this. They’ll just keep it as a buffer zone so there won’t be a conflict.’ We never even dreamed that something like this would happen,” says fellow fighter Zdenko Biki.

years turned into decades…

According to witness statements, Zlatko was captured at Ristić’s farm and taken in the direction of Negoslavci. There, his brother Branko says, he was recognised by a man who knew the family, but that did not save his life. “He told him: ‘I know you, you’re Veruška’s son. Why are you here? I’ll let you go home now.’ He took him to the back yard, fired a burst into his back and killed him,” Branko says. The years passed and every new piece of information raised hope. They searched for him among the living, on lists of prisoners and in the stories of returnees. They believed even in things that seemed impossible to others. “We even had information that the Serbs had taken them to the mines in Aleksinac to work. Mum used to dream that Zlatko was alive, that he was working in a mine in Serbia, that he had lost his memory and that he had a wife and two children,” Branko says.

zlatko was finally found, three and a half long decades later

Zlatko’s remains were found two years ago at Petrovačka dola. Branko asked Minister Tomo Medved for only one thing – that the news of the discovery not be published before he personally told his mother. He spent two days gathering the strength for that conversation. “Mum is always watching the TV. The news came at around five and I arrived at four. I called all the children to come in. She was surprised and happy. And then I hugged her and told her. That scream… it cannot be described,” Branko recalls.

For 35 years Veruška had no grave she could go to. In front of the image of Our Lady in the courtyard she lit candles, prayed and waited for the son she had last hugged in August 1991. Now she finally knows where her beloved son is. On his grave reads the name she had spoken in her prayers for decades. Behind the letters remains a life cut short at the age of 26 and a mother who waited decades for an answer. Now that she has received it, she still asks the same question.

“Why him of all people? Zlatko, you shouldn’t have gone. But we couldn’t stop him. That was his fate from birth and that’s that,” concluded Veruška Bataković.

World.title: Estonia's Foreign Ministry summons Russian chargé d'affaires
World.content:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) has summoned Russia's chargé d'affaires over recent attacks on Kyiv and to announce Estonia's decision to close its eastern border.

The Russian diplomat was summoned by the ministry Friday to protest Russia's large-scale missile and drone attacks on Kyiv in recent days. Thursday's strikes damaged several European diplomatic missions, including the Austrian and Dutch embassies.

The Foreign Ministry also informed the chargé d'affaires that Estonia will be closing all road border checkpoints along its border with Russia from December 1 in response to what it called Russia's hostile activities.

"Putin continues to systematically attack Ukrainian cities, infrastructure and people," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said, adding that Russian strikes are targeting energy, economic and transport infrastructure as well as hospitals, schools, cafes and cultural institutions.

He noted that nearly 700 civilians have been killed or injured in the past week alone.

"Until Russia ends its aggression and takes responsibility for its actions, our efforts must focus on two objectives: increasing pressure on Russia and providing comprehensive support to Ukraine," Tsahkna said.

'It's our duty to protect Estonia and the EU border'

He described the Estonian government's Friday decision to close the road border with Russia for at least the next six months as an important security measure, saying the move would limit opportunities for Russia to recruit people, conduct influence operations, organize sabotage and evade sanctions through cross-border movement.

"It is our duty to protect Estonia's security and the European Union's external border," the minister stressed, adding that Estonia also must not allow Russia to sow fear and uncertainty or divert attention away from supporting Ukraine.

World.title: Estonian racing driver Paul Aron leaves Alpine Formula One team
World.content:
Estonian racing driver Paul Aron has parted ways with Formula One team Alpine by mutual agreement after two seasons as a reserve driver, to pursue a full-time race seat.

According to motorsport outlet Gpblog, starting a third season as a reserve at the U.K.-based outfit held little appeal for the 22-year-old, as he wants to return to full-time racing.

"BWT Alpine Formula One Team and Paul Aron have mutually agreed to release Paul from his role as reserve driver and his other obligations within the team, in order to allow him to pursue other opportunities in motorsport." the team said in a statement released on Friday.

"The team extends its sincere thanks to Paul for his work as a reserve driver over the past two seasons and wishes him all the best for the future.," the statement went on.

With Argentine driver Franco Colapinto and France's Pierre Gasly locked in as Alpine's main race drivers for next season, no full-time race seat was open for Aron at the team, which traces its lineage back to the Toleman, later Benetton, team of the 1980s.

Over the past two years, Aron, 22, has taken part in several Grands Prix, but only at free practice sessions, with Alpine and also with Sauber and Audi.

International motorsport media report that Aron could move to the all-electric Formula E series, where several teams are reportedly interested in signing him.

Earlier this week, Aron tested a Formula E car for Fortescue Zero Racing at the Jarama circtui in Spain. While he was involved in a crash there, he was unhurt.

Two years ago, he competed in the Berlin ePrix for Envision Racing, finishing 13th and 14th.

Formula E is the electric cars counterpart to Formula One.

World.title: Ukrainian defense firms showcase latest battlefield tech in Tallinn
World.content:
Ukrainian defense companies are in Tallinn, showcasing their latest battlefield technology at Open Arms Fest as they seek European partners to expand production.

The two-day Tallinn leg of the Open Arms Fest, organized by the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry and its embassy in Tallinn, is being held at the Port of Tallinn Cruise Terminal, where defense company FirePoint stole the spotlight Thursday with a particular replica missile.

The company's technology recently helped bring down part of the Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea, as seen in footage that has since gone viral.

The attack also highlighted Ukraine's use of mesh modems carried by relay drones to maintain communications and control links without ground-based infrastructure or SpaceX's Starshield. Russia has used the same system to attack Ukrainian infrastructure.

"I can't say exactly how long it took the adversary, but our network's capabilities were already developed a year ago," said Ukrainian Capt. Valerii Churkin. "They've just started deploying them more widely now."

Open Arms Fest kicked off in Oslo late last month, followed by two-day events in Stockholm and Helsinki before making its way to Tallinn. Ukraine is looking to move some production to Europe, as manufacturing at home remains vulnerable to Russian attacks.

"Localizing production in Ukraine isn't safe," explained festival project manager Kateryna Soliar, adding that moving production to Europe also makes economic sense. "Europeans, in turn, are interested in drawing on Ukrainians' recent battlefield experience."

Ukraine has what Europe lacks

Churkin, a former deputy defense minister tasked with introducing modern warfare methods in Ukraine, now works on similar issues within one of its military units. He said Ukraine's advantage lies in its ability to rapidly develop and refine technology based on battlefield feedback.

"What Ukraine has and Europe lacks is a fast development cycle and rapid feedback on technologies," he said. "Things can change completely in six months — or even just a few weeks in some fields, like electronic warfare."

This summer, Estonia and Ukraine signed a framework agreement on drone cooperation at the NATO summit in Ankara, with Estonia providing investment while Ukraine contributes technology.

World.title: Road conditions to take a turn for the wintry this weekend
World.content:
Roads in parts of Estonia will become slippery starting Friday evening as air and road temperatures drop below freezing in many areas, potentially causing wet road surfaces to freeze.

According to the Estonian Environment Agency's forecast, intermittent rain is expected on Friday, with sleet and snow in some areas beginning late in the evening. These changeable weather and road conditions are expected to persist until Sunday evening, although the risk of slippery roads will remain on Monday.

The Transport Administration's road maintenance partners are prepared to carry out deicing operations, but drivers should be aware that roads can become slippery quickly and sometimes unexpectedly.

The Transport Administration reminds drivers that the posted speed limit is not always a safe driving speed. Drivers should monitor road and driving conditions and adjust their speed accordingly. Overtaking should be avoided in winter road conditions, but if necessary, drivers should allow significantly more time to complete the maneuver.

Before setting off, drivers should make sure their vehicles are ready for winter conditions and that their brakes, lights and windshield wipers are in working order. Drivers whose vehicles are still fitted with summer tires should exercise particular caution.

All passenger cars must be equipped with winter tires by December 1 at the latest.

Drivers are advised to check the TarkTee website for the latest road conditions before setting off.

World.title: Estonia seeks exemption from asylum seeker relocation program
World.content:
The Riigikogu's European Union Affairs Committee has backed a plan to seek a full exemption from the European Union's asylum seeker relocation mechanism for next year, arguing that Estonia is already hosting a large number of Ukrainian war refugees receiving temporary and international protection.

Estonia is among the EU countries where migration pressures place a significant burden on reception and asylum systems. For that reason, the government plans to request a complete exemption from contributing to the solidarity mechanism next year.

Kadri Tali, chair of the European Union Affairs Committee, said EU interior ministers will agree on the annual solidarity reserve for the coming year at a meeting of the Justice and Home Affairs Council on December 3.

"The 2027 solidarity reserve is primarily intended to help Cyprus, Greece, Spain and Italy manage migration pressures. Because of the war in Ukraine, Estonia has also found itself facing a significant migration situation and is therefore seeking an exemption from contributing to the solidarity reserve," Tali said.

Estonia is seeking a full exemption. Tali noted that if that is not possible, Estonia is prepared to contribute financially or provide experts and equipment, but it will not participate in the relocation of asylum seekers.

"In 2026, Estonia received a reduction in its solidarity contribution and paid €560,000 into the solidarity reserve. Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Croatia, Austria and Poland are in a similar position and are also seeking full exemptions from solidarity contributions," she added.

According to the explanatory memorandum outlining Estonia's position, next year's solidarity reserve would amount to 35,000 relocations or €700 million in financial assistance.

The European Commission's annual migration report, published on November 6, identified Greece, Cyprus, Italy and Spain as countries under migration pressure during the second solidarity cycle.

Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, France, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovenia and Finland were identified as being at risk of migration pressure, while Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Croatia, Austria and Poland were classified as facing a significant migration situation.

Estonia was placed in the latter category primarily because, relative to its gross domestic product and population, it has recorded a large number of Ukrainian war refugees receiving temporary and international protection over the past five years.

The European Union Affairs Committee unanimously supported Estonia's position on implementing the migration and asylum pact's solidarity reserve in 2027. The position will be presented at the Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting on December 3–4.

World.title: Meelis Maripuu: Are we afraid of our history or ashamed of it?
World.content:
The Museum for the Victims of Communism, scheduled to open in a scaled-back form on June 14 next year, has reached a dead end, Meelis Maripuu writes. With no clear decision on future funding for the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory and the museum, there is no guarantee the institution will be able to operate after opening.

This week, European Union member states imposed sanctions on a Russian company involved in organizing disinformation campaigns. The Propastop blog's analysis, "Monuments once again as a weapon of Russian propaganda," shed light on another chapter of Russia's information warfare.

In recent days, an active campaign has been launched based on the fact that, following the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, Estonia reached a political consensus and removed most Soviet occupation monuments from public spaces. Russia has always viewed these monuments as symbols of its presence and superiority.

As part of the current campaign, this is being portrayed as support for Nazism, with the aim of once again reinforcing Russia's image as the "liberator" of World War II. Beyond the Russian domestic audience, the message is also aimed at Western European publics, where the legacy of the Cold War still provides fertile ground for such narratives.

World War II triggered a crisis in our society that lasted more than 50 years. We lost nearly one-fifth of our population: tens of thousands were murdered, imprisoned, deported or forced to flee their homeland.

While the identity of Estonians as an independent people in the early decades of the 20th century was shaped by the National Awakening, the Russification era and, above all, the War of Independence, the identity of Estonia and Estonians in the 21st century has been shaped by the occupations of the recent past.

Although the Soviet occupation ended with a liberating moment that gave society a tremendous positive boost, it is still decades of Soviet terror that define us. Recovering from that experience has required far more time and resources than recovering from World War I and the War of Independence.

Over the years, several authors have argued that our society has become overly attached to narratives of suffering and continues to define itself largely through historical injustice, hindering its ability to move forward.

"The possibility that the institute's research activities may be terminated cannot be ruled out."

Indeed, the observation that "almost every Estonian family suffered under Soviet repression" has become such a common phrase that it no longer seems to require proof. It creates the impression that we have surrounded ourselves with stories of our ancestors' suffering, stories that today's young people grow up hearing. And, supposedly, those stories prevent them from fully embracing the progressive world around them.

At the same time, researchers of repression repeatedly encounter what is known as intergenerational silence. Parents who experienced repression remain silent to protect their children, while children do not ask because they sense their parents' pain. Under the communist regime, this was a pragmatic choice because speaking openly could bring new punishment.

After Estonia regained independence, that obstacle disappeared. During the initial years of intense efforts to uncover the past, many stories were recorded, and hopefully even more were passed on within families. The Estonian Institute of Historical Memory has also documented these experiences and made them available through the oral history portal Kogu Me Lugu.

A museum alone cannot reach everyone. Just as important is the story of every family, and if those stories are not told, they disappear.

The struggle with Russia over the image of the "liberator" has continued with varying success for decades. One landmark event was the Bronze Night riots of April 2007, which ultimately led the government to relocate the Bronze Soldier, known as Alyosha, from Tõnismägi to the Military Cemetery.

On August 23, 2018, Estonia's national memorial to the victims of communism was opened at Maarjamäe. Earlier that spring, the government tasked the Ministry of Justice with establishing a Museum and Research Center for the Crimes of Communism in the former Patarei Prison, delegating responsibility for the project to the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory.

The museum's focus is on commemorating the violence and victims of communist regimes. Its exhibition will provide an overview of the activities of communist regimes in our region and around the world, as well as their continuing impact today.

The museum is intended to serve as a leading educational and research center in its field while supporting Estonia's strategic communication efforts.

With funding from the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, the institute has advanced the project step by step. However, budget cuts have ultimately forced us to leave one-third of the planned exhibition unfinished.

As we prepare to open the Patarei museum, we naturally meet many different people. We are also interested in their personal stories and regularly test public awareness of the subjects we address.

If we are to believe the loud criticism that Estonian society is trapped in a victim narrative, then one would expect young people, who have grown up in that environment, to possess an obvious understanding of these topics.

Yet when meeting with a group of university students, the question arose as to why the museum is scheduled to open specifically on June 14.

To spare readers the embarrassment, I will point out that June 14 marks Estonia's only official national day of mourning, commemorating the mass deportations of June 1941. National flags are flown at half-staff on that day.

Unfortunately, not a single student present made the connection between June 14 and a museum dedicated to the victims of communism.

That encounter made me wonder what stories about the years of Red Terror have been shared by well-known public figures, stories that might resonate with others. After all, we are constantly told that almost every Estonian family experienced Soviet repression and that these stories are discussed almost too much.

"The museum's focus is on commemorating the violence and victims of communist regimes."

Artificial intelligence now provides convenient tools for obtaining at least an initial impression. While the students' lack of understanding of our recent history and national commemorations was disappointing but not especially surprising, examining the public statements of opinion leaders and prominent figures produced a genuine surprise.

Active politicians were deliberately excluded from the search. Former Prime Minister Kaja Kallas, for example, is well known for her detailed knowledge of the darker chapters of her family history.

Among entrepreneurs, musicians, journalists and other public figures, however, there were only a handful of fragments, a few touching memories. Beyond that, there was emptiness and silence.

Are we afraid of our history or ashamed of it? Is this a subconscious attempt to shield ourselves from uncomfortable thoughts?

We saw something similar when a destroyed Russian tank was displayed in Tallinn on the first anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some people objected that "children should not be shown ugly things."

We ultimately removed many Soviet monuments from public spaces, yet the Soviet memorial complex at Maarjamäe remains trapped in an endless game of reinterpretation, and even that exists largely in words rather than action.

The Museum for the Victims of Communism, which is due to open in a reduced form on June 14 next year, has now reached a dead end.

Liisa Pakosta, the minister of justice and digital affairs responsible for the project, has argued in the media that the Patarei museum is essentially a private initiative, albeit an important one, that the state simply cannot afford to fund and that private donors should take over.

Formally, that is true, since the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory is a private foundation. However, we launched this project based on government instructions and have invested public funds in it for years.

Because there is still no certainty about how and to what extent the institute and the museum will be funded, there is no guarantee that the museum will actually operate after it opens. At present, there is no staff funding in place. The possibility that the institute's research activities may be terminated cannot be ruled out.

The generations with firsthand experience of Soviet society are inevitably leaving active public life, one by one, to be replaced by new generations.

Our post-Soviet opening to the world is now a full generation in the past, and the illusion of an increasingly liberal and globalized world during the intervening decades has created a sense of alienation and silence about our own origins.

At the societal level, such silence can lead to important lessons being forgotten and past mistakes being repeated.

This is happening at a time when the world around us, and we along with it, have entered a new global crisis. If we fail to engage with our own history, we inevitably contribute to the fulfillment of Russia's information warfare objectives.

World.title: Estonia switches to lower winter speed limits Friday
World.content:
On Friday, the Transport Administration will begin removing signs allowing a maximum speed of 110 kilometers per hour on Estonia's main highways, with lower winter speed limits taking effect.

On road sections equipped with variable speed limit signs, the maximum permitted speed will be up to 110 kilometers per hour during daylight hours when driving conditions are good. The speed limit will remain at 100 kilometers per hour on 2+1 roads and certain sections of 2+2 roads.

Higher speed limits will be introduced in areas where road conditions are suitable, the Transport Administration said.

On the Maardu–Haljala section of the Tallinn–Narva highway, a 2+2 road with numerous left-turn and U-turn locations and a higher risk of accidents involving wildlife and pedestrians, the speed limit will remain at 90 kilometers per hour for the winter.

"Drivers should remember that the maximum permitted speed is not always safe. They must pay attention to road and driving conditions and adjust their speed accordingly," said Siim Vaikmaa, head of the Transport Administration's Traffic Management Center.

On the Laagri–Ääsmäe section of the Tallinn–Pärnu–Ikla highway, the Peetri–Mäo section of the Tallinn–Tartu–Võru–Luhamaa highway and the Väo–Kanama section of the Tallinn Ring Road, the Transport Administration's Traffic Management Center may set speed limits of up to 110 kilometers per hour during daylight hours when driving conditions are good and up to 100 kilometers per hour after dark, using variable speed limit signs.

Driving conditions are assessed based on measurements from roadside weather stations in the area.

This winter, speed limits of up to 110 kilometers per hour will remain in effect on a total of 249 kilometers of roads, while limits of 100 kilometers per hour will apply to another 107 kilometers.

Starting December 1, all passenger cars must be equipped with winter tires.

World.title: Gallery: Tallinn Christmas Market's one more year of cheer in current form
World.content:
The sights and smells of Estonian Christmas are back in Tallinn's Town Hall Square as its famous holiday market opens for one last season under its current operator.

Tallinn Christmas Market officially opens Friday evening with the annual lighting of Tallinn's Town Hall Square Christmas tree. The 15-meter spruce was brought to the capital from Hara village in Lahemaa.

At noon on Christmas Eve, Mayor Peeter Raudsepp will proclaim the traditional Christmas Peace from a window of Tallinn's historic Town Hall.

This winter, the market will stay open later into the holiday season, including on New Year's Eve.

Tallinn Christmas Market. November 2026. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Food and drink stalls will remain open on December 31, with a live broadcast of the New Year's Eve concert in nearby Freedom Square shown onstage. A DJ will take over after midnight.

The City of Tallinn is preparing to take over the iconic market's operation, ending nearly a decade of management by 5+ Capital. Organizing its final season in Town Hall Square will cost the private operator approximately half a million euros.

The Christmas market will remain open through Orthodox Christmas Eve on January 6.

Tallinn Christmas Market. November 2026. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR
