World.title: 2,000 trees felled in Faridabad reserve forest, officer dismissed without inquiry
World.content:
The Haryanagovernment on Friday dismissed from service a Range Forest Officer (RFO) posted in Faridabad over his alleged involvement in the illegal felling of around 2,000 mature trees in the Alipur Reserve Forest, officials said. Two others, including a forester and a forest guard, have also been dismissed, while an Indian Forest Service (IFS) officer has been suspended in connection with the case, they said.

The government invoked Article 311(2)(b) of the Constitution to dismiss the officials without holding a departmental inquiry, citing their alleged connivance with contractors and the impracticability of conducting such an inquiry.

RFO Afjal Khan was dismissed through an order issued by Additional Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Forestry), Haryana, Dr Navdeep Singh. The two juniors, including foresters Ankit Kumar and Sandeep, were also dismissed via a separate order.



Earlier, IFS officer Jhalkar Uyake, Deputy Conservator of Forests, Faridabad, was placed under suspension on November 18 under Rule 3(1) of the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969, over allegations of negligence in preventing the illegal felling.

According to Khan’s dismissal order, the matter came to light following a report submitted by the Conservator of Forests, South Circle, Gurugram, on November 14. It reported that a large number of trees, including Mesquite and Eucalyptus, had been felled and their timber unauthorisedly removed from the reserve forest under the guise of jungle clearance for ridge-making and plantation work.

An assessment report submitted by the Chief Conservator of Forests (Protection-II), Gurugram, on November 16, further revealed that contractors engaged for ridge-making and plantation had selectively felled fully grown trees belonging to Class-I, Class-II and Class-III categories. The report allegedly established that the illegal activity was carried out by contractors in connivance with Ankit Kumar and Sandeep, Khan and Uyake.

The scale of the alleged operation was evident from the recovery of around 19 truckloads of timber from Punhana in Nuh district. The timber was subsequently transported back to the Faridabad Forest Division, with the recovered quantity assessed at approximately 2,724 quintals till November 15.



An interim report submitted by the Chief Conservator of Forests (Protection-II) on November 19 also highlighted the extent of damage to the reserve forest. The dismissal order stated that most of the illegal felling had taken place between September and early November 2026, allegedly in violation of directions issued by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in PIL No. 392 of 2025 and PIL No. 70 of 2026.

Holding the incident to be a serious case of environmental degradation and financial loss to the state exchequer, the order said Khan, as the officer in charge of the range, was primarily responsible for protecting forests under his jurisdiction.

Invoking Article 311(2)(b) of the Constitution and Rule 7(16) of the Haryana Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 2016, the government dispensed with a departmental inquiry before ordering his dismissal. The order cited the Supreme Court’s 1985 judgment in Union of India vs Tulsiram Patel and the Haryana government’s instructions dated December 6, 2022, governing the exercise of these exceptional powers.

It reasoned that a departmental inquiry was not reasonably practical as the felling had taken place inside a restricted reserve forest area and contractors had allegedly acted in connivance with the very officials responsible for protecting it. Independent witnesses to the incidents were unlikely to be available, it said, adding that the officials concerned could not themselves be relied upon as witnesses.



The order further alleged that Khan had connived in the large-scale illegal felling for personal pecuniary gains, concluding that the gravity of the alleged misconduct warranted his immediate dismissal from government service.

Meanwhile, in a communication dated November 18, the Haryana government directed the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (HoFF), Haryana, Panchkula, to initiate necessary action for registration of an FIR against the officers and officials concerned for their alleged negligence and involvement in the illegal felling.

The direction followed a proposal submitted by the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests on November 17. The department was also asked to apprise the government of the action taken.

World.title: Tamil Nadu’s investment agency denies mass resignations, EPS says Vijay should clarify
World.content:
Guidance Tamil Nadu, the state government’s investment promotion agency, has denied reports of mass resignations and sought to play down allegations of confidential information being leaked to Andhra Pradesh. This, even as AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami accused the C Joseph Vijay-led TVK government of tarnishing the reputation of professionals who helped attract investments to the state.

The agency was responding to reports that at least 15 Guidance employees had resigned after the TVK government assumed office, with two asked to quit on June 30. Three former employees subsequently joined the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board (APEDB), triggering allegations of industrial espionage and diversion of investments.

World.title: Indian national Nikhil Gupta gets 19-year US prison term for plot to kill Khalistani separatist
World.content:
A US court on Friday sentenced Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 235 months (about 19.5 years) in jail for his involvement in a murder-for-hire plot against Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh on American soil.

Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in relation to the plot to murder Pannun in New York.

Judge Victor Marrero of the Southern District of New York announced 235 months prison term to Gupta after an 80-minute hearing, news agency PTI reported.



Pannun also made a statement, claiming he has not been able to do his regular legal practice for over 1200 days since the threat to his life was uncovered.

World.title: Rajkot man murders landlord cousin, his wife after dispute over ‘eviction notice’
World.content:
A family spat in Rajkot turned tragic on Thursday evening after a man went on an assault spree on his relatives with a wooden log, killing his cousin and the latter’s wife and leaving two other female relatives with severe injuries.

The Rajkot Rural police arrested Ashok Gobar Dholakiya for the murder of his cousin Prakash Bachhu Dholakiya (35) and the latter’s wife Vilas (32) on Friday, said Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) Naveen Chakravarty.

According to Chakravarty, Ashok has been living in a house owned by Prakash, who is the son of his father’s brother.



“Prakash had asked Ashok to move out of the house and there had been tensions in the family over this issue for the last couple of months,” said the officer.

World.title: Minister insists referendum on new provinces 'will happen'
World.content:
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Friday insisted that a referendum on the formation of new provinces “will happen”.

The remarks come after PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari delivered a no-holds-barred speech on Tuesday that covered the question of new provinces.

Bilawal had expressed his opposition to the creation of provinces and the idea of holding a referendum for such a move in his speech. He cautioned that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces, particularly in Sindh, could lead to bloodshed.

However, the federal government maintains that a referendum is a legal and constitutional method of gauging public opinion on new provinces and that no political party should have reservations regarding it.

Speaking to the Geo News programme ‘Naya Pakistan’ on Friday, Chaudhry, when asked about the referendum, insisted that developing consensus on the matter should be a priority for the ruling coalition.

“National consensus is very important on the issue of new provinces,” the minister said, highlighting that the PTI-led opposition was also in favour of it.

Chaudhry said that the process of taking the public’s opinion cannot be stopped if a single party opposes it.

“The referendum will happen,” the minister insisted, adding that the PML-N would undertake “every last effort” to convince the PPP.

“A referendum is neither non-constitutional nor undemocratic; the public’s opinion can be sought on any important matter,” he remarked.

Asked about the timeline for the proposed move, Chaudhry said it was premature to talk about it. However, he added that “things will be clarified soon”.

Asked if PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif was on board with the referendum, Chaudhry answered in the affirmative.

“One hundred per cent. The prime minister does not make any major decisions without his opinion,” he added.

On being asked if the PPP may join the opposition with the PTI and the Jamiat-Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F), Chaudhry maintained that the party included “mature and seasoned politicians”, expressing hope that it would continue in its role as a coalition partner.

“I believe matters will not reach a point where they might have to exit the coalition, as we will make sure to onboard them on the decision and vice versa,” he added.

In response to a question over Bilawal’s recent remarks and whether they were “justified”, he said that the PPP chairman had the right to present the party’s perspective on the formation of new provinces. However, he warned Bilawal against invoking other matters and targeting the PML-N.

“Attacking us [PML-N] or invoking other matters that have nothing to do with the debate related to the provinces was uncalled for.”

Chaudhry was also asked whether the government’s stance on the creation of provinces and the proposed referendum had been delivered to President Asif Ali Zardari in his meeting with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi a day earlier.

To this, he said that various matters had been discussed during the meeting in Islamabad. However, the main topic was the recent verbal confrontation between the coalition partners, he added.

Chaudhry said that during the meeting, both President Zardari and PM Shehbaz decided to resolve all the differences through dialogue. He added that the matters between the allied parties had returned to “usual”.

“Most of the matters have backtracked,” the minister remarked.

The PML-N leader said the party leadership would decide when to bring the party’s perspective on new provinces to the media.

Chaudhry also said that before making the remarks publicly, Bilawal should have taken PM Shehbaz into confidence.

“It is clear that the PPP will not exit the coalition,” he reiterated, referring to Bilawal’s comments about the prime minister completing his five-year term in office.

Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

On November 12, Naqvi also floated the idea of holding a referendum to gauge public opinion on the issue, saying the exercise could settle the contentious debate once and for all.

However, Bilawal, in his hard-hitting speech on Tuesday, termed the referendum an “unconstitutional move”, vowing that his party would stand against any such measure.

Bilawal, as well as Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and other senior party leaders, has repeatedly declared that the division of Sindh was neither legally nor politically acceptable to the party.

Soon after Bilawal’s remarks, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar defended the move, saying it was a legal and constitutional method of gauging public opinion.

Meanwhile, the JUI-F voiced its support for Bilawal’s opposition to a referendum, warning that it could be misused. The party termed Bilawal’s statements “realistic” and viewed them in high regard.

Against this backdrop, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan has also called for a nationwide referendum on the creation of new administrative units, proposing that the exercise be held before the start of 2027 to allow people to decide the future administrative structure of the country.

Asif hopes ‘resolution will soon be reached’

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, speaking to Geo News show ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’, expressed hope that “some resolution will be reached” between the coalition partners on the issue of creating new provinces; however, he warned that certain politicians, without naming anyone, wanted to maintain “personal fiefdoms” over provinces.

“We have to drop this idea that a certain province in its current form is a personal fiefdom [..] I don’t want to take any names, but this is unacceptable,” he remarked, urging politicians to avoid pursuing personal agendas.

“I don’t want to sabotage any evolving situation, but the personal agendas of politicians have been brought to the surface,” he said, pointing out that the PPP had been pushing for a province in South Punjab for a long time.

Asif maintained that the creation of provinces was “not a political, but rather an administrative division for improved service delivery”.

However, Asif expressed confidence that a resolution will soon be found.

At the same time, referring to Bilawal’s comments warning of bloodshed in case of division of Sindh, Asif warned, “When you warn of bloodshed, you are attacking the state [..] they (PPP) should have clarity on this.”

On being asked if PM Shehbaz was making efforts towards the creation of fresh administrative units and if it meant that he had the “blessing” of Nawaz, Asif said, “Can anyone advance independently without Nawaz Sharif’s blessing [..] he is our leader [..] we want to pursue a solution where all stakeholders are on the same page.”

Asif also called on president Zardari to “intervene” so matters may be resolved.

World.title: Petrol price reduced by Re1 per litre; diesel increased by Rs2 per litre
World.content:
The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Re1 per litre while raising that of diesel by Rs2 per litre, after snapping a 12-day streak of consecutive reductions in the rate of petrol the previous day.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs322 per litre and HSD at Rs357 on Nov 21 (Saturday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

Following Tuesday’s reduction of the petrol price to Rs325 per litre, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar highlighted the government’s “proactive measures including policy changes and structural reforms in petroleum policy” that had brought prices back down from their April 3 peak and provided relief through a fuel subsidy scheme.

“The government of Pakistan remains committed to continue making all possible efforts to ease the financial burden on the common man amid global challenges,” he said.

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: CTD says 3 terrorists, including mastermind of Kohat police lines attack, killed in IBO
World.content:
PESHAWAR: The Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) on Friday claimed to have killed three terrorists of the banned Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), including the mastermind of the Kohat Police Lines attack in September.

The three were killed in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) carried out in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat, following information about presence of the group members in the area, a CTD statement said.

According to an official statement, the Kohat CTD received intelligence that armed terrorists of the banned IMP had set up a checkpoint on Bazeed Khel Road in Kohat. Following the lead, the CTD and district police launched a joint IBO at around 6:30pm.

“When police and CTD teams reached the location, the terrorists opened indiscriminate fire. The teams effectively retaliated in self-defence,” the statement said.

After the exchange of fire, a search operation was conducted in the area where the teams found the bodies of the suspected terrorists, while some of their associates escaped.

The statement read that according to preliminary information, two of the suspected terrorists killed had been identified as Abdul Hai and Abdul Rashid.

Hai belonged to Kohat and was the mastermind of the Kohat Police Lines suicide attack, in which at least 21 people, including 15 police officials, were martyred and over 100 were wounded.

Both he and Rashid were also wanted in a bank robbery case in Balitang, in which Rs6 million was looted, it said.

The identity of the third terrorist killed had not yet been established, according to the statement. It added that a search operation was ongoing in the area to track and arrest the fleeing terrorists.

Three SMGs and nine magazines were recovered from the possession of the killed terrorists, it said.

“Further investigation into the incident is continuing, while all available resources are being used for the arrest of the terrorists who fled,” the statement added.

KP police chief Zulfiqar Hameed and the CTD’s Additional Inspector General Jawad Qamar reiterated their resolve that operations against terrorists would continue until the last terrorist was eliminated.

In the two-pronged assault in September, an explosives-laden vehicle detonated near a mosque in Kohat district’s old Police Lines, followed by terrorists storming the compound and attacking police facilities. KP police later said eight terrorists were killed in retaliatory action by police and security forces.

According to a recent report from the Centre for Research and Security Studies, Pakistan recor­ded a sharp 83 per cent increase in violence-linked fatalities during the third quarter of 2026, re­­versing a declining trend reported in the first and second quarters as terrorism and counter-terrorism deaths surged nationwide.

Balochistan and KP remained the epicentres of violence, jointly accounting for 98pc of all fatalities during the period. Balochistan recorded 829 deaths, nearly 59pc of the national total, while KP reported 556 fatalities, accounting for more than 39pc.

World.title: 'I would love to see him be back': Trump urges Nvidia to give Jensen Huang 'second chance'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday called for AI giant Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang after he was ousted as CEO over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go? I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump told reporters.

Huang resigned as chief of the chip giant at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funnelled restricted chips to that country.

Earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Trump did not discuss Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting this week.

Responding to a question, Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC that Huang had not come up in Trump’s talks with Xi, held earlier this week in Shenzhen.

Speaking about the Trump administration’s support for the domestic AI sector, Bessent stressed that the US “must stay ahead” of China in that realm.

“Our best protection against the foreign SI and exploits by foreign actors is for our labs to maintain their substantial lead, and in effect, they are our shield against SI,” he said, using the administration’s term for AI technology.

“There’s no turning back on this. What we have to do is make sure that our labs maintain their leads through their continued innovation, through their access to the best chips, and through smart policy.”

Bessent said Trump and Xi had agreed on certain guardrails on the use of AI in the military domain.

“President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” he said.

On the threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks, Bessent again stressed that the best defence his country had was to allow its AI companies “to continue at the frontier and to provide us with the best defence against these other models”.

World.title: Bilawal wants PM Shehbaz to become first premier to complete 5-year term
World.content:
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said on Friday that he wanted Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to become the first premier to complete a five-year term in office.

Since the country came into being in 1947, no elected prime minister has ever completed their five-year term.

Addressing an event in Karachi, Bilawal, citing the economic crisis resulting from the US-Israeli war on Iran, called for “empowering” PM Shehbaz so that he could present a way forward to tackle the crisis.

“My objective is that I want to strengthen the hand of the prime minister [..] usually politicians create difficulties or plot his fall and secure the seat for themselves. I will not do that […] I am saying that I want Shehbaz Sharif to be the first prime minister […] to complete a five-year term,” Bilawal said.

Bilawal noted that the prime minister had not been “given the chance” to focus on the economic issues so far.

“What can he do? Whenever he [PM Shehbaz] makes a plan, some federal minister objects and presents their own agenda to divert the topic at hand.”

The PPP chairman insisted he wanted the premier to complete his term as he foresaw difficulties ahead for the country.

“I am saying this because I know that there is no consideration for the people of Pakistan. Whether one province is created or a 1,000, the only worry the public has is having access to meals twice a day,” Bilawal said, recalling his party’s slogan of ‘roti, kapra, makan’ as primary concerns for the public.

Bilawal reiterated that the premier’s “hand should be strengthened” so he can draw attention to the economic issues facing the country. In that regard, he also underscored the need for a “national effort”.

“While I am praying for the success of the prime minister, I also believe that if we are to face the real issues of the country, one or two political parties alone cannot achieve this. It has to be a national effort,” Bilawal said.

He added that it did not matter whether the government “liked” Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman or PTI founder Imran Khan, who Bilawal said had President Asif Ali Zardari and his sister Faryal Talpur “imprisoned.”

Bilawal asserted that he would not do politics “based on ego and personal vendettas” as he believed that it was not “more important than national interest”.

He called on the government to engage the opposition, particularly the PTI, in dealing with the country’s issues.

“My political differences with Khan sahib and his own mistakes aside, his party still has a majority representation in the opposition. And if we have to face these issues collectively then we will have to engage them, entice them and request them to play their role in [parliamentary] committees,” the PPP chairman said.

Bilawal added that the PPP would continue to work as per its “ideology and others may follow suit should they wish”.

“We cannot force someone, but it is my right to present my stance, and it is the prime minister’s right to decide whether he wants to take into account my suggestion,” he said.

Bilawal claimed that the PPP’s sole focus was to draw attention to the public’s grievances and expressed the hope to succeed in doing so.

The development comes amid renewed tensions between coalition partners, the PPP and the PML-N, triggered by a hard-hitting speech delivered earlier this week by Bilawal.

In the no-holds-barred address, Bilawal had warned against new provinces, constitutional tweaks, criticised the treatment of the opposition and past decisions taken by the ruling coalition.

Bilawal had also warned against “political revenge” in politics. “What a weird country this is; since 1947, whoever becomes the prime minister goes to jail, whoever gets out of jail goes to sit in the Prime Minister’s House,” he remarked.

The PPP chairman had referred to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s recommendation of holding a referendum to decide on the creation of new administrative units and said: “In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one.”

He also remarked that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse” — seemingly reacting to Naqvi’s statement in July that the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

In the aftermath, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and other leaders from the ruling PML-N criticised the Bhutto scion for his remarks.

Despite this, Bilawal went on a media blitz on Wednesday, articulating the PPP’s grouse with the federal government and questioned many of its past decisions. This led to PM Shehbaz and Naqvi going to meet his father, President Asif Ali Zardari.

According to the brief official readout issued by the Presidency, the three men reviewed the current political situation, and resolved that all pending issues would be resolved through dialogue and discussion.

While leaders from both parties remained tight-lipped over what transpired during the meeting, observers termed it an attempt at ‘damage control’ or ‘mending fences’ after Bilawal adopted a decidedly aggressive tone against the ruling PML-N.

World.title: FO rejects India's 'undiplomatic, irresponsible' remarks about Pakistan's mineral wealth
World.content:
The Foreign Office (FO) on Friday categorically rejected the “undiplomatic and irresponsible” remarks made by India at the United Nations regarding the country’s mineral wealth.

At the UN Security Council (UNSC) Arria-formula meeting on natural resources and conflict, on Thursday India’s Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish had “directly accused the Pakistan military of looting the country’s natural resources for personal gain and triggering domestic political turmoil to keep control over them”, according to Indian news agency ANI.

The remarks had come after Pakistan raised the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) during the meeting, which has been held in abeyance by India following the attack in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26.

In response to Harish’s remarks, Pakistan’s First Secretary Ansar Shah rejected the “frivolous and highly inappropriate remarks”.

On Friday, the FO spokesperson was also asked about the Indian remarks during his weekly press briefing, to which he rejected the “undiplomatic and irresponsible” comments.

“Such baseless accusations merit no attention and were immediately and effectively rebutted by Pakistan’s representative during the same meeting,” he said, adding that the remarks constituted “an unacceptable interference in Pakistan’s internal affairs” and were antithetical to the UN Charter.

In a detailed statement released shortly after, the FO said: “Such diatribe, so typical of India, can only be rubbished.”

“Instead of addressing Pakistan’s legitimate concerns with respect to India’s hydro-terrorism, India has resorted to unsubstantiated insinuations about Pakistan’s institutions and leadership,” the statement said.

The statement highlighted that India’s hostility towards Pakistan’s development of its mineral resources was “equally evident in its persistent efforts to undermine Pakistan’s stability”.

“Pakistan has repeatedly raised concerns, supported by evidence, regarding India’s sponsorship and support of terrorist activities in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, aimed at disrupting development and depriving local populations of the benefits of their natural resources,” the statement said.

“India’s continuing descent into a Hindutva-inspired extremism-fascist polity, led by a religious fundamentalist regime is well known,” it added.

“Indian accusations and distortion of facts are a futile attempt to hide its international isolation, and only aimed at distracting attention from India’s domestic situation and its weaponisation of shared resources, as evident from its illegal and unilateral action to hold the IWT in abeyance,” the statement said.

The FO said that in August, the Court of Arbitration ruled that the treaty remains binding and fully in force and there was no legal basis for its unilateral suspension or termination.

“India’s refusal to accept this ruling raises serious questions about its commitment to treaty obligations and international law,” it said.

“Instead of misusing the platform of the UN for peddling lies, India will be well advised to implement its obligations under the UNSC resolutions on Jammu and Kashmir, where Indian occupation forces continue to perpetrate gross violations of human rights for decades,” it said.

“A state that is a serial violator of UN Charter, UNSC resolutions, sovereignty of neighbouring states, and binding treaty obligations, that patronises systematic discrimination against its Muslim, Sikh, Christian, and Dalit minorities, engages in disinformation and terrorism as instruments of state policy and remains in forcible occupation of a territory whose people it denies the internationally guaranteed right to self-determination, has no standing whatsoever,” the FO remarked.

“Instead of pointing fingers, India should introspect and change its behaviour,” it concluded.

World.title: Indian man jailed over US murder plot against Sikh separatist
World.content:
An Indian man was sentenced on Friday to more than 19 years in a US prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill a Sikh separatist on American soil, allegedly on behalf of Indian intelligence.

The case strained ties between Washington and New Delhi, which denied any involvement in Nikhil Gupta’s foiled ploy to assassinate dual US-Canadian citizen Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.

Gupta pleaded guilty in February to all three counts he faced: murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

US federal prosecutors alleged that an Indian intelligence officer, who remains at large, directed the plot and recruited Gupta in May 2023 to hire a hitman to carry out the murder.

Pannun, the intended target, is affiliated with a New York-based group called Sikhs for Justice that advocates for the secession of Punjab.

Canada separately alleged in 2023 that India arranged a plot on its soil that ended in the killing of a Sikh separatist, who was a naturalised Canadian citizen.

Hardeep Singh Nijjar, 45, was shot dead by masked gunmen outside the Sikh temple he presided over after being wanted by Indian authorities for alleged terrorism offences and conspiracy to commit murder — accusations he denied.

India dismissed Ottawa’s allegations, which sent relations into freefall, with both nations expelling a slew of diplomats.

World.title: Corruption vulnerabilities identified in govt institutions in bid to undertake ‘self-accountability’, says law minister
World.content:
The federal government has identified weaknesses that could create opportunities for corruption in ten institutions through a comprehensive ‘National Risk Assessment of Corruption Vulnerabilities’ survey, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said on Friday.

In a press conference alongside Information Minister Ataullah Tarar and Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani, the law minister, who joined via video, maintained that the report was not a “charge sheet”.

Rather, it identified weaknesses that needed to be addressed through reforms to prevent corruption and promote “merit and transparency”, he said.

Speaking about the assessment, Tarar said the Ministry of Law and Justice had coordinated with various agencies and institutions to prepare the report, which examined vulnerabilities across federal institutions using different indicators.

“Let me also say that no other government has made efforts like this until today,” the minister claimed, adding that the survey would also be shared with international agencies.

The minister detailed that ten institutions had been examined in depth because of the nature of their operations, particularly those involving finance-related matters, which presented opportunities for corruption.

He also highlighted “positive” steps taken by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during his governance. He cited power generation projects and reforms in the electricity and energy sectors, saying the government, in collaboration with relevant departments, had undertaken a detailed and lengthy exercise to address various issues in the sector.

“As a result of these reforms, the government is expected to save Rs3,500 billion in the electricity and energy sectors,” he said.

He also recalled the privatisation of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) last year, which Tarar said was conducted through an open auction and competitive bidding process after previous attempts failed to materialise.

“You will see positive changes in that in the coming days,” he added.

The minister also referred to the government’s plans to right-size departments deemed unnecessary. As an example, Tarar highlighted the closure of Pakistan Public Works Department (PWD), which he said faced allegations of corruption and “wastage” of money.

“It was closed and a package finalised for its employees. Some legal amendments are pending in the Assembly,” he said, adding that the government saved billions of rupees through its closure. “Now this work will be executed through smaller institutions or provincial departments.

Shifting his attention back to the report, the law minister stated that the report had highlighted “checks and balances, misuse of authority” to stop financial leakages.

“This has been done for the guidance of the federal institutions. Consider it a precautionary step,” he added.

“Twenty-five institutions were selected, over 300 indicators were used and the role of regulatory authorities was taken into consideration as well, and the need for planning reforms was felt,” he said, reiterating that the report was not a “charge sheet”.

He said the institutions were selected based on financial linkages, including the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), Pakistan Railways, Sui Northern, National Highway Authority, as well as the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) and discos.

In FBR’s role, Tarar held that the agency’s “good work” had increased the number of taxpayers from 3.7 million to 7m.

“Similarly, for Discos, there were complaints of electricity theft and now more than 2.1m smart meters have been installed,” the minister added.

He also noted the digitisation of toll collection on motorways as well as reforms around pensions and the digitisation of BISP via digital wallets.

The law minister said the objective of the report was to move towards “self-accountability” and ensure federal institutions operate on the basis of merit and transparency without any lapses.

He said the report had outlined a strategy for 400 reform measures, while 74 “reform blocks” had been presented. He added that the completion period for the steps outlined was between two and five years.

Concluding his address, the law minister reiterated: “Instead of waiting around for others to point out our weaknesses, we should identify them ourselves and present them in front of the people, as this is part of the prime minister’s vision of good governance.”

The information minister, speaking at the press conference, maintained that the report was an effort to set “improved targets by identifying weaknesses in the system”.

He added that the report was a continuation of the federal government’s efforts to ensure transparency, “as it had previously done in the closure of Pak-PWD, PASSCO and Utility Stores Corporation”.

In November last year, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its Governance and Corruption Diagnostic Assessment (GCDA), had highlighted persistent corruption challenges in Pakistan driven by systemic weaknesses across state institutions.

The lending agency had demanded immediate initiation of a 15-point reform agenda to improve transparency, fairness and integrity.

The report had estimated that Pakistan could boost economic growth by about 5 to 6.5 per cent over five years if it implemented a package of governance reforms beginning within the next three to six months.

The report revealed systemic governance weaknesses across state functions and noted that the country was exposed to corruption risk generated by weaknesses in budgeting and reporting of fiscal information, and management of public financial and non-financial resources, particularly in capital spending, public procurement and the management and oversight of state-owned enterprises.

It also identified an overly complex and opaque tax system administered by tax and customs authorities operating with insufficient capacity, management and oversight.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
