World.title: Saudis make deal with Japan to replenish depleted oil stockpiles
World.content:
Saudi Arabia reached an agreement to help replenish Japan’s depleted crude stockpiles and expand the kingdom’s own storage capacity in the Asian country.

The accord is further evidence of how major producers and consumers are taking steps to boost energy security after the U.S.-Iran war caused the greatest oil supply disruption in history.

Tokyo will buy as much as 8 million barrels of Saudi crude for its national petroleum reserve, subject to favorable market conditions, according to a joint statement on Friday carried by the Saudi Press Agency.

World.title: Takaichi meets with leaders of Chile and Peru in bid to boost ties
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met with her Chilean and Peruvian counterparts in Tokyo Friday to boost ties with the two countries.

The Latin American countries are home to critical mineral resources that would be a major asset for Japan.

“We confirmed that Chile, as a major supplier of copper and lithium to Japan, will deepen its cooperation and coordination with Japan to strengthen the resilience of supply chains for critical minerals,” Takaichi said in a joint news conference after meeting with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast, adding that they had also agreed to strengthen defense cooperation.

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also met with his Chilean counterpart Fernando Barros on the sidelines of the leadership summit to further discuss the strengthening of security cooperation.

A similar pledge to cooperate on securing critical mineral supply chains was made at a meeting earlier on Friday with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. Peru is a major supplier of copper to Japan.

Tokyo has sought alternative sources of rare earth minerals since China choked off exports to Japan in January this year in response to Takaichi’s comments in support of Taiwan.

Takaichi meets with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast in Tokyo on Friday. | JIJI

In addition to agreeing to collaborate with both Chile and Peru on agriculture, education, information and communications technology, and economic investment, Japan pledged disaster response support — particularly through the transfer of disaster response equipment to Peru — as part of its El Nino assistance.

Friday’s meetings marked the first bilateral summits between Takaichi and her Chilean and Peruvian counterparts since Kast and Fujimori took office earlier this year.

Japan and Chile are preparing to mark the 130th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027, and a logo commemorating the anniversary was publicly unveiled at Friday’s post-summit news conference.

Citing Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s 2014 visit, Kast extended an invitation to Takaichi to meet again in Chile and encouraged Japanese companies to participate in the Choose Chile Summit planned for March 2027.

World.title: Japanese see current ties with China and Russia as worst on record, survey shows
World.content:
A record share of Japanese people views ties with China and Russia negatively, a government survey showed, underscoring the diplomatic challenges facing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Some 93% of respondents described Japan-China relations as poor or somewhat poor, the highest since the government began posing the question in 1986, according to preliminary results of a Cabinet Office survey released Friday. The figures aren’t fully comparable as the survey methodology changed in 2020. A record 93.7% also viewed ties with Russia negatively.

The findings come at the end of a week of high-profile diplomacy in Asia, where Takaichi came face to face with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. Her relations with both have been strained. A yearlong standoff with China persists, and ties with Russia worsened after Moscow arrested a Japanese journalist in October and seized assets of Japan Tobacco this month.

Tokyo’s relationship with Beijing has deteriorated since Takaichi told parliament last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan’s survival, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its right to collective self-defense. Beijing demanded she retract the remarks. China also imposed export restrictions and launched personal attacks against the Japanese leader.

At this week’s summit in Shenzhen, Takaichi exchanged handshakes and smiles with Xi, though the two held no formal talks. Her reception in China was otherwise distant, with a cool welcome at the airport and a place in the back row of the leaders’ family photo.

Takaichi also spoke with Putin for 30 minutes and raised Russia’s seizure of Japanese assets and the arrest of the Japanese journalist, but Russia has yet to acknowledge that the meeting took place. Moscow’s takeover of Japan Tobacco’s Russian operations is expected to push the company into a net loss for the year ending December, the company said Thursday.

The souring view of China and Russia contrast markedly with Japanese sentiment toward South Korea. Some 62% of respondents expressed affinity toward the country, up from 35% in 2020. South Korea is an important partner in addressing global challenges, a Foreign Ministry official who oversaw the survey said, adding that bilateral ties have become increasingly vital amid a difficult regional security environment.

The survey targeted 3,000 adults nationwide from Sept. 17 to Oct. 25. Preliminary results were based on responses received by Oct. 16, with final findings due next year.

World.title: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries to take on launch operations for Japan’s H3 rocket
World.content:
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will transfer launch operations for the country’s flagship H3 rockets to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI), beginning with the next launch, science minister Yoshihiro Seki said Friday.

The H3 is a two-stage liquid-fuel launch vehicle jointly developed by JAXA and MHI. It experienced failures with its first unit in 2023 and the No. 8 unit in December last year, but has since achieved success in three consecutive launches, indicating a sufficient level of technical maturity.

The transfer will take place in stages, starting with the H3-22 configuration, which has two LE-9 liquid-fuel engines and two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters. Among the rocket’s three configurations, the H3-22 has the strongest track record, with five of its seven launches having been successful.

JAXA will continue to conduct launch operations when newly developed components, such as an improved version of the LE-9 engine, are put into practical use, according to the ministry. The transfer to MHI will occur after confirming technical reliability.

World.title: From ukiyo-e to ‘Godzilla,’ where do Japanese monsters stand in the Asian imagination?
World.content:
Japan’s yōkai have come a long way from the shadows of local folklore. These uncanny, impish creatures haunt the global imagination, evident in their presence on the walls of Hong Kong’s M+ contemporary art museum, part of the ” Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia ” exhibition.

On display until April 4, 2027, the show exhibits some 430 works, surveying two centuries of Asian storytelling through paintings, textiles, manga, anime and multimedia art. Japanese works form one of its strongest threads: From ukiyo-e prints and “Godzilla” posters to “Akira” sketches and Mariko Mori’s video art depicting a cyborg shaman, the exhibition demonstrates how Japan has been shaping Asia’s fantasy landscape.

It’s no coincidence that Japan’s yōkai art flourished during the period featured in the first chapter, “Spirits Among Us: Fantasy in the 1800s.” In the late 19th century, Japan faced demons both foreign and domestic, the latter in the form of a coup and civil war that would end more than two centuries of shogunate rule. Kyosai Kawanabe’s 1874 ukiyo-e “School for Spooks” lampoons the new Meiji government with a scene depicting Shoki, the Chinese “king of ghosts,” dressed in Western garb instructing a classroom of ghoulish yōkai students.

World.title: Indonesia’s Prabowo and China’s Xi discuss future South China Sea cooperation
World.content:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto met with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday to discuss the economy and investment partnerships as well as developments in cooperation in the South China Sea, the Indonesian government has said.

Both countries saw prospects for partnership in the strategic waterway of the South China Sea, including progress in discussions on areas for joint development, Prabowo’s office said on Friday.

“Our relationship, we think, keeps growing stronger,” Prabowo told Xi in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit. “We have reached a more aligned understanding.”

World.title: Red card drama at World Cup inspired Kozo Tashima’s run for FIFA presidency
World.content:
Japanese soccer official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red card at the World Cup was what prompted him to run for the role of FIFA president against Gianni Infantino.

FIFA suspended forward Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after U.S. President Donald Trump said he had personally asked Infantino to review the sanction.

The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, fueled opposition to Infantino’s reelection as president.

World.title: Over 15,000 register interest in class action after Rakuten Securities breach
World.content:
At least 15,000 people have registered interest in a law firm’s bid to pursue a class-action lawsuit against Rakuten Securities following a massive data breach earlier this month, a lawyer overseeing claimants said Friday.

Rakuten Securities announced on Tuesday that login credentials and branch codes for around 11.25 million accounts, as well as personal information such as addresses, names, phone numbers, income and withdrawal bank details for 4.47 million accounts, were exposed in a security breach that took place on Nov. 11.

Makino Law Office in Tokyo, which is organizing the potential legal action, said that the breach was more serious than other incidents, as it could provide bad actors with a list of people along with their assets and addresses, and could also be used to make scams seem legitimate.

Even if customers do not experience any losses related to the potential leak, they may still be entitled to damages due to emotional distress, details on the law firm’s website soliciting claimants said.

Rakuten Securities told customers to consider locking their accounts to temporarily suspend transactions and services, and to remain vigilant against impersonators, but said they had not identified any cases of wrongdoing so far.

The securities company has not announced if they will be compensating any customers for the leak.

Makino Law Office, which is also representing plaintiffs in a similar class-action suit announced last month against Times Car services, created its site related to the Rakuten Securities incident earlier this week, urging those affected to sign up.

It will consider whether to go ahead with filing the lawsuit depending on how many people register their interest and what measures Rakuten Securities take following the security incident.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said that the Financial Services Agency was monitoring the “regrettable” situation and had instructed Rakuten Securities to report back to the agency on how it happened.

“It should respond earnestly and do everything possible to alleviate concerns,” Katayama said, adding that the company should take action toward protecting its customers.

In the Times Car case, Park24, the parent company of vehicle-sharing and rental service operator Times Mobility, offered ¥3,000 to each affected user, including those who had images of personally identifying documents such as a driver’s license accessed in the breach.

The lawsuit led by Makino Law Office seeks ¥50,000 for each customer who had images of personal identification documents leaked, and ¥30,000 for every other affected customer.

World.title: Hong Kong slams ‘biased’ US report accusing city of expanding security powers
World.content:
Hong Kong has slammed an annual report by a US congressional commission that accused the government of expanding its security powers, including restricting media coverage of the Wang Fuk Court fire, the city’s deadliest blaze in decades.

The Hong Kong government on Friday evening condemned the report issued by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) a day earlier, calling its accusations “biased slanders and smears”.

It urged the United States to “discern facts from fallacies” and stop interfering in Hong Kong affairs.

World.title: Hong Kong proposes tougher building safety penalties after deadly Tai Po blaze
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have proposed tripling the maximum fine for using defective materials or seriously deviating from approved construction plans, from HK$1 million to HK$3 million (US$382,437), as part of a sweeping overhaul of building safety rules following the deadly Tai Po fire last year.

The Development Bureau also said on Friday that the government would issue a technical memorandum clearly defining the responsibilities of authorised people and technical directors to prevent professionals from shirking accountability.

The reforms follow last November’s blaze at Wang Fuk Court, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. Multiple safety violations were found to have exacerbated the fire, including the use of flammable scaffolding netting and foam boards covering windows under renovations at the estate.

World.title: Beijing’s Hong Kong point man hopes CUHK-Shenzhen uses ‘unique strengths’ in GBA growth
World.content:
Beijing’s point man on Hong Kong affairs visited the Shenzhen campus of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), calling on the institution to leverage its unique strengths while serving the development of the Greater Bay Area.

Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, paid a visit to the institution on Friday morning, according to a release from the office.

After listening to a briefing from the university’s president, Xu Yangsheng, a professor in automation and computer-aided engineering, Xia affirmed the university’s educational direction, the office said.

World.title: Tai Po fire: memorial events for victims won’t be blocked, Eric Chan says
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities will not obstruct residents from holding memorial activities to mark the first anniversary of the deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze, the city’s No 2 official has said.

Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said on Friday that the government was willing to offer help to organisations in holding memorial events.

“I have heard that some groups claim they were pressured to cancel certain memorial events. I want to clarify and reiterate that Hong Kong is a place governed by the rule of law, and as long as any memorial activity is lawful, the government definitely allows it,” he said.

World.title: Hong Kong joins global drug body ahead of schedule, boosting regulatory ambitions
World.content:
Hong Kong has joined a global body for drug regulators ahead of schedule, a move health authorities say brings the city closer to establishing its own internationally recognised regulatory authority.

The city was admitted as the 20th regulatory member of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) at an assembly meeting in Prague on Tuesday.

Hong Kong is poised to become a crucial “bridgehead” for mainland Chinese drugs to reach global markets amid current geopolitical tensions.

World.title: HKUST turns a 35-year-old vision into impact for the future of regional innovation
World.content:
HKUST council chairman Professor Harry Shum Heung-yeung says: “The concept of the Greater Bay Area was envisioned by our founding president, Professor Woo. He understood the importance of this area, not only for Hong Kong, but also for the future of the motherland.”

Woo was also an early advocate of deeper integration between Hong Kong and mainland China, recognising the region’s potential as a hub for talent, research and innovation long before the Greater Bay Area entered public discourse.

“He didn’t just want to build a university,” says HKUST president Professor Nancy Ip Yuk-yu. “He envisioned an institution where education, research and innovation come together to create impact for society.”

The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) marks its 35th anniversary this year, having established itself as one of Asia’s most highly ranked universities with a reputation built around research excellence, entrepreneurship, innovation and national development. Behind this success is the vision of its founding president, the late Professor Woo Chia-wei.

Guided by this vision, HKUST became one of the first Hong Kong universities to establish a research institute in Shenzhen in 1999. Today, that presence has evolved into an innovation network spanning Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Foshan and Shanghai.

The foundation laid by Woo has enabled HKUST to build one of the region’s most vibrant research and innovation ecosystems. Under government-led initiatives, the university hosts seven InnoHK centres along with three State Key Laboratories to conduct frontier research in artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, robotics, renewable energy and biomedicine, with a strong focus on translating discoveries into real-world impact.

HKUST has nurtured an entrepreneurial culture, resulting in its giving birth to more than 2,000 start-ups, including 11 unicorns and 23 successful exits through initial public offerings as well as mergers and acquisitions. Among its most notable examples is drone technology company DJI, founded by HKUST alumnus Frank Wang.

Professor Nancy Ip (right), president of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, brings a background in neuroscience to her role, while Professor Harry Shum, chairman of the university council, is a tech industry veteran and AI expert.

Looking ahead, Shum sees enormous potential in emerging fields such as the low-altitude economy – commercial activities that take place in airspace below 1,000 metres (3,281 feet) – and artificial intelligence. HKUST researchers with years of experience in developing these technologies, in addition to robotics, communications and autonomous systems, are contributing to the Hong Kong government’s low-altitude economy regulatory sandbox programme.

Shum also believes AI’s greatest promise lies in accelerating scientific discovery, transforming fields ranging from mathematics and materials science to drug development.

After 35 years, HKUST continues to champion cutting-edge research by translating bold scientific ideas into technological breakthroughs with real-world impact.

As it enters its next chapter, HKUST sees the Northern Metropolis, and particularly the development’s future San Tin University Town, as a natural extension of the institution’s founding mission. The megaproject across northern Hong Kong is designed to create housing, jobs and tech-driven growth alongside cross-border links with Shenzhen.

Central to this vision is the proposed establishment of Hong Kong’s third medical school. Ip believes the facility will offer an opportunity to pioneer a new model of medical education that draws on HKUST’s unique strengths in science, engineering, artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship.

“We envision a ‘closed-loop’ ecosystem where clinicians identify challenges at the bedside and work closely with scientists, engineers and industry partners to develop solutions. These innovations can then be brought back into the clinical setting to benefit patients,” she says.

HKUST has grown beyond its Clear Water Bay campus, expanding into mainland China with operations including a Guangzhou campus. Photo: SCMP/May Tse

She believes the Northern Metropolis can become a dynamic convergence point for talent, research, industry and healthcare innovation. “By integrating medicine, technology and entrepreneurship, we hope to nurture a new generation of clinician-scientists and innovators, while contributing to Hong Kong’s development as an international hub for medical and health innovation.”

Thirty-five years after its founding, HKUST remains guided by the vision that inspired its creation: advancing knowledge, nurturing talent and translating discovery into impact.

World.title: Waiting time for Hong Kong public housing at 10-year low
World.content:
The waiting time for Hong Kong’s public housing fell to its lowest level in a decade in the 12 months to end-September, dropping to 4.4 years from 4.8 years at the end of the previous quarter.

The Housing Bureau said on Friday that for general applications, composite waiting times – which cover standard public rental flats and homes under the Light Public Housing (LPH) scheme – had declined across urban areas, extended urban areas and the New Territories districts.

At the end of September, about 96,100 families and single elderly people were on the general application waiting list for a standard public rental flat, some 4,400 fewer than at the end of the previous quarter, the bureau said.

World.title: Hong Kong plans EV battery levy of HK$6 per kg on suppliers from 2028
World.content:
Hong Kong plans to impose a recycling levy of about HK$3,000 (US$380) on each electric vehicle battery, with suppliers rather than vehicle owners required to pay the charge as demand grows for the handling of retired batteries.

The Environmental Protection Department said on Friday that the levy, expected to be implemented in 2028, would be raised gradually and reach about HK$15,000 in 2043 for a battery typically weighing 500kg (1,102lbs).

Asked whether suppliers would pass the extra costs on to EV owners, the department said “market forces” would determine whether that happened.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.title: China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.content:
China has successfully tested two large unmanned cargo aircraft: one with a 5-ton payload capacity and the other capable of flying 3,000 kilometers, laying the groundwork for future commercial and emergency transportation systems.

On Tuesday, the country announced that the Changying-8, a domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, had completed a test delivery. Three days prior, another domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, the W5000, also completed its maiden flight.

The milestones come as China’s drone market is expected to exceed 140 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) by the end of 2026, with the industrial drone segment alone projected to reach 84 billion yuan, up 12.5% from last year.

China began testing large cargo drones as early as 2017 and incorporated the concept of the “low-altitude economy” into government policy in 2021. The Civil Aviation Administration of China has also laid out a roadmap to establish an air transportation system for unmanned aircraft by 2035.

During its delivery test, the Changying-8, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation, released a cargo pallet at an altitude of 300 meters before returning to its base.

The aircraft, whose maiden flight took place in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, on March 31, has a maximum range of over 3,000 kilometers, measures 17 meters in length, has a 25-meter wingspan, and an 18-cubic-meter cargo compartment volume, domestic media reported.

In the event of extreme disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and mudslides destroying roads and bridges, the aircraft can be used to transport up to 3.5 metric tons of goods, equal to over 700 disaster-relief tents, the head of the Changying-8’s development team told state news agency Xinhua.

According to its engineers, future applications could include transportation of regional cargo, emergency supplies, and cold-chain deliveries, domestic media reported.

On Saturday, the W5000, an unmanned cargo aircraft developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, also completed its maiden flight in northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

The aircraft flew for about 30 minutes at an altitude of 1,000 meters, completing a series of test maneuvers before landing. The test focused on the aircraft’s flight stability and the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, electronics, and ground-based monitoring and control systems.

With a maximum payload capacity of 5 metric tons, the W5000 is billed as one of the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft by payload capacity. Made of carbon fiber and weighing less than 6 metric tons, the aircraft measures over 22 meters in both length and wingspan and can fly at a cruising speed of 526 kilometers per hour, with a maximum range of 2,600 kilometers, domestic media reported.

Hu Zhendong, founder, chairman, and CEO of Air White Whale, said the W5000 could reduce logistics costs per ton-kilometer by more than 60% compared with comparable crewed cargo aircraft.

The W5000 is expected to begin commercial operation by the end of next year, according to domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: The W5000, billed as the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft, on display at Airshow China 2024 in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, Nov. 12, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.title: Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.content:
One of the wildest boss fights in China’s latest hack-and-slash blockbuster game begins with a calligraphy brush. Soul, the protagonist of Phantom Blade Zero, released late last month, dots the eyes of a lion-dance head, performing a traditional Chinese ritual believed to awaken the eponymous beast.

Cue the violence. Two performers animate the lion, lunging at Soul with blades spinning on its head and flames pouring from its mouth. The fight then spills onto elevated wooden poles, where Soul and the lion-dance master leap from perch to perch, trading blows to pounding Chinese drums and screaming electric guitar.

In the game its creator originally envisioned, Soul had just 66 lives to survive this fight and every other. Use them up, and hours of progress across the campaign would be gone for good.

The restriction was meant to mirror the game’s story: Soul has just 66 days to find a replacement for his damaged heart. But Beijing-based developer S-Game eventually abandoned the compulsory death limit, introducing three difficulty settings and making the original challenge optional.

S-Game founder Liang Qiwei called the compromise “one of the countless difficult decisions we made in developing Phantom Blade Zero.” His studio spent four years and a reported 300 million to 400 million yuan ($45 million to $60 million) creating a game it hoped would introduce wuxia — Chinese martial arts fantasy — to audiences around the world.

To bring its combat to life, S-Game recruited Hong Kong action star Donnie Yen, enlisted martial arts experts, and brought traditional performers into motion-capture studios. The finished game features more than 50 bosses and 55 weapons, each offering different ways to fight.

The scale of the undertaking drew inevitable comparisons with Black Myth: Wukong, China’s breakout global gaming hit of 2024. Chinese gamers even dubbed Phantom Blade Zero “the village’s second college student,” hoping the conditions for success would align twice.

So far, it has. Video game rating site IGN gave Phantom Blade Zero a 9 out of 10, praising its “memorable boss fights, compelling combat, and limitless swagger.” Its PC version scored 88 on review aggregator Metacritic, surpassing the 81 Black Myth: Wukong received.

Released on Oct. 29, with a standard edition priced at 268 yuan ($40) and a deluxe edition at 328 yuan, the game sold more than 4 million copies in its first 72 hours, topping Steam’s bestseller chart and generating an estimated 1 billion yuan in gross sales.

Unlike Wukong, which drew on the beloved Chinese classic “Journey to the West,” Phantom Blade Zero had to win over players with a far less familiar fictional universe, one Liang had spent two decades developing.

Punk fiction

In 2006, while studying architecture at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, Liang began developing Rain Blood, an independent role-playing game inspired by Taiwanese wuxia novelist Gu Long. Built using software intended for amateur game developers, it introduced Soul, an assassin serving the Order, a secretive organization of martial artists.

Over the following years, Liang, who later earned a master’s degree in architecture from Yale University, expanded the fictional universe through a series of PC and mobile games, retaining its characters, history, and storytelling conventions. In 2017, he began developing concepts for Phantom Blade Zero.

This time, Soul is fighting for his own survival. Framed for the murder of the Order’s leader and gravely wounded, he is kept alive by a venom-infused replacement heart that will last just 66 days. He must uncover the conspiracy, clear his name, and find a way to survive.

His search takes him through a bleak, rain-soaked world where ancient Chinese temples house enormous machinery, and traditional martial arts coexist with mechanical prosthetics. Liang calls the distinctive blend of wuxia and industrial technology “kungfupunk.”

Geng Youzimin, a researcher at Peking University’s Video Game and Art Research Center who has followed the series for years, recognized much of the old Rain Blood universe in the new game, from its character names and dialogue to its cold, gray atmosphere.

While many Chinese wuxia games emphasize storytelling over action, Geng was particularly impressed by Phantom Blade Zero’s side quests and the portrayal of jianghu — the loosely governed world of wandering martial artists, rival factions, and secret societies familiar to readers of wuxia fiction.

“The jianghu often represents a world in which an existing power structure governing a region has collapsed, while a new one has yet to emerge,” he said.

In one such quest, a Shadow Warden sent to capture Soul instead seeks his help to escape the organization he serves. He even discards the numerical identity assigned by his masters and chooses a name for himself. Though he ultimately fails to break free, he secretly helps Soul defeat his enemies, even at the cost of his own life.

Yet not all of the older series’ conventions have been as warmly received. Some players mocked the game’s grandiose names as adolescent melodrama, including “Dark Demon Castle,” where Soul fights a boss portrayed by Donnie Yen. Others found its dialogue overly straightforward.

Geng, who welcomed those familiar touches as a longtime fan, said the pushback underscores how tastes have shifted since the franchise’s indie beginnings. “When this IP first emerged, these elements were popular,” he said, adding that today, the same stylistic quirks have become “baggage” that risks alienating a wider audience.

For Cao Yuan, a game content creator in his 30s who had never played S-Game’s earlier titles, the moral ambiguity of its world struck a chord. “The game incorporates many such blurred boundaries between good and evil,” he said.

Cao also found Soul’s struggle more relatable. “I have no weapons, no resources, nothing at all, but I still have to fight my way into the jianghu,” he said. “That experience feels very close to real life.”

The fire-breathing lion that confronts Soul took shape in a Shanghai motion-capture studio, where a troupe from China’s southern Guangdong province performed a traditional lion-dance routine. Combat director Yang Liu and his team used the recordings to develop the fight, exaggerating the performers’ head tosses and tail swings into attacks.

Even the vegetables suspended above the arena draw on cai qing, or “plucking the greens,” a southern Chinese lion-dance ritual in which the lion retrieves greenery symbolizing prosperity and spits it out to spread good fortune.

In the game, Soul can collect the vegetables to boost his power; later, when the lion-dance master finally breaks free of the force controlling him, he offers Soul the greens.

The music, helmed by Bo Caisheng, a composer who’s worked on animated productions and video games, draws on the same traditions, beginning with drums performed live before introducing percussion evocative of the northern Shanxi province and electric guitar. Bo described his approach as “using Chinese music as the skeleton and Western music as the flesh.”

Tang Zhi, 35, grew up in central China’s Hunan province, where he was familiar with lion dancing from neighboring Guangdong. A Beijing-based developer relations executive, he’s followed Phantom Blade Zero since its early trailers.

“When you jump around on the plum blossom poles and fight the boss, it immediately reminds you of the martial arts performances you watched as a child,” he said.

Game theory

For all the intricate martial arts choreography onscreen, pulling off spectacular moves in Phantom Blade Zero requires surprisingly few commands.

In a fight against a wooden puppet, flashes of blue signal an attack the player can block, while red warns of one that must be dodged. Each response takes a button press, though timing is crucial: dodge at precisely the right moment, and Soul executes “ghoststep,” instantly slipping behind his opponent.

Another button unleashes an elaborate finishing sequence, launching the puppet into the air before Soul slashes its neck as it lands.

Liang wanted to make such combat accessible to newcomers while giving experienced players room to test their skills and explore its depth. Those less interested in mastering the fighting system could concentrate on the story or simply enjoy the cinematic choreography.

“And in the era of livestreaming and short videos, the gameplay itself will become content for a wider audience,” Liang wrote on social media.

Players can combine 30 primary weapons and 25 secondary weapons, including broadswords and twin daggers, each with their own moves and finishing animations. A sha qi, or “killing intent” meter, replenished by well-timed blocks and weapon switches, encourages fast, aggressive combat.

For Zhang Yingshen, 35, a game content creator who works in public relations for a foreign gaming company, the combat was exhilarating without the frustration he associated with learning other action games.

“It’s a game where positive feedback practically spills out of the screen,” he told Sixth Tone.

But Zhang admitted that he eventually wanted more of a challenge. “About halfway through the game, I felt it was a little easy, so I switched to the highest difficulty setting. But even that wasn’t challenging enough,” he said.

Players can switch between three difficulty settings as they progress, but the toughest challenge is reserved for those who complete the main story. Only then can they unlock “66 Days,” a separate mode that limits them to 66 lives — the restriction Liang originally intended for every player.

But Zhang’s experience at a Phantom Blade Zero playtest in Beijing left him with reservations about the combat system’s staying power. “We (and other uploaders) were worried that players might feel exhausted after 10 to 20 hours of gameplay,” he said.

Yet he found that the game’s more than 50 bosses and interconnected, three-dimensional maps gave players plenty to explore across Liang’s sprawling jianghu world.

“Throughout the game, you constantly feel like you’re discovering something new around every corner, and you always maintain a sense of freshness about the world,” Zhang said.

He Wei, a professor at Beijing Normal University’s School of Arts and Communication, sees Phantom Blade Zero’s fusion of wuxia and industrial machinery as an attempt to create a distinctive style that international audiences can readily embrace.

But he argued that incorporating Chinese traditions was only part of the challenge. “Gameplay is the vessel, while culture is the soul. Only when the two are integrated can a game spread culture far and wide,” he said.

He nevertheless considers Black Myth: Wukong stronger in artistic vision and cultural depth, particularly in its character designs. “From the character concept art to the finished designs, the illustrated portraits of characters are more sophisticated and demonstrate greater depth,” he said.

Geng, from Peking University, cautioned against expecting other Chinese developers to reproduce Wukong’s extraordinary cultural impact. “Black Myth: Wukong was a phenomenon. The cultural discourse it carried, or the cultural responsibilities it took on, were things that neither the game itself nor its development team could ever have fully anticipated,” he said.

Nor did the commercial success of Wukong and Phantom Blade Zero resolve Geng’s doubts about the sustainability of AAA development. Such games demand enormous investment and large-scale production, and require high returns to justify their costs.

“AAA games will always represent the ultimate ideal for many game developers, the crown jewel of their ambitions. But commercially, they are increasingly more like luxury goods,” he said.

For Liang, bringing a fictional world he had spent two decades developing to a mass audience meant balancing his desire for creative expression with his responsibilities to paying players. After a playtest in Beijing, he described himself as “a service provider” who had to give players more than their money’s worth.

“Making games is a process of dissolving one’s own ego and sinking it into the earth,” he wrote on social media, “where it can grow into a flourishing tree nourished by the soil.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A scene from the video game “Phantom Blade Zero.” From @影之刃零 on Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.title: China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.content:
China has proposed its first regulation on vocational skills certifications, cracking down on fraudulent credentials and tightening oversight of certification bodies.

The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security released the draft regulation on Nov. 12, with public feedback open until Dec. 12. No date has been set for when the rules will take effect.

China now has more than 220 million skilled workers — including electricians, AI trainers, and elderly-care workers — accounting for about 30% of its workforce, according to the ministry. Vocational skills certificates can bring benefits such as cash subsidies, children’s school enrollment, and fast-tracked residency applications.

Fraudulent vocational skills certificates have proliferated online in recent years, prompting a nationwide crackdown on bogus credentials in 2022.

The proposed regulation would tighten oversight of certification bodies, barring them from making misleading claims or leaking exam questions. In addition, certificates can be issued only to candidates who pass the required assessments, rather than those who simply pay to obtain them.

The draft also outlines that organizations responsible for vocational qualification assessments would be barred from offering related training. Institutions that issue certificates without first registering with the government, as well as those that forge, alter, or trade certificates, may face suspension, confiscation of illegal earnings, and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan ($1,500 to $15,000).

The rules also outline penalties for examiners who engage in misconduct, candidates who cheat, and officials who fail to perform their duties properly. Employers will be encouraged to use workers’ certified skill levels as a key factor in determining pay.

Previously, workers obtained vocational qualifications through government-organized exams. Starting in 2020, however, China phased out most government-issued vocational qualifications, shifting responsibility to registered and supervised third-party organizations. By the end of 2025, 32,000 such organizations were in operation nationwide.

Cheng Xiezhong, a law professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media that the shift had “helped expand the pool of skilled workers” but had also led to uneven standards among certification bodies and a widespread increase in bogus certificates.

An investigation by domestic media this June found vocational certificates openly advertised on multiple Chinese e-commerce platforms. In one case, a reporter paid just 300 yuan for a mechanical equipment installer certificate showing passing scores on tests they had never taken.

Previous reports also found that some training providers issued course completion certificates rather than recognized vocational credentials. Others lured young jobseekers into “training loan” scams, persuading them to borrow thousands of yuan for courses.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Heade image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.title: Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.content:
Chinese AI model DeepSeek has reportedly begun limiting use of its free chatbot by reducing the number of characters users can input and discontinuing inactive conversations after seven days.

DeepSeek users began reporting seeing an error message — “Due to server overload, the use limit has been reached” — on Monday when they tried to continue chats inactive for a week or when they tried to input larger volumes of text, according to posts on microblogging platform Weibo.

According to domestic media, users of the large language model (LLM) can now only enter around 40,000 characters at a time (a page of Chinese text typically ranges from 500 to 800 characters). Previously, the chatbot had no publicly stated text limit. Once users reach their daily limit, DeepSeek displays an error message.

It is reportedly the first time DeepSeek, headquartered in China’s eastern city of Hangzhou, has restricted free-user access since its launch in January 2025.

According to its official status page, DeepSeek has experienced 57 outages or performance degradations this year, without providing additional explanation. Domestic media reported that disruptions in the first half of the year mainly involved slower responses, delays in data generation, and occasional request failures. After October, prolonged global outages began to occur more frequently.

Usage caps apply only to individual users, but because DeepSeek has no related paid plan, those who hit their capacity cannot pay for more. App developers, who pay to use DeepSeek through an application programming interface, or API, a connection that shares data between their software and the AI model, are subject to separate limits and per-use billing.

As of Wednesday, DeepSeek had not announced a reason for the new rules or whether it might lift them. Developers who spotted references to a “Coding Plan” in the website’s code have speculated that the company may soon implement a paid subscription plan for individual users.

Online, users debated the new limits, with many expressing outrage and complaining that the company had not rolled out a paid plan option for individual users before the usage limit. “I feel like I’m a widow who just lost her husband,” wrote one user on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote.

Others sympathized with DeepSeek, arguing that data is costly or hypothesizing that the company was clamping down on users developing companion relationships with its AI, alluding to China’s ban on AI products designed to mimic human personalities that took effect on July 15.

Data from OpenRouter, a U.S.-based platform that provides access to numerous AI models through one interface, showed DeepSeek’s latest model processing 59.2 trillion tokens the week of Nov. 9 to 15, topping OpenRouter’s weekly token usage chart.

Long chats are more costly for LLM developers because models must parse more information with each reply. Industry watchers told domestic media that the higher costs mean DeepSeek may now have to choose between training new models, serving paying API customers, and providing free chats.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng has long said the company has moved toward developing its artificial general intelligence capabilities — the drive to create an AI that can match or surpass humans across a wide range of tasks — rather than consumer revenue.

Earlier this year, Liang said computing power is the biggest factor holding the company back. He also described near-term business opportunities targeting customers as “sesame seeds,” a Chinese turn of phrase describing small gains not worth chasing at the expense of a bigger payoff.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019257/Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.title: Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019257/Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.content:
In 1903, 22-year-old Lu Xun, then a student in Japan, wandered into a bookstore in Jimbocho, Tokyo’s famed book district, where his attention was caught by a science fiction novel titled “A Journey to the Moon in Ninety-Seven Hours and Twenty Minutes.” Translated into Japanese by Inoue Tsutomu and believed to have been written by an American author, the novel appealed to Lu Xun’s own ambition to popularize scientific knowledge in China, where modern science education was still in its infancy. Enthusiastic about the genre’s potential, he quickly set about translating it into Chinese.

His version, “Yuejie Lüxing” (“A Journey to the Moon”), published the same year and among the earliest Chinese translations of science fiction, marked the beginning of his prolific career as a translator, long before he became celebrated as the “founding father of modern Chinese literature” for his novels and essays.

Today, we know that Inoue had misidentified the original author. The novel was, in fact, Jules Verne’s “De la Terre à la Lune: trajet direct en 97 heures 20 minutes,” published in 1865 and widely translated into English in the 1870s. Misled by its setting — in post-Civil War America, where members of the Baltimore Gun Club plan to fire a projectile at the moon — Inoue assumed the author was American. Lu Xun, following this assumption, opened his translation with original passages describing America in extravagant detail to provide context for his Chinese readers.

The curious story of this translation and mistranslation of Verne’s novel illuminates how literary forms and ideas traveled across borders at the turn of the 20th century, particularly in East Asia following the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), when waves of Chinese students — including Lu Xun — went to study in Japan.

It was in Tokyo, amid the intellectual riches of Jimbocho, where he spent much of his leisure time, that Lu Xun was drawn to translation. Japan’s Meiji Restoration, which restored imperial rule in 1868, had already spurred a flood of translations from European languages into Japanese. Eager to take advantage of this wealth of material, Lu Xun, by then proficient in Japanese, with a working knowledge of German and some Russian, immersed himself in these texts. On one hand, he translated texts from cultures he perceived as more scientifically and technologically advanced, with the aim of promoting science education among his own people; on the other hand, he gradually developed an interest in writers from marginalized communities and nations, believing their experiences would resonate with China, which had endured decades of foreign invasion and exploitation. Later, recounting his decision to translate the exiled Russian writer and activist Vasily Eroshenko, he made clear that he saw translation not simply as an aesthetic pursuit, but as a means of giving voice to the oppressed.

It is worth remembering that Lu Xun, then an unknown young student named Zhou Shuren, had yet to adopt his most famous pen name that would be enshrined in modern Chinese literature. In 1918, he published “A Madman’s Diary,” a pioneering work of modern Chinese fiction inspired by a short story of the same name by Russian writer Nikolai Gogol. He later wrote the celebrated novella “The True Story of Ah Q,” published in 1921, helping establish vernacular Chinese as a language of modern literature. He is remembered as a pioneer of the New Culture Movement, which championed “Mr. Democracy” and “Mr. Science” just as China transitioned from monarchy to republic.

But in 1903, a literary career was not yet his ambition. Funded by a Qing government scholarship to study in Japan, he began by taking language courses, translating scientific essays, science fiction, and literary works along the way, before enrolling in medical school in Sendai City, 370 kilometers north of Tokyo, in 1904.

He would soon abandon medicine to pursue his own literary and intellectual revolution, with translation as his chosen medium. Back in Tokyo in 1906, Lu Xun remained enrolled at a German-language school, but rather than attend classes, he devoted his time to translating, writing, and publishing. He shared a small room with his younger brother, Zhou Zuoren (1885–1967), who had joined him in Japan.

The brothers sent their translations to publishers in China. Translation was poorly paid a century ago, just as it often is today. Zhou Zuoren later recalled with resignation: “… manuscript fees were truly meager. Typically, the translation of Western-language texts only earned two yuan per 1,000 characters — and this was a net amount, with all punctuation and black spaces excluded from the calculation.”

Nevertheless, the brothers pursued their work with passion, publishing “Collection of Stories from Abroad” in 1909. Reflecting their intellectual ambitions, the collection featured revolutionary literature from “peripheral” nations whose experiences echoed China’s own. They hoped such works could change minds and contribute to social progress. Funded by Jiang Yizhi, a banker from China’s eastern Zhejiang province, the collection sold poorly, with just 21 copies of the first volume and 20 of the second sold in six months, according to Lu Xun’s preface to a later edition.

Like translators today, those of the past could find their intellectual lives both poor and rich: financial hardship drove them to scrimp and work harder, while literature’s riches tempted them to procrastinate. We might imagine these “revolutionary figures” readily sacrificing leisure for national salvation, but their personal accounts tell a more relatable, even comforting, story.

After Lu Xun returned to Tokyo from Sendai, the brothers moved to the wider Kanda-Jimbocho area. After moving a few times, they rented the former residence of renowned Japanese novelist Natsume Sōseki with three friends and named their share-house Wushe, “the house of five.” As admirers of Natsume, they even shopped at the same grocery stores he had frequented and followed his recommended reading list. Personal accounts suggest that Lu Xun spent much of his stipend on books, economizing on food and other daily necessities as a result, which also helps explain why he shared a room with Zhou Zuoren.

Tightening their belts for books while working on their envisioned projects, Zhou Zuoren described a conflict with Lu Xun when they shared a room: “He kept urging me to translate, but I brushed him off. One day, he suddenly flew into a rage, raised his fist, and beat me on the head several times.” As a translator who habitually procrastinates, I can’t bear to imagine what life would be like if I shared a room with my editor.

Translation was more than just work for the Zhou brothers. They lived a “translated” way of life. Kanda-Jimbocho, where they lived, served as a “universal library” and remains Tokyo’s most celebrated book district. Much like Chinese students abroad today who frequent bookstores such as Strand Bookstore, Daunt Books, Shakespeare and Company, or Kinokuniya, the brothers visited Jimbocho’s bookshops almost daily.

The brothers devoured texts across languages and genres. They kept detailed records of their favorite bookstores, even rating the quality of their books and service. Their daily lives involved constant movement between languages as they learned new ones and absorbed political, social, and literary theories, whether in their original languages or in translation.

This broad and intensive engagement transformed their intellectual horizons, offering access to ideas from around the world. As Zhou Zuoren later recalled, Lu Xun would read and write until dawn, sleep until late morning, get up to smoke, and then repeat the cycle.

Later, figures such as Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People’s Republic of China; Guo Moruo, a writer, poet, and communist leader; Tian Han, the playwright who wrote the lyrics to China’s national anthem; and Feng Zikai, a pioneer of modern Chinese comics, would undergo similar intellectual journeys shaped by translation while studying in Tokyo. They, too, explored different paths toward China’s modernization through their engagement with translated texts, ideas, and ways of life.

In a 1931 letter to fellow writer and revolutionary Qu Qiubai, Lu Xun argued that “translations not only introduce new things but also new ways of expression.” By incorporating unfamiliar syntax into modern Chinese through translation, whether “ancient, dialectal or foreign,” he believed “we can later make it our own.”

His goal was to shape modern Chinese into a truly global language through translation, one flexible enough to absorb diverse forms of expression and capable of conveying ideas from around the world. Arguably, in his imagination, modern Chinese was a language born of translation, one that proudly celebrates its linguistic inheritances. Tian Han and Feng Zikai shared similar convictions, believing that drama and comics — beyond translation in the narrow linguistic sense — embodied cosmopolitan ideals and egalitarian possibilities more vividly than other forms.

To fully appreciate Lu Xun’s significance in modern Chinese literature and language, we cannot examine his fiction alone. In many ways, his identity as a translator — both in the literal sense and in the broader, metaphorical sense of absorbing influences from other cultures and passing them on — was fundamental to his intellectual and literary work.

At a time when cultural exchange has become increasingly complex and contentious, Lu Xun’s story as a translator offers a fresh perspective on what it means to be truly global.

(Header image: Lu Xun (left) with Kaizōsha publishing house president Sanehiko Yamamoto (center) and Japanese bookseller Kanzo Uchiyama (right) at Shingetsutei in Shanghai, Feb. 11, 1936. From the collection of the Lu Xun Museum.)

World.title: Lesson in Endurance: China’s Schools Start Later to Ease Burden on Students
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019288/Lesson in Endurance: China’s Schools Start Later to Ease Burden on Students
World.content:
Parents across China have for years raised concerns about how long children spend in school each day, with some high school students logging at least 15 hours in class.

In recent weeks, education authorities nationwide have been pushing back start times for all grades to ease the burden.

Schools in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, reportedly began introducing changes in November. A parent told the Yangtze Evening Post that their child, a high school freshman, now starts studying at 7:15 a.m. and finishes after-school study sessions at 9:20 p.m., a 45-minute reduction from the previous schedule of 6:40 a.m. to 9:30 p.m.

Jiangyin, a city about two hours east by road, also announced across-the-board adjustments on Nov. 5. Classes now start at 8 a.m. at primary schools, 7:40 a.m. at middle schools, and 7:20 a.m. at high schools.

During an edition of the show “Zhengfeng Hotline” broadcast live on Jiangsu TV on Oct. 27, Jiang Yong, director of the provincial education department, said, “The issue of excessively long school hours is severe. As the education authority, we feel a profound sense of remorse.”

Paying attention

According to the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey of families, individuals, and communities conducted by researchers at Peking University, 46% of full-time high school students study for more than 12 hours on a typical weekday, while for nearly 25% it’s over 14 hours. Including weekdays and rest days, high school students average 68.6 hours of study time per week.



In 2024, China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) published its Third National Time Use Survey, which for the first time included data on how children and adolescents spend their time. In 2024, China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) published its Third National Time Use Survey, which for the first time included data on how children and adolescents spend their time.

For a 2026 article published in Youth Studies, researchers from Renmin University of China and Peking University analyzed survey data relating to students aged 6 to 17. They found that high school students spend on average 10 hours and 54 minutes engaged in education-related activities on weekdays and six hours and 29 minutes on weekends. That adds up to about 67.5 hours.

These activities cover in-class instruction, after-class study, off-campus tutoring, and commuting to and from school.

However, for some, 67.5 hours is merely a baseline. The study reveals a direct correlation between a parent’s education level and how long their child spends studying.

For those with only a middle school education or lower, their children study an average of eight hours and two minutes a day. If the parent holds a high school diploma or a university degree, that time rises by 15 or 29 minutes, respectively.

Study time also varies by location and school quality.

The CFPS shows that high school students in China’s four municipalities — Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, and Chongqing — as well as provincial capitals study 73.5 hours a week, nearly five hours more than the national average. Meanwhile, for students at key schools, which receive preferential funding and attract high-quality teachers, the figure rises to 75.1 hours.

Both comparisons suggest students in urban high schools and top-tier institutions endure a heavier academic burden.

But why are children spending so long in class? Xiong Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, argued in an article for Southern Weekly that keeping students on campus longer makes them easier to manage, especially amid pressures to boost academic performance and meet parents’ expectations regarding supervision.

No nodding off

Children in primary education face similarly long days. The NBS’ Third National Time Use Survey shows that elementary school students spend eight hours a day on educational activities. That climbs to nine hours and 22 minutes for those in middle school.

This coincides with evidence that suggests this age group already isn’t getting enough shut-eye.

According to a 2021 Ministry of Education notice on improving young people’s sleep, primary school students should get a minimum of 10 hours a day, middle school students nine hours, and high school students eight hours. Measured against these standards, the Youth Studies research article points out that nearly 22% of 6-year-olds and 42% of 11-year-olds are getting insufficient sleep.

Although the recommended daily sleep duration is lowest for older students, about 20% of survey respondents aged 16 and 17 still weren’t getting enough sleep. Researchers explain that the relatively low proportion compared with younger age groups could be because boarding is more common at the high school level, meaning a “more fixed daily schedule.”

As more schools push back start times, some parents see a chance for change. But whether students will get more sleep depends on other factors, including homework load and the length of evening study sessions.

A later start for students will make a difference only if the time it frees up is reserved for rest.

This article, reported by Chen Liangxian and edited by Lü Yan, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.title: China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.content:
China will include a CAR T-cell therapy in its national health insurance scheme for the first time, making a blood cancer treatment that once cost over 1 million yuan ($150,000) per dose more accessible.

The National Healthcare Security Administration announced on Nov. 14 that relmacabtagene autoleucel, or relma-cel, made by Shanghai-based biotech firm JW Therapeutics and sold under the brand name Carteyva, will be covered by insurance starting Jan. 1. The therapy has three approved uses for different types of lymphoma and costs 1.29 million yuan per dose.

CAR T-cell therapy is primarily used to treat types of lymphoma and involves extracting and genetically modifying a patient’s own immune cells to target cancer cells, before infusing them back into the body. China approved its first CAR T-cell therapy product in 2021.

Most of China’s population is covered by the country’s national insurance scheme: 1.33 billion were enrolled in basic medical insurance by the end of 2025. Only drugs listed in the national insurance catalog can be partially reimbursed through the medical insurance fund. For drugs not listed, patients must usually bear 100% of the cost.

For years, CAR T-cell drugs were excluded from the national insurance list because an unwritten industry rule held that drugs priced above 300,000 yuan rarely secured coverage, limiting patient access, according to Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper.

The rate of CAR T-cell drug use as a second-line treatment for large B-cell lymphoma in China is about one-sixth of that in the United States, while use as a third-line treatment is about one-10th of the rate in the U.S. and Europe.

Carteyva was one of five CAR T-cell therapies included last year in China’s first commercial insurance list for high-cost innovative drugs. This year, those drugs became eligible for national coverage. Two CAR T-cell drug manufacturers, including JW Therapeutics, entered insurance coverage negotiations on Sept. 6.

“Two or three years ago, we wouldn’t have dared to imagine this,” Tian Feng, JW Therapeutics chairman and CEO, told The Paper.

China records about 101,500 new lymphoma cases each year. Carteyva is available at more than 200 certified hospitals nationwide.

The updated national reimbursement list adds 107 drugs covering oncology, chronic diseases, mental illnesses, rare diseases, and pediatric medications. A separate commercial insurance list, which covers drugs outside the basic scheme, includes 12 new treatments.

“This is a historic moment for lymphoma patients in China,” Tian said, adding that when he and the company received the news, “everyone really felt that the treatment of lymphoma patients in China had entered a new, very exciting era.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.title: A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.content:
A TV drama about a doctor who returns to his small hometown after being fired from a prestigious city-based position has become a hit among young Chinese, who resonate with its message of finding purpose away from competitive urban areas.

“Small Town Remedy” has been hotly discussed since its Nov. 4 finale. Premiering Oct. 21, the show follows Liu Zhengliang, played by A-list actor Xiao Zhan, a young neurosurgeon who returns to his hometown in northeastern China — or Dongbei — from a major hospital following a botched surgery in which his patient dies.

The show’s popularity comes amid a broader shift in attitudes among young Chinese, who increasingly seek a more sustainable work-life balance and self-care amid growing fatigue stemming from relentless competition and conventional definitions of success.

Socially awkward and unfamiliar with local customs, Liu initially struggles to return to life at home after leaving his post in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen. The series depicts how his brother, childhood friends, and former hospital colleagues gradually help him overcome the trauma of his failed operation, among other personal struggles, such as the death of his mother.

Fans have reported being drawn to the drama’s lighthearted tone and the witty humor commonly associated with China’s Northeast, despite tackling heavy subject matter such as illness, death, and grief.

Its popularity has also sparked an online trend of learning the Dongbei dialect, with video lessons gaining traction on social media. One related hashtag — “‘Small Town Remedy’ Dongbei dialect listening test” — had amassed nearly 1.4 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Monday.

The 29-episode drama has earned an average rating of 8 out of 10 on review platform Douban and reached an audience of 148 million across all streaming platforms, according to data from domestic streaming platform iQiyi. Related hashtags on short-video platform Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, had also garnered more than 8 billion views.

Since the show’s finale, online users have been debating what Liu’s next move should be. Some suggest that as a talented young doctor, he should return to a major hospital to pursue better career prospects, while others say he’d be better off staying in his hometown, where he’d have the emotional space to continue recovering and potentially find greater purpose using his medical skills.

“Everyone wants to go to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, but if life away from home is too difficult, returning to your hometown is not a step backward, nor is it something to be ashamed of,” one user wrote beneath a post discussing the show on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “One’s hometown can be a great choice, too.”

“As urbanization continues, more and more young people are facing the same dilemmas as Liu Zhengliang,” another Xiaohongshu user wrote in a comment under the same post, referring to Liu’s struggles with cultural identity and homesickness. “I think the theme of this show really suits the times.”

In one widely discussed scene, Liu and his girlfriend see off his younger brother as he leaves for Beijing in search of better job opportunities. Overwhelmed by the farewell, the female protagonist, played by Jiang Yan, questions the seemingly inevitable exodus from their hometown.

“Were we born in Dongbei only to leave it behind?” she asks. “The winters here may be cold, but people’s hearts are warm ... Will leaving Dongbei necessarily bring happiness? Don’t those who leave ever miss home?”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Small Town Remedy.” From Douban)

World.title: PBA great PJ Simon, the ‘Scoring Apostle,’ dies at 46
World.content:
Philippine basketball mourns the sudden passing of former PBA star PJ Simon, who died after collapsing during a game

MANILA, Philippines – Former PBA star Peter June “PJ” Simon died on Friday, November 20, after collapsing in a basketball game. He was 46.

The Purefoods/Magnolia franchise confirmed his passing in a social media post.

“Isa si PJ sa pinakamagandang ehemplo ng isang professional basketball player (PJ is one of the best examples of a professional basketball player),” the team said. “You competed with quiet confidence, carried yourself with humility, and wore #8 with a pride everyone could feel.”

“You represented the franchise in the best way possible, and that is why you are beloved not just by Hotshots fans, but every Filipino basketball fan.”

Though no official cause of death was given, multiple videos online showed Simon being fanned by teammates on the sideline and eventually carried off-court after an apparent mid-game collapse in what looked like a recreational match in Davao City.

Drafted 43rd overall in 2001, Simon quickly established himself as one of the greatest PBA draft steals, eventually carving out a legendary 16-year career entirely with the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise, and earning the iconic moniker “The Scoring Apostle.”

Forming a feared guard duo with fellow franchise icon and shooter James Yap, Simon provided excellent production mostly off the bench, enough to earn him eight PBA All-Star selections and win Mr. Quality Minutes twice.

Alongside fellow stars like Yap, Marc Pingris, and Mark Barroca, Simon immortalized himself in PBA lore in 2014 after helping Purefoods — named the San Mig Coffee Mixers at the time — win the ultimate PBA title trifecta, the rare Grand Slam, under head coach Tim Cone.

“This is so sudden, Part. I didn’t expect it at all,” Yap wrote in Bisaya in a social media post.

“Thank you for everything, Part, for all the times we spent together that I will never forget. We still have a basketball tour to do. This is painful, Part.”

In 2019, Magnolia handed Simon the rare honor of retiring his iconic jersey No. 8, after the Cotabato native helped the franchise win eight PBA titles with averages of 10.1 points in under 22 minutes across nearly 700 games.

After the 2001 PBA draft, Simon started to make a name for himself in the defunct Metropolitan Basketball Association and the Philippine Basketball League, becoming a two-time PBL champion and one-time MVP, before finally suiting up for Purefoods in 2004.

After retiring from the PBA in 2020, Simon made a brief return to the pro ranks in 2024 with the Davao Occidental Tigers of the Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League before again hanging up his sneakers a year later.

“We’ll always remember the eight championships and the Grand Slam. We’ll miss that signature one-hander from midrange. We’ll always think of the clutch shots and heat checks of ‘The Scoring Apostle,'” the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise said.

“Most of all, we’ll miss the person we got to share those moments with.”

Simon is survived by his wife, Jehza, and two children. – Rappler.com

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
