World.title: 1 in 8 Filipino students were vape users in 2024 – DOH
World.content:
'TOBACC-OFF'. Youth advocates against tobacco, nicotine, and vapes during the press conference announcing the 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey findings on November 20, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Some users of e-cigarettes in the Philippines were only 7 years old when they started vaping, the 2024 Global Tobacco Survey finds

MANILA, Philippines – One in eight Filipino students aged 13 to 15 years old were users of electronic cigarettes or vape in 2024, the Department of Health (DOH) said on Friday, November 20.

According to the DOH’s 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey, the rate of students who used vapes within the month they participated in the study was at 12.8%. It was a decrease from 14.1% in 2019.

But the survey also found that 26.7% of students have “used electronic cigarettes in their entire life,” slightly higher than the 24.6% in 2019.

“What we see as a potential room for us to actually act on, we can see that those who actually experiment… only half of those are actually current users of electronic cigarettes,” Dr. Alethea de Guzman, director of the DOH Epidemiology Bureau, said in a press conference.

Health Assistant Secretary Lester Tan said it was alarming that there are e-cigarette users who started at 7 years old, according to the survey.

Department of Health

De Guzman said that smoking is the number one risk factor for non-communicable diseases.

She pointed to the accessibility of vape and to the information about these products for the apparent increase in the use of e-cigarettes.

“Are our youth being targeted by the industry, by those that are selling and distributing these products?” De Guzman said.

According to the survey, e-cigarette use is the most prevalent among Filipino youth at 12.8%, followed by cigarettes (7.1%), smokeless tobacco (5.7%), and other smoke tobacco (4.1%).

Alethea also noted that the figure of current e-cigarette users was higher than the figure for current cigarette users.

“However, this rate shows cigarette smoking persists among the youth with those age 16 years and above having around twice as higher rate at 13.1% versus the younger age group was 6.2% to 7.1%,” she said.

“The rate for current use is increasing as the students get older,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Au Quilala, executive director of the Philippine Legislators’ Committee on Population and Development (PLCPD), said that while it is the responsibility of adults to prevent young ones from accessing cigarettes and vapes, it is the government’s duty to enforce existing laws.

Republic Act No. 11900 or the Vaporized Nicotine and Non-Nicotine Products Regulation Act provides that 18 years old is the minimum allowable age for the purchase, sale, and use of these products.

It also prohibits the sale, promotion, advertising, and product demonstration of vapes within 100 meters of the perimeter of a school, playground, or other facility frequented by minors.

“It is important that we amend RA 11900. Children should not have access to vapes. I hope we raise the minimum age to access vape or cigarette,” Rizza Duro, Philippine Smoke-Free Movement national coordinator, said in Filipino.

Move to fight secondhand smoke

Exposure to secondhand smoke also increased across settings of home, enclosed public places, and outdoor places, according to the survey.

There was also high exposure to secondhand smoke in school properties in 2024, Alethea noted.

Department of Health

Health advocates rallied for the passage of the smoke-free and vape-free environment bill, which seeks to protect public health from exposure to secondhand cigarette smoke and vape aerosol in all public spaces and workplaces, especially those frequented by children.

The proposed measure has moved forward in the House of Representatives following its approval in the chamber’s health committee on November 11, the PLCPD said.

Amid the legislative push, Dr. Dominic Maddumba, DOH Health Promotion Bureau head, said the agency had released a template ordinance for local government units to implement a smoke-free and vape-free environment.

He said the DOH is also stepping up efforts on making smoking and vaping cessation services accessible.

But they will also study the messaging against the use of vape and tobacco products as graphic pictures may have already lost their effectiveness.

Over 8,000 students across 96 schools participated in the 2024 Global Youth Tobacco Survey. The DOH presented findings coming from over 6,000 students aged 13 to 15 years old. – Rappler.com

World.title: Defense witness can’t explain discrepancy in Cale88 sales, cash inflow
World.content:
DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo's testimony on Cale88 raises more suspicions about the banana chips exporter's inward remittances from China

MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness for Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, November 20, admitted he could not explain the discrepancy between the cash inflows and declared sales revenues of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company being linked to the Vice President.

On Day 45 of the impeachment trial, the defense presented Ceferino Rodolfo, Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) undersecretary for industry development and investment promotions, to establish the legitimacy of Cale88.

Rodolfo testified that Cale88 is registered as an export enterprise under the DTI-Board of Investments (BOI) and has complied with the agency’s registration requirements. He also identified the company as a micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME).

In his interjection, Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian questioned the huge disparity between Cale88’s declared sales and its reported cash inflows, asking Rodolfo to explain the possible reasons behind the discrepancy.

“In relation to the operations of the company and the documents they submitted to us, we don’t see any reason for the inward remittances to exceed the declared sales revenue submitted to us,” Rodolfo said.

Rodolfo later admitted that it was his first time encountering such a discrepancy involving a company. He stressed, however, that he was not qualified to explain the figures, saying Cale88’s president, treasurer, operating officer, and export sales manager would be in a better position to do so.

Cale88, a banana chips production company partly owned by Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible.” He likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was a symptom of money laundering.

Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said the central issue was not Cale88’s legitimacy as a registered company but allegations that it may have been used as a front for money laundering.

“What we want to see is proof or records – waybills, shipping records,” Lacson said.

“I know you said earlier that those are with the Customs, but we are all wondering, at least, if the defense could refute the forensic financial analysis, and erase our doubts that Cale88 might have been used,” he added.

Defense counsel Michael Poa clarified that Rodolfo’s testimony was only preliminary, assuring senator-judges that the defense would present other witnesses to address the allegations.

“We understand what you are looking for. We have witnesses for that,” Poa said.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said on October 6 that an investigation by her office showed that Cale88 Food Corporation received remittances from Chinese companies, including entities linked to China’s state-owned sector.

Prior to that, Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura told the impeachment court that Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs).

The National Security Council (NSC) responded to these disclosures last October by saying it would look into the reported inflow of Chinese funds to Cale88.

Vice President Duterte has generally been silent and uncritical about China’s harassment of Philippine vessels in the West Philippine Sea, which critics say could be linked to her family’s business ties with Chinese companies.

Trial schedule

In a related development, the Senate impeachment court has set a new schedule for the trial as it takes a brief break to give way for the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.

Impeachment Court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero initially announced that the trial would resume on Thursday, November 26, reverting to its original schedule of 10 am to 2 pm. However, lead defense counsel Sheila Sison asked for the indulgence of the court, saying their witnesses are unavailable on November 26 and November 27.

“We would like to be candid to the court and say that our next witnesses are not available on November 26 and 27. Also given that we are only informed today that there will be hearings for next week and as you know, this is not our only commitment and we had also made commitments to our other engagements,” Sison said.

“We are not interested in a protracted, prolonged trial of this case and as this court has seen, the defense has been prudent with the time of this court, has not abused this court, and has not wasted three months time presenting witnesses that will eventually be withdrawn,” she said.

House prosecutor Terry Ridon asked for Sison’s remarks to be stricken from the records. He also called for consequences to be placed on the defense for lessening the days of presentation.

Escudero said he would take under advisement Ridon’s manifestation. He also said the impeachment proceedings will resume next month with the following schedule:

December 1 to 4: 10 am – 3 pm

World.title: Martin Romualdez’s co-accused surrenders to NBI
World.content:
SURRENDER. Samchan President Felicito Guevarra surrenders to the National Bureau of Investigation on Thursday, November 19, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – One of the co-accused of former House speaker Martin Romualdez has surrendered to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), the bureau said on Friday, November 20.

The NBI said Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation president Felicito Guevarra surrendered the day before on November 19. Through his counsel, the accused, who faces a plunder case alongside Romualdez, relayed his plan to surrender.

“On 19 November 2026, at approximately 9:00 am, NBI agents proceeded to the agreed meeting place at Santuario de San Antonio Parish, 3117 McKinley Road, Forbes Park, Makati City,” said the NBI.

“At approximately 10:00 am, Guevarra voluntarily submitted to NBI custody in the presence of his counsel,” it added.

Guevarra was read his rights during the surrender and was later brought to the NBI headquarters to undergo standard booking procedures for arrested or surrendered suspects.

On Friday, NBI agents returned the warrant to the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan and presented Guevarra before the 3rd Division, where their case is pending.

Guevarra surrendered after the Office of the Ombudsman moved to cancel his passport. The investigative body said it granted the Samchan president conditional immunity because they will use his testimony to further strengthen their case.

“The Office granted Mr. Guevarra conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case. The immunity rests on his full and truthful testimony,” the Ombudsman said.

“Mr. Guevarra personally handled Samchan’s operations. His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed,” it added.

If Guevarra breaks any condition, the Ombudsman said it will revoke the immunity. The conditions are as follows:

cooperate fully and truthfully with the prosecution

turn over all of Samchan’s records and devices

remain in the country

stay under the Department of Justice’s protection

Romualdez, Guevarra, former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co, and Josely Serenio are facing plunder, a non-bailable offense, due to alleged P7.44 billion in kickbacks from government projects.

The Ombudsman filed the plunder charge against them with the Sandiganbayan on September 7. On the same day, the 3rd Division issued a warrant of arrest against the accused.

Romualdez was subsequently arrested and has been detained in the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14. But his co-accused remained at large, until Guevarra’s surrender. – Rappler.com

World.title: Duterte in ICC jail, but victims’ families still afraid – Callamard
World.content:
LAUNCH. Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard calls for justice for drug war victims during the November 20 launch of 'Walang Pahimakas' in Quezon City, on November 20, 2026.

'How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?' asks Amnesty International secretary general Agnes Callamard

QUEZON CITY, Philippines – Former president Rodrigo Duterte is detained in The Hague, but the families of those killed in his war on drugs are still afraid to seek justice in the Philippines.

Nearly a decade after the killings began, their fear has not gone away.

“How can it be that Duterte is in prison in The Hague, and yet people are scared here now?” Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard asked Friday, November 20.

Callamard, returning to the Philippines after a Duterte-era immigration ban was lifted, raised the question during the launch of Walang Pahimakas (No Farewell), an anthology of poems remembering those killed in the anti-drug campaign.

REMEMBERING. Amnesty International officials and editors of Walang Pahimakas discuss poetry, remembrance, and accountability for drug war killings, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

She had spent the previous 48 hours meeting victims’ families. Their message, she said, was that justice remained beyond their reach.

“How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?” she asked.

“That is an indictment not of President Duterte. It is an indictment of the current government.”

Her remarks came 10 days before the scheduled opening of Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

The former president faces charges of crimes against humanity, including murder and attempted murder, over killings allegedly committed during his anti-drug campaign and earlier operations in Davao City. He has denied wrongdoing.

Callamard welcomed the coming proceedings but said the Marcos administration must also deliver accountability through independent investigations, witness protection, and prosecution of those responsible for unlawful killings.

Poetry for those who never came home

At the book launch in Quezon City, National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario, better known as Rio Alma, read his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran (Pagkatapos ni Francisco Goya), written on May 3, 2020.

RIO ALMA. National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario reads his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran, a warning against injustice and abuse of power, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

“Pag nahimlay ang katwiran, lumalabas ang halimaw.” (When reason falls asleep, the monster emerges.)

Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo, writing as Layad Ya Ikigai, read Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a poem in Kankanaey about a family whose hopes for their child’s future are shattered by loss.

POETRY. Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo reads her Kankanaey poem Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a story of sacrifice, hope, and loss, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

Their works are among those featured in Walang Pahimakas, Amnesty International Philippines’ first published book, with contributions from more than 70 writers and artists.

First unveiled at the Manila International Book Fair in September, the anthology tells the stories of people whose deaths were often reduced to police reports, statistics, and the familiar claim that suspects had fought back.

Its editors, poets Ronald Atilano and Harold Fiesta, said the collection challenges the narratives that helped normalize the killings.

Atilano described the poems as testimony against forgetting, recalling how violence could be presented as necessary or even as service to the nation.

Fiesta said poetry could not bring back the dead, but it could keep their stories from disappearing.

“Those who were denied a proper goodbye should not also be denied remembrance,” he said.

During the launch, Amnesty presented a symbolic check for P69,300 to representatives of victims’ families, representing sales of Walang Pahimakas and Suong at the Manila International Book Fair.

SUPPORT. Amnesty International presents ₱69,300 in proceeds from book sales at the Manila International Book Fair to support families of drug war victims, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

Back after being barred

Callamard last visited the Philippines in 2017, when she was serving as United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions.

Her criticism of Duterte’s anti-drug campaign and calls for an investigation into the killings drew the administration’s ire. In 2018, she was barred from entering the country and declared an undesirable alien.

The immigration restriction was lifted in September 2026.

“A ban may keep a person out, but it cannot suppress the truth,” she said.

Callamard’s return comes as Duterte faces proceedings before the ICC, which is investigating alleged crimes committed while the Philippines was still a party to the Rome Statute.

Play Video

Police figures recorded more than 6,000 deaths during anti-drug operations under Duterte. Human rights organizations have estimated a much higher toll, including killings attributed to unidentified assailants.

Amnesty International Philippines section director Ritz Lee Santos III said accountability through Philippine courts remains limited.

Citing the organization’s assessment, Santos said only five cases involving nine police officers had resulted in convictions, despite thousands of deaths. (READ: [Pinoy Criminology] The hidden impact of Duterte’s drug war)

He questioned how families could pursue justice when filing complaints meant spending money on transportation, missing work, and risking their safety.

“A mother should be able to ask these questions without being passed from one office to another,” he said.

Amnesty International called on the government to investigate unlawful killings, protect witnesses, and replace punitive drug policies with voluntary treatment, healthcare, and evidence-based harm reduction programs.

Callamard, who plans to attend the opening of Duterte’s trial in The Hague, said international proceedings should not become an excuse for inaction in the Philippines.

She also warned that sanctions and political pressure against the ICC, particularly from the United States, threatened an institution on which victims of serious crimes depend when domestic justice systems fail them.

As the launch ended, the poems returned attention to the people at the center of the case: children who waited for parents who never came home, families still looking for answers, and survivors who remain afraid to speak.

Callamard promised them that Amnesty International would continue pressing for investigations and accountability.

“You are not alone, we stand by you and we will fight with you.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
World.content:
FILE PHOTO: An Anthropic, PBC (ANT) sign at One Times Square on the day Anthropic holds their initial public offering (IPO) at the NASDAQ Market site in New York City, US, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton/File Photo

Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending

Anthropic shares fell 6% in premarket trading on Friday, November 20, pulling back after a strong market debut that vaulted the AI lab into the ranks of the most valuable US companies but failed to revive investor enthusiasm for the sector.

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending.

The stock was at $91.24, below Thursday’s close, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about $1.7 trillion and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

The shares are likely to remain in focus for signs of volatility as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

“A decline in share value is normal following a high-profile listing, but we don’t know if that decline will be in line with other IPOs or more volatile, and that should raise alarms for investors,” said Tejal Patel, executive director at the SOC Investment Group.

Anthropic shares closed on Thursday at 13% below their opening price, reinforcing concerns trading could remain volatile in the first few weeks as some investors seek quick gains.

“We would not describe the valuation as cheap. At this valuation, the growth plan is largely priced in,” said Harrison Rolfes, senior research analyst of private company coverage at PitchBook.

“Large IPOs have historically delivered modest returns in their first year.”

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.

Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, and futures pointed to another day of declines on Friday.

Parallels with SpaceX

Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment.

Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms, Bloomberg News reported on Friday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Anti-narcotics agents nab 2 suspects, seize P4M in meth in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
Two suspects arrested in a drug sting on Friday, November 20, in Barangay Lilod Saduc, Marawi City. ( Photo courtesy Marawi City Police Office)

MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur – A joint buy-bust operation on Friday, Nov. 20, by the Philippine National Police Regional Drug Enforcement Unit and the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao ( BARMM) netted two men allegedly involved in illegal drug trade at Lilod Saduc village here.

Colonel Caezar Cabuhat, Lanao del Sur police director, identified the suspects as Abduljalil Pondiong Acraman, 21, alias Tapah, and Samera Dipatuan Ali, 38, alias Jam, both residents of Barangay Rorogagus in this city.

READ: 2 arrested, P6.8M in suspected meth seized in Sulu drug sting

Article continues after this 

Cabuhat said the poseur-buyer, with the aid of a confidential informant, met with the subject persons to the agreed place of transaction.

At the site, Tapha and Jam sold the undercover agent one bag of meth for P600, 000.

On the actual consummation of the illegal drug transaction, authorities arrested the suspects and seized, among others, the meth that, in all weighed 600 grams with an estimated value of P4.08 million, and a Yamaha NMAX motorcycle.

The operation was led by the Regional Drugs Enforcement Unit in collaboration with Regional Intelligence Division PROBAR, Provincial Drug Enforcement Unit -Privincial Special Operstions Group, Marawi Police Station, 1st Provincial Mobile Force Company, 1403rd Regional Mobile Force Battalion 14-A and Provincial Intelligence Unit of Lanao del Sur police. /jpv

World.title: Kids’ welfare group calls out comedian over ‘sexual’ playground joke
World.content:
Council for the Welfare of Children logo in the background of Angelo Tapales, social welfare undersecretary and executive director of the CWC | PHOTO: Facebook page of Undersecretary Angelo M. Tapales – Council for the Welfare of Children

MANILA, Philippines — The Council for the Welfare of Children (CWC) on Friday called out a comedian over “sexualized humor” involving playground “and their association with children.”

Comedian Mr. JP Aguilera of Pencilbox Comedy posted on Facebook: “Sabi ng doktor ko watch what you eat, kaso kumokonti na yung mga playground (My doctor said to watch what you eat, but playgrounds are getting fewer).”

READ: Only 1 of 5 ‘Machong Chismisan’ hosts appears at NBI following subpoenas

Article continues after this 

This joke, the CWC said, “uses playgrounds and their association with children as a sexual reference, raising serious concerns about the use of minors as subjects of sexualized humor.”

“Children should never be reduced to objects of sexual innuendo or made the subject of jokes that trivialize their vulnerability,” it also said.

The CWC noted that the Sec. 4 of the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (OSAEC) and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (CSAEM) Act “strictly prohibits the acts of sexualizing children by presenting them as objects of sexual fantasy or making them conversational subjects of sexual fantasies, in any online or digital platform.”

According to this law, any person found guilty of committing this act shall suffer the penalty of reclusion temporal (12 years and 1 day to 20 years of imprisonment) in its maximum period and a fine of up to P1 million.

The CWC calls on Aguilera and Pencilbox Comedy “to seriously reflect on the implications of the material and exercise greater responsibility in their future performances and content.”

Article continues after this 

Aguilera and Pencilbox Comedy have yet to issue a statement.

Last month, hosts of podcast Machong Chismisan became the subject of a complaint before the National Bureau of Investigation after one of them mocked Kris Aquino’s firstborn son Josh, who is on the autism spectrum. They have since apologized for their remarks. /jpv

World.title: 9 airports, major railway projects eyed for PPPs before Marcos exits
World.content:
Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon during the airport inspection. INQUIRER / GABRYELLE DUMALAG

MANILA, Philippines – The government is lining up nine airports and three major railway projects for public-private partnership (PPP) arrangements before President Marcos ends his term in June 2028, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said Friday.

Dizon announced the plans during the 11th Pilipinas Conference organized by think tank Stratbase Institute, where he outlined the administration’s efforts to complete delayed infrastructure projects and improve the country’s transportation system.

READ: PPP projects rack up P2.81-trillion pipeline

Article continues after this 

He said Mr. Marcos had directed him to “shake it up some more,” particularly in addressing the daily struggles of commuters.

The President also instructed the Department of Transportation (DOTr) to prioritize unfinished infrastructure projects, including bridges, bypass roads and flood control structures.

As part of these efforts, Dizon said the administration was pursuing PPPs for airports and railway systems, which he described as an important part of Mr. Marcos’ legacy.

“The president, I think when he started, said that PPPs are the most important legacy that the President, this administration, is going to leave behind,” he said.

Airports

Article continues after this 

The DOTr will initially pursue a bundled PPP covering the airports in Davao, Siargao and Bicol, which is expected to be awarded in the first quarter of 2027.

The proposal was submitted through an unsolicited offer by the group operating Clark International Airport, covering the development and operation of the three airports.

Article continues after this 

The agency is also eyeing solicited PPPs for Iloilo airport in the first half of 2027, followed by the airports in Bacolod, Puerto Princesa, Busuanga, General Santos and Tacloban.

Dizon said these projects would bring the total number of airports under PPP arrangements to nine before Mr. Marcos leaves office in June 2028.

“For airports, we have already privatized the most PPPs that any other administration has…nine airports will be PPPed by the time the President exits in June of 2028,” he said.

“That will really change the way our airports are run,” he added.

Railway projects

Beyond airports, the DOTr is also preparing PPP arrangements for three major railway projects, including the Light Rail Transit Line 2 (LRT-2), the Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) and an automated fare collection system covering the country’s major railway networks.

The LRT-2 PPP will be pursued with assistance from the International Finance Corp. of the World Bank, while the MRT-3 project will receive support from the Asian Development Bank. Both are targeted for next year.

READ: Dizon says 5 MRT-3 stations to be modernized by 2027

Dizon said the MRT-3 project would be pursued as a long-term PPP with a 25-year concession.

The DOTr is also planning a solicited PPP for an automated fare collection system covering LRT-1, LRT-2, MRT-3, the Metro Manila Subway and the North-South Commuter Railway.

Procurement for the system is expected to begin early next year.

Other infrastructure projects

Apart from the PPP plans, Dizon also announced the expected opening of two major toll road projects.

READ: Calax, CCLink seen boosting economic activity in Cavite, Laguna

The Cavite-Laguna Expressway (CALAX) is already 97 percent complete, and Dizon said he would recommend to Mr. Marcos that it be opened before Christmas as a “Christmas gift” to Filipinos.

World.title: Authorities intercept P19.5-M in contraband cigarettes in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
P13 million worth of illegal cigarettes intercepted at a checkpoint of Task Force Marawi and police in Marawi City on Friday morning, November 20.( Photo by Richel V. Umel, Inquirer Mindanao)

MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur – Police and military authorities intercepted contraband cigarettes worth some P19.5 million in separate operations in Lanao del Sur province on Friday, November 20.

Colonel Caezar Cabuhat, Lanao del Sur police director, told the Inquirer that the first incident happened at past midnight on Friday when law enforcers raided a warehouse in Bara-as village of Picong town.

READ: Police bust P7.8M smuggled cigarettes in Lanao del Sur

Article continues after this 

The raid, according to Cabuhat, yielded some 145 master cases of Capital, four master cases of Canon and five master cases of Platinum cigarettes, all undocumented, with a total estimated value of P6.5 million, per Bureau of Customs assessment.

The second haul of contrabands were seized at a checkpoint of the Army’s 4th Mechanized Infantry Battalion-Task Force Marawi in Barangay Cadayunan, Marawi City.

The operation, jointly led by Lieutenant Colonel Rogelio Lopez and Police Lieutenant Colonel Muhiddin Pagayawan, yielded 192 master cases of Titan and 121 master cases of Casa Blanca undocumented cigarettes valued at P13 Million.

The illicit items were reportedly transported from Picong, Cabuhat said.

The recent seizures bring to P39 million the total contraband cigarettes intercepted by authorities in Lanao del Sur, so far, for the month of November.

Marawi City Vice Mayor Majul Usman Gandamra lauded the police and Army for their “relentless joint efforts” against illegal activities. /jpv

World.title: Highlights:  Day 45 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Nov. 20, 2026
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said Friday that the defense’s sluggish presentation of witnesses and requests to defer trial dates validate the prosecution’s earlier decision to withdraw three of four Articles of Impeachment and proceed only with Article II, the allegation that Vice President Sara Duterte amassed unexplained wealth and failed to declare it in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

Luistro said the prosecution had manifested before open court on October 13 that it would no longer pursue those three articles, and argued that more time would have been consumed had that move not been made.

READ: Highlights: Day 44 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Nov. 19, 2026

Article continues after this 

On Day 45 of the trial, the defense presented Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who testified that the Board of Investments found no irregularities in Cale88 Foods Corp.’s export transactions involving Chinese companies.

Cale88, the banana chips manufacturing company linked to Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, had drawn scrutiny after prosecutors showed the firm received around P319 million in remittances from China.

Rodolfo also confirmed under questioning by Presiding Officer Francis Escudero that the company’s name combines the surnames of Carpio and his business partner, Lourdes Lebosada.

Prosecution counsel Erwin Matib asked Rodolfo whether Duterte’s tree-planting activities were connected to a Board of Investments requirement for enterprises to plant at least 100 forest trees to qualify for incentives, given the link between those activities and Cale88’s BOI registration. Rodolfo said he did not know.

Public prosecutor Manila Rep. Joel Chua and prosecution spokesperson Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong both reminded the defense that the core issue surrounding Cale88 is not whether the company is properly registered, but its allegedly undeclared income.

Article continues after this 

Separately, Presiding Officer Escudero ordered the issuance of a show-cause order against Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., after Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo moved for the order following Panelo’s remarks that some senator-judges were showing bias against Duterte.

Panelo had singled out Senator-Judges Raffy Tulfo, Francis Pangilinan, and Risa Hontiveros, saying it was not their job to challenge the credibility of defense witnesses.

Article continues after this 

Escudero noted that although Panelo is not listed as Duterte’s counsel, he may be asked to explain why he should not be held in contempt under Rule 71 of the Rules of Court.

Panelo maintained his remarks were constitutionally protected, citing Supreme Court rulings on freedom of expression and the public’s right to criticize judicial authorities.

World.title: Albay energizes P130.5-M Cullat substation
World.content:
The newly energized P130.5-million Cullat Substation in Daraga, Albay, features a 20-megavolt-ampere transformer and a monitoring system designed to improve power distribution in the municipality and neighboring areas. The facility is expected to help meet growing electricity demand and support future investments in Albay’s 2nd District. (Photo By Michael B. Jaucian)

DARAGA, Albay — Daraga’s new 20-megavolt-ampere (MVA) Cullat Substation was blessed and energized on Friday, Nov. 20, marking a major step toward improving power distribution capacity in the municipality and other areas in Albay’s 2nd District.

The project was initiated through the efforts of Ako Bicol Party-list, with funding provided through national government assistance to the Albay Electric Cooperative (ALECO).

READ: Upgraded ALECO substation unveiled in Ligao City, Albay

Article continues after this 

Ako Bicol Party-list Rep. Alfredo “Pido” Garbin Jr. said the facility is expected to help meet the growing electricity demand of the Bicol International Airport and accommodate future investments in Daraga, Camalig, and Legazpi City.

“We expect the electricity supply to be reliable, efficient, and stable. We will not hesitate to invite investors because we are confident that ALECO can meet their electricity requirements,” he said.

Daraga Mayor Vic Perete said a reliable power supply is crucial to attracting investors, expanding business opportunities, and supporting the municipality’s bid for cityhood.

Camalig Mayor Carlos Irwin Baldo Jr. also expressed hope that the newly energized substation would help reduce frequent brownouts, preventing losses among consumers and business owners.

The P130.5-million facility features a 20-MVA transformer and a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system to improve monitoring and operational efficiency.

Article continues after this 

The new facility doubles the capacity of the earlier 10-MVA substation proposal identified in ALECO’s development plan.

The project forms part of a broader P367-million government assistance package for power infrastructure improvements in Albay.

Article continues after this 

Officials said the additional capacity would help strengthen electricity distribution and prepare Daraga and neighboring areas for increased commercial activity, infrastructure development, and population growth. /jpv

World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Rejects ‘Unfair’ Rohingya Genocide Ruling at ICJ
World.content:
NAYPYITAW—A historic ruling by the top UN court that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority was “not fair,” the regime’s presidential spokeswoman said Friday.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court’s president said.

Asked about the ICJ decision at a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw, spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe called it unfair.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she said, noting the 9-6 vote.

“So this was not a unanimous decision,” she added. “I would say it is not fair.”

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.

“There is no evidence before the court that, in the conduct of the clearance operations, Myanmar distinguished between civilians and alleged (Rohingya) fighters,” the judgment said.

It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges have determined that a state committed genocide.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh during the crackdown, the court said.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

No enforcement

The court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with specific sums to be determined later.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling may heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy.

China, an enduring partner after the coup, raised concerns of judicial overreach after the ICJ ruling.

One of the ICJ’s judges is from China and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The U.S. reacted with caution, stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the international court.

Despite determining in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Washington has more recently pushed back on another case before the court, involving accusations by South Africa that U.S. ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Lashes Out at Beijing, Scammer Whac-a-Mole Continues in Shan, and More
World.content:
Min Aung Hlaing hints at Chinese hand in resistance’s Operation 1027

Putschist president Min Aung Hlaing is still groping for an explanation for Operation 1027, the humiliating Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that stripped his regime of most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on the offensive.

He insisted the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

Then came the interesting part: “There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he added.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country, few observers were left in doubt that it was a swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance.

The comments echoed Min Aung Hlaing’s complaints at the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

They come after Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun delivered a body blow to Naypyitaw by urging “high-level autonomy” for ethnic minorities, a suggestion that flies in the face of the military regime’s centralization doctrine.

Regime chief fingers neighbors for sustaining ‘insurgents’

In the same outburst, Min Aung Hlaing also accused the two neighbors that have made the biggest effort to accommodate his regime—China and Thailand—of sustaining “insurgents” by encouraging trade through border crossings they control.

He started with Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and MNDAA, which now control much of Myanmar’s border with China. “In Kachin, the KIA runs border gates at the Chinese border. In northeastern Myanmar, the MNDAA runs Chinshwehaw gate,” he said.

“Taxation from illegal trade has sustained and financed insurgents,” he complained.

In Kachin, the regime has also lost control over the lucrative rare earth mines, which are now a major source of revenues for the KIA. The situation is not much different in northern Shan, where the regime has lost key border crossings with Yunnan as well as rare earth and other mineral resources.

On the surface, he was only accusing Thailand of directly facilitating trade through resistance-held territory at the Thaw Le Hta crossing in Hpapun, avoiding direct accusations against China except by inference and association.

Chinese Customs figures show a steady increase in cross-border trade through crossings controlled by the MNDAA and its allies. Trade through the Chinshwehaw border crossing alone reached 5.01 billion yuan (about US$700 million) so far this year. The central regime is reduced to heavy-handed efforts to “tax” this trade once goods reach military-controlled areas.

China steps up media ‘outreach’ in Myanmar to shape narrative

China stepped up efforts to shape Myanmar’s information space this week, gathering regime-aligned media figures, officials and commentators in Yangon to promote President Xi Jinping’s four flagship global initiatives.

Speaking at a symposium at the Wyndham Grand Yangon Hotel on Tuesday with over 160 participants, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia highlighted growing bilateral cooperation in security, governance and people-to-people exchanges. Myanmar is the first country to sign up to all four of Xi’s initiatives, which also include AI.

Ma listed the usual talking points, from law-enforcement cooperation to combat cross-border crimes, including online scam operations, to cultural and media exchanges aimed at strengthening “mutual understanding.” Echoing Chinese President Xi Jinping and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, she called for key projects of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) to be hurried along.

The event brought together stalwart regime propagandists like Lower House MP Aye Chan, Myanmar Press Council Chairman Dr. Tin Tun Oo, Myanmar Narrative Think Tank chairman Ko Ko, plus figures from regime and regime-aligned media.

Days earlier, Myanmar Foreign Ministry-backed think tank MISIS and state-owned China Media Group gathered academics, media representatives and officials in Yangon to discuss future areas of China-Myanmar cooperation aligned with Beijing’s 15th Five-Year Plan.

The forums follow a similar gathering hosted by Ma in May, when she called on regime-linked media and opinion leaders to tell “beautiful stories” about China.

Chinese-run scam industry lives on in southern Shan

Myanmar’s regime says it arrested 23 Chinese nationals and seized three assault rifles in a raid on an alleged online scam and gambling operation in Laihka Township in southern Shan State on Wednesday.

They were detained at a makeshift compound deep in the forest comprising a workshop, living quarters and a kitchen. A tally compiled from regime media reports suggests some 90 Chinese scammers have been arrested in raids since February in Laihka, which has emerged as a new scam hotspot since 2025.

They take advantage of the lawless environment amid competing territorial claims of local militias as well as the Shan State Progressive Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), and the Restoration Council of Shan State/Shan State Army (RCSS/SSA).

Even as a docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry broadcast on Chinese state media last month sold the 2024 crackdown on scam hubs in northern Shan State’s Laukkai as an unmitigated success, the criminal gangs simply scattered across eastern and southern Shan instead. According to the independent Institute for Strategy and Policy–Myanmar, operations have since been identified in at least 17 Shan townships including Tangyan, Tachileik and Muse.

Meanwhile, ASEAN and the U.S., meeting in Manila this week, adopted what was billed as a “partnership work plan” to tackle online scams and thereby increase international pressure on Myanmar’s regime. Regime leader Min Aung Hlaing was not invited to the summit.

Complied by Thurein Lynn

World.title: US Warns Against ‘Politicization’ of ICJ, Studying Myanmar Ruling
World.content:
WASHINGTON—The U.S. State Department reacted with caution to the International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying Washington was examining the decision while stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the body.

Washington’s wary response comes as the United States determined in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But it has more recently pushed back on another case before the top UN court, involving accusations by South Africa that US ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” said a State Department spokesperson on Thursday.

“We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official added, referring to the Myanmar ruling.

The US statement comes as the top UN court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation.

The decision marked the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges determined a state committed genocide. It is likely to be viewed as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority.

The US official said Thursday: “We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”

The official also called for more burden-sharing in the humanitarian response for Rohingya refugees.

For more than one million Rohingya living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling offered hope for accountability.

World.title: Five Key Points From Historic ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority—the first time the UN top court has determined a state responsible for the world’s worst crime.

Here are the key points from the 191-page ruling, which took nearly three hours to read out in court and is the second-longest in the ICJ’s 80-year history.

Genocide

This was what the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya victims were waiting for: did the atrocities they suffered clear the high bar under international law to be labelled a genocide?

In the end, the ICJ—known for dressing up its rulings in impenetrable legalese—was refreshingly clear.

Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said the ruling, which was passed by nine votes to six.

By the same margin, the court found Myanmar had failed in its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention to prevent the crime.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take “immediate and effective steps” to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of genocidal acts.

Myanmar must stop any ongoing acts of genocide and prevent similar violations of the Convention in future.

To prove genocide, judges have to be satisfied not only that genocidal acts have occurred but also there was intention to destroy a given community—a notoriously tricky legal hurdle.

However, the judges ruled that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people.

Safe return

Having concluded that genocide occurred, the court also issued rulings on the consequences for Myanmar—so-called “remedies” in the legal jargon.

It ordered several actions from Myanmar.

The authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

They must also “return or replace in kind all individual and collective property” that was lost in the violent crackdown.

The Rohingya must also be offered “physical and psychological rehabilitation” for the harms they suffered, the judges ruled.

Reparations

The Rohingya are entitled to “adequate compensation” for the harms caused by the genocide.

The ICJ did not set an amount, saying that would be determined at a later phase.

It gave Myanmar two years to file a report setting out the “amount and modalities” of compensation.

After receiving the report, the ICJ will decide whether Myanmar’s proposal is sufficient.

Investigations

The ICJ is a court that settles disputes between countries, unlike its neighbor the International Criminal Court, which weighs individual responsibility.

However, the ICJ ruling tasks Myanmar with conducting a “prompt” investigation into anyone suspected of committing genocidal acts.

Judges ruled that previous efforts in Myanmar to probe atrocities were insufficient.

“Myanmar has not genuinely investigated or, if warranted, prosecuted its soldiers and commanders and punished them,” the ICJ said.

Scale of killings

The court said that an estimate of at least 10,000 deaths in the crackdown, established by an independent UN fact-finding mission, was “supported by the record.”

“The evidence before the court demonstrates the pervasive and lethal nature of the violence… and establishes that thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed by the Myanmar security forces,” said the ICJ.

The court said there were approximately 815,000 Rohingya in Rakhine State at the time of the crackdown, meaning those killed constituted 1.2 percent of the population.

The majority of the survivors fled to neighboring Bangladesh.

The ICJ also said there were at least 1,834 acts of rape during the 2017 “clearance operations.”

World.title: ICJ Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
World.content:
The United Nations’ top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017, in a historic decision.

In the case brought by the Gambia, the ICJ delivered the first ruling in its 80-year history finding a state responsible for committing genocide.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, delivering the court’s verdict.

Iwasawa said around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 “clearance operations,” which also involved widespread sexual violence and violence against children, as the Rohingya fled en masse to Bangladesh.

“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

The ICJ president said Myanmar had failed to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible for acts punishable under Article III of the Genocide Convention.

The Myanmar military also disseminated and promoted hate speech in a systematic and coordinated way during the 2017 operation, the court said.

The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of those who fled the violence to their homes. It also ruled that Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators and prosecute and punish those found responsible, and provide compensation. The amount would be determined in future proceedings, it said.

The ruling cannot be appealed. Rather than prosecuting individuals, the verdict determined that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide.

As a result of the military operation in Rakhine, over one million Rohingya now live in what is effectively the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh. For some of them, the case offered a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the World Court has found a state responsible for committing genocide—and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

Horsey pointed out that the court lacks the power to enforce the orders contained in its ruling.

“What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it,” he said.

Myanmar should comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya, said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” she said.

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, said international governments should not welcome putschist president and former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya.

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said.

All other states, including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must also uphold these obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law, taking every measure within their power to prevent and punish genocide, Callamard said.

She urged the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

The Myanmar military’s 2017 “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee amid widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.
