World.title: Australia strikes deal on AI talks with China
World.content:
Australia and China will hold talks on artificial intelligence as the two countries look for new ways to work together on the rapidly developing technology.

The agreement was reached during a meeting between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing overnight on Friday, where the leaders also discussed trade, climate change, health and tourism.

Mr Albanese spent about six hours in the Chinese capital for high-level talks, having met President Xi Jinping earlier that morning in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Anthony Albanese met Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

At that meeting Mr Xi declared there had been a "complete turnaround" in China's relations with Australia despite the two countries' ongoing "differences".

Mr Albanese is due to return to Australia on Saturday after 11 days of international travel for the COP31 UN climate talks, ASEAN summit in Manila and APEC in China.

Anthony Albanese has held meetings with several world leaders on his 11-day trip, including Donald Trump and Andy Burnham. (Ryohei Moriya/The Yomiuri Shimbun via AFP)

During the trip, Australia signed a new defence cooperation with the Philippines and Mr Albanese took part in meetings with several world leaders including US President Donald Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Mr Albanese also used his APEC speech to directly tell Russian President Vladimir Putin to end his illegal invasion of Ukraine "now".

"I have a responsibility to put Australia's position clearly and directly, and that is what I did," the prime minister said.

Australia commits to AI talks with China

The new AI dialogue with China would allow the two governments to share their experiences of the technology as governments grapple with how it should be regulated.

Attendees ahead of the business round table in Beijing. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Speaking at a business round table in Beijing, Mr Albanese said AI had the potential to transform productivity and living standards.

"That's why Australia is developing AI standards, because we're serious about shaping the future of AI, not being shaped by it," he said.

The agreement to hold an AI dialogue comes just days after Australia signed a separate declaration with the United States partly designed to reduce reliance on China for critical technologies.

The US deal committed members to identifying vulnerable supply chains, protecting sensitive technology from theft or foreign interference, and reducing dependence on countries that could disrupt access to the infrastructure needed for AI.

Australian and Chinese leaders attended the ninth Australia-China CEO Roundtable, along with senior executives from some of the countries' biggest businesses. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Australia–China relationship in a 'mature' place

During their formal annual meeting, Mr Li told Mr Albanese the improvement in relations between Australia and China had taken considerable work.

"These achievements have not come easily, they are the result of our joint efforts," he said.

He said closer ties had delivered benefits to people in both countries and argued a stable relationship was particularly important given international tensions.

Albanese meets Xi Jinping Anthony Albanese meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

"Facts have shown that a more mature, stable and productive China–Australia relationship will only benefit the two countries, but also the region and beyond," he said.

Mr Albanese acknowledged the trust he had developed with Mr Li through their repeated meetings, saying the pair were now able to speak directly by phone when issues arose.

He also said the countries had shown they could manage disagreements while continuing to work together.

Mr Albanese said they could demonstrate to the region "that there can be different political systems, differences that can be negotiated wisely, but all in the spirit of recognising that working together is very much in our interests".

Mr Albanese and Mr Li also attended the ninth Australia–China CEO Roundtable, which brought together senior executives from some of the countries' biggest businesses.

World.title: IDF refuses ABC requests for evidence journalist was Hamas operative
World.content:
Israel's military has ignored or declined to answer the ABC's multiple requests for evidence a Palestinian journalist it engaged as a freelancer in Gaza was a Hamas operative.

It comes after reports in The Australian newspaper that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) had evidence the man held a role in Hamas's military wing as observer and deputy squad commander.

Roshdi Al Sarraj was killed by an Israeli air strike on October 22, 2023, two weeks after Hamas' deadly attacks on Israel triggered the war in Gaza.

Al Sarraj was engaged by the ABC in 2023 in the very early stages of the war to provide video for its 7.30 program.

Since the war began, Israel has controlled all access to the Gaza Strip — and blocked international media from accessing and reporting independently there.

The ABC has repeatedly requested access and has only been allowed in for two very limited periods.

The first was in August 2025 when the ABC travelled to the Kerem Shalom aid depot in the far south of the strip, away from fighting and populated areas.

The second was in October that same year when the ABC was taken to the edge of Gaza City weeks after the ceasefire was announced.

These were embeds, where journalists are taken into areas under the strict supervision of the IDF and do not interact with locals.

In October 2026, the IDF included Al Sarraj in its publication of The Press Files — a website listing 170 Palestinians killed in the war who it claimed were terrorists masquerading as journalists.

The level of detail attached to each name varied.

Some included photos of the journalists carrying out their work alongside photos of them in military outfits brandishing weapons, or appearing on posters designed by the terrorist organisations they worked for labelling them as martyrs for the cause.

Others included details such as military ID numbers and documents the IDF said it discovered during raids of Hamas command centres showing service records — both the originals in Arabic and seemingly machine-translated versions in English.

The IDF said the people in the list had been lauded as slain journalists when they should actually be condemned as terrorists.

It listed Al Sarraj as a member of Hamas.

However, the evidence provided in many cases has been scant and not conclusive of a terrorist affiliation.

Al Sarraj is the only person on the list the IDF said had worked for the ABC.

From October to November 20, there was only a grainy photo of the man wearing a flak jacket labelled "press".

In the original publication, an ID number was also listed, but this was not a military identifier, rather a Palestinian ID number the likes of which are given to every Palestinian in Gaza and the West Bank under a system which Israel has oversight of.

Liberal senator Sarah Henderson recently corrected the parliamentary record over this distinction, after mistakenly asserting that the IDF had Al Sarraj's military ID.

The Press Files listed Al Sarraj as an operative in Hamas' military wing, based on multiple intelligence sources, but has, until now, not publicly cited what the sources are.

Following the publication of The Press Files, the ABC made repeated requests for further information from the IDF about the sources.

No evidence was provided and the ABC's approaches went largely ignored.

On November 20, The Australian newspaper reported on a document which the IDF said showed Al Sarraj was a Hamas operative.

A redacted document supplied by the IDF, allegedly showing that "Rushdi Yahya Rushdi al-Sarraj" was a "Deputy Squad Commander", "Soldier" and "Observer" for Hamas (translations provided by IDF). (Supplied: IDF)

Screenshots of the heavily redacted document published by the paper purport to show Al Sarraj's military ID number as well as note that he joined Hamas as a foot soldier in 2011 when he was 19 and was promoted in 2018 at the age of 26.

The IDF told the paper it discovered the document in November 2023, just weeks after Al Sarraj was killed.

Following this reporting, the ABC has again made multiple requests for a copy of the document but has not yet received a response.

The document relied on by The Australian has since been made available on the IDF's The Press Files website, along with other details on Al Sarraj's profile.

The IDF did not reply directly to the ABC but posted the screenshot of the document on social media platform X.

There are no identifying markers on the document to suggest where it is from or what the list is for, and every line has been blurred other than that which includes Al Sarraj's name.

The Committee to Protect Journalists, an independent non-profit organisation which investigates cases of killed journalists, has maintained Al Sarraj was a civilian journalist.

In a statement to the ABC, the CPJ said its September 2026 investigation into Al Sarraj "did not identify any evidence" he was a combatant.

"Our rigorous investigation required CPJ researchers to interview at least two new credible independent sources on each individual, in addition to in-depth, desk-based research," the statement said.

What did the ABC do to verify this claim with the IDF?

On Saturday, October 3,the ABC first asked the IDF's International Press Desk about its listing of Al Sarraj as a Hamas militant, including requesting evidence of the allegation.

The usual approach is to message the press team via WhatsApp.

One day later, the IDF requested an extension in time to provide a response. Then it stopped responding altogether.

The ABC made three follow-up requests on October 5 and 6, but no response was provided and correspondence was ignored by the IDF.

On October 6, a request for comment on a separate story was immediately acknowledged, and a response to that story was provided a week later.

The ABC again followed up its questions about Al Sarraj and the military press team claimed it had been experiencing "internet issues" and was "looking into getting an answer".

When pressed on when a response would be provided, and why previous messages had been read and ignored, the IDF said it understood the "frustration" but insisted giving "the best answer possible" can take time.

What did the IDF tell the ABC?

The IDF eventually responded on Wednesday, October 14, just under two weeks after the initial query.

The IDF told the ABC it had thoroughly reviewed the information and published it alongside the sources that could be disclosed:

"In the case of the journalist in question, the information available to the IDF unequivocally indicates his affiliation with the Islamic Jihad. "The IDF bases its assessments on information collected and examined by professional authorities, including the cross-referencing of information from multiple sources. "The information published regarding the journalists is based on reliable findings indicating their affiliation with terrorist organizations and their involvement in activities on their behalf."

The reference to Palestinian Islamic Jihad did not match The Press Files's listing of Al Sarraj as a member of Hamas.

When the ABC sought to clarify this, the IDF's message in the chat to the ABC was quickly edited to say "Hamas".

A further message asking for evidence to back up the IDF's assertion was read and ignored.

When the ABC became aware of The Australian's latest reporting, prior to its article being published, the broadcaster again requested the material.

The IDF has yet to respond to the ABC's latest questions but has posted a statement criticising the ABC on X.

World.title: Tim Tszyu hunting 'legacy-defining' win on Gold Coast
World.content:
Tim Tszyu knows all about the highs boxing can deliver.

He knows a fair bit about the lows, too.

Three years ago, Tszyu, the WBO junior middleweight world title holder, was eyeing up unification and US domination.

Three defeats in four fights later, his career was on the trash heap.

"You learn more about your character," Tszyu told ABC Sport from his Rockdale gym.

"You realise life isn't just going to go on an upward scale. It goes up and down. You've got to ride through the waves.

"One thing I learned was don't get too high from your wins, don't get too low from your losses, maintain a stable way of living and keep approaching every day with the foundation of something to work towards.

"That's how it's always been for me."

Tim Tszyu is headlining the event, with Jermell Charlo lower on the card. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Three wins later, including against American legend Errol Spence Jr, the 32-year-old is fighting for another world title, this time at the 160-pound-limit against WBA middleweight champion Erislandy Lara.

Not everyone is happy about Tszyu's return to the top.

"We all know he don't deserve a world title fight," American fighter Jermell Charlo told media on Wednesday via Zoom link from the United States.

"You didn't work your way up [at middleweight] for real. He fought a 147-pounder [welterweight] that just happened to overlap 154 [junior middleweight].

"Errol Spence wasn't the Errol Spence we all know, right?

"He can't beat Lara. Styles make fights, and this is just stylistically a bad fight for Tim.

"Lara's going to destroy Tszyu."

Tim Tszyu is leaving no stone unturned in his bid for glory. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo, a former unified champion in Tszyu's former weight division, light middleweight, may have a vested interest in shooting down Tszyu's chances.

Tszyu was supposed to face Charlo in January 2023, but the bout collapsed after Charlo broke his hand in sparring.

Despite Tszyu still being keen, Charlo wanted to hunt bigger fish and stepped up two weight divisions to take on Canelo Álvarez in a big-money blockbuster.

The WBO were not amused, stripping Charlo of his title the second he stepped into the ring, elevating Tszyu.

Tszyu has rebuilt his reputation since, while Charlo has stagnated.

Tim Tszyu knows the threat Erislandy Lara poses. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo has not fought since losing to Canelo, returning as the third-billed fight on December's spectacular Gold Coast card.

"Don't forget that, Charlo," Tszyu said, mockingly.

"You're on my undercard."

Tszyu's resurrection into a world title challenger has been nothing short of remarkable.

And although Lara will pose an enormous test of Tszyu's resilience, "He's going to present a lot of challenges," Tszyu noted, with the Australian backing himself to claim victory.

A big part of Tszyu's recovery has been his partnership with former three-weight world champion Jeff Fenech.

"He just came on board at a time where I really needed it," Tszyu said.

Tim Tszyu has been training with Jeff Fenech and Billy Hussein. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Despite that, Fenech has been dealing with several health challenges of late, including a third heart operation in October.

"I wouldn't say it impacted my training camp. I was more impacted personally because I felt like a lot was missing from Jeff," Tszyu said.

"But then when Billy [Hussein] came on board, we just started flowing with things, and we've just been working ever since."

Fenech is one of just two Australian male fighters to win championships in different weight classes (IBF bantamweight, WBC super-bantamweight and WBC featherweight), the other being Liam Paro (IBF super lightweight and welterweight titles).

"Playing it safe all the time is not the way I do things," Tszyu said.

"You got to chase the hard stuff. The tricky stuff. The legacy-defining type stuff."

World.title: An ex-Queensland premier's cherished link to legendary Wallabies family
World.content:
Holding the future Queen Elizabeth II when she was a toddler and joining King George V to shoot pheasants aren't stories every Australian rugby union player gets to tell.

Nor is sending British newspapers into a frenzy over a rumoured engagement to marry.

But for Jim and Arnold Tancred, these were some of the tales they shared during their rugby careers a century ago.

Jim, a mobile prop, and younger brother Arnold, an aggressive back-rower, were members of the legendary 1927/28 NSW Waratahs, which captivated the rugby world on their tour of Great Britain, Ireland and France (as well as Sri Lanka and Canada).

One of their older siblings, Harry, also played for NSW during his career.

The trio was posthumously recognised as Australian representatives and awarded Wallaby numbers 192 (Harry), 231 (Jim) and 241 (Arnold) following a decision to grant Test status to the Waratahs' matches against international teams between 1920 and 1928.

Jim Tancred's playing career was celebrated at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test last month. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

To celebrate 100 years since Jim (christened James) played for the Waratahs against the All Blacks, 22 of his direct descendants, along with spouses and friends, attended last month's Bledisloe Cup Test in Sydney.

Among those commemorating the milestone was Jim's granddaughter, former Queensland premier Anna Bligh.

"We had caps made. We all sat together in the stands. It was great," Anna tells ABC Sport.

Anna's brother, Stephen Tancred, adds: "We rounded up the family from Perth, Melbourne, Sydney, Darwin and country Queensland.

"We had three of Jim's daughters there. They're all in their 80s, and we had a great-great-great-grandchild who was 13."

It wasn't the only occasion Jim's descendants came together to remember his career.

Jim and Arnold Tancred were welcomed home by their family following the 1927/28 Waratahs tour. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

Anna and Stephen's mother, Frances, was one of nine children born to Jim and his wife Mary, and a coveted family photo was recreated to coincide with her 90th birthday.

The original image captured Jim and Arnold's family outside their home in the Sydney suburb of Rozelle as they welcomed the brothers back from the Waratahs' tour in early 1928.

The Tancreds' return to Rozelle was recently recreated by Jim's descendants. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

"It was such a proud moment for the family," Anna says.

"The photo is quite precious."

Playing for the Waratahs

When writing about the Tancred brothers, Australian rugby historian Jack Pollard noted they were "sometimes described mistakenly as New Zealanders".

Born in Sydney, they spent part of their childhood in New Zealand after parents Thomas and Anna moved the family of 10 children to the Shaky Isles.

Much of their rugby education took place across the Tasman.

Harry Tancred was the first of the brothers to play for the Waratahs. (Supplied: Rugby Australia/Classic Wallabies)

Harry even represented New Zealand in rugby league but was permitted to rejoin the union ranks.

Once the family returned to Australia, it was Harry, a robust number eight, who first represented the Waratahs when he twice faced the New Zealand Māori (now Māori All Blacks) in 1923.

Jim, who like Harry and Arnold played for the Glebe-Balmain club in Sydney, made his Waratahs debut in 1926, appearing in two internationals against the All Blacks.

A caricature of Jim Tancred appeared in The Daily Telegraph in 1928. (Supplied: The Daily Telegraph)

But the highlight of Jim's playing days was his selection alongside Arnold for the 1927/28 Waratahs tour.

The Waratahs, away from Sydney for 252 days, dazzled crowds in Great Britain, Ireland and France with a breathtaking display of "running rugby".

They won three of their five internationals and played more than 30 matches in total.

"It was such a big thing in those days to represent your country and tour internationally," Anna Bligh says.

"It meant being away for many weeks at a time because they travelled by ship."

Jim played the third and final international of his career against France, with the Waratahs winning 11-8 in Paris.

He was headbutted by opposition prop Jean Morère during the match, only for Waratahs teammate Ted "Bluey" Greatorex to violently square up with the Frenchman.

The Waratahs captivated spectators with their attacking brand of rugby. (Supplied: Official 1927/28 Waratahs Report)

Standing at 5'10" (1.78 metres) and weighing 78 kilograms, Jim would be considered a small front-rower by today's standards.

His modest physique, though, complemented the Waratahs' attacking game.

"The Waratahs' forwards were mobile," says Stephen Tancred, who played for the Stanthorpe Kookaburras during a proud bush rugby career.

"They would have the set-play and then join in with the backs. That was the essence of running rugby."

Arnold Tancred appeared in three internationals for the Waratahs. (Rugby Australia/Classic Wallabies)

All three of Arnold's internationals came on tour, against Ireland, Wales and Scotland.

A dislocated shoulder ended his tour early, meaning he and Jim never played an international together.

Waratahs Tour (internationals) Won 5-3 vs Ireland

Won 18-8 vs Wales

Lost 10-8 vs Scotland

Lost 18-11 vs England

Won 11-8 vs France

Arnold's ferocious tackling shocked spectators, especially in England, where rugby was regarded as a "gentlemen's game".

"Even though the Waratahs were known for running rugby, they had some really good defenders," Arnold's grandson Toby Tancred says.

"Dad [Arnold's son John] has told me stories about them getting booed at games because of the hard defence.

"That was Arnold's forte."

Meeting the royals

It wasn't just rugby keeping the Waratahs busy on tour.

While in England, they enjoyed afternoon tea with the Duke (who would become King George VI) and Duchess of York at their Piccadilly residence.

The Waratahs' meeting with Princess Elizabeth made newspaper headlines. (Supplied: The Arrow)

The Waratahs were introduced to the duke and duchess's one-year-old daughter, Elizabeth, who 24 years later would be crowned queen of the United Kingdom.

Jim Tancred was among the players to take a shine to "Baby Betty".

"The family story is he jiggled Elizabeth on his knee," Anna Bligh laughs.

Another meeting with the royal family involved pheasant shooting with King George V at his Sandringham estate.

Arnold Tancred (left) and his teammates met King George V (third from left). (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

According to the official tour report, written by manager E Gordon Shaw and captain Johnnie Wallace, the king "gave us each a pheasant from the day's bag".

So what happened to the pheasants?

This was a topic of conversation when Jim's descendants came together at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test a month ago.

They were joined by the daughter of star 1927/28 Waratahs centre Cyril Towers, Marguerite Howard, whose husband Jake and son Pat played for the Wallabies.

Anna Bligh (left) with Marguerite Howard at the Sydney Bledisloe Cup Test. (Supplied: Anna Bligh)

"Marguerite asked, 'Does your family have the pheasant?'" Anna recalls.

"We said, 'What pheasant?'

"She said, 'The king apparently gave all the players stuffed pheasants in a glass case. My mother claimed it was the ugliest thing she had ever seen.'"

The Waratahs fraternised with more than royals while abroad.

Arnold Tancred was rumoured to have become engaged on the Waratahs tour. (Supplied: South Wales Argus)

Arnold Tancred sent tongues wagging among the British press when it was reported he was engaged to marry Vera Morgan, whom he met at a dance in Swansea, Wales.

"The marriage will probably take place in a year's time, when Miss Morgan will go out to Australia," the South Wales Argus newspaper reported on January 6, 1928.

Alas, it wasn't to be.

"There is nothing at all in our friendship," Arnold told London's The Evening Standard.

"And there is no likelihood of our becoming engaged."

Business giants

Given rugby was amateur at the time, Jim, Arnold and Harry cut their playing careers short because of their business interests.

As a family of butchers, they helped established Tancred Brothers in the 1920s, quickly becoming giants of Australia's meat industry.

Arnold and Harry remained in Sydney while Jim ran the Queensland arm of the business, which went public in 1955, after moving his family to Toowoomba.

"They had a fair bit of go about them," Stephen Tancred says.

"They pioneered slaughtering in the country and shipping chilled meat to the city."

Arnold managed and coached the Wallabies on their 1947/48 tour of Great Britain, Ireland and France.

Arnold Tancred (second from right) training with the 1947/48 Wallabies squad. (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

Newspaper reporters following the tour suggested he was prickly, and his players considered him tough on the training paddock.

"I think what was more notable than his playing career is he was the coach of the 1947/48 Wallabies," Toby Tancred says.

"He trained them like bastards."

The Tancred name lives on in rugby, with Toby's three sons showing promise.

The eldest, Arnie, was a member of the Waratahs' 2024 preseason squad, George represented Australian Schoolboys last year, while Tomma played in the Riverview first XV, which was named AAGPS co-premiers in August.

Arnie (left), George (centre) and Tomma Tancred are making names for themselves in rugby. (Supplied: Toby Tancred)

A well-known racehorse owner, Harry, who was christened Henry Eugene, served as Sydney Turf Club chairman (1953-59), with the prestigious H E Tancred Stakes named in his honour.

Jim stayed connected to rugby in Toowoomba and, like Harry, racehorses were among his passions.

He was a punter, too, once betting 1,000 pounds on the horse he owned, On Cor, when it won the 1948 February Handicap at Doomben.

"We knew he liked the GGs [horses] and a flutter," Anna Bligh says admiringly.

Tragically, Jim died suddenly of a heart attack at his home in 1965, at the age of 62.

His brothers Arnold and Harry also died from heart-related conditions, aged 59 and 64 respectively.

Anna, who was five at the time of Jim's death, remembers her grandfather as "larger than life" and a family man "taken from them far too young".

She learned more about Jim during her political career, especially his generosity.

Anna Bligh was Queensland premier between 2007-12. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

A chance meeting with Wallabies great, prominent businessman and ex-lord mayor of Sydney, the late Sir Nicholas Shehadie, left Anna beaming with pride.

"When Shehadie finished his rugby career, he was very keen to go into business and couldn't find a bank that would give him money without someone going guarantor for him," Anna says.

"My grandfather offered to do it.

"Shehadie said, 'I owe my success to your grandfather being prepared to back me', which has always made me feel good about my grandfather.

"It's nice when you hear a story like that."

World.title: Students rally across Europe over cost of living, war and education cuts
World.content:
From the shadows of the mighty Colosseum in Rome to Parliament Square in London, and in dozens of other cities across Europe, thousands of young Europeans gathered to make their voices heard.

The issues being chanted about as protesters waved flags and placards and let off flares were wide-ranging, encompassing everything from the cost of living, climate change and education budgets to housing affordability, rising defence spending and mandatory military service.

Students take to the streets of Milan during Friday's general strike. (Reuters: Claudia Greco)

However, the Gen Z protesters have been united by a shared belief that decisions about their future are being made without them or at their expense.

Describing the day of action as Europe's biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition (the organisation behind the action) said it had planned demonstrations in 400 cities in countries including Belgium, Croatia, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom.

Protesters make their voices heard in Berlin on Friday. (Reuters: Christian Mang)

The rally in the German capital Berlin was among the largest, with thousands of demonstrators marching through the streets as part of the "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z takes charge) protest.

The placards they waved carried slogans such as "Fight for our future, not their wars", "A smart head does not fit under a steel helmet", and "You cannot make cuts to the climate crisis".

Protester Jasmin Hamadi said she took part in the march to "take a stand and push for a change, because things cannot go on like this".

Masked demonstrators throw a road sign toward riot police officers in Rome on Friday. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

In Rome, riot police were on stand-by as thousands of young people marched through the streets past the world-famous Colosseum and towards the education ministry.

A small group of masked activists threw firecrackers and other projectiles, but otherwise it was mostly peaceful as the demonstrators demanded their cost-of-living concerns be taken seriously by Italian authorities.

Student protester Lucia Lamorgese said she felt the rising cost of living was making life "impossible", while another demonstrator, Luca Cornani, said he joined the rally to demand more money be spent on education and healthcare instead of defence.

Demonstrators gather in Parliament Square in London on Friday. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Outside the UK's Houses of Parliament, protesters were met by a rival right-wing group of activists, but police kept the two groups apart.

High school student Irene Mark, 16, who came to the rally with her mother told the ABC she feels government should be investing in opportunities for young people, not wars.

"I'm scared that I won't ever be able to do anything in my future if they don't want to fund it," Irene said.

Irene Mark was among those students at the London protests. (ABC News: Syan Vallance)

Fellow high-schooler Antoni Cienciala said he hoped more young people would join the growing protest movement.

"Wherever you are, just stand up, fight for what you believe in, show up to these protests," he said.

"It may seem silly sometimes, but it's worth it, history will sort of look on you favourably if you do, so show up."

A demonstrator in Cologne makes a point during the protests. (Reuters: Jana Rodenbusch)

In France, the rally was more muted than recent protests about the poor state of education facilities, which evolved into a wider movement against high living costs and plunged France into its worst unrest in years.

"I think a lot of us who are young people, no matter where they were, in Paris or in London or in New York or any random place around the world, it's up to us to fight for the future that we think that we deserve," protester Evelyn said at the Paris march.

Larger demonstrations are expected in Paris over the weekend.

With major European elections on the horizon in the new year, governments in each country are grappling with how to respond to the growing protest movement, and their demands to cut defence spending, in the face of an increasingly unstable and violent global geopolitical environment, headlined in their region by Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

World.title: Citizen scientists are hunting for bugs in Australia's backyards
World.content:
Deb Taylor was out for a walk on her property in regional New South Wales when she spotted a strange bug.

"We were just bumbling around. The dogs were swimming, the horses and the cows were grazing," she said.

"And I just saw it sitting on a leaf."

The brown and black beetle wasn't particularly "pretty", but she didn't recognise it. So she snapped a few photos and uploaded them to online citizen science database iNaturalist.

A biologist quickly identified the insect as Anastetha raripila and said, as far as he could tell, it was the only photograph of the bug alive in the wild.

"I was absolutely hooked," Ms Taylor said.

Native bees are just some of the insects captured for Bugs In my Backyard Week. (iNaturalist: Thyreus nitidulus/debtaylor142/CC BY-NC 4.0)

Citizen scientist snapshots

This week, citizen scientists like Ms Taylor have been out in force for the second-ever Bugs in my Backyard Week.

The initiative, run by citizen science group Bug Hunt, has Australians upload their insect finds to iNaturalist to capture a "springtime snapshot" of the nation's bugs.

There have been almost 30,000 observations of insects submitted across Australia this week.

Jess Ward-Jones, co-coordinator of Bug Hunt, said the project helps people connect with the outside world.

"Projects like this provide an opportunity for people to be curious and engage with the wildlife around them," Ms Ward-Jones said.

"It's super easy to take part. Just download iNaturalist, make an account and start snapping bugs."

Deb Taylor has uploaded observations of thousands of insects and arachnids to iNaturalist. (Supplied: Alison Kuiter)

Uploading insects and spiders to databases like iNaturalist is invaluable to scientists, who use the data for research like the spread of introduced pest species such as fire ants.

"Seventy per cent of fire ant records come from citizen scientists in the Brisbane area," Ms Ward-Jones said.

" Having people on the ground all over the place really adds that value to that constant monitoring. "

Spotting rare insects

The project also provides scientists with evidence of extremely rare native insects.

"This project last year discovered a species of ant that we thought was extinct for decades on the Eyre Peninsula," Ms Ward-Jones said.

"Researchers from Adelaide got to go out there, and now we know a lot more about it."

The photo of the critically endangered dinosaur ant (Nothomyrmecia macrops) in South Australia came as a surprise after scientists spent almost 50 years looking for it in Western Australia instead.

Many of the 4,500 spider and insect observations Ms Taylor has taken over the last few years were not just new to her, but potentially new to science.

"I've got a lot of insect observations where they're not identified to genus, let alone species, because they just haven't been described," she said.

" I think it's important that I go out there and document as much as possible. "

A wrap-around spider from the genus Dolophones, which Deb Taylor has not been able to identify. (Supplied: Deb Taylor)

While it may take more work to find insects than other animals like birds, Ms Ward-Jones said the "inconspicuous" critters were worth looking a bit harder for.

"Invertebrates make up 95 per cent of our species diversity in Australia and provide ecosystem services all the time," she said.

"They keep our soils healthy, our water clean, our air clean. They keep plants healthy. They're just these little workers that we never see, working hard to keep everything functioning."

Bogongs are bouncing back

Ms Ward-Jones said that the bogong moth has just overtaken the European honeybee as the most submitted species for this year's count.

Documenting bogong moths marked with blue paint dots helps scientists track the species' migration. (Supplied: Western Sydney University)

"It's not only a native, but also a threatened species," she said.

"Obviously, it might not have been ideal to have hundreds of bogong moths fly into your house, but the result is that people got to learn about this threatened species that went through a massive population decline."

Ms Taylor has also noticed an increase in some other species that has surprised her.

"About the same time we had the great bogong moth migration come through … we started seeing a butterfly here that I had never seen before, a chequered swallowtail," she said.

"I'm thinking there has to be some correlation, like it can't be a coincidence."

Deb Taylor has seen more lime swallowtails in her local area at the same time as the bogong moth. (iNaturalist: Lime Swallowtail/debtaylor142/CC BY-NC 4.0)

Even after years of snapping photos, Ms Taylor is still spurred by the thought that new insects are out there to find.

"I actually saw my first green and gold carpenter bee today. I've never seen one before," she said.

"It constantly surprises me that I'm still finding so much.

" It's like real life Pokemon hunting! "

World.title: This crime caper reveals a brash Australian bank heist by way of Belfast
World.content:
Sometimes truth is stranger than fiction. So is it with Chasing Millions, the Australian-Irish co-production that dramatises the wild tale of a Belfast bank connected to National Australia Bank (NAB) being robbed of over $50 million.

Fast Facts about Chasing Millions What: A real-life crime drama that's played for brutal laughs Directed by: Stephen Burke Starring: Madeleine Madden and Christopher Eccleston When: In cinemas November 19 Likely to make you feel: Like Irish and Australian humour gel well

Doctor Who star Christopher Eccleston plays cranky Northern Irish Detective Crayford, opposite Madeleine Madden from Mystery Road and Tomorrow When the War Began, as Australian Federal Police officer Diana, in a Christmas movie with a darkly funny twist.

The brazen heist occurred on December 20, 2004, right in the bustling city centre abuzz with shoppers.

One of the biggest bank jobs ever pulled off, involving kidnapping and rumours of IRA involvement, the real-life whodunnit remains stubbornly unsolved, with most of the money never recovered — though there's a twist to that, too.

"Stephen Burke, the writer/director, had to leave a lot of things out," Eccleston chuckles, with a mischievous twinkle. "It's like Donald Trump. If you put this orange guy with a wig in a graphic novel, it stretches credulity."

Chasing Millions is a Christmas movie with a darkly funny twist. (Supplied)

Colonial context

Burke loosely adapted the bizarre tale with Australian writer Katherine Thomson, best known for A Place to Call Home, in a film that also boasts a score by Midnight Oil veteran Jim Moginie.

Thomson's presence on set was a comfort for Arrernte, Kalkadoon and Bundjalung actor Madden.

"It's almost like starting school on the first day, and the nerves that come with not knowing how you're going to fit in," the Sydneysider says. "But being able to sit down with Katherine, shifting some of the language to make it a bit more Australian, and Stephen being open to that made it much easier."

Diana is technically off duty in Belfast before being deployed to the robbery case by the AFP. She's trying to trace the grandmother she never met, who had to give Diana's late mum up for adoption, with subtle nods to both the Magdalene laundries and the Stolen Generations folded into the story.

"That was really moving," says Madden, who comes from a long line of Aboriginal activists and artists, including civil rights hero Charles Perkins, filmmaker aunt Rachel Perkins and cinematographer brother Tyson Perkins.

" We have this shared colonial context and history, and there was a real sense of familiarity, being there in Ireland, chatting with our Irish cast and crew that put me at ease," Madden adds. "Everyone was on the same page. "

The majority of Chasing Millions was shot south of the border, in the Republic of Ireland. (Supplied)

And that page is about placing these very different cops in their truths.

"It's about identity, and people figuring out who they are in the world," Madden says. "It's also about being able to find meaning and purpose in other people."

Muscle memory

The majority of Chasing Millions was shot south of the border, in the Republic of Ireland, with Crayford suspicious of what he sees as a tenuous peace, post-Troubles, following the Good Friday Agreement of 1998.

Eccleston, who broke through in crime drama Cracker with Robbie Coltrane, adopts a convincing Ulster accent here. He previously played a Northern Irishman in Michael Winterbottom's 1999 romance With or Without You and in Andrea Harkin's 2018 missing person drama Come Home.

"The first guy was a Protestant from East Belfast, the second was from West Belfast, and now I'm from East Belfast," he says. "There's a world of difference, not just religiously, politically and culturally, but also in the accent, and I'm obsessed with all that."

To keep in character, Eccleston maintained the accent during the five-week shoot. "I'm not a method actor, but it helps," he says. "Just for muscle memory."

Eccleston loves the lyricism of the Irish tongue and "Their absolute delight in the surrealism of language," he says. "Speaking with the sparkies on the set and the prop people, they're all using language in such a poetic way, and you just have to go for that."

Madden praised the improvisational skills of her Northern Irish co-stars, including Amy Molloy, who plays one of the robbers, and Kerri Quinn, who is Inspector McClary.

"One of my favourite improvised lines was when Amy said, 'Why don't you smile and give your face a joy ride?'" Madden says. "It's just so brilliant, and apparently that's a real Belfast thing."

Eccleston favoured Quinn's bluer, "Get your fingers out of your f***ing holes".

" When Kerri came up with that, we had a problem," he says. "We had to go again because everybody on the set fell apart laughing. "

Madeleine Madden's Diana is technically off duty in Belfast before being deployed to the robbery case by the AFP. (Supplied)

Good cop/bad cop

Chatting to the pair, it seems like that would have been a regular occurrence. Madden and Eccleston bounce off each other boisterously and boast grand good cop/bad cop chemistry on screen.

Madden drew on her good-humoured sibling rivalry.

"My older sister once described me as being like a bird that keeps pecking at a snake, and the snake just dies from being so annoyed," Madden grins.

"I was like, 'Thank you.' It's a very honest way that an older sister would view a younger sister, and I kind of see that being the same with Diana and Crayford."

Christopher Eccleston says Chasing Millions is about the Troubles and the tenuous peace, but it's still really funny. (Supplied)

Madden enjoyed pecking at Eccleston. "He's a real force to be reckoned with," she says. "We had so much fun."

Eccleston concurs. "Chasing Millions is about the Troubles and the tenuous peace, but it's still really funny," he says. "And I love it as an audience member and as an actor, when a project asks me to laugh, cry and be terrified."

He wishes more films credited the viewer with the intelligence to grasp complexity and nuance.

" Because that's life, isn't it? Life's tragicomic! "

Chasing Millions is in Australian cinemas from November 19

World.title: No longer plain grain: A rural town’s towering new identity
World.content:
Artists are putting the finishing touches on a $1.85 million mural in the Lockyer Valley, turning four decommissioned silos into a towering Forest Hill landmark.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For weeks now, residents of a small Lockyer Valley town have watched as four gigantic decommissioned grain silos transform from a plain white eyesore into one of Queensland’s biggest pieces of public art. The $1.85 million project, which includes a car park and viewing platform on the other side of the train tracks, is nearing completion on the old GrainCorp silos by the train line at Forest Hill. Like the rest of the community, Anna Williams, whose sister runs Caffe Sorella in town, has been eagerly tracking the changes as the mural has taken shape over the past couple of months. What was once a “bit of an eyesore”, as Williams described it, has become a towering tribute to the town’s pioneering past. “It was all kept secret – we didn’t really know what was actually happening, and then all of a sudden it just developed, and it’s just beautiful,” she said. “People have been coming [to check the progress]. The first time they saw it, it was painted a pink or brown colour, and then all of a sudden you see a sketch of a boy and a girl – all right, what’s coming next? “And then there’s the train, all of that. So they come back and they see it take shape.”



What they have seen is their town reflected in paint, a young girl holding a Queenslander-style home in her hands, a boy playing with a steam train. And the Lockyer Valley rolling off into the distance. “It’s just beautiful,” Williams said. The artists behind the mural are Brisbane-based Jordan Bruce, of the Brightsiders collective fame, and Joel “The Zookeeper” Fergie from the Sunshine Coast. Artists Joel Fergie (‘The Zookeeper’) and Jordan Bruce of the Brightsiders during a painting break on Tuesday. Cameron Atfield The Forest Hill mural is the fourth piece of giant silo art to be painted in Queensland, and the closest to Brisbane by some margin.



“It’s become a bit of a way for towns to share their identity, what they’re about, what’s a drawcard to the area, what they’d like to be known for,” Fergie said. “We’ve had ‘big’ things around regional Australia [pineapples, bananas, merinos etc], and for the last 10 years, it’s big silos being painted.” The pair have been on the job now since early October, with (weather permitting) a few weeks left until completion. Both have temporarily relocated to nearby Gatton while painting the silos, about a 90-minute westerly drive from Brisbane. It’s quite the job. The four silos are 26 metres tall and about 15 metres wide – a huge artistic canvas by any standard. And it has been far from easy going, particularly when perched on an elevated platform atop a crane. “There are certain areas on this job where, because of the power line in particular, you might need to park further away [from the mural] – then it gets a bit hairy, especially if the wind’s up,” Bruce said.



“We do have good machines that are safe, but there’s no way to stop being scared at different points – at above 20 or 22 metres, you start to feel it.” Fergie said that was why the more intricate parts of the mural were closer to the ground than the top. The artists aren’t too fond of heights. Lockyer Valley Regional Council “A lot of the detail sits on the bottom two thirds, so we’ve tried to keep that top section quite sparse,” he said. “That just means you’re not up there all day every day painting trees right at the top, partly because we don’t love being up there all day every day. “It’s pretty scary when you’re 26 metres up on a machine that you just hope’s been serviced really well.” Bruce said the design, which was a closely held secret before work commenced, came from a period of community consultation with the locals.



“The first time we came out here, Joel had a vision of a child playing with a train, and that created a bit of a jump-off point,” he said. “It was partly about how to interact with what’s already happening, so you can imagine when the train comes past, if you get the photo at the right time, it’ll look like the boy’s playing with an actual train.” Lockyer Valley Mayor Tanya Milligan said the mural was about seven years in the making – and she had high hopes for its potential as a drawcard to Forest Hill. “For our council, it’s a once-in-a-generation opportunity. It’ll attract visitors. It will position Forest Hill and the Lockyer Valley as a must-see destination,” she said. Forest Hill’s two pubs will be hoping for more customers. Cameron Atfield “I’ve seen a few murals in my time, and I’m trying not to be biased, but this mural will be absolutely magnificent.”

World.title: Don’t tell me not to bark! I’m just fulfilling my destiny
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion Don’t tell me not to bark! I’m just fulfilling my destiny If Mal Lanyon wants tips on lowering crime, he should get in touch with Frank, the world’s most fearsome guard dog. Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist November 21, 2026 — 5:30am

November 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The diary of a dog: Who’d be a dog? My human companions live in a rough neighbourhood. Birds constantly squawk in the back garden. Three wheelie bins lurk ominously in the front yard. And children insist on walking past, chatting in their high-pitched voices, on the way to school each morning. And, so, I bark. Not constantly. That’s annoying. Just a series of brief volleys to warn others of the threat. Three months on patrol, and Frank has a 100 per cent success rate in protecting Man and home. I bark at the birds. I bark at the wheelie bins. And, with my paws leaning on the sill of the front window, I bark at the children as they walk past chatting, or at least pretending to chat as they plan their horrendous attack on our household. I have been on duty in this household for three months. Dear diary, I hope you won’t think me egotistical if I list my successes so far.



1: Number of bird attacks on humans in our backyard: zero. 2: Number of wheelie bins which have gone mad and attacked my humans: zero. 3: Number of local schoolchildren deciding to commit a violent home invasion of our house: zero. It’s a success rate of 100 per cent. If Mal Lanyon wants tips on lowering crime, he should get in touch. So, what thanks do I get for these achievements? None. Not a single dried sardine snack. Not a whiff of cheese – a delicious product I know they have, right there in the fridge. Not even a scratch behind the ears. It’s just, “Frank, will you please stop barking?”



Why employ a dog – feeding him, watering him, housing him – if you make no use of his skills? I come equipped with ears which, swivelling like two satellite dishes, can catch the sound of trouble a whole suburb away. Then there’s my nose, a piece of gear so well-engineered that science has not been able to match it, from identifying drugs at an airport to sniffing out cancer in a hospital patient. I’m also fast on my feet. I can go from back garden to front door – the thundering sound of my paws on floorboards – all while the delivery guy is still catching his breath. Why employ a dog – feeding him, watering him, housing him – if you make no use of his skills? And yet confronted with this symphony of skills, this apex of athleticism, this pure doggedness of dog, it’s just, “Frank, Frank, Frank, will you please calm down?” What if I were to acquiesce to their demands? What if I agreed to be deskilled? I’d be nothing. I’d be a Beethoven who has abandoned his piano. An Einstein kept from his calculations. A Mother Teresa who has turned her back on the poor.



More crucially: what if there were to be robbery? You know the truth. I’d be the first to be blamed. The dog would be the one in the doghouse. “I thought you had a dog?” a friend might say. “Isn’t he called Frank? What was Frank doing during the home invasion? I suppose the dear old thing was snoozing.” And then a derisive laugh, at my expense. Well, I’m not having it. If occasionally, very occasionally, I bark at a threat that proves illusory, it’s better than an invasion of violent primary school children – one that leaves all the valuables stolen, all the humans dead, and me with my paws bound with cable ties. Frank hard at work, ready to stop chatty schoolchildren from staging a home invasion. Meanwhile, in the brief breaks between threatening incidents, we play soccer, with Man kicking the ball into the air. I soar upwards and, nine balls out of ten, achieve the most spectacular of headers. At five months of age, I’m too young to win a place in the Socceroos, I know that. But surely, it’s only a matter of time. My main problem is guessing the direction of the ball after Man has kicked it. He is, I fear, the worst player since the game was invented. Once we are back inside the house, I follow Man from room to room. We go down the hallway to the bedroom, back up to the kitchen, and again down to the bedroom. And then back to the kitchen. One day, I feel certain, he’ll do something interesting, although this outcome is yet to eventuate.



Still, if you are interested in watching a man pick up a teacup from his bedside table and walk it up to the dishwasher, only to remember he’s forgotten the other cup and so repeating the journey, turning on and off the bedroom light each time, then it’s a son et lumière display that will leave you dazzled. Later, at 9pm, I go to sleep on the bed in the front room, ready for the morning. I sleep until I hear it. Childish voices. Going to school. Outside my house. How dare they! I throw a few warning shots their way, my paws resting on the sill of the front window. It won’t stop the children from executing a home invasion, but at least this way they’ll choose the house two doors down. That household is “protected” by an elderly Labrador. From him, I hear hardly a snuffle. I assume the dear old thing is snoozing.

World.title: Fake farewells fool nobody, but a great encore is worth the wait
World.content:
CultureMusicThe Verdict Opinion Fake farewells fool nobody, but a great encore is worth the wait A good encore should raise the roof. After all, this is show business. Michael Dwyer Journalist November 21, 2026 — 5:30am

November 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We know they’re coming back. The exit was too casual, it’s still dark out here and the stage lights are throbbing like jazz hands. Look around, though. That punter’s checking his public transport app. That one’s rubbing her temples. Could the band not just play Wonderwall and then leave the stage? Loathe it or just dislike it, the encore is inescapably a thing. But sometime between Elvis leaving that building in Shreveport, Louisiana 70 years ago and the modern musician’s all-but-contracted toilet break a few songs before the end of the show, the curtain call caper shifted from pandemonium to charade. I blame the artist. Not least Roger Daltrey. “I call it bullshit time,” the Who’s moonlighting singer announced before he led his Ultimate Rock Symphony offstage and back on at Colonial Stadium in March 2000. Way to kill the vibe, Rog. What might have been a romping climax left this fan with a 26-year-long grudge. A memorable encore requires commitment and imagination. Richard Clifford Daltrey’s long antipathy – “The encores, the bloody encores. We hate ’em,” he told a press conference in 1975 – says the quiet bit out loud for many. Fair enough for the Who, I guess. They’d smashed everything to pieces during My Generation. But begrudging the return says more about the artist’s lack of imagination than the ritual itself.



Sam Fender’s recent Australian tour offered an example of the thing done right. After the communal uproar of his signature hit Seventeen Going Under, he returned alone under a spotlight for The Dying Light and suddenly the encore was an invitation to listen again. The band joined later, swelling towards the final blast of Hypersonic Missiles, but that moment of solitude reset the emotional scale. Turns out you can bring a crowd closer by giving them less to shout about. “If you own a cape, rock star, this is the time to put it on.” Indulging the past is fine too, but a surprise payoff is the difference between escalation and obligation. A risky, under-rehearsed cover version. Dragging the support band back up. Even bagpipes and a kilt can work – just make sure you’re Jimmy Barnes first. Mike Skinner knew he’d have to come back for a few random hits after performing the Streets’ A Grand Don’t Come For Free in its entirety last summer, but he kept himself interested by crowd-surfing the length of the venue each night.



It’s not like every performer can be Rufus Wainwright, magicking up a whole Mardi Gras of dancing fools with fruit on their heads to take over the concert hall as he re-costumes as Judy Garland for a roof-raising re-entry. But if you own a cape, rock star, this is the time to put it on. And if not, why not? This is show business. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Civilians are always landing planes in movies. Call me cynical, but I doubt I could wing it John Bailey Contributor Speaking of James Brown, you don’t even need to physically leave to make people suddenly realise how much they’re going to miss you. Even threatened departure is drama on a stick, as long as you commit fully enough to make the audience want to play along. Walking off with your biggest hit still in your pocket is where the eye-rolling starts. Deep Purple moved Smoke On the Water back into the main set decades ago. “We wanted to teach it a lesson,” singer Ian Gillan told me, like a boss. If the air guitars are still plugged in and wailing after that, that’s an encore you deserve. As we grow more jaded out here in the dark, making the charade feel real is the part of the deal that’s slipping. I was a more credulous young man when I first saw Leonard Cohen in 1980, but when he came back eight times I was convinced I was witnessing history. Surely this hadn’t happened in Adelaide.

World.title: Women are retiring with $51,000 less in super. Here’s how to fight back
World.content:
November 21, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ladies we have a problem: an average $51,000 retirement funding shortfall versus men, according to Super Members Council’s analysis of ATO data. That’s 26 per cent less. Ten years ago, the deficit was 20.5 per cent. Yet most Aussie women are doing little about it. The gender pay gap may be improving, but women still earn nearly 20 per cent less than men. Michaela Pollock While most of us have – probably painfully – cut spending in the past three months, we are wrestling with the present rather than focusing on the future. Indeed, just 16 per cent of us feel we can balance today’s priorities with our financial goals. The gender pay gap – which last week was confirmed at still 19.7 per cent by the Workplace Gender Equality Agency – gets baked in like a poisoned money mushroom with every super contribution. Then it can widen over years of reduced pay compared to men.



So, let’s ‘man up’ your super in three swift steps: M is for Manage it: According to Australian Retirement Trust’s Women’s Future indicator, 63 per cent of us checked our super balance in the past year, but only 17 per cent reviewed or changed investment options. Yet, there is a great tool to do so. Half of all women said their current stage of life was holding back their ability to build wealth. Start by sanity checking your fund’s performance on the ATO’s YourSuper comparison tool. Log in via myGov and find this tool on the ATO site. It will compare your existing super fund and its performance against that of several alternative funds. The average median Balanced super fund put on 9.4 per cent last financial year, according to superratings.com.au, but you want performance that is solid over the long term, so your real benchmark is 7.7 per cent a year over 10 years.



Even a 1 per cent lower return over a lifetime will see someone on $100,000 aged 30, and with $50,000 in super to date, with an end balance that is $157,509 less than it could have been – $519,432 as opposed to $676,941. In fact, that’s the difference on MoneySmart’s excellent superannuation calculator between the 6.1 per cent forecast returns of a Balanced fund option holding up to 70 per cent in growth assets like shares, and a conservative fund that will contain far fewer growth assets, around 4.9 per cent. And that’s the other thing you need to check when you manage your super: the type of fund in which you are invested. In general, the younger you are, the more risk you can take on. A is for Accelerate it (for ‘free’): You may not be aware just how much free and discounted super money is out there – that is, if you are a low-income earner and particularly if you’re in a caring life-phase which has you earning less (and probably working harder). Half of all women said their current stage of life was holding back their ability to build wealth, found Australian Retirement Trust. Almost a third of women said caring responsibilities had reduced the hours they could work or the income they could earn, rising to 50 per cent of partnered women supporting children.



There are two strategies that families in particular should use to help equalise the super of a lower-earning spouse. The first of these is the co-contribution. You need to be working in some form to qualify for this, you also need to pay in $1000 after tax – $19 a week. Editor's pick Opinion

Christmas The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor But you get – for free – up to $500 paid into your super by the government each year you qualify. A qualifying condition is that you earn less than $64,293 a year. The amount phases down from a $500 top up after your wage hits $49,293. The second super opportunity, if you can afford it, is a spouse contribution. Here, a higher earning spouse pays into the super account of a lower earning spouse, on less than $40,000. They don’t need to be working, so this is especially good during unpaid time working even harder to raise children.



An after-tax contribution of $3000 – about $58 a week – nets the payer a tax offset of up to $540. This one phases down from $540 after a $37,000 wage, until it disappears at $40,000. A tax offset is a beautiful thing. It is a straight-up discount on your tax bill, so not only will a family’s overall super balance build more equally, the family tax bill will reduce. So, what is the most powerful way of redressing the super detriment versus men? N is for Nullify the disadvantage: Actuarial firm Rice Warner crunched the numbers on this… purely from a longevity perspective, given that women typically live about four years longer than men, female workers needed to be paid 2 per cent more in superannuation to ensure the same level of income as males throughout retirement. On the face of it, it seems discriminatory. But actually, it levels the playing field. And this was borne out when the firm took the modelling to the Human Rights Commission and was granted permission to pay female workers 2 per cent more on the grounds of fairness.



So use that as your guide. Could you salary sacrifice 2 per cent extra, remembering that it wouldn’t even cost you this much from your pay as it would be before tax? Because, ladies, it could change your life. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: The retirement question most of us never ask – until it’s too late
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementRetirement living Opinion The retirement question most of us never ask – until it’s too late Bec Wilson Money contributor November 21, 2026 — 5:01am

November 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ask any Australian approaching retirement what they’re planning for, and they will probably tell you their target super balance. They want to have $300,000, $500,000, $750,000 or a magic million dollars in their super account before they pull the ripcord. But ask them what they want their retirement to look like, and the answers become a lot more hazy, idealistic and uncertain. A big trip or three, more time with the family, golf, and maybe a caravanning trip around Australia. And there’s nothing wrong with any of those ambitions. But I hate to break it to you – they’re not that helpful in building a retirement plan. How we live and spend in retirement is changing. Getty Images I talk about retirement a lot, and I’m constantly surprised by how much attention we give to accumulating money and how little we spend working out what we actually want to do with it. And this week, I’ve been contemplating these things in a much more personal way. A lot of us do when big life changes land at the end of the year.



My youngest son, the last of three kids, finished school this week. No more lunch packing, school drop-offs, school fee payments or uniform washing for me. And, the end of an intense, 23-year phase of raising children. (Now I’m just coaching, part-funding and prodding young adults.) Alongside that, I’ve worked and organised my life around everyone else’s priorities and schedules. But now I’m starting to wonder what the next 20 or 30 years might look like for me. And I’m curious – really curious. What could I do differently? How much do I want to work? Where do I want to live? What do I want to spend more time doing, and who do I want to spend it with? And only then will I be able to answer – what financial choices could I be making now to give myself the freedom to do these things? I’m not alone. Tens of thousands of Australians are preparing to retire this year-end, while others are heading towards the summer holidays wondering whether they want to return to the same job.



We’re all at different stages of the journey towards retirement. But there’s enormous value in getting curious, long before we’re forced into big decisions. The earlier you start asking these questions, the more time you have to do something with the answers. Too many Australians today only start seriously thinking about retirement at 64 or 65, when they realise they haven’t saved enough, or that the life they’ve imagined costs more than they expected. In my retirement programs and speeches, I often ask people to picture an ordinary Tuesday in retirement. By then, they can’t go back and save more in their 50s, pay down their mortgage or spend a few years reshaping their careers into more flexible work. That’s why I think we need to change our approach to retirement planning. Rather than waiting until we’re almost ready to stop working, we should start getting curious about it much earlier. And then working out what it will take to make the future we want, possible.



It’s one of the reasons I’m kicking off Epic Retirement Month, a four-week, free public education initiative encouraging Australians to go back to basics and get curious about their future retirement. Not just the financial side, but the life they’re actually planning for and how to bring it to life. You’ll see it running in these pages, and on my reels and podcast for the next four weeks. Editor's pick Opinion

Financial planners Your retirement savings shouldn’t be someone else’s sales target Bec Wilson Money contributor This week I interviewed American behavioural scientist Hal Hershfield, who has spent years studying our relationship with our future selves. His research suggests we can think about our future selves almost as though they’re strangers. And when you think about it – it makes a lot of sense. It’s difficult to prioritise the needs of a future self you barely know, can’t imagine and don’t prioritise when you’ve got bills to pay in a crappy economy, a busy life to juggle and many demands from work and kids. But Hershfield’s work points to something really useful we can all grab onto: the more vividly we can imagine our future lives, the easier it can become to connect with them and start making decisions that will benefit us later.



And that is where modern retirement planning really needs to start. Not with a superannuation calculator or a target retirement date – but with a bit of curiosity and imagination for the 20, 30 or 40 years that might lie ahead. In my retirement programs and speeches, I often ask people to picture an ordinary Tuesday in retirement. And not the Tuesday you’re cruising Europe or driving the van through the Kimberley. Just an ordinary Tuesday, maybe five years after you stop working. Where are you living? Who are you spending your time with? What gets you out of bed in the morning? Do you still do a little bit of work? Do you have some good friends nearby? And are you fit and healthy enough to do all the things you enjoy? Picture that then work backwards. What does that future life ask you to do today to get there? That’s how you build a retirement plan. Maybe you need to save more, sooner. Or perhaps you need to pay down your debt, or rethink where you live. You might have to make a more conscious effort to build friendships outside of work. Or put a real focus on your strength, flexibility and nutrition.



You could start working less, or making more room in your life for the priorities that really are at the top of your list. And maybe you could even find time to start some of these things now, without waiting for retirement. Editor's pick Opinion

Jobs Lost your job? Do these four things before you touch your savings Paridhi Jain Money contributor Because getting curious about retirement isn’t just about planning for a better life later. It’s also about recognising the choices you have today, while you’ve still got time to make them. So here’s something to try this weekend. Imagine yourself five or 10 years from now, living the ordinary life you’ve pictured. Then, write a short letter from that future version of yourself to the person you are today. What would they thank you for doing? What might they wish you had done earlier or differently? And what advice would they give you about the choices you’re making right now?



If you have a partner, try it separately and then compare notes. You might find your ideas overlap, or discover you’ve got quite different expectations about the years ahead. And don’t worry about getting it right – there’s no right answer. It’s just a way to start thinking about what you want while you’ve still got time to make the choices that could help you get there. We’ve spent decades encouraging Australians to save more for retirement. It’s certainly important. But I think it’s a lot easier to save, improve your health, pay down debt and make better choices when you know what you’re doing it all for. Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. World.title: How a priceless Faberge egg ended up permanently living at sea
World.content:
InspirationCruises How a priceless Faberge egg ended up permanently living at sea Julietta Jameson November 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When we hear the word “Faberge”, chances are we think “egg”. The Russian jewellery house is renowned for the bejewelled ovoid creations that characterised the prolific gift-giving of the Romanov court, and are now among the world’s most-prized objets d’art. Journey in Jewels, the contemporary Faberge egg created for the ship. The egg can unfurl to reveal a secondary bejewelled egg. I’m standing in the main reception area of Regent Seven Seas Grandeur with some of my new cruise friends as we admire Journey in Jewels, the contemporary Faberge egg created for the ship. It seems an unlikely place to encounter one, but this is the first and only Faberge egg to permanently live at sea.



That’s because the ship’s godmother is Sarah Faberge, great-granddaughter of Peter Carl Faberge, best known for creating Faberge eggs made in the style of genuine Easter eggs, but using precious metals and gemstones. Our voyage is themed on the jewellery house, and Sarah herself is on board. 



We laugh, then riff on how funny it would be if he suddenly produced the egg from his pocket during his evening show. I mention that it’s probably worth millions. The Kelch Rocaille egg. The Houston Museum of Natural Science houses the McFerrin Faberge Collection, which includes a number of the famous eggs. HMNS/Rathke “What?” The magician’s face goes a little white. Then we notice cameras pointed in our direction, and realise whoever is directing them may not appreciate the joke. We disperse rather quickly, probably looking far more suspicious than we intend.



Journey in Jewels isn’t an Imperial egg but is unmistakably Faberge. Graduated blue guilloche enamel, pearls, emeralds, tsavorites, sapphires, hand-carved mother-of-pearl clouds and opals reference the colours and moods of the sea rather than imperial Russia. A mechanical movement opens the outer shell to reveal its hidden surprise. By rotating a pearl-set “helm” at the base of the stand, seven enamelled blades open to reveal a second egg nestled inside. A vanity case from the early 20th century in silver, gold and pink guilloche enamel accented with diamonds. HMNS/Mike Rathke “People think of the eggs,” says Faberge historian Tim Adams during the voyage. “But they represent only a tiny part of what Faberge produced.” At its peak, the House of Faberge employed about 500 craftsmen and created an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 objects. Alongside the famous eggs came clocks, fans, perfume bottles, cigarette cases, carved stone animals, flowers, desk accessories and jewellery. As Jennifer McFerrin-Bohner, director of the McFerrin Foundation and daughter of renowned collectors Art and Dorothy McFerrin, puts it during one of her onboard talks, “Anything someone wanted to buy, he would create.”



The Houston Museum of Natural Science in Texas provides a home to the McFerrin Collection. Built over decades, that collection spans more than 600 Faberge objects, from Imperial treasures to whimsical hardstone animals, fans, clocks and jewellery. Perhaps the biggest surprise is Faberge’s flower studies. Adams describes them as being “as rare as the Imperial Easter eggs”. To create them, Faberge maintained a greenhouse on the roof of his St Petersburg headquarters so craftsmen could study exotic blooms before recreating them in stone. As Adams puts it, “Pictures just do not do these things justice.” With Russia firmly on Australia’s “do not travel” list, America’s great Faberge collections have become the easiest way to understand the house outside its homeland. A gold, enamel and diamond brooch created for the Nobel Brothers Company in the late 19th or early 20th century. HMNS/Mike Rathke Along with the Houston Museum of Natural Science, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts in Richmond hosts one of the world’s finest public Faberge collections, assembled by Lillian Thomas Pratt, an American lover of Russian art.



Alongside several Imperial Easter eggs are exquisitely crafted everyday objects, including delicate cigarette cases. Adams notes that a single cigarette case could combine engraving, chasing, stone-setting and enamelling – “the whole art of the goldsmith” in one object. Hillwood Estate, Museum & Gardens, a decorative arts and historic house museum in Washington, DC, explains why so much Faberge is found in the United States. Opera glasses decorated with rose gold and silver trim and diamond-set floral festoons. HMNS/Mike Rathke Following the Russian Revolution, Soviet authorities sold many Imperial treasures overseas to raise foreign currency. Known in her lifetime as America’s wealthiest woman, General Foods founder and philanthropist Marjorie Merriweather Post acquired many of them. Hillwood was her home, and she endowed the property, along with her collections, as a public institution. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York places Faberge within the wider story of European decorative arts. Here, it becomes clear that the eggs are simply the headline acts in a much larger story of innovation, artistry and technical mastery.



Related Article ★★★★★

Ship reviews Travel can’t get any closer to flawless than on board this ship In my own journey, I go from looking at a pretty egg and having a bit of a joke about it, to realising I am looking at the latest expression of nearly two centuries of craftsmanship. It is no longer simply an exquisite object on display aboard a luxury ship, but a reminder that the House of Faberge has constantly evolved, finding new ways to celebrate artistry and innovation. THE DETAILS CRUISE

Regent’s Spotlight Voyages program offers a Spotlight on Wine with Mercante Wine Merchants, an eight-night cruise from Rome to Venice on Seven Seas Grandeur, home of Journey in Jewels. Departs July 11, 2027, from $10,230 a person. See rssc.com
