World.title: Summer is coming. Here’s what you should know about sharks
World.content:
The idea that there are more sharks around now is wrong, says marine biology adjunct professor Colin Simpfendorfer: “On the other hand, there are certainly more people in the water.”

Last summer was one of the worst on record for shark bites. With a hot season ahead, should swimmers and surfers be worried? One survivor and two experts weigh in what works – and what doesn’t.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 21 edition of the Good Weekend. See all stories .

GLENN ORGIAS, 51, is an energy trader and writer who lives in Bondi, Sydney. On February 12, 2009, he was bitten by a shark while surfing at Bondi Beach. He spent 10 days in ICU, more than five weeks in hospital, and lost his hand and part of his forearm. Since his attack, he’s written two books – a memoir called Man in a Grey Suit, and Teeth Kicker, a crime novel about – well, a loan shark. “There was a lot going on the night I was attacked. Paul [de Gelder, a navy diver] was attacked the day before [by a bull shark in Sydney Harbour]; there’d been a huge amount of flooding in Queensland, which had pushed a lot of fresh water into the ocean; and it was really stormy here in Sydney, so the water was reasonably murky. It was dusk, and the light was getting low. There would’ve been 20 or 30 guys out that night. It was big surf – very lumpy, not very nice – but it had been flat for two weeks, so no one had surfed for ages and everyone was keen to get out there. It was breaking a fair way offshore. I’d just got a wave and was paddling back towards the pack – about 80 metres from shore, 20 metres from the lineup – when I was attacked. Glenn Orgias at Bondi Beach, where he still surfs despite being mauled there during a shark attack. “Fear’s not something that will stop me doing it,” he says. Brent Lewin The shark just slammed into me from below. It knocked me right off my board and pulled me under by my left arm. I didn’t know what was happening. I couldn’t see anything – I never actually saw it – but I remember it shook me really aggressively, sort of ran me through the water. The whole thing was so quick – less than a minute, maybe less than 30 seconds – I didn’t really know what was going on. Then it suddenly let me go and I popped up. The other surfers didn’t come for me. It was a difficult situation – they initially scattered, as you would, because I was screaming. I managed to get back on my board and got my arm – what was left of it – back onto the board. I just started paddling. I was very fearful it was going to circle back and come again. I felt like a sitting duck. I just went hell-for-leather and paddled really hard one-handed and caught a wave. Just on my stomach. It was the best wave of my life – the wave that saved my life, absolutely. When I got in [to the shallows], my board got sucked back out behind me, dragging on my leash, and I couldn’t get out. I was there in the shallows, holding my arm, just stuck up to my thighs in the water. And then one of the local guys here who I know quite well grabbed me and helped me up onto the sand.



There were a lot of people on the beach that night. Someone called the ambulance, which took about 45 minutes to come. But Bondi’s one of the best places in Australia to be attacked by a shark: there were three doctors literally right there. I’d lost a fair bit of blood, and later on one of them – an emergency doctor from Prince of Wales [Hospital in Randwick] – told me that when he looked at me, he thought it was 50-50 I’d have a cardiac arrest on the sand and not make it. ‘The shark slammed into me from below. It knocked me off my board and pulled me under by my left arm.’ Glenn Orgias Straight after the attack, when I woke up in hospital, I thought I’d never surf again. I remember my wife, Lisa – who was six months pregnant – saying, “I want to move away from the beach.” And I was the same – I didn’t want to even see the ocean. But by the next day, we’d both calmed down; we both decided we wanted to stay. And I knew I wanted to surf again. Since the attack, I’ve learnt a bit about what happened, though of course you can’t be sure. I think it was a test bite from the shark. Another guy in the water that day got bumped just before I was bitten, and – I’m speculating – I think it was the same shark: I think it was noticing a lot of surfers, trying to figure it out. The teeth marks from my bite, and my wetsuit, suggest it was a juvenile white shark, maybe about four years old, about 200 kilograms – around the age where they transfer from eating finned fish to mammals, like seals. So they’re just learning, and with something big, they want to test it out. They’re looking for fat and meat. So when it got my arm it gave it a bit of a go, then it was like, “Yeah, feeling a bit weird … not worth my time”. So it let go. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster I only learnt all that later, of course. When I think back, I think our understanding of sharks now is at a completely different scientific level than when I was attacked; and I didn’t understand the contributing factors towards shark attack the way I do now. For instance, the night I was attacked, there were the floodwaters and the runoff; it was dusk; it was overcast and cloudy and not easy for sharks to see. There were a lot of bait fish around; and it was February, which is a very common month for shark attacks. So there were lots of risk factors which the average Joe – including me – didn’t really know at the time. Now there are drones and tagging and tracking and just a lot more information to help you. When I decide to go out these days, I think I recognise that I’m making an actual decision, consciously, based on a whole lot of factors. For myself, my basic rules are: if a beach is closed, I don’t go. I don’t surf at sunset or sunrise – basically, if the sun isn’t on the water, I don’t go. If it’s really murky after rain, I’ll give it a couple of days. I do sometimes feel fearful, but fear’s not something that will stop me doing it. It’s just a feeling, and I just try to manage it, accept it and let it pass. And usually it does. Often I’ll go out and I don’t feel any fear at all.



I’m not an expert and I’m not really capable of offering anyone advice. But my personal feeling is that what’s most valuable is the continuing development of scientific knowledge and education around sharks: their habits, behaviours, biology. Just in the past year, the drones have started putting out a lot of information, which I think is useful. I don’t love shark nets: they didn’t save me, and I think they trap a lot of wildlife. I’m not 100 per cent against them, but I’ve always questioned their value. I feel the same about drum lines. My major thing is I don’t really want a whole lot of wildlife getting killed unnecessarily when it’s not really having a very big impact on shark attacks. I think the biggest impact will come with people really understanding that “today is a potentially dangerous day”, based on the science. I think the scientists are doing a good job. These days, sometimes I’ll surf every day of the week; sometimes, if it’s flat for a while, I won’t go at all. But I guess I average a couple of times a week. [Last summer, at the peak of the attacks] I stayed out of the surf for two weeks, probably longer than most people. I probably do take a more cautious approach than others. I certainly don’t feel immune. And if I did get attacked again, people are going to think I’m a real idiot! Like getting struck twice by lightning. Loading Chris Pepin-Neff is an associate professor in public policy at the University of Sydney. For the past 20 years, they have worked in the sub-specialty of “human-shark studies”, looking at media coverage, policymaking, and public opinion and emotion surrounding sharks. They have worked on human-shark risk assessment and safety measures all over the world, including Australia, South Africa, Réunion Island and the United States. “I always look at three things: shark activity, human activity, environmental conditions. Last summer was a perfect storm: warm water temperatures, record summer rain, superabundance of bait fish. It was a singularity – totally incomparable to any other time. And I’d suggest we’re not going to have another year like we’ve just had. But that said, there’s going to be extraordinary levels of unpredictability this year: we’ve got El Niño, it’s going to be hot – we just don’t know what’s going to happen. It can be helpful to think in terms of attractants and deterrents. Attractants are things that attract sharks. So, say you have a harbour beach, with a jetty nearby. You’ve got boats, with sewage that attracts small fish: attractant. You’ve got fishermen gutting fish off the jetty: attractant. Then you’ve got high water temperature and low water clarity, environmental conditions that raise the level of bait fish: attractant. So a lot of attractants, which equals high risk. My mum’s passed now, but she was a big swimmer. Would I let her go swimming between the boats in that sort of scenario? No way. To me, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. Chris Pepin-Neff: enclosure nets can be effective, but the use of gill nets, which sit offshore and create partial barriers, is “insane and dangerous”. Wolter Peeters



What you want is to remove attractants and add deterrents – things that trigger avoidant behaviour in sharks. So one thing I always recommend is that if you’re swimming at an unprotected beach, you should be swimming in pairs or groups. That’s particularly true for children: everybody needs a buddy. And that’s because we want to trigger sharks’ avoidance response by being more intimidating. Big multiple splashes, like swimmers between the flags – a great big mess in the water – that’s intimidating, because sharks don’t know what that is: it doesn’t read like potential prey. One swimmer is not intimidating. A surfer on a surfboard is not intimidating. So sharks come up and they’re curious, maybe defensive. That’s when they might take a bite. You can also do a few things to make yourself less inviting. Don’t wear jewellery – your watch, your necklace – because it could look flashy, like fish gills that are moving. Don’t wear yellow: in the shark-bite community – and I’ve not seen a scientific study on this, but dear god, I know it’s true – it’s referred to as “yum yum yellow”. Don’t wear flesh-coloured clothes. You don’t want to look like a seal, but I’d rather be black than look like flesh. Or a fish. Don’t wear silvery, bluey things. ‘Don’t wear jewellery ... Don’t wear yellow ... Don’t wear flesh-coloured clothes.’ Chris Pepin-Neff I’ve done assessments on Réunion Island, in Florida; the same rules apply. You just have to be mindful that the ocean is an active ecosystem. It’s wrong to assume that the ocean is like a resort pool that’s always safe, and the shark is always dangerous. The fact is, the shark isn’t always dangerous and the beach is really never safe. The ocean is the wild. We do ourselves a disservice when we pretend otherwise. This is why the research on culling has shown that it doesn’t work. Because if the attractant is never removed, you have to kill every single shark in the ecosystem. And then you’ve got to kill every shark under that, and under that, all the way down. Apex predator, meso-predator, on and on: white sharks and bull sharks, then dusky sharks and bronze whalers. It would never end. A white shark circles kayakers. Westpac Life Saver Rescue Helicopter Netting is difficult. Not all nets are created equal. Enclosure nets in the right context work very well. I’ve seen them in operation in Capetown; I recommended one at Cottesloe in Western Australia. An enclosure net doesn’t kill anything, doesn’t catch anything. It’s not an environmental disaster. It comes right in to the beach – water on three sides, sand on the fourth. You put it out for three hours on a Sunday morning for Nippers or whatever, then you pull it back in. It’s completely safe – nothing can get in, nothing can get out.



I think other kinds of nets [such as the gill nets at many beaches, which sit off-shore in the middle of a water column as partial barriers, while leaving the majority of the area un-netted] are insane and dangerous. The reality is that when fish get caught in those nets, they struggle. Those struggles send out low-frequency vibrations that sharks can sense over long distances: it’s one of the ways they detect prey. So those vibrations are literally like ringing a dinner bell for sharks to come in toward the nets – and the beach. They are literally the last thing you should put in front of the flags. The irony is that people don’t actually want [gill] nets. I’ve gone all over the world – and remember, I only go to beaches after clusters of fatal shark bites – looking for people who want them, and the highest number I can get is between seven and nine per cent. I did a survey here at Waverley at Bondi. The question was: “If a shark net was taken out and there was a fatal shark attack at Bondi afterwards, would you hold the politician responsible?” Six hundred people, scientific study; 70 per cent of people said, “No, we wouldn’t.” We also asked, “Would you go back to that beach if the net was taken out?” And three out of four people said, “Yes.” Related Article Good Weekend 'They'll have an uprising on their hands': the fight to save wild horses But for politicians, that 30 per cent is too much of a risk. Politicians are trying to manage the public holding them accountable for shark bites – not the occurrence of shark bites themselves. What’s the threshold of risk and courage a politician would need to take shark nets out, pray to God there are no incidents, and if there is, be able to sustain nine weeks of front page coverage blaming them? That’s a very, very hard question. I’ve seen it asked all over the world, but never more than in Australia. And the fact is, no politician is courageous enough to take that risk. And so the state government has been entirely disingenuous on the subject of shark nets in NSW. There were shark nets in the water when at least three of the last shark attacks here occurred, and yet the government has doubled down on the effectiveness of shark nets. I’m not talking about my friends at the DPI [Department of Primary Industries] or my scientist colleagues, I’m talking about the politicians who said, “Oh, well, this cluster goes to prove that we need more shark nets.” It has not proven that. It has proven that shark nets are less effective and potentially more dangerous even than we thought. They’ve had 100 years to find one study that says they work and they can’t. And I can find five studies that say that gill nets catch sharks and other marine life, and attract sharks closer to the beach. And not only studies: DPI pictures and videos show that 40 per cent of sharks are caught on the inside of the nets. The fact is, shark nets don’t protect beachgoers. Shark nets protect politicians. “The ocean is the wild. We do ourselves a disservice when we pretend otherwise.” Getty Images One of the major political off-ramps for governments wanting to stop using nets is drumlines. The old kind are baited buoys that basically drown the shark. The new kind, smart drumlines, have a pinger that alerts people, who come and drag the shark out to sea. The response has to be quick, otherwise there’s an 80 per cent mortality rate – but it’s potentially an excellent resource for tagging and other scientific data collection; and the research shows that dragging a shark away is traumatic enough for the animal that it stays out of the area for between three and six months. So it’s a very effective non-lethal measure. Although there is some bycatch, it’s very low – far lower than nets.

World.title: No longer plain grain: A rural town’s towering new identity
World.content:
Artists are putting the finishing touches on a $1.85 million mural in the Lockyer Valley, turning four decommissioned silos into a towering Forest Hill landmark.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For weeks now, residents of a small Lockyer Valley town have watched as four gigantic decommissioned grain silos transform from a plain white eyesore into one of Queensland’s biggest pieces of public art. The $1.85 million project, which includes a car park and viewing platform on the other side of the train tracks, is nearing completion on the old GrainCorp silos by the train line at Forest Hill. Like the rest of the community, Anna Williams, whose sister runs Caffe Sorella in town, has been eagerly tracking the changes as the mural has taken shape over the past couple of months. What was once a “bit of an eyesore”, as Williams described it, has become a towering tribute to the town’s pioneering past. “It was all kept secret – we didn’t really know what was actually happening, and then all of a sudden it just developed, and it’s just beautiful,” she said. “People have been coming [to check the progress]. The first time they saw it, it was painted a pink or brown colour, and then all of a sudden you see a sketch of a boy and a girl – all right, what’s coming next? “And then there’s the train, all of that. So they come back and they see it take shape.”



What they have seen is their town reflected in paint, a young girl holding a Queenslander-style home in her hands, a boy playing with a steam train. And the Lockyer Valley rolling off into the distance. “It’s just beautiful,” Williams said. The artists behind the mural are Brisbane-based Jordan Bruce, of the Brightsiders collective fame, and Joel “The Zookeeper” Fergie from the Sunshine Coast. Artists Joel Fergie (‘The Zookeeper’) and Jordan Bruce of the Brightsiders during a painting break on Tuesday. Cameron Atfield The Forest Hill mural is the fourth piece of giant silo art to be painted in Queensland, and the closest to Brisbane by some margin.



“It’s become a bit of a way for towns to share their identity, what they’re about, what’s a drawcard to the area, what they’d like to be known for,” Fergie said. “We’ve had ‘big’ things around regional Australia [pineapples, bananas, merinos etc], and for the last 10 years, it’s big silos being painted.” The pair have been on the job now since early October, with (weather permitting) a few weeks left until completion. Both have temporarily relocated to nearby Gatton while painting the silos, about a 90-minute westerly drive from Brisbane. It’s quite the job. The four silos are 26 metres tall and about 15 metres wide – a huge artistic canvas by any standard. And it has been far from easy going, particularly when perched on an elevated platform atop a crane. “There are certain areas on this job where, because of the power line in particular, you might need to park further away [from the mural] – then it gets a bit hairy, especially if the wind’s up,” Bruce said.



“We do have good machines that are safe, but there’s no way to stop being scared at different points – at above 20 or 22 metres, you start to feel it.” Fergie said that was why the more intricate parts of the mural were closer to the ground than the top. The artists aren’t too fond of heights. Lockyer Valley Regional Council “A lot of the detail sits on the bottom two thirds, so we’ve tried to keep that top section quite sparse,” he said. “That just means you’re not up there all day every day painting trees right at the top, partly because we don’t love being up there all day every day. “It’s pretty scary when you’re 26 metres up on a machine that you just hope’s been serviced really well.” Bruce said the design, which was a closely held secret before work commenced, came from a period of community consultation with the locals.



“The first time we came out here, Joel had a vision of a child playing with a train, and that created a bit of a jump-off point,” he said. “It was partly about how to interact with what’s already happening, so you can imagine when the train comes past, if you get the photo at the right time, it’ll look like the boy’s playing with an actual train.” Lockyer Valley Mayor Tanya Milligan said the mural was about seven years in the making – and she had high hopes for its potential as a drawcard to Forest Hill. “For our council, it’s a once-in-a-generation opportunity. It’ll attract visitors. It will position Forest Hill and the Lockyer Valley as a must-see destination,” she said. Forest Hill’s two pubs will be hoping for more customers. Cameron Atfield “I’ve seen a few murals in my time, and I’m trying not to be biased, but this mural will be absolutely magnificent.”

World.title: Don’t tell me not to bark! I’m just fulfilling my destiny
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion Don’t tell me not to bark! I’m just fulfilling my destiny If Mal Lanyon wants tips on lowering crime, he should get in touch with Frank, the world’s most fearsome guard dog. Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist November 21, 2026 — 5:30am

November 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The diary of a dog: Who’d be a dog? My human companions live in a rough neighbourhood. Birds constantly squawk in the back garden. Three wheelie bins lurk ominously in the front yard. And children insist on walking past, chatting in their high-pitched voices, on the way to school each morning. And, so, I bark. Not constantly. That’s annoying. Just a series of brief volleys to warn others of the threat. Three months on patrol, and Frank has a 100 per cent success rate in protecting Man and home. I bark at the birds. I bark at the wheelie bins. And, with my paws leaning on the sill of the front window, I bark at the children as they walk past chatting, or at least pretending to chat as they plan their horrendous attack on our household. I have been on duty in this household for three months. Dear diary, I hope you won’t think me egotistical if I list my successes so far.



1: Number of bird attacks on humans in our backyard: zero. 2: Number of wheelie bins which have gone mad and attacked my humans: zero. 3: Number of local schoolchildren deciding to commit a violent home invasion of our house: zero. It’s a success rate of 100 per cent. If Mal Lanyon wants tips on lowering crime, he should get in touch. So, what thanks do I get for these achievements? None. Not a single dried sardine snack. Not a whiff of cheese – a delicious product I know they have, right there in the fridge. Not even a scratch behind the ears. It’s just, “Frank, will you please stop barking?”



Why employ a dog – feeding him, watering him, housing him – if you make no use of his skills? I come equipped with ears which, swivelling like two satellite dishes, can catch the sound of trouble a whole suburb away. Then there’s my nose, a piece of gear so well-engineered that science has not been able to match it, from identifying drugs at an airport to sniffing out cancer in a hospital patient. I’m also fast on my feet. I can go from back garden to front door – the thundering sound of my paws on floorboards – all while the delivery guy is still catching his breath. Why employ a dog – feeding him, watering him, housing him – if you make no use of his skills? And yet confronted with this symphony of skills, this apex of athleticism, this pure doggedness of dog, it’s just, “Frank, Frank, Frank, will you please calm down?” What if I were to acquiesce to their demands? What if I agreed to be deskilled? I’d be nothing. I’d be a Beethoven who has abandoned his piano. An Einstein kept from his calculations. A Mother Teresa who has turned her back on the poor.



More crucially: what if there were to be robbery? You know the truth. I’d be the first to be blamed. The dog would be the one in the doghouse. “I thought you had a dog?” a friend might say. “Isn’t he called Frank? What was Frank doing during the home invasion? I suppose the dear old thing was snoozing.” And then a derisive laugh, at my expense. Well, I’m not having it. If occasionally, very occasionally, I bark at a threat that proves illusory, it’s better than an invasion of violent primary school children – one that leaves all the valuables stolen, all the humans dead, and me with my paws bound with cable ties. Frank hard at work, ready to stop chatty schoolchildren from staging a home invasion. Meanwhile, in the brief breaks between threatening incidents, we play soccer, with Man kicking the ball into the air. I soar upwards and, nine balls out of ten, achieve the most spectacular of headers. At five months of age, I’m too young to win a place in the Socceroos, I know that. But surely, it’s only a matter of time. My main problem is guessing the direction of the ball after Man has kicked it. He is, I fear, the worst player since the game was invented. Once we are back inside the house, I follow Man from room to room. We go down the hallway to the bedroom, back up to the kitchen, and again down to the bedroom. And then back to the kitchen. One day, I feel certain, he’ll do something interesting, although this outcome is yet to eventuate.



Still, if you are interested in watching a man pick up a teacup from his bedside table and walk it up to the dishwasher, only to remember he’s forgotten the other cup and so repeating the journey, turning on and off the bedroom light each time, then it’s a son et lumière display that will leave you dazzled. Later, at 9pm, I go to sleep on the bed in the front room, ready for the morning. I sleep until I hear it. Childish voices. Going to school. Outside my house. How dare they! I throw a few warning shots their way, my paws resting on the sill of the front window. It won’t stop the children from executing a home invasion, but at least this way they’ll choose the house two doors down. That household is “protected” by an elderly Labrador. From him, I hear hardly a snuffle. I assume the dear old thing is snoozing.

World.title: Fake farewells fool nobody, but a great encore is worth the wait
World.content:
CultureMusicThe Verdict Opinion Fake farewells fool nobody, but a great encore is worth the wait A good encore should raise the roof. After all, this is show business. Michael Dwyer Journalist November 21, 2026 — 5:30am

November 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We know they’re coming back. The exit was too casual, it’s still dark out here and the stage lights are throbbing like jazz hands. Look around, though. That punter’s checking his public transport app. That one’s rubbing her temples. Could the band not just play Wonderwall and then leave the stage? Loathe it or just dislike it, the encore is inescapably a thing. But sometime between Elvis leaving that building in Shreveport, Louisiana 70 years ago and the modern musician’s all-but-contracted toilet break a few songs before the end of the show, the curtain call caper shifted from pandemonium to charade. I blame the artist. Not least Roger Daltrey. “I call it bullshit time,” the Who’s moonlighting singer announced before he led his Ultimate Rock Symphony offstage and back on at Colonial Stadium in March 2000. Way to kill the vibe, Rog. What might have been a romping climax left this fan with a 26-year-long grudge. A memorable encore requires commitment and imagination. Richard Clifford Daltrey’s long antipathy – “The encores, the bloody encores. We hate ’em,” he told a press conference in 1975 – says the quiet bit out loud for many. Fair enough for the Who, I guess. They’d smashed everything to pieces during My Generation. But begrudging the return says more about the artist’s lack of imagination than the ritual itself.



Sam Fender’s recent Australian tour offered an example of the thing done right. After the communal uproar of his signature hit Seventeen Going Under, he returned alone under a spotlight for The Dying Light and suddenly the encore was an invitation to listen again. The band joined later, swelling towards the final blast of Hypersonic Missiles, but that moment of solitude reset the emotional scale. Turns out you can bring a crowd closer by giving them less to shout about. “If you own a cape, rock star, this is the time to put it on.” Indulging the past is fine too, but a surprise payoff is the difference between escalation and obligation. A risky, under-rehearsed cover version. Dragging the support band back up. Even bagpipes and a kilt can work – just make sure you’re Jimmy Barnes first. Mike Skinner knew he’d have to come back for a few random hits after performing the Streets’ A Grand Don’t Come For Free in its entirety last summer, but he kept himself interested by crowd-surfing the length of the venue each night.



It’s not like every performer can be Rufus Wainwright, magicking up a whole Mardi Gras of dancing fools with fruit on their heads to take over the concert hall as he re-costumes as Judy Garland for a roof-raising re-entry. But if you own a cape, rock star, this is the time to put it on. And if not, why not? This is show business. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Civilians are always landing planes in movies. Call me cynical, but I doubt I could wing it John Bailey Contributor Speaking of James Brown, you don’t even need to physically leave to make people suddenly realise how much they’re going to miss you. Even threatened departure is drama on a stick, as long as you commit fully enough to make the audience want to play along. Walking off with your biggest hit still in your pocket is where the eye-rolling starts. Deep Purple moved Smoke On the Water back into the main set decades ago. “We wanted to teach it a lesson,” singer Ian Gillan told me, like a boss. If the air guitars are still plugged in and wailing after that, that’s an encore you deserve. As we grow more jaded out here in the dark, making the charade feel real is the part of the deal that’s slipping. I was a more credulous young man when I first saw Leonard Cohen in 1980, but when he came back eight times I was convinced I was witnessing history. Surely this hadn’t happened in Adelaide.

World.title: Women are retiring with $51,000 less in super. Here’s how to fight back
World.content:
November 21, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ladies we have a problem: an average $51,000 retirement funding shortfall versus men, according to Super Members Council’s analysis of ATO data. That’s 26 per cent less. Ten years ago, the deficit was 20.5 per cent. Yet most Aussie women are doing little about it. The gender pay gap may be improving, but women still earn nearly 20 per cent less than men. Michaela Pollock While most of us have – probably painfully – cut spending in the past three months, we are wrestling with the present rather than focusing on the future. Indeed, just 16 per cent of us feel we can balance today’s priorities with our financial goals. The gender pay gap – which last week was confirmed at still 19.7 per cent by the Workplace Gender Equality Agency – gets baked in like a poisoned money mushroom with every super contribution. Then it can widen over years of reduced pay compared to men.



So, let’s ‘man up’ your super in three swift steps: M is for Manage it: According to Australian Retirement Trust’s Women’s Future indicator, 63 per cent of us checked our super balance in the past year, but only 17 per cent reviewed or changed investment options. Yet, there is a great tool to do so. Half of all women said their current stage of life was holding back their ability to build wealth. Start by sanity checking your fund’s performance on the ATO’s YourSuper comparison tool. Log in via myGov and find this tool on the ATO site. It will compare your existing super fund and its performance against that of several alternative funds. The average median Balanced super fund put on 9.4 per cent last financial year, according to superratings.com.au, but you want performance that is solid over the long term, so your real benchmark is 7.7 per cent a year over 10 years.



Even a 1 per cent lower return over a lifetime will see someone on $100,000 aged 30, and with $50,000 in super to date, with an end balance that is $157,509 less than it could have been – $519,432 as opposed to $676,941. In fact, that’s the difference on MoneySmart’s excellent superannuation calculator between the 6.1 per cent forecast returns of a Balanced fund option holding up to 70 per cent in growth assets like shares, and a conservative fund that will contain far fewer growth assets, around 4.9 per cent. And that’s the other thing you need to check when you manage your super: the type of fund in which you are invested. In general, the younger you are, the more risk you can take on. A is for Accelerate it (for ‘free’): You may not be aware just how much free and discounted super money is out there – that is, if you are a low-income earner and particularly if you’re in a caring life-phase which has you earning less (and probably working harder). Half of all women said their current stage of life was holding back their ability to build wealth, found Australian Retirement Trust. Almost a third of women said caring responsibilities had reduced the hours they could work or the income they could earn, rising to 50 per cent of partnered women supporting children.



There are two strategies that families in particular should use to help equalise the super of a lower-earning spouse. The first of these is the co-contribution. You need to be working in some form to qualify for this, you also need to pay in $1000 after tax – $19 a week. Editor's pick Opinion

Christmas The two debt traps to avoid this Christmas – and what to do instead Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor But you get – for free – up to $500 paid into your super by the government each year you qualify. A qualifying condition is that you earn less than $64,293 a year. The amount phases down from a $500 top up after your wage hits $49,293. The second super opportunity, if you can afford it, is a spouse contribution. Here, a higher earning spouse pays into the super account of a lower earning spouse, on less than $40,000. They don’t need to be working, so this is especially good during unpaid time working even harder to raise children.



An after-tax contribution of $3000 – about $58 a week – nets the payer a tax offset of up to $540. This one phases down from $540 after a $37,000 wage, until it disappears at $40,000. A tax offset is a beautiful thing. It is a straight-up discount on your tax bill, so not only will a family’s overall super balance build more equally, the family tax bill will reduce. So, what is the most powerful way of redressing the super detriment versus men? N is for Nullify the disadvantage: Actuarial firm Rice Warner crunched the numbers on this… purely from a longevity perspective, given that women typically live about four years longer than men, female workers needed to be paid 2 per cent more in superannuation to ensure the same level of income as males throughout retirement. On the face of it, it seems discriminatory. But actually, it levels the playing field. And this was borne out when the firm took the modelling to the Human Rights Commission and was granted permission to pay female workers 2 per cent more on the grounds of fairness.



So use that as your guide. Could you salary sacrifice 2 per cent extra, remembering that it wouldn’t even cost you this much from your pay as it would be before tax? Because, ladies, it could change your life. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. World.title: The retirement question most of us never ask – until it’s too late
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementRetirement living Opinion The retirement question most of us never ask – until it’s too late Bec Wilson Money contributor November 21, 2026 — 5:01am

November 21, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ask any Australian approaching retirement what they’re planning for, and they will probably tell you their target super balance. They want to have $300,000, $500,000, $750,000 or a magic million dollars in their super account before they pull the ripcord. But ask them what they want their retirement to look like, and the answers become a lot more hazy, idealistic and uncertain. A big trip or three, more time with the family, golf, and maybe a caravanning trip around Australia. And there’s nothing wrong with any of those ambitions. But I hate to break it to you – they’re not that helpful in building a retirement plan. How we live and spend in retirement is changing. Getty Images I talk about retirement a lot, and I’m constantly surprised by how much attention we give to accumulating money and how little we spend working out what we actually want to do with it. And this week, I’ve been contemplating these things in a much more personal way. A lot of us do when big life changes land at the end of the year.



My youngest son, the last of three kids, finished school this week. No more lunch packing, school drop-offs, school fee payments or uniform washing for me. And, the end of an intense, 23-year phase of raising children. (Now I’m just coaching, part-funding and prodding young adults.) Alongside that, I’ve worked and organised my life around everyone else’s priorities and schedules. But now I’m starting to wonder what the next 20 or 30 years might look like for me. And I’m curious – really curious. What could I do differently? How much do I want to work? Where do I want to live? What do I want to spend more time doing, and who do I want to spend it with? And only then will I be able to answer – what financial choices could I be making now to give myself the freedom to do these things? I’m not alone. Tens of thousands of Australians are preparing to retire this year-end, while others are heading towards the summer holidays wondering whether they want to return to the same job.



We’re all at different stages of the journey towards retirement. But there’s enormous value in getting curious, long before we’re forced into big decisions. The earlier you start asking these questions, the more time you have to do something with the answers. Too many Australians today only start seriously thinking about retirement at 64 or 65, when they realise they haven’t saved enough, or that the life they’ve imagined costs more than they expected. In my retirement programs and speeches, I often ask people to picture an ordinary Tuesday in retirement. By then, they can’t go back and save more in their 50s, pay down their mortgage or spend a few years reshaping their careers into more flexible work. That’s why I think we need to change our approach to retirement planning. Rather than waiting until we’re almost ready to stop working, we should start getting curious about it much earlier. And then working out what it will take to make the future we want, possible.



It’s one of the reasons I’m kicking off Epic Retirement Month, a four-week, free public education initiative encouraging Australians to go back to basics and get curious about their future retirement. Not just the financial side, but the life they’re actually planning for and how to bring it to life. You’ll see it running in these pages, and on my reels and podcast for the next four weeks. Editor's pick Opinion

Financial planners Your retirement savings shouldn’t be someone else’s sales target Bec Wilson Money contributor This week I interviewed American behavioural scientist Hal Hershfield, who has spent years studying our relationship with our future selves. His research suggests we can think about our future selves almost as though they’re strangers. And when you think about it – it makes a lot of sense. It’s difficult to prioritise the needs of a future self you barely know, can’t imagine and don’t prioritise when you’ve got bills to pay in a crappy economy, a busy life to juggle and many demands from work and kids. But Hershfield’s work points to something really useful we can all grab onto: the more vividly we can imagine our future lives, the easier it can become to connect with them and start making decisions that will benefit us later.



And that is where modern retirement planning really needs to start. Not with a superannuation calculator or a target retirement date – but with a bit of curiosity and imagination for the 20, 30 or 40 years that might lie ahead. In my retirement programs and speeches, I often ask people to picture an ordinary Tuesday in retirement. And not the Tuesday you’re cruising Europe or driving the van through the Kimberley. Just an ordinary Tuesday, maybe five years after you stop working. Where are you living? Who are you spending your time with? What gets you out of bed in the morning? Do you still do a little bit of work? Do you have some good friends nearby? And are you fit and healthy enough to do all the things you enjoy? Picture that then work backwards. What does that future life ask you to do today to get there? That’s how you build a retirement plan. Maybe you need to save more, sooner. Or perhaps you need to pay down your debt, or rethink where you live. You might have to make a more conscious effort to build friendships outside of work. Or put a real focus on your strength, flexibility and nutrition.



You could start working less, or making more room in your life for the priorities that really are at the top of your list. And maybe you could even find time to start some of these things now, without waiting for retirement. Editor's pick Opinion

Jobs Lost your job? Do these four things before you touch your savings Paridhi Jain Money contributor Because getting curious about retirement isn’t just about planning for a better life later. It’s also about recognising the choices you have today, while you’ve still got time to make them. So here’s something to try this weekend. Imagine yourself five or 10 years from now, living the ordinary life you’ve pictured. Then, write a short letter from that future version of yourself to the person you are today. What would they thank you for doing? What might they wish you had done earlier or differently? And what advice would they give you about the choices you’re making right now?



If you have a partner, try it separately and then compare notes. You might find your ideas overlap, or discover you’ve got quite different expectations about the years ahead. And don’t worry about getting it right – there’s no right answer. It’s just a way to start thinking about what you want while you’ve still got time to make the choices that could help you get there. We’ve spent decades encouraging Australians to save more for retirement. It’s certainly important. But I think it’s a lot easier to save, improve your health, pay down debt and make better choices when you know what you’re doing it all for. Bec Wilson, bestselling author of How to Have an Epic Retirement, is a retirement educator and founder of the Epic Retirement Institute. World.title: How a priceless Faberge egg ended up permanently living at sea
World.content:
InspirationCruises How a priceless Faberge egg ended up permanently living at sea Julietta Jameson November 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When we hear the word “Faberge”, chances are we think “egg”. The Russian jewellery house is renowned for the bejewelled ovoid creations that characterised the prolific gift-giving of the Romanov court, and are now among the world’s most-prized objets d’art. Journey in Jewels, the contemporary Faberge egg created for the ship. The egg can unfurl to reveal a secondary bejewelled egg. I’m standing in the main reception area of Regent Seven Seas Grandeur with some of my new cruise friends as we admire Journey in Jewels, the contemporary Faberge egg created for the ship. It seems an unlikely place to encounter one, but this is the first and only Faberge egg to permanently live at sea.



That’s because the ship’s godmother is Sarah Faberge, great-granddaughter of Peter Carl Faberge, best known for creating Faberge eggs made in the style of genuine Easter eggs, but using precious metals and gemstones. Our voyage is themed on the jewellery house, and Sarah herself is on board. 



We laugh, then riff on how funny it would be if he suddenly produced the egg from his pocket during his evening show. I mention that it’s probably worth millions. The Kelch Rocaille egg. The Houston Museum of Natural Science houses the McFerrin Faberge Collection, which includes a number of the famous eggs. HMNS/Rathke “What?” The magician’s face goes a little white. Then we notice cameras pointed in our direction, and realise whoever is directing them may not appreciate the joke. We disperse rather quickly, probably looking far more suspicious than we intend.



Journey in Jewels isn’t an Imperial egg but is unmistakably Faberge. Graduated blue guilloche enamel, pearls, emeralds, tsavorites, sapphires, hand-carved mother-of-pearl clouds and opals reference the colours and moods of the sea rather than imperial Russia. A mechanical movement opens the outer shell to reveal its hidden surprise. By rotating a pearl-set “helm” at the base of the stand, seven enamelled blades open to reveal a second egg nestled inside. A vanity case from the early 20th century in silver, gold and pink guilloche enamel accented with diamonds. HMNS/Mike Rathke “People think of the eggs,” says Faberge historian Tim Adams during the voyage. “But they represent only a tiny part of what Faberge produced.” At its peak, the House of Faberge employed about 500 craftsmen and created an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 objects. Alongside the famous eggs came clocks, fans, perfume bottles, cigarette cases, carved stone animals, flowers, desk accessories and jewellery. As Jennifer McFerrin-Bohner, director of the McFerrin Foundation and daughter of renowned collectors Art and Dorothy McFerrin, puts it during one of her onboard talks, “Anything someone wanted to buy, he would create.”



The Houston Museum of Natural Science in Texas provides a home to the McFerrin Collection. Built over decades, that collection spans more than 600 Faberge objects, from Imperial treasures to whimsical hardstone animals, fans, clocks and jewellery. Perhaps the biggest surprise is Faberge’s flower studies. Adams describes them as being “as rare as the Imperial Easter eggs”. To create them, Faberge maintained a greenhouse on the roof of his St Petersburg headquarters so craftsmen could study exotic blooms before recreating them in stone. As Adams puts it, “Pictures just do not do these things justice.” With Russia firmly on Australia’s “do not travel” list, America’s great Faberge collections have become the easiest way to understand the house outside its homeland. A gold, enamel and diamond brooch created for the Nobel Brothers Company in the late 19th or early 20th century. HMNS/Mike Rathke Along with the Houston Museum of Natural Science, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts in Richmond hosts one of the world’s finest public Faberge collections, assembled by Lillian Thomas Pratt, an American lover of Russian art.



Alongside several Imperial Easter eggs are exquisitely crafted everyday objects, including delicate cigarette cases. Adams notes that a single cigarette case could combine engraving, chasing, stone-setting and enamelling – “the whole art of the goldsmith” in one object. Hillwood Estate, Museum & Gardens, a decorative arts and historic house museum in Washington, DC, explains why so much Faberge is found in the United States. Opera glasses decorated with rose gold and silver trim and diamond-set floral festoons. HMNS/Mike Rathke Following the Russian Revolution, Soviet authorities sold many Imperial treasures overseas to raise foreign currency. Known in her lifetime as America’s wealthiest woman, General Foods founder and philanthropist Marjorie Merriweather Post acquired many of them. Hillwood was her home, and she endowed the property, along with her collections, as a public institution. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York places Faberge within the wider story of European decorative arts. Here, it becomes clear that the eggs are simply the headline acts in a much larger story of innovation, artistry and technical mastery.



Related Article ★★★★★

Ship reviews Travel can’t get any closer to flawless than on board this ship In my own journey, I go from looking at a pretty egg and having a bit of a joke about it, to realising I am looking at the latest expression of nearly two centuries of craftsmanship. It is no longer simply an exquisite object on display aboard a luxury ship, but a reminder that the House of Faberge has constantly evolved, finding new ways to celebrate artistry and innovation. THE DETAILS CRUISE
