World.title: Summer is coming. Here’s what you should know about sharks
World.content:
The idea that there are more sharks around now is wrong, says marine biology adjunct professor Colin Simpfendorfer: “On the other hand, there are certainly more people in the water.”

Last summer was one of the worst on record for shark bites. With a hot season ahead, should swimmers and surfers be worried? One survivor and two experts weigh in what works – and what doesn’t.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This story is part of the November 21 edition of the Good Weekend. See all stories .

GLENN ORGIAS, 51, is an energy trader and writer who lives in Bondi, Sydney. On February 12, 2009, he was bitten by a shark while surfing at Bondi Beach. He spent 10 days in ICU, more than five weeks in hospital, and lost his hand and part of his forearm. Since his attack, he’s written two books – a memoir called Man in a Grey Suit, and Teeth Kicker, a crime novel about – well, a loan shark. “There was a lot going on the night I was attacked. Paul [de Gelder, a navy diver] was attacked the day before [by a bull shark in Sydney Harbour]; there’d been a huge amount of flooding in Queensland, which had pushed a lot of fresh water into the ocean; and it was really stormy here in Sydney, so the water was reasonably murky. It was dusk, and the light was getting low. There would’ve been 20 or 30 guys out that night. It was big surf – very lumpy, not very nice – but it had been flat for two weeks, so no one had surfed for ages and everyone was keen to get out there. It was breaking a fair way offshore. I’d just got a wave and was paddling back towards the pack – about 80 metres from shore, 20 metres from the lineup – when I was attacked. Glenn Orgias at Bondi Beach, where he still surfs despite being mauled there during a shark attack. “Fear’s not something that will stop me doing it,” he says. Brent Lewin The shark just slammed into me from below. It knocked me right off my board and pulled me under by my left arm. I didn’t know what was happening. I couldn’t see anything – I never actually saw it – but I remember it shook me really aggressively, sort of ran me through the water. The whole thing was so quick – less than a minute, maybe less than 30 seconds – I didn’t really know what was going on. Then it suddenly let me go and I popped up. The other surfers didn’t come for me. It was a difficult situation – they initially scattered, as you would, because I was screaming. I managed to get back on my board and got my arm – what was left of it – back onto the board. I just started paddling. I was very fearful it was going to circle back and come again. I felt like a sitting duck. I just went hell-for-leather and paddled really hard one-handed and caught a wave. Just on my stomach. It was the best wave of my life – the wave that saved my life, absolutely. When I got in [to the shallows], my board got sucked back out behind me, dragging on my leash, and I couldn’t get out. I was there in the shallows, holding my arm, just stuck up to my thighs in the water. And then one of the local guys here who I know quite well grabbed me and helped me up onto the sand.



There were a lot of people on the beach that night. Someone called the ambulance, which took about 45 minutes to come. But Bondi’s one of the best places in Australia to be attacked by a shark: there were three doctors literally right there. I’d lost a fair bit of blood, and later on one of them – an emergency doctor from Prince of Wales [Hospital in Randwick] – told me that when he looked at me, he thought it was 50-50 I’d have a cardiac arrest on the sand and not make it. ‘The shark slammed into me from below. It knocked me off my board and pulled me under by my left arm.’ Glenn Orgias Straight after the attack, when I woke up in hospital, I thought I’d never surf again. I remember my wife, Lisa – who was six months pregnant – saying, “I want to move away from the beach.” And I was the same – I didn’t want to even see the ocean. But by the next day, we’d both calmed down; we both decided we wanted to stay. And I knew I wanted to surf again. Since the attack, I’ve learnt a bit about what happened, though of course you can’t be sure. I think it was a test bite from the shark. Another guy in the water that day got bumped just before I was bitten, and – I’m speculating – I think it was the same shark: I think it was noticing a lot of surfers, trying to figure it out. The teeth marks from my bite, and my wetsuit, suggest it was a juvenile white shark, maybe about four years old, about 200 kilograms – around the age where they transfer from eating finned fish to mammals, like seals. So they’re just learning, and with something big, they want to test it out. They’re looking for fat and meat. So when it got my arm it gave it a bit of a go, then it was like, “Yeah, feeling a bit weird … not worth my time”. So it let go. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster I only learnt all that later, of course. When I think back, I think our understanding of sharks now is at a completely different scientific level than when I was attacked; and I didn’t understand the contributing factors towards shark attack the way I do now. For instance, the night I was attacked, there were the floodwaters and the runoff; it was dusk; it was overcast and cloudy and not easy for sharks to see. There were a lot of bait fish around; and it was February, which is a very common month for shark attacks. So there were lots of risk factors which the average Joe – including me – didn’t really know at the time. Now there are drones and tagging and tracking and just a lot more information to help you. When I decide to go out these days, I think I recognise that I’m making an actual decision, consciously, based on a whole lot of factors. For myself, my basic rules are: if a beach is closed, I don’t go. I don’t surf at sunset or sunrise – basically, if the sun isn’t on the water, I don’t go. If it’s really murky after rain, I’ll give it a couple of days. I do sometimes feel fearful, but fear’s not something that will stop me doing it. It’s just a feeling, and I just try to manage it, accept it and let it pass. And usually it does. Often I’ll go out and I don’t feel any fear at all.



I’m not an expert and I’m not really capable of offering anyone advice. But my personal feeling is that what’s most valuable is the continuing development of scientific knowledge and education around sharks: their habits, behaviours, biology. Just in the past year, the drones have started putting out a lot of information, which I think is useful. I don’t love shark nets: they didn’t save me, and I think they trap a lot of wildlife. I’m not 100 per cent against them, but I’ve always questioned their value. I feel the same about drum lines. My major thing is I don’t really want a whole lot of wildlife getting killed unnecessarily when it’s not really having a very big impact on shark attacks. I think the biggest impact will come with people really understanding that “today is a potentially dangerous day”, based on the science. I think the scientists are doing a good job. These days, sometimes I’ll surf every day of the week; sometimes, if it’s flat for a while, I won’t go at all. But I guess I average a couple of times a week. [Last summer, at the peak of the attacks] I stayed out of the surf for two weeks, probably longer than most people. I probably do take a more cautious approach than others. I certainly don’t feel immune. And if I did get attacked again, people are going to think I’m a real idiot! Like getting struck twice by lightning. Loading Chris Pepin-Neff is an associate professor in public policy at the University of Sydney. For the past 20 years, they have worked in the sub-specialty of “human-shark studies”, looking at media coverage, policymaking, and public opinion and emotion surrounding sharks. They have worked on human-shark risk assessment and safety measures all over the world, including Australia, South Africa, Réunion Island and the United States. “I always look at three things: shark activity, human activity, environmental conditions. Last summer was a perfect storm: warm water temperatures, record summer rain, superabundance of bait fish. It was a singularity – totally incomparable to any other time. And I’d suggest we’re not going to have another year like we’ve just had. But that said, there’s going to be extraordinary levels of unpredictability this year: we’ve got El Niño, it’s going to be hot – we just don’t know what’s going to happen. It can be helpful to think in terms of attractants and deterrents. Attractants are things that attract sharks. So, say you have a harbour beach, with a jetty nearby. You’ve got boats, with sewage that attracts small fish: attractant. You’ve got fishermen gutting fish off the jetty: attractant. Then you’ve got high water temperature and low water clarity, environmental conditions that raise the level of bait fish: attractant. So a lot of attractants, which equals high risk. My mum’s passed now, but she was a big swimmer. Would I let her go swimming between the boats in that sort of scenario? No way. To me, it’s a disaster waiting to happen. Chris Pepin-Neff: enclosure nets can be effective, but the use of gill nets, which sit offshore and create partial barriers, is “insane and dangerous”. Wolter Peeters



What you want is to remove attractants and add deterrents – things that trigger avoidant behaviour in sharks. So one thing I always recommend is that if you’re swimming at an unprotected beach, you should be swimming in pairs or groups. That’s particularly true for children: everybody needs a buddy. And that’s because we want to trigger sharks’ avoidance response by being more intimidating. Big multiple splashes, like swimmers between the flags – a great big mess in the water – that’s intimidating, because sharks don’t know what that is: it doesn’t read like potential prey. One swimmer is not intimidating. A surfer on a surfboard is not intimidating. So sharks come up and they’re curious, maybe defensive. That’s when they might take a bite. You can also do a few things to make yourself less inviting. Don’t wear jewellery – your watch, your necklace – because it could look flashy, like fish gills that are moving. Don’t wear yellow: in the shark-bite community – and I’ve not seen a scientific study on this, but dear god, I know it’s true – it’s referred to as “yum yum yellow”. Don’t wear flesh-coloured clothes. You don’t want to look like a seal, but I’d rather be black than look like flesh. Or a fish. Don’t wear silvery, bluey things. ‘Don’t wear jewellery ... Don’t wear yellow ... Don’t wear flesh-coloured clothes.’ Chris Pepin-Neff I’ve done assessments on Réunion Island, in Florida; the same rules apply. You just have to be mindful that the ocean is an active ecosystem. It’s wrong to assume that the ocean is like a resort pool that’s always safe, and the shark is always dangerous. The fact is, the shark isn’t always dangerous and the beach is really never safe. The ocean is the wild. We do ourselves a disservice when we pretend otherwise. This is why the research on culling has shown that it doesn’t work. Because if the attractant is never removed, you have to kill every single shark in the ecosystem. And then you’ve got to kill every shark under that, and under that, all the way down. Apex predator, meso-predator, on and on: white sharks and bull sharks, then dusky sharks and bronze whalers. It would never end. A white shark circles kayakers. Westpac Life Saver Rescue Helicopter Netting is difficult. Not all nets are created equal. Enclosure nets in the right context work very well. I’ve seen them in operation in Capetown; I recommended one at Cottesloe in Western Australia. An enclosure net doesn’t kill anything, doesn’t catch anything. It’s not an environmental disaster. It comes right in to the beach – water on three sides, sand on the fourth. You put it out for three hours on a Sunday morning for Nippers or whatever, then you pull it back in. It’s completely safe – nothing can get in, nothing can get out.



I think other kinds of nets [such as the gill nets at many beaches, which sit off-shore in the middle of a water column as partial barriers, while leaving the majority of the area un-netted] are insane and dangerous. The reality is that when fish get caught in those nets, they struggle. Those struggles send out low-frequency vibrations that sharks can sense over long distances: it’s one of the ways they detect prey. So those vibrations are literally like ringing a dinner bell for sharks to come in toward the nets – and the beach. They are literally the last thing you should put in front of the flags. The irony is that people don’t actually want [gill] nets. I’ve gone all over the world – and remember, I only go to beaches after clusters of fatal shark bites – looking for people who want them, and the highest number I can get is between seven and nine per cent. I did a survey here at Waverley at Bondi. The question was: “If a shark net was taken out and there was a fatal shark attack at Bondi afterwards, would you hold the politician responsible?” Six hundred people, scientific study; 70 per cent of people said, “No, we wouldn’t.” We also asked, “Would you go back to that beach if the net was taken out?” And three out of four people said, “Yes.” Related Article Good Weekend 'They'll have an uprising on their hands': the fight to save wild horses But for politicians, that 30 per cent is too much of a risk. Politicians are trying to manage the public holding them accountable for shark bites – not the occurrence of shark bites themselves. What’s the threshold of risk and courage a politician would need to take shark nets out, pray to God there are no incidents, and if there is, be able to sustain nine weeks of front page coverage blaming them? That’s a very, very hard question. I’ve seen it asked all over the world, but never more than in Australia. And the fact is, no politician is courageous enough to take that risk. And so the state government has been entirely disingenuous on the subject of shark nets in NSW. There were shark nets in the water when at least three of the last shark attacks here occurred, and yet the government has doubled down on the effectiveness of shark nets. I’m not talking about my friends at the DPI [Department of Primary Industries] or my scientist colleagues, I’m talking about the politicians who said, “Oh, well, this cluster goes to prove that we need more shark nets.” It has not proven that. It has proven that shark nets are less effective and potentially more dangerous even than we thought. They’ve had 100 years to find one study that says they work and they can’t. And I can find five studies that say that gill nets catch sharks and other marine life, and attract sharks closer to the beach. And not only studies: DPI pictures and videos show that 40 per cent of sharks are caught on the inside of the nets. The fact is, shark nets don’t protect beachgoers. Shark nets protect politicians. “The ocean is the wild. We do ourselves a disservice when we pretend otherwise.” Getty Images One of the major political off-ramps for governments wanting to stop using nets is drumlines. The old kind are baited buoys that basically drown the shark. The new kind, smart drumlines, have a pinger that alerts people, who come and drag the shark out to sea. The response has to be quick, otherwise there’s an 80 per cent mortality rate – but it’s potentially an excellent resource for tagging and other scientific data collection; and the research shows that dragging a shark away is traumatic enough for the animal that it stays out of the area for between three and six months. So it’s a very effective non-lethal measure. Although there is some bycatch, it’s very low – far lower than nets.

World.title: Country Life: A young deer farmer's journey to the top
World.content:
Reuben Danen's work day usually starts with a scenic drive.

"The Ashburton South Branch is our northern boundary, and then the Hinds River is our Southern boundary," he told Country Life while shifting a mob of red deer stags.

Farming with a view - Mt Somers is the backdrop at Lincoln Hills. RNZ/Anisha Satya

With over 4000 animals and 720 hectares of hilly land to traverse, a good chunk of Danen's week is spent in his Hilux.

It's part of the gig at Lincoln Hills farm, a breeding and finishing property in Mt Somers, and part of Geraldine's Peel Forest Estate.

Audio player for " A day farming deer with Reuben Danen " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2718221%2Fcountry-life-a-young-deer-farmer-s-journey-to-the-top

A day farming deer with Reuben Danen Country Life Download MP3 12m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Reuben Danen (left) and farm manager Dan Hall drafting velvet stags. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Danen has been on the job here for almost a year, and it's one he's worked towards since finishing high school.

"I always had quite an interest in deer, grew up hunting a lot," he said.

"I always kept university as an option, but sitting in a classroom for another three or four years wasn't the best option for me."

Hundreds of hinds and stags graze and wander Lincoln Hills' paddocks. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Danen's first foray into farming was avocado orchards and a beef farm in Tauranga, where he grew up.

"I happened to be working for a lady ... I mentioned that I was actually quite keen to move down to the South Island, and she gave me a phone number of a bloke on a sheep and beef farm from White Rock, North Canterbury.

"Said to give him a ring, he might give you a job, so I did, and he did."

A few jobs later, he found his way to Lincoln Hills, where he now works alongside farm manager Dan Hall.

He said a good deer farmer is patient and plans ahead.

"Your stockmanship always needs to be sort of two steps ahead, reading the situation.

"Deer have a flight or fight instinct. Ninety nine percent of the time they choose flight.

"But how you manage them and having a well set up farm is the main thing."

Velvet stags - a fresh summer coat hides under their shaggy top layer. RNZ/Anisha Satya

He said things have changed a lot since the initial boom of deer farms in the 80s, in both the animals themselves, and they way they're cared for.

"We put a very large emphasis on the welfare of the animals.

"If it's very windy or lightning storms or whatever, you don't go near them, give them their space - you get what you give."

It's that range of knowledge that netted him the title of 2026 Young Deer Farmer of the Year - although Danen didn't go into it expecting a win, only finding out about it a few days before the competition.

"It was held at Peel Forest Estate ... and the bosses almost, I guess, told me I was doing it, or suggested that it would be good for me anyway."

Contestants tried their hands at practical tests, like tractor driving, fencing, and grading velvet.

"The competition was set up for people who have never done a lot of those things before," Danen said.

"So [the judges] did a really good job of judging you on your willingness to learn and how you handled those situations relative to your experience."

Danen said the competition was a great opportunity for newer farmers to build their understanding of the sector, and their contact lists.

"I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who's starting off.

"I think everyone, including myself, came away with a lot of good knowledge.

World.title: Country Life: Cutting the food bank queues in a food-rich land
World.content:
Una Stephens remembers a time when nutritious food was abundant and kids were healthy.

"You look around now and our kids are eating processed colours in their kai.

"My personal drive is to create kai that does put that little red spark back in the little ones' faces," she told Country Life.

Una Stephens RNZ/Sally Round

Stephens was helping to host visitors at Te Māra o Puanga Kairau, a traditional māra kai or food garden, in Motueka.

On land owned by Wakatū Incorporation the garden produces food for the local community and is trialling growing at scale taewa (Māori potato) and several different types of kūmara.

The visitors - growers, exporters, grassroots groups and researchers - were there to learn and contribute to a food strategy for Te Tauihu - the region straddling Tasman, Nelson and Marlborough - an initiative led by Wakatū Inc and the Riddet Institute.

"Te Tauihu is a food-rich region, so we can grow a lot of things, but actually, whilst we can grow a lot of things, we have some challenges in terms of how that food is actually distributed fairly across our region and our community," Wakatū deputy chair Miriana Stephens said.

Audio player for " Feeding the future: Te Tauihu's local food challenge " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2718220%2Fcountry-life-cutting-the-food-bank-queues-in-a-food-rich-land

Feeding the future: Te Tauihu's local food challenge Country Life Download MP3 25m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Stephens opened the Food Security in a Changing World conference in Motueka last week where speakers noted the irony of New Zealand's farmers feeding approximately 40 million people worldwide while one in three of the country's households struggled to put nourishing food on the table.

They spoke about the opportunities and challenges ahead and the need for fairer local distribution of food without sacrificing economic prosperity from food exports.

Moko Morris of the Kore Hiakai Zero Hunger Collective said the situation was very serious.

"There are more lines outside the food banks. The pātaka kai around the country are often empty after being filled quite quickly … and we're also seeing that police officers, schoolteachers are coming to food banks."

As part of the conference's "Motueka Call", communities were urged to grow and share more local food, support local producers and cut food waste, culminating in a regional food strategy to be finalised by September 2028.

Miriana Stephens (C) of Wakatū Incorporation at the November 2026 Motueka gathering to discuss the draft of the Te Tauihu Regional Food Strategy RNZ/Sally Round

Māori-owned Wakatū Inc is one of the largest landowners in Te Tauihu, and exports wine and fruit around the world, and it had a role to play, Stephens said.

"Perhaps we have land that we can open up for community gardens. I think it really is around the responsibility of our leaders to think differently.

"We need to collaborate. There's many wonderful initiatives going on in the community, so part of the conference is actually to find out what is going on. You know, we tend to really love working in silos.

"It's not always about money, but we've got people power."

A display of gourds and information at Te Māra o Puanga Kairau RNZ/Sally Round

Consultant and organic grower Rob Simcic said over 70 years much of the region's food production infrastructure had been lost, and reviving it would help fill local plates.

"It could look like a processing facility at the wharf in Golden Bay for local fish, so that there's greater access to kaimoana."

Capital and support were required but green shoots were appearing in the region, he said.

"We're about to have the re-emergence of concentration facilities for our berry industry with a new company starting that up in the region.

"The opportunity for mobile abattoirs so that we can have more localised [meat processing], that would mean so much to a relatively remote region like Te Tauihu.

"We know that some of the infrastructure is tired, so how do we get behind that? And we also know we've got a lot of wonderful innovators that can support us on that journey," Stephens said.

"But also, we're very wasteful, also as a community. So, there's value in that waste."

Food waste was among considerations as Switzerland worked towards its Agriculture and Food Climate Strategy 2050, according to another speaker, Dr Fabian Wahl of the Swiss research centre Agroscope.

He told the audience that an estimated one quarter of Switzerland's arable land produced food which went to waste.

"I think we need to bring back the meaning of food to the society, that food is not a fast-moving consumer good. Food is our source of life."

Wahl was impressed by the Te Tauihu meeting's "bottom-up approach" towards a national food strategy.

"I think it's very, for me, very positive to see how also in small areas all actors are working together and creating the input."

A traditional food storage structure at Te Māra o Puanga Kairau in Motueka RNZ/Sally Round

PhD student Catherine Trought presented her early research into different countries' approach to food policy, governance and trade-offs.

"So how does health, environment, the economy, culture, how do they all work together?" she asked.

"Because if you have one dominating another, then you might get unintended consequences. If the economy dominates, then you might have people not having access to healthy food."

She said Canada had an approach New Zealand might be able to follow.

"A long period of consumer advocacy led to a strategy that the government released which was across health, environment, economy, culture in 2019, but just this year they put out one that's particularly focused at food security so it's about the domestic food supply getting more Canadian food to Canadians."

A volunteer fills boxes at the Christchurch City Mission food bank. RNZ / Niva Chittock

Moko Morris cautioned communities should not bear the full weight of ensuring people did not go hungry.

"We value that communities are resilient, but we need the government to come to the party and upscale, deep scale and support organisations who are moving from a food response, from a food bank, towards food security, kai motuhake."

One of the champions of the Motueka food scene, Angela Morris, showed the delegates around her own extensive market garden which produced food for her café and food business, Toad Hall.

"We are growing healthy communities via healthy food.

World.title: New Zealander found with explosive-making instructions, extremist material jailed in Australia
World.content:
A New Zealand man has been jailed in Australia after he was found with violent extremist material, including instructions on how to make an explosive.

The 25-year-old was sentenced to one year and two months' imprisonment at the Perth District Court on Friday, Australian Federal Police (AFP) said.

He had pleaded guilty in August to four charges - one count of possessing violent extremist material and three counts of transmitting such material.

Local newspaper The West Australian named the man as Brendon McLeod and described him as an "online gaming addict". It reported the videos included footage of the Christchurch mosque attack and ISIS killings.

His sentence was backdated to 23 February 2026, when he was arrested and taken into custody after arriving at Perth Airport on a flight from overseas.

During a bag exam, Australian Border Force (ABF) officers found "concerning videos" on the man's mobile phone, including some containing instructions on how to make an explosive device.

Australian Police have previously said the videos also included "violent killings overseas linked to varying ideologies".

Later forensic examinations of the phone and a desktop computer seized from a central Perth property identified additional violent extremist material.

AFP Counter Terrorism Commander Paula Hudson said sharing "appalling material" damaged social cohesion and amplified the trauma felt by communities.

"Let me be extremely clear - this harmful content holds no place in our society. The sharing and distribution of extremist material, including images and videos of graphic acts of violence such as beheadings, shootings, bombings, rape and violent assaults is unacceptable in our community," she said.

"This disruption should serve as another, serious warning to those fuelling dangerous, violent extremist content online - the AFP, and its partners in law enforcement and national security are watching - and we have never taken our focus off those seeking to harm our community. We will identify you and bring you to justice."

ABF Acting Commander John Eldridge said officers were highly skilled and capable in detecting indicators of criminality and national security threats at the border.

World.title: Strong social bonds likely to be behind sperm whale stranding - expert
World.content:
The sperm whales that stranded in the Far North in recent days are likely to be females and calves with strong social bonds, a marine mammal expert says.

On Friday, Te Rūnanga Nui o Te Aupōuri chief executive Tipene Kapa-Kingi said 22 parāoa had died at Ninety Mile Beach and people from iwi around the area were dealing with the tāonga with customary practices passed on from tīpuna.

The whales became stranded on Thursday at Te Oneroa-a-Tōhe, the northen point of the beach.

University of Otago Emeritus Professor Liz Slooten said it's likely to be a matriarchal group returning from winter around Tonga or Fiji.

Otago University professor Liz Slooten. Supplied

"Even the fact that it was a group suggests that it's females and calves rather than males, males do not move around in groups that size."

Female calves stayed with their mothers for life, while males became more solitary as they got older, she said.

The usual migration pattern was for females to move south to around the level of Cook Strait for summer, and males to go on to Antarctica for summer feeding, Slooten said.

Strong social bonds within the group were likely to be behind the stranding.

"What tends to happen is if one individual from that group is in trouble, either they are sick or they are confused, or for whatever reason they find themselves close to shore and at risk of stranding, then the rest of the group won't leave them."

Slooten likened it to when a human got in trouble in the water and family members or friends went in to help and got in trouble themselves.

It was not unusual for sperm whales and pilot whales to strand around New Zealand because of their social bonds, she said.

World.title: UFC Qatar: Navajo Stirling v Jiří Procházka - what you need to know
World.content:
UFC Qatar: Navajo Stirling v Jiří Procházka

7am Sunday, 22 November

ABHA Arena, Doha, Qatar

Live blog updates on RNZ

The UFC returns to Qatar for the second time with a New Zealand fighter headlining the event again.

Navajo Stirling will fight former light heavyweight champion Jiří Procházka with potential title implications on the line.

A win over Procházka would make it hard for the UFC to deny him a shot at the belt, currently held by City Kickboxing teammate, Carlos Ulberg.

Meanwhile, Dan Hooker will be hoping to have this hand raised for the first time in over two years and halt a three-fight losing streak when he takes on American Brian Ortega.

The co-main event is a featherweight match-up between former bantamweight champion Aljamain Sterling and rising star Kevin Vallejos.

Flyweights Kyoji Horiguchi and Asu Almabayev, and middleweights Jared Cannonier and Ikram Aliskerov round out the main card.

New Zealand's Carlos Ulberg punches Jiri Prochazka of Czechia in a light heavyweight title bout during UFC 327. Carmen Mandato/Getty Images

Stirling's golden opportunity

The event's feature fight will be Stirling's first time headlining a UFC card in a 25-minute showdown with fan favourite Procházka.

Stirling is coming off a career-best performance against another former light heavyweight champion in Jan Blachowicz.

The 29-year-old earned performance of the night honours with a first-round TKO finish, his third in his last three fights, making him the bookies favourite on Sunday.

A win over Procházka could see Stirling handed a title shot in a division desperate for new talent.

After winning and vacating the belt in 2023 due to injury, Procházka has failed in his last three attempts as the challenger.

The last being against current champion and Kiwi Ulberg, who overcame a leg injury to knock out the unorthodox Czech fighter in the first round at UFC 327 in April.

Stirling's age and novelty as a fresh face puts him in the driver's seat for a title shot with a win over Procházka.

However, it also could present another challenge entirely, a potential clash with teammate Ulberg for the light heavyweight crown.

Stirling has previously said he didn't want to fight Ulberg, and believed he could bide his time with youth on his side.

What's Stirling saying?

Stirling - "Prior to UFC I was definitely a fan of Jiri, I knew who he was before the UFC did and here I am fighting him. But at the end of the day, I'm just going to go and smash his face in.

"I love violence, I just enjoy smashing peoples faces in, just teeing off and watching them squirm on the ground a little bit is always fun. I think that's why I was born to do this, I'm a weapon. I'm carrying that energy into the fight, no mercy.

"I can impose my game on anyone, I have so many tools, I can fight forward, I can go back, I can scrap if I want. In this sport, to be a name you have to beat a name."

Hooker's bid to end losing skid

Having headlined Qatar's UFC debut last year, Hooker returns in hopes of ending his losing streak against former two-time featherweight challenger Ortega.

That main event defeat to Aman Tsarukyan was the start of a three-fight skid - all finishes -, with his last loss against UFC newcomer Salahdine Parnasse in September.

His opponent on Sunday hasn't fared much better in recent times, with his last win also coming in 2024.

New Zealand's Dan Hooker looks on after his loss to France's Benoit Saint Denis at UFC 325. STEVEN MARKHAM

Ortega last fought for the featherweight title in 2021, losing by decision to UFC great Alexander Volkanovski.

Sunday's fight presents the opportunity for Hooker or Ortega to find a new wind in the organisation, or risk flirting with it being the end of their UFC career.

The other Sterling

Much like the headline billing, the co-main event is another classic rising star against a former champion.

Vallejos is coming off back-to-back performance of the night honours, and another against Sterling could propel him up the featherweight rankings.

Sterling was the previous bantamweight champion, and defended the belt three times before losing his title in 2023.

Since then, he's won his last three of four fights, including a victory over Ortega.

New Zealand women's bantamweight Michelle Montague was originally slated to fight Jacqueline Cavalcanti this Sunday, but the bout has been pushed back to December.

Where and what time?

UFC 321 returns to Doha in Qatar a year on from its debut.

The 7700-capacity Ali Bin Hamad al-Attiyah Arena will host the event.

The main card gets underway at 7am Sunday (NZT), with preliminary fights starting at 4am.

Who else is on the card?

Main card:

Light heavyweight: Navajo Stirling v Jiří Procházka

Featherweight: Aljamain Sterling v Kevin Vallejos

Lightweight: Dan Hooker v Brian Ortega

Flyweight: Kyoji Horiguchi v Asu Almabayev

Middleweight: Jared Cannonier v Ikram Aliskerov

World.title: Forest & Bird, NZDF cyber attacks likely unrelated, expert says
World.content:
A cybersecurity expert says attacks on Forest & Bird and the Defence Force (NZDF) this week are likely a coincidence.

The environmental advocacy group was alerted to a hack on Wednesday, where people's names, phone numbers, and email addresses were accessed.

The NZDF also shut down its public websites after a breach on Friday of a database associated with a discount scheme for Defence Force families.

Cogent chief information security officer Anthony Grasso said two attacks in quick succession wasn't surprising, with New Zealand increasingly targeted by criminal gangs.

"We are reporting on this really regularly. If you look back even 18 months, two years ago, it wasn't this regular. We've got onto their radar."

He suspected those behind the hack at Forest & Bird were after donor money, with a criminal gang a likely culprit.

"They know what that group of people are interested in and then send on following phishing emails saying, 'Your donation didn't go through' or something along those lines and branded Forest & Bird.

"It's basically a scam to get money out of people would be my guess."

Regarding the NZDF security breach, Grasso said he couldn't rule out a foreign intelligence agent, but said a gang could also be responsible.

"Often they are looking for an exploit that they can use ... they may not actually have the right context of the information provided.

"It could just go into a big spamming machine for all we know."

The NZDF website, as seen around 7pm on 20 November, 2026. Screenshot / NZDF

Grasso didn't expect to get answers but said he'd be interested to know what may have been taken and what the impact was.

Speaking generally, he said the country needed to lift its game and maintained cybersecurity was about getting good advice not necessarily spending "loads of money".

Forest & Bird chief executive Sam Rowland told RNZ it had taken immediate steps to secure its systems, including a forensic search of the website that uncovered malicious files hidden to read data.

Rowland said Police, the National Cyber Security Centre, and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner had been notified.

Supporters were also warned that the stolen data could be used to create scam emails, phone calls or convincing text messages, and they should be cautious about unexpected messages even if they contained personalised information.

The Defence Force said preliminary inquiries indicated a database associated with the Force4Families Defence Discounts scheme had been accessed.

The database included names and email addresses of registered users, a spokesperson said.

They said individuals who may have been affected had been contacted and given advice on how to protect themselves from malicious activity.

World.title: Former Filthy Few gang president James Henry Wilson denied parole
World.content:
Former gang leader and convicted murderer James Henry Wilson has been denied parole.

The former Filthy Few motorcycle gang president has been serving a life sentence for the 1999 murder of his ex-girlfriend Jo-Anne van Duyvenbooden at her home in Tauranga.

In July, Wilson was acquitted by the Supreme Court of the 1987 murder of Red Fox Tavern publican Chris Bush.

Wilson sought a guided release to a community reintegration programme, which the parole board denied.

He will next see the parole board in November 2027 for further consideration.

Panel convenor Kathryn Snook asked Wilson to describe the man he was in 1999.

"I was fully immersed in the gang and drug culture," he said.

"I was addicted to methamphetamine, now I'm drug-free, no gang involvement, looking forward to spending my life with my wife and family. Now my family comes first. Back then, drugs and the gang came first."

Snook asked if he had reflected on how his offending had impacted others.

"I'm certainly not proud of it. I can't imagine ... Well, I can imagine, because I did it. But I can't imagine ever being in that position again," he said.

"I used to see methamphetamine as a miracle drug, now I see it as a blight. I've got no interest in it, I see the damage it's done."

Wilson said the murder he committed was "a foreign act to me now".

"When you're on methamphetamine, you're fully immersed in the psychosis of methamphetamine use. There's no filter to your thinking or your actions. From where I am now, I can't even consider behaving like that."

A support person from the Department of Corrections said Wilson had done "an outstanding job" in the prison's garden, and said he would soon be moved to a self-care facility where they hoped to develop a similar garden.

Board member Jeremy Skipworth. Pool

A family member told the board he was "a changed man".

"I speak to him every Saturday. We talk mostly about old people stuff, the veggie garden, painting, landscaping, nothing violent and nothing to even indicate he's had a criminal history," he said.

"If someone overheard our conversation they'd think we're two old mates from the pub, except we don't drink."

Board member Alan Hackney questioned Wilson on whether he had any remaining connections to the Filthy Few.

"I get the occasional letter from ex-members," Wilson said.

"I'm sure they still have some contact with the club, but they're not active members."

Wilson had not worked outside the prison since 2016, when he was caught smuggling tobacco back into the prison on behalf of another inmate.

Because of that, board member Jeremy Skipworth noted he hadn't had a chance to prove he could behave "outside the wire".

"We need to be careful moving forward that you have changed in the way you tell us you have, and that's by testing in less constrained circumstances," he said.

Wilson's lawyer, Christopher Stevenson KC, said he believed his client's gang days were over.

"He wants to get something more out of life," he said.

"He's now in his developed years and he understands what's at risk now."

The parole board decided to decline Wilson's application, and said parole would be reconsidered the following November.

World.title: Trying to get your head around Sandpapergate? We're here to help
World.content:
Do you know absolutely nothing about cricket, but want to get your head around the ongoing Sandpapergate scandal?

Here's a quick guide to the drama — absolutely zero knowledge of cricket rules needed.

What is Sandpapergate?

During a Test match against South Africa in March 2018, Australia's Cameron Bancroft was caught using an object, which was later revealed to be sandpaper, to rough up one side of a ball.

Loading...

Uneven wear on the ball can cause it to move through the air in unpredictable ways.

That would have made it harder for the South African batters to see and hit it and therefore, given Australia an unfair advantage.

A whole lot happened in the fallout, but the dust mostly settled after an investigation by Cricket Australia (CA), completed just four days after the match, found only three players were involved in the plan to use sandpaper.

Who were the major names in Sandpapergate?

Steve Smith The captain Read more Read more Smith was Australia's captain at the time. The CA investigation found Smith: Was aware of the plan to tamper with the ball

Did not try to prevent the plan from going ahead

Had a hand in concealing the evidence during the game

Sought to mislead match officials

Misled the public in statements about the plan Punishment: Banned for 12 months from all international and domestic cricket. David Warner The vice-captain Read more Read more Warner was Australia's vice-captain at the time. The CA investigation found Warner: Hatched the plan to tamper with the ball

Told Bancroft to carry out the plan

Did not report his knowledge of the plan prior to, during, or after the match

Misled match officials by concealing his knowledge of and involvement in the plan Punishment: Banned for 12 months from all international and domestic cricket; leadership ban. Cameron Bancroft The operative Read more Read more The CA investigation found Bancroft: Carried out Warner's instructions to tamper with the ball

Sought to conceal evidence

Sought to mislead match officials

Misled the public in statements about the plan Punishment: Banned for nine months from all domestic and international cricket. Darren Lehmann The coach Read more Read more Lehmann was the head coach of the team at the time. The CA investigation cleared him of any direct involvement, but he announced his resignation shortly after the scandal broke. The Australian cricket squad Read more Read more The Cricket Australia investigation found the rest of the squad was not involved in the plan to tamper with the ball. Those players were: Pat Cummins

Peter Handscomb

Josh Hazlewood

Jon Holland

Usman Khawaja

Nathan Lyon

Mitchell Marsh

Shaun Marsh

Tim Paine

Jhye Richardson

Chadd Sayers

Mitchell Starc

Why are we talking about it now?

That's thanks to Usman Khawaja.

In an autobiography published this month, he said the entire team had known about the plot to tamper with the ball.

"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," he told the Sydney Morning Herald.

He also said sandpaper had been used to rough up the ball in the Test prior to the one in which Bancroft was caught.

Who said what since Sandpapergate reignited The Sandpapergate saga has seen a definitive split between some of Australia's greatest cricketers. Here's what everyone has said so far.

While Khawaja declined to name names, his account implicated several men who still play for the national team, including current captain Pat Cummins.

Warner added his weight to Khawaja's account, saying it was "100 per cent accurate", adding that the CA investigation at the time was "rushed and botched".

Since then, we've seen a long line of people coming forward to offer their versions of events.

On November 13, Cummins categorically denied Khawaja's comments.

" Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," he said at one stage in a 68-minute press conference."In his book, Uzzy's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. "

But a 4,000-word article written by Cameron Bancroft and published in the West Australian on Wednesday cast significant doubt on denials by Cummins and others.

Bancroft said Cummins's press conference was "the final straw" and had left him feeling "angry, betrayed and alone".

Where Khawaja had dodged questions about precisely who knew what, Bancroft's article offered unprecedented detail about what he said happened.

He said he had discussed the condition of the ball with Cummins and that Lehmann, now an ABC commentator, knew about the use of sandpaper.

Lehmann declined to offer a detailed response on Wednesday, saying he needed time to read Bancroft's account.

If you want to dive a little deeper, you can find a definitive breakdown of everyone's accounts here.

So, what next?

CA announced on Wednesday it would launch a voluntary forum for players and staff involved in the infamous Test match to discuss their recollections of the incident.

When asked if a future investigation was on the table, CA chief Todd Greenberg stressed that "the investigation has been completed".

"The forum is designed [for] people who weren't interviewed or weren't offered the opportunity or didn't feel like they had the opportunity to contribute," he said.

World.title: Lions disrupt high school graduation ceremony with consecutive picks
World.content:
Brisbane has disrupted a high school graduation ceremony by drafting classmates Kodah Edwards and Archie Van Dyk with consecutive picks in the second round of the AFL draft.

The Lions were left with three consecutive second-round selections after failing to match a bid from Sydney for their academy prospect Caylen Murray in the first round, and chose Edwards with the 27th pick and Van Dyk with the 28th.

Incredibly, Edwards and Van Dyk weren't the only players to be selected from the same high school ceremony, with Port Adelaide grabbing Angus White out of the same ceremony with the 47th pick later in the night.

However, the celebration of the entire draft came at the 33rd pick when the Western Bulldogs matched Adelaide's bid for academy prospect Khaled El Souki.

El Souki's draft party took place in a warehouse with approximately 100 people in attendance with fireworks exploding and Lebanese drummers banging away in the background upon his selection.

There was also some father-son romance at the back end of the draft as Cooper Hodge (the son of Luke Hodge) landed at Hawthorn, while Aidan McCartney (the son of Jason McCartney) landed at North Melbourne and Harper Banfield (the son of Drew Banfield) was selected by West Coast with the final pick.

Former No.1 pick Jamarra Ugle-Hagan was re-drafted by Gold Coast alongside fellow veteran Elliott Himmelberg with one of the final picks of the night.

World.title: Cricketers' association slams 'disgraceful' treatment of Sandpapergate players
World.content:
The CEO of the Australian Cricketers' Association, Paul Marsh, has labelled the media treatment of Australian Test players as "absolutely disgraceful".

Marsh has criticised the media coverage of players linked to the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal which has seen media teams taking videos and photos outside players' houses, most notably of Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins.

"We've got media camped outside and hounding players' families in their private homes and with their personal activities and it's disgraceful in my view," Marsh told ABC Sport.

"This has been an issue where people's integrity's being questioned, left, right and centre."

The union leader has called for the media companies to consider their actions

"There's a human toll to this that I think is being disregarded in a lot of quarters," he said.

"The scrutiny, the accusations, the fact their families are being hounded here, like, this is really difficult.

"I'm really concerned about the players' well-being at the moment as a collective.

"The reality of this is, this is hurting I think everyone that's involved."

Steve Smith says he did not want to speak to the press on his return to the New South Wales set-up ahead of Sunday's Shield game. (Supplied: Channel 10)

Questions around who knew details of the 2018 Cape Town sandpaper plot have blown up in the past two weeks since the publication of Usman Khawaja's memoir, and a newspaper article by the player at the centre of the scandal, Cameron Bancroft.

Bancroft said that the entire 2018 team knew about the sandpaper plot.

Those allegations directly contradict other Australian players who played in the 2018 tour including Cummins, who held an extensive media conference denying any knowledge of the sandpaper plot.

Marsh is calling for space and perspective.

"Understandably people want to understand that the black and white of what might have happened here but I'm just not convinced we're going to get to that," he said.

"What I do think we need to do is find a way to get the players and others that were involved together and talk about this and actually try to find a way through.

"I do think that they might need everyone here to give a bit."

Pat Cummins spoke in front of a press conference for 68 minutes, but has also been door-stopped outside his home. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

He said mistakes were made by all parties in 2018 that are adding to the current febrile environment.

"I think there was a lot of pressure put on the team at the time from Cricket Australia, and I think they need to take some responsibility," Marsh said.

"I think time again, maybe the whole playing group should have taken a collective responsibility for this, whether they knew or they didn't know.

"I think that also needs to be an understanding that one person's recollection of what happened here, might be different to somebody else's — [that] doesn't mean that anyone's not telling the truth."

Cricket Australia (CA) this week announced the formation of a forum to allow players to discuss their recollection of events in 2018 behind closed doors.

But the proposal has been criticised because it won't take the form of an inquiry to find a set of agreed facts and because the CA board will decide what it will and won't release after the forum is completed.

CA hasn't released the terms of reference for the forum, nor has it named a person to oversee it.

Marsh said while he was supporting the attempt to find a way to move forward, he said he was still waiting on the details of the forum.

Steve Smith has not made any comments since the release of Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr. (Supplied: Channel 10)

"I'd probably rather understand exactly what they're proposing before I get into assessing it," he said.

He said the Australian players want what's best for Australian cricket.

"Let's work out how we can get there because if we don't do that, I feel like we're going to stay in the place that we're at the moment, which is hurting everyone," he added.

He said while he accepted the public want to know who knew what regarding the sandpaper plot, that may be impossible.

"I think we all would love to have a, you know, an accepted set of facts, but the reality of this is we don't," he said.

"I've had lots of conversations with players the last two weeks, and you know, players with no reason to tell me any differently than what is the truth.

"Players are saying, 'I don't remember the meeting that's been referred to here' or the next person saying, 'I think we had that meeting', and this is what we're dealing with at the moment.

"I would just ask consider the human element of what these guys are going through at the moment."

World.title: AFLW physicality helps resilient Tayla Harris 'feel alive'
World.content:
Tayla Harris has always been a player for the big moments.

The Melbourne forward is renowned for high-flying marks and picture-perfect kicks.

But with Melbourne down by seven points in the fourth quarter of its qualifying final against Geelong, it was Harris's grit that delivered.

Harris, knowing how ex-Melbourne coach Mick Stinear talks about the inside and outside layers of a contest, realised Cats star Nina Morrison would win the ball in the latter.

She made her move, flattening Morrison with a perfectly timed, legal and brutal bump.

It set the tone as Tom Wilson's Melbourne completed a turnaround from 28 points down to beat Geelong and reach Saturday's preliminary final against Carlton at Princes Park.

"That's how I play," Harris said.

Tayla Harris's physicality isn't always reflected in the stats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Martin Keep)

"I would like to think that people know that I only ever play with fair intent.

"And our game requires some pretty impactful moments.

"And I'll cop it back, no problem — and I do often. A few Geelong players got me good.

"Hell yeah, this is how I feel alive."

Harris, 29, knows her impact goes beyond the stat sheet.

"What I do with my physicality and presence I know has an impact on our team in a positive way, so I'll continue to do whatever's required in that moment," she said.

"If it's putting your body on the line, if it's spoiling or if it's running hard, whatever it might require, all of us would agree that, particularly in finals, those little moments matter."

Two years ago, bumping and clunking overhead marks appeared a pipe dream.

Tayla Harris struggled with injuries to her shoulders 12 months ago. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The ruck-forward had surgery on her loose shoulders, one after the other, but never doubted she would return.

"I'm pretty determined when it comes to overcoming adversity or being told that I can't," Harris said.

"I'm pretty bullish on proving to myself that I can."

Having dealt with two trades, plus a failed trade to Hawthorn and a rise to fame and highly publicised social media abuse, there is not much Harris can not handle.

"My career hasn't been one that's been straightforward and all roses, which I'm really thankful for because it builds resilience," Harris said.

"And the adversity that I have faced has made me a better player, but more importantly, person.

"When it was hitting the fan, it's all happening. And then you feel like the world's collapsing in and then next minute it's all good again. But that's life."

Harris practises breathwork and maintains her boxing fitness, a throwback to a childhood that juggled football with waterskiing and skateboarding.

"I'd spend hours on the street trying to do a kickflip, and I'd fail 100 times, and then I would maybe get one and think that I was Tony Hawk," she said.

"I'm so glad that I grew up that way and with my parents not letting me believe that failure was a bad thing — it was just part of it.

"The only way that you're ever going to get anywhere is to fail.

"One thing I know for sure is I will continue to get it wrong and continue to make mistakes and continue to fail, so to speak, but that's the only way I'll ever keep growing or get better."

Inaugural AFLW star Harris would love to play for several more years.

But first, the 2022 premiership winner wants another flag.

"We believe we can go all the way. But we are absolutely set on this next game that we have," Harris said.

"We recently watched a Kobe Bryant press conference and they'd gone up 2-0 in the playoffs and the journalist had said 'why aren't you smiling?'

"And he's got a straight face and goes, 'Job's not done.'

"So that's our philosophy at the moment and we're certainly not looking ahead. But we certainly believe."

AAP

World.title: Media locked out of Steve Smith training session at SCG
World.content:
Steve Smith has returned to training in a covert session with New South Wales as the hierarchy closes ranks around Australia's star batsman.

Smith arrived at the Sydney Cricket Ground today through a back entrance, and media were locked out of watching the ex-Test captain bat in the nets.

The 37-year-old has maintained his silence amid a fresh furore surrounding the sandpaper scandal.

After returning from New York earlier this week, Smith is expected to play for the Blues in their Sheffield Shield game against Queensland at the SCG starting on Sunday.

Smith has not played any cricket since suffering a neck injury in the second Test on last month's tour of South Africa.

Current Test captain Pat Cummins and his national cohorts Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also could feature in the NSW side in the final round of Shield games before Australia name a squad for the first Test against New Zealand starting December 9.

Those four bowlers did not attend Blues training yesterday.

Smith has not spoken publicly since the release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which has triggered an unheralded split in Australian cricket.

Khawaja wrote that all players were aware of Australia's ball tampering in the infamous Test match against South Africa in 2018.

That version was rejected as nonsense by Cummins, but has been supported by David Warner, Cameron Bancroft and Chadd Sayers.

Cummins bluntly denied any knowledge of Australia using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town.

But Bancroft, in a written account issued on Wednesday night, said all players knew the plan.

Smith, Test skipper at the time, was banned by Cricket Australia for 12 months and stripped of the captaincy.

Warner was also suspended for a year and removed from the vice-captaincy, while Bancroft, who was caught by television cameras in Cape Town with sandpaper, was banned for nine months.

AAP

World.title: F1 is in Las Vegas, and teams are fighting to hit prize money jackpot
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has won the F1 drivers' championship, his Mercedes team is constructors' champion, and there are just three rounds left in the season.

But the final trio of grand prix, starting this Sunday (AEDT) in Las Vegas, are not just for show.

These three races, for every team other than Mercedes, are the most important three weekends of the 2026 season.

Why? It's all about the money.

While fans mostly focus on the drivers' championship, it is the constructors' championship that carries the most significance for teams.

The prize money handed out at the end of the year is tied to where you finish in the team's championship. The higher you finish, the more money you receive.

While the exact figure each season is not made public, UK outlet The Independent published a rough guide to potential earnings this season, based of figures gathered from 2025.

Potential F1 2026 prize money *as per The Independent, all figures are in USD 1st — $140m 2nd — $131m 3rd — $122m 4th — $113m 5th — $104m 6th — $95m 7th — $87m 8th — $78m 9th — $69m 10th — $60m 11th — $51m

As the champion, Mercedes is expected to be awarded about $US140 million ($208 million).

But the other 10 teams in this year's championship have not solidified their spot in the championship, meaning there is plenty to race for in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There is a maximum of 129 points a team can win to finish the season; they would need their drivers to finish first and second in all three grand prix.

Ferrari currently sits in second place with 510 points, 95 ahead of Red Bull. The Scuderia just need 34 more points from the final three races to be certain of second place.

But the battle for third between Red Bull and McLaren should be a belter.

Red Bull sits on 415 points, led by superstar Max Verstappen, who sits second in the drivers' championship with 279 points to his name.

Red Bull sits just 17 points ahead of McLaren, which has been an up-and-down season for drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

The difference between third and fourth this season appears to be worth roughly $US9 million ($13.3 million), and every point will be crucial.

F1 constructors' standings before Las Vegas 1: 652 — Mercedes CHAMPION 2: 512 — Ferrari 3: 415 — Red Bull 4: 398 — McLaren 5: 112 — Racing Bulls 6: 69 — Alpine 7: 31 — Haas 8: 28 — Audi 9: 12 — Williams 10: 7 — Aston Martin 11: 0 — Cadillac

"We'll do our best to make sure it goes down to the wire and in our favour," McLaren race director Randy Singh told the F1 Nation podcast this week about his team's battle with Red Bull.

"We're treating it like a mini championship on our side, so we're just aiming to do our best at each race."

Racing Bulls appears all but set to place fifth, and Alpine looks to be safe in sixth, with any team below them needing to increase their season tally by more than double just to match them before this weekend's action.

The final five teams in the championship: Haas (31), Audi (28), Williams (12), Aston Martin (7) and Cadillac (0) are separated by just 31 points.

Haas and Audi are separated by just three points with three rounds to go, while Williams and Aston Martin are separated by just five.

If either of these teams can secure a remarkable and unlikely podium placing in the final three races, they will almost certainly leapfrog at least one rival and bag themselves a few extra million dollars.

F1 to have full-time stewards from 2027

Formula 1 will have full-time stewards from next season in a bid to create greater consistency in officiating.

Stewards play a crucial, and at times defining, role in races, as they are in charge of regulating rule breaches and handing out penalties.

Until now, stewards for F1 races have been selected from a pool on a race-by-race basis.

But with the demand for greater consistency in how rules are enforced and penalties handed down, a full-time group will be introduced.

It is expected that a team of 12-15 stewards will make up the team, with a smaller pool starting next season, supported by members of the current stewards pool used.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship; it is also an investment in the future of our sport," FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said.

World.title: NRL and NRLW 2027 draw released, with lengthy wait for grand final rematch
World.content:
The NRL will introduce a Super Sunday to accommodate Perth's entry in the 2027 season, with an extra game added to the end of each weekend as part of an 18-team competition.

League officials revealed the draw for next year on Friday, with Parramatta and the Gold Coast to kick off the season in Las Vegas alongside Melbourne and Wests Tigers.

The Dolphins, North Queensland and South Sydney have emerged as the biggest winners, while Melbourne and Brisbane have been served two of the most difficult schedules.

NRL round one, 2027 Sunday, February 28 Parramatta Eels vs Gold Coast Titans, Las Vegas

Melbourne Storm vs Wests Tigers, Las Vegas Thursday, March 4 Sydney Roosters vs Brisbane Broncos, Sydney Football Stadium Friday, March 5 New Zealand Warriors vs Canterbury Bulldogs, Mt Smart Stadium

St George Illawarra Dragons vs North Queensland Cowboys, Jubilee Stadium Saturday, March 6 Dolphins vs Cronulla Sharks, Dolphin Stadium

Newcastle Knights vs Penrith Panthers, Hunter Stadium Sunday, March 7 Perth Bears vs Manly Warringah Sea Eagles, Perth Stadium

Canberra Raiders vs South Sydney Rabbitohs, Canberra Stadium

Under the newly constructed draw, no team will have more than one five-day turnaround, with 16 of them shared evenly across the league.

The vast majority of weekends will consist of one game on a Thursday night, two on a Friday and then three on both a Saturday and Sunday.

The NRL had previously steered away from a 2pm Sunday time slot early in the season due to hot weather, but that is no longer possible in the new fixture.

Sunday night games will also be a constant across the majority of the year, with the Bears hosting five of those to ensure more daytime football due to the west coast time difference.

Newcastle will have to wait until round 10 to try to exact revenge on the Sydney Roosters for last year's grand final, with a rematch set for Saturday, May 8.

That is the longest wait for a grand-final rematch since Canberra and the Roosters in the COVID-hit 2020 draw.

The Roosters will have a number of grudge matches locked in before the Knights clash, given they face Brisbane in the opening round and arch-rivals South Sydney in round two.

Payne Haas could feel the wrath of a Lang Park crowd for three straight weeks in 2027, with the ex-Bronco able to set up camp in Brisbane for the month of May.

South Sydney recruit Haas is set to travel to Lang Park to meet Brisbane for the first time in round 10.

After coming up against the Broncos on Thursday, May 6, South Sydney will then face North Queensland at Lang Park the following Sunday for Magic Round.

Assuming Haas is then picked for NSW in State of Origin, he will then feature in the series opener at the same ground on May 26 for the Blues.

Wests Tigers will have to wait only four weeks to take on their former halfback Jarome Luai, after his exit for Parramatta for next season.

Luai's signing with the PNG Chiefs for 2028 derailed the Tigers' season before he was released from his contract a year early to head to the Eels.

The NRLW draw was also released on Friday, with the competition having a trio of prime-time Thursday night matches.

Reigning premiers Sydney will host Wests Tigers to open the season on Thursday, July 1.

St George Illawarra will host Parramatta in round 10, while the Gold Coast hosts Brisbane in round 11 in the other two Thursday night clashes.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Young Aussies stun Argentina at under-17 World Cup
World.content:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he's one of the most exciting talents in Australian football as he inspired the Joeys to a shock 2–0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style in Qatar.

The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and then produced an audaciously cheeky finish 11 minutes later to seal the opening-day win on Thursday (Friday AEDT) as Carl Veart's side provided a magnificent return to the global boys' competition for the first time in seven years.

Against one of the powerhouse soccer nations, Australia had their backs to the wall, having to make 31 clearances as Argentina enjoyed two-thirds of the possession and 22 shots on goal, but Akon ended up hailing their second-half heist as "amazing".

The 17-year-old livewire provided the real star quality, and it was soon evident why the Sky Blues had wanted to keep him back in Australia for their A-League Men campaign.

He caused havoc from the start down the right flank, his neat through ball in the fifth minute almost resulting in a goal for Central Coast Mariners' Luke Becvinovski.

Akon then struck after the break following another dangerous foray down the right flank that ended with his shot across goal deflecting off the hapless Alvaro Guich and into the net.

In the 71st minute, Mariners' Oli O'Carroll expertly picked off an Argentina attack before Brisbane's Emmett Shaw released Akon with a slide-rule left-foot pass, the winger going on to dummy the goalkeeper before slotting into an empty net.

It only got worse for Argentina when substitute Benjamin Vallejos got sent off for a reckless challenge in stoppage time.

But it wasn't all about Akon, a considerable talent who's already made his national U23 bow.

At the other end, Charlie Wilson-Papps, the young goalie who's on Premier League Brighton's books, made half-a-dozen fine saves and kept a clean sheet.

"I do it for my teammates. I do it for my family at home. So to make them proud is the most important thing," said Akon, as he clutched the player-of-the-match trophy afterwards.

His only worry came with the video checking of his goal. "Ah, that was nerve-racking, man. Because at 1-0, it was a very scary game. So to be able to seal it like that, the coach was telling me it was a goal.

"The first goal? It wasn't really my goal, but I just wanted to do the Tim Cahill, start off the tournament like that. So, yeah, the knee side had to come with it.

"Now, the group, we're really confident, really confident in our ability, and I think that showed today."

Next up on Sunday for the Joeys will be Denmark, who lost 4–0 to Mozambique in their group C opener on Thursday.

AAP

Tech.title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards, while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk, if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason.

For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon. That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be.

I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

Tech.title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.

The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.

The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.

Gemini for Home was announced last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.
